
## `html/target-blank-rel` — Links that open a new tab set rel="noopener"

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/conventions` at `error` · `codelaw:html/security` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-html/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/target-blank-rel.md

### What it checks

An `<a>` or `<area>` with `target="_blank"` and an `href` (or a `<form>` with an `action`) has `rel="noopener"` or `rel="noreferrer"`.

**Why:** Without it, older browsers give the opened page a handle on this one (`window.opener`), which it can use to redirect it.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Example</a>
```

##### Do

```html
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Example</a>
```

## `html/tel-non-breaking` — Phone numbers don't wrap

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the text then contains non-breaking characters, which copy and search keep)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/tel-non-breaking.md

### What it checks

The text of a `tel:` link uses non-breaking spaces and hyphens.

**Why:** A phone number broken over two lines is hard to read and to copy.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignoreClasses` | `string[]` | `[]` | classes that already prevent wrapping |
| `ignoreStyle` | `boolean` | `true` | skip links styled `white-space: nowrap` or `pre` |

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<a href="tel:5551234">555 1234</a>
```

##### Do

```html
<a href="tel:5551234">555&nbsp;1234</a>
```

## `html/text-content` — Buttons have text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the button's name needs a human)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/text-content.md

### What it checks

A `<button>` has text a screen reader can announce: content, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or an image with `alt`.

**Why:** Without it the button is announced as just "button".

### How to fix

1. Add visible text, or an `aria-label` that says what the button does.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<button type="button"><svg width="16" height="16"></svg></button>
```

##### Do

```html
<button type="button" aria-label="Close"><svg width="16" height="16"></svg></button>
```

## `html/th-scope` — Header cells in complex tables have scope

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are `scope="col"` and `scope="row"`, the default by where the header stands (the first row heads columns, a row's first cell heads the row); the reviewer confirms it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/th-scope.md

### What it checks

In a table whose headers are not just the first row or just the first column, every `<th>` has `scope` (`row`, `col`, `rowgroup` or `colgroup`).

**Why:** Screen readers announce each cell with its headers; `scope` tells them which headers belong to which cells.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `strict` | `boolean` | `false` | check simple tables too |

### How to fix

1. Add `scope="col"` to column headers and `scope="row"` to row headers.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<table>
  <tr><th>Name</th><th>Age</th></tr>
  <tr><th>Ada</th><td>36</td></tr>
</table>
```

##### Do

```html
<table>
  <tr><th scope="col">Name</th><th scope="col">Age</th></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Ada</th><td>36</td></tr>
</table>
```

## `html/todo-marker` — HTML TODO comments carry a ticket and, when asked, a date

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a ticket and a date are facts about the work that only the author knows; the engine can't invent them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/markers` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/todo-marker.md

### What it checks

A comment line that opens with a marker tag (`TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` by default) in a `<!-- … -->` comment carries a ticket, and a date when the project asks for one: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): text`. The ticket and the date go in the parentheses, in either order, either one optional unless required; any other item in them (an owner's name) is ignored. The tag must start the comment line, so a sentence that merely mentions a TODO is not a marker.

A date that is written is always enforced, whether or not `require_date` is set: it is **expired** from the as-of date on (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date, never the clock: [SR-BASELINE](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md) decision 9) and is a **warning** for the `warn_days` before it. A date that is not a calendar day is reported too. With no as-of date, only the missing and the malformed are reported.

**Why:** A TODO with no ticket has no owner and no place to be tracked, and one with no date never comes due; both outlive the people who wrote them. Naming a ticket ties the comment to the work, and a date makes the comment fail loudly the day it is overdue instead of rotting quietly.

**Configuration** is the `[todo]` table of `codelaw.toml` ([SR-CONFIG](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0110_config.md) decision 11a), one for every language:

```toml
[todo]
tags           = ["TODO", "FIXME", "HACK"]   # the words that open a marker
require_ticket = true                         # a ticket is required (default)
require_date   = false                        # a date is required (default: only a written date is enforced)
ticket_pattern = "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\\d+"        # a whole ticket must match this regular expression
warn_days      = 14                           # warn this many days before the date
```

**A repo full of bare TODOs** gets every one of them at once. Take them into the baseline (`codelaw baseline`) and pay them down, or set `require_ticket = false` and let the rule enforce only the dates that are written.

### How to fix

1. Open or find the ticket for the work and write it in the parentheses: `TODO(ABC-123): …`.
2. When the project asks for a date (`require_date`), or the work has a deadline, add it: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): …`.
3. For an expired marker: do the work and delete the comment; or, if the work really moves, change the date and say why in the text.
4. If the comment is not a to-do, rewrite it so it does not open with the tag.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<!-- TODO: swap in the final copy -->
<h1>Welcome</h1>
```

##### Do

```html
<!-- TODO(WEB-5): swap in the final copy -->
<h1>Welcome</h1>
```

## `html/unique-landmark` — Repeated landmarks have distinct names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the names need a human)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/unique-landmark.md

### What it checks

When a landmark appears more than once (two `<nav>`, two `<aside>`, …), each has a unique, non-empty `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

**Why:** Screen-reader users jump between landmarks by name; two unnamed `<nav>` are indistinguishable.

### How to fix

1. Give each landmark of the same kind its own `aria-label`, or point `aria-labelledby` at its heading.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<nav><a href="/">Home</a></nav>
<nav><a href="/help">Help</a></nav>
```

##### Do

```html
<nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/">Home</a></nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer"><a href="/help">Help</a></nav>
```

## `html/unrecognized-char-ref` — Character references exist and are terminated

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the reference only lacks its `;` (`&copy` is `&copy;`), which renders the same; a name HTML doesn't know gets the known names within two edits as a suggestion)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/unrecognized-char-ref.md

### What it checks

Every named character reference (`&name;`) is one HTML defines, and ends with `;`.

**Why:** An unknown reference is shown literally, and an unterminated one may be read with the text after it.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignoreCase` | `boolean` | `false` | compare names without case |
| `requireSemicolon` | `boolean` | `true` | report references without `;` |

### How to fix

1. Correct the name, or escape the `&` as `&amp;` if no reference was meant.
2. End the reference with `;`.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<p>Price: 5&euros; &copy 2024</p>
```

##### Do

```html
<p>Price: 5&euro; &copy; 2024</p>
```

## `html/valid-autocomplete` — autocomplete values are valid

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the field names within two edits of an unknown token are choices, nearest first; a field that doesn't fit its input type, or a token with none near, is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-autocomplete.md

### What it checks

`autocomplete` holds a valid token list: optional `section-*`, then `shipping`/`billing`, then `home`/`work`/… for contact fields, then one field name that fits the input type, then optional `webauthn`. `<form>` takes only `on` or `off`.

**Why:** Browsers ignore an invalid value, so autofill and password managers can't help the user.

### How to fix

1. Pick the field name that describes the data (the WHATWG autofill list).
2. Order the tokens as described above, or use `off`.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="emial">
```

##### Fixed

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
```

##### Do

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="number" name="n" autocomplete="off">
```

## `html/valid-for` — A label points at a control

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the ids of the document's labelable controls are choices, nearest the written one first; a document with none is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-for.md

### What it checks

A `<label for>` refers to the id of a form control a label can name (`input`, `select`, `textarea`, `button`, `meter`, `output`, `progress`).

**Why:** Pointed at a `<div>` or `<span>`, the label names nothing, and clicking it does nothing.

### How to fix

1. Point `for` at the control's id, or make the target a form control.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<label for="name">Name</label>
<div id="name"></div>
<input id="full-name">
```

##### Fixed

```html
<label for="full-name">Name</label>
<div id="name"></div>
<input id="full-name">
```

##### Do

```html
<label for="name">Name</label>
<input type="text" id="name">
```

## `html/valid-id` — Ids are well-formed

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming an id breaks the CSS, scripts and links that use it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-id.md

### What it checks

An `id` is not empty and has no whitespace; it starts with a letter and uses only letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

**Why:** Whitespace makes the id unusable; other characters need escaping in CSS selectors and are easy to get wrong.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relaxed` | `boolean` | `false` | only require a non-empty id without whitespace |

### How to fix

1. Rename the id, and update everything that refers to it.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<div id="1st item"></div>
```

##### Do

```html
<div id="first-item"></div>
```

## `html/void-content` — Void elements have no end tag

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`</br>` is read as a second line break, so removing it changes the rendering)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/void-content.md

### What it checks

Void elements (`<br>`, `<img>`, `<input>`, `<meta>`, …) are written without an end tag.

**Why:** They can't have content; browsers ignore most such end tags, and read `</br>` and `</p>` as new elements.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<input type="text" name="q"></input>
```

##### Do

```html
<input type="text" name="q">
```

## `js/accessor-pairs` — A setter has a getter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the getter returns is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/accessor-pairs.md

### What it checks

An object or class that defines a setter for a property also defines its getter (the upstream default checks setters only).

**Why:** A write-only property reads back as `undefined`, which is almost never what the author meant.

### How to fix

1. Add a getter for the same name that returns the stored value.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const box = {
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const box = {
  get value() {
    return this._v;
  },
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const box = {
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const box = {
  get value() {
    return this._v;
  },
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const box = {
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```ts
const box = {
  get value() {
    return this._v;
  },
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const box = {
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
const box = {
  get value() {
    return this._v;
  },
  set value(v) {
    this._v = v;
  },
};
```

## `js/arguments-usage` — Rest parameters rather than arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the rest parameter needs a name and its uses change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/arguments-usage.md

### What it checks

`arguments` is not read inside a function.

**Why:** A rest parameter is a real array, is named, and works in arrow functions.

### How to fix

1. Add `...args` to the parameter list and use `args` instead of `arguments`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function sum() {
  return [].reduce.call(arguments, (a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function sum(...nums) {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function sum() {
  return [].reduce.call(arguments, (a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function sum(...nums) {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function sum() {
  return [].reduce.call(arguments, (a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function sum(...nums) {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function sum() {
  return [].reduce.call(arguments, (a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function sum(...nums) {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

## `js/array-callback-return` — A callback to map, filter, reduce and the like returns a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the callback should return is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/array-callback-return.md

### What it checks

A block-bodied callback passed to an array method that uses its return value — `map`, `filter`, `find`, `findIndex`, `findLast`, `findLastIndex`, `every`, `some`, `reduce`, `reduceRight`, `flatMap`, `sort`, `toSorted`, `Array.from`'s mapper — returns a value. ESLint follows every code path; this port reports a callback that has no `return` with a value at all (one that only throws is left alone).

**Why:** Without a `return` the callback gives `undefined`, so `map` fills the array with it and `filter` keeps nothing.

### How to fix

1. Return the value the method expects from every branch of the callback, or use `forEach` or a loop if no value is wanted.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const names = users.map((user) => {
  user.name.trim();
});
```

##### Do

```js
const names = users.map((user) => {
  return user.name.trim();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const names = users.map((user) => {
  user.name.trim();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const names = users.map((user) => {
  return user.name.trim();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const names = users.map((user) => {
  user.name.trim();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const names = users.map((user) => {
  return user.name.trim();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const names = users.map((user) => {
  user.name.trim();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const names = users.map((user) => {
  return user.name.trim();
});
```

## `js/array-constructor` — An array literal rather than the Array constructor

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/array-constructor.md

### What it checks

An array of given elements is written `[a, b]`, not `new Array(a, b)` or `Array(a, b)`, and an empty one `[]`. `Array(n)` with one argument, which makes an array of that length, is left alone.

**Why:** The constructor means two different things depending on how many arguments it gets; the literal means one.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const pair = new Array(left, right);
```

##### Do

```js
const pair = [left, right];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const pair = new Array(left, right);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const pair = [left, right];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const pair = [left, right];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const pair = [left, right];
```

## `js/arrow-body-style` — No braces around a single returned expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/arrow-body-style.md

### What it checks

An arrow function whose body is only `return expr;` is written with the expression body (the upstream default, `"as-needed"`). An object literal is left alone, since it needs parentheses.

**Why:** The braces and `return` add two lines for nothing.

### Examples

##### Do

```jsx
  return x * 2;
```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  return x * 2;
};
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/assertions-in-test-cases` — A test makes an assertion

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the test should check is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/assertions-in-test-cases.md

### What it checks

A test (`it`, `test`, `specify`) given a function calls something that asserts: `expect`, `assert`, a `should` chain, `sinon.assert` or a `cy` command.

**Why:** A test that asserts nothing passes whatever the code does.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
});
```

##### Do

```js
it("saves the user", () => {
  save(user);
  expect(store.get(user.id)).toEqual(user);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  save(user);
  expect(store.get(user.id)).toEqual(user);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expect(store.get(user.id)).toEqual(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  save(user);
  expect(store.get(user.id)).toEqual(user);
});
```

## `js/aws-iam-all-privileges` — No IAM policy granting every action

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`


#### JSX


#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
new iam.PolicyStatement({ actions: ["s3:GetObject"], resources: [bucket.arnForObjects("*")] });
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/aws-restricted-ip-admin-access.md

### What it checks


#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do


#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do

## `js/bool-param-default` — An optional boolean parameter has a default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the default value is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/bool-param-default.md

### What it checks

An optional parameter typed `boolean` (`flag?: boolean`) is given a default value instead.

**Why:** Without a default the parameter is `true`, `false` or `undefined`, and the code must handle three cases where two were meant.

### How to fix

#### TypeScript


##### Do

```ts
function render(compact = false) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function render(compact?: boolean) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function render(compact = false) {}
```

```js
  y();
```

```js
  y();
```

```jsx
  y();
```

#### TSX

## `js/camelcase` — camelCase names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the rename covers every use in this file; names read from other files or from strings are for the reviewer)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/camelcase.md

### What it checks

A variable, function or parameter declared with a lower-case first letter is named in camelCase, not snake_case: `user_name` is `userName`. Constants in ALL_CAPS, leading and trailing underscores, and PascalCase class names are left alone. ESLint also checks property names; this port checks the names a file declares.

**Why:** One naming convention lets a reader tell a local from a property from a constant at a glance.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const user_name = read();
print(user_name);
```

##### Do

```js
const userName = read();
print(userName);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const user_name = read();
print(user_name);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const userName = read();
print(userName);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const user_name = read();
print(user_name);
```

##### Do

```ts
const userName = read();
print(userName);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const user_name = read();
print(user_name);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const userName = read();
print(userName);
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
  log(error);
}
```

```jsx
  run();
} catch (e) {
```

##### Do

```jsx
  run();
} catch (error) {
  log(error);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  run();
} catch (e) {
  log(e);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
try {
  run();
} catch (error) {
  log(error);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  run();
} catch (e) {
  log(e);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
try {
  run();
} catch (error) {
  log(error);
}
```

## `js/class-methods-use-this` — A class method uses this

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (making the method static changes how callers reach it; the author decides)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/class-methods-use-this.md

### What it checks

An instance method of a class — not the constructor, not `static` — uses `this` or `super` somewhere in its body (an arrow function inside counts; a nested `function` does not).

**Why:** A method that never touches its instance is a function in a class's clothing; as `static`, or a plain function, it says it needs no instance.

### How to fix

1. Mark the method `static` and call it on the class, or move it out of the class as a function.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Price {
  format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Price {
  static format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Price {
  format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Price {
  static format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Price {
  format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Price {
  static format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Price {
  format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Price {
  static format(value) {
    return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}
```

## `js/class-name` — Class names in PascalCase

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice and changes every use)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/class-name.md

### What it checks

A class name matches `^[A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$` (the upstream default).

**Why:** One naming style tells classes from functions and values at a glance.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the code as the message says.

### Examples


##### Do

```js

```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/comma-or-logical-or-case` — No comma or || in a case

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting the case is a structural edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/comma-or-logical-or-case.md

### What it checks

A `case` value is not a comma or `||`/`&&` expression.

**Why:** The expression is evaluated to one value, so `case 1, 2:` matches only 2 and `case "a" || "b":` only "a".

### How to fix

1. Write one `case` label for each value, falling through to the same body.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (k) {
  case "a" || "b":
    run();
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (k) {
  case "a":
  case "b":
    run();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (k) {
  case "a" || "b":
    run();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (k) {
  case "a":
  case "b":
    run();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (k) {
  case "a" || "b":
    run();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (k) {
  case "a":
  case "b":
    run();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (k) {
  case "a" || "b":
    run();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (k) {
  case "a":
  case "b":
    run();
}
```

## `js/complexity` — A function's cyclomatic complexity stays under a maximum

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting a function changes its structure; where to cut and what to call each piece is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/complexity.md

### What it checks

A function's cyclomatic complexity is 1 plus the number of ways control can branch inside it: each `if` (an `else if` too), `?:`, `for`, `for…in`/`for…of`, `while`, `do…while`, `case` (not `default`), `catch`, and each `&&`, `||` and `??` (their assignment forms `&&=`, `||=` and `??=` as well). A function nested in another is counted on its own and not in the outer one. `count_optional_chain` adds each `?.`. The rule reports on the function's name when more than `max` (20 by default) is reached: `route has a complexity of 24 (max 20)`. `ignore_names` is a regular expression for names to exempt.

**Why:** Each branch is another path a reader must hold in mind and a test must cover. Past about twenty a function is not understood, only trusted. The limit is a prompt to split, not a goal in itself.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `20` | the highest cyclomatic complexity a function may have |
| `count_optional_chain` | `boolean` | `false` | count each optional chain, `a?.b`, as a branch |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; functions named like this are exempt |

### How to fix

1. Find a branch that decides one thing (a `switch` over a kind, a run of `if`s that validate input) and extract it into a well-named function that returns the result.
2. Replace a long `if`/`else if` chain on one value with a lookup table or a small map of handlers.
3. Return early on the guard cases so the main path has fewer nested branches.
4. If the function is complex on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule js/complexity`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
function label(n) {
  if (n === 0) return "zero";
  if (n === 1) return "one";
  if (n === 2) return "two";
  return "many";
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
const LABELS = ["zero", "one", "two"];
function label(n) {
  return LABELS[n] ?? "many";
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```jsx
function Badge({ a, b }) {
  if (a && b) return <b>both</b>;
  return <i>{a || b ? "one" : "none"}</i>;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```jsx
function Badge({ count }) {
  return <i>{count}</i>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
function label(n: number): string {
  if (n === 0) return "zero";
  if (n === 1) return "one";
  if (n === 2) return "two";
  return "many";
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
const LABELS = ["zero", "one", "two"];
function label(n: number): string {
  return LABELS[n] ?? "many";
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```tsx
function Badge({ a, b }: { a: boolean; b: boolean }) {
  if (a && b) return <b>both</b>;
  return <i>{a || b ? "one" : "none"}</i>;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```tsx
function Badge({ count }: { count: number }) {
  return <i>{count}</i>;
}
```

## `js/consistent-conditional-object-spread` — Spread a conditional object one way

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (if the condition is a truthy non-object (a number or a string), `&&` spreads it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/consistent-conditional-object-spread.md

### What it checks

A conditional object spread is written `...(cond && {…})`, not `...(cond ? {…} : {})`.

**Why:** Spreading `false`, `null` or `undefined` into an object adds nothing, so the empty branch is noise.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug ? { verbose: true } : {}) };
```

##### Do

```js
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug && { verbose: true }) };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug ? { verbose: true } : {}) };
```

##### Do

```jsx
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug && { verbose: true }) };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug ? { verbose: true } : {}) };
```

##### Do

```ts
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug && { verbose: true }) };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug ? { verbose: true } : {}) };
```

##### Do

```tsx
const opts = { ...base, ...(debug && { verbose: true }) };
```

## `js/consistent-existence-index-check` — Check indexOf against -1 the same way

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/consistent-existence-index-check.md

### What it checks

An index from `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `findIndex` or `findLastIndex` held in a variable is tested with `=== -1` or `!== -1`, not `< 0`, `>= 0` or `> -1`.

**Why:** These methods return -1 for "not found"; comparing with -1 says that, and reads the same everywhere.

### How to fix

1. Write `i === -1` for `i < 0`, and `i !== -1` for `i >= 0` or `i > -1`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i >= 0;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i !== -1;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i >= 0;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i !== -1;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i >= 0;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i !== -1;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i >= 0;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function has(list, x) {
  const i = list.indexOf(x);
  return i !== -1;
}
```

## `js/consistent-json-file-read` — Read JSON files as text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Don't


##### Do


#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const pkg = JSON.parse(await readFile(path, 'utf8'));
```

## `js/consistent-return` — return undefined explicitly beside valued returns

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the behaviour is unchanged, but whether `undefined` is the right value is the author's to confirm)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/consistent-return.md

### What it checks

A function that returns a value with some `return` statements does not also use a bare `return;`. Upstream also reports falling off the end of such a function; that needs control flow and is left out.

**Why:** A bare `return` beside valued ones looks like a forgotten value; `return undefined` says the empty result is meant.

```js
  return list.get(id);

```

##### Do

```js
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return undefined;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx

  if (!list) return undefined;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return undefined;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function find(list, id) {
  if (!list) return undefined;
  return list.get(id);
}
```

## `js/consistent-this` — An alias of this is named that

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the alias is renamed through the file; the reviewer checks no other `that` is in scope)

##### Do

## `js/constructor-for-side-effects` — No object constructed only for its side effects

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

#### TSX

## `js/constructor-super` — A derived class's constructor calls super(); a base class's does not

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are `super(...arguments)` first in the constructor (the default: what an implicit constructor does) or `super()`; which the parent needs is the reviewer's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/constructor-super.md

### What it checks

A class that extends another must call `super()` in its constructor before it returns, and a class
that extends nothing must not call `super()` at all.

**Why:** Without `super()` the instance is never initialised and the constructor throws; in a base
class `super()` is a syntax error.

### How to fix

1. In a class with `extends`, call `super(...)` with the arguments the base class expects, before any use of `this`.
2. In a class without `extends`, remove the `super()` call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super(...arguments);
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super(...arguments);
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

### Differences from the source

Paths are followed in straight-line order: a `super()` on any branch counts as called.

## `js/cookie-no-httponly` — Cookies are HttpOnly

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (whether the page needs the cookie in script is the author's call; the change closes access that something may rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`


#### JSX


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`

## `js/custom-error-definition` — Custom errors set name and extend Error

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the constructor must call `super`, and its body changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/custom-error-definition.md

### What it checks

A class whose name ends in `Error` extends `Error` (or another error class). Upstream also checks the `name` property and the constructor; this port checks the base class.

**Why:** Without `extends Error` the object has no stack trace and fails `instanceof Error`.

### How to fix

1. Add `extends Error`, call `super(message)` first in the constructor, and set `this.name` to the class name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class TimeoutError {
  constructor(message) {
    this.message = message;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class TimeoutError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class TimeoutError {
  constructor(message) {
    this.message = message;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class TimeoutError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  constructor(message) {
    this.message = message;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class TimeoutError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  constructor(message) {
    this.message = message;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class TimeoutError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
  }
}
```

## `js/default-case` — A switch has a default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (what the default does with an unmatched value is chosen: a quiet `break` or a thrown error)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/default-case.md

### What it checks

A `switch` has a `default` clause, or a `// no default` comment at its end.

**Why:** Without one, a value no case handles passes silently.

### How to fix

1. Add `default:` that handles or reports the unexpected value, or a `// no default` comment.

### Examples

```js
switch (x) {

    a();
```

```js
switch (x) {
```

```js
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
  default:
    throw new Error(`Unexpected ${x}`);
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
    break;
  default:
    fail(x);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
}
```

##### Fixed (break)

```jsx
  case 1:
    a();
  default:
    break;
}
```

##### Fixed (throw)

```jsx
switch (x) {

  default:
    throw new Error(`Unexpected ${x}`);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
    break;
  default:
    fail(x);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
}
```

##### Fixed (break)

```ts
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    a();
  default:
    break;
}
```

##### Fixed (throw)

```ts

  case 1:
    a();
  default:
    throw new Error(`Unexpected ${x}`);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
    break;
  default:
    fail(x);
}
```

##### Fixed (break)

## `js/default-case-last` — default comes last

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (moved automatically when no clause falls into another across the move: `default`, the clause before it and the last clause each end with `break`, `return`, `throw` or `continue`; otherwise moving it changes which statements run, and it is moved by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/default-case-last.md

### What it checks

The `default` clause of a `switch` is its last clause.

**Why:** A `default` in the middle is easy to miss and makes fall-through order hard to follow.

### How to fix

1. Move the `default` clause to the end, checking any fall-through into or out of it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (x) {
  default:
    a();
    break;
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
  default:
    a();
    break;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (x) {
  default:
    a();
    break;
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
  default:
    a();
    break;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (x) {
  default:
    a();
    break;
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
  default:
    a();
    break;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (x) {
  default:
    a();
    break;
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (x) {
  case 1:
    b();
    break;
  default:
    a();
    break;
}
```

## `js/default-param-last` — Default parameters come last

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (reordering parameters changes every call site)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/default-param-last.md

### What it checks

Parameters with default values come after the ones without.

##### Do

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/dom-node-dataset` — Use dataset for data- attributes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`.dataset` gives `undefined` where `getAttribute` gave `null`, and keys like `data-x-1` map to `x-1`; the author confirms the reads)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/dom-node-dataset.md

### What it checks

`data-*` attributes are read and written through the element's `dataset`, not `setAttribute`/`getAttribute`/`removeAttribute`/`hasAttribute`.

**Why:** `dataset` maps `data-user-id` to `userId` and back, and reads as property access.

### How to fix

1. Replace `el.setAttribute("data-user-id", v)` with `el.dataset.userId = v`, `getAttribute` with a read, `removeAttribute` with `delete el.dataset.userId` and `hasAttribute` with `"userId" in el.dataset`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
el.setAttribute("data-id", id);
```

##### Do

```js
el.dataset.id = id;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
el.setAttribute("data-id", id);
```

##### Do

```jsx
el.dataset.id = id;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
el.setAttribute("data-id", id);
```

##### Do

```ts
el.dataset.id = id;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
el.setAttribute("data-id", id);
```

##### Do

```tsx
el.dataset.id = id;
```

## `js/eqeqeq` — === rather than ==

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`===` compares without converting, so code that relied on `"1" == 1` changes behaviour; the author confirms the types match)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/eqeqeq.md

### What it checks

`==` and `!=` are written `===` and `!==`. Comparisons with `null` are left alone (`x == null` tests for both `null` and `undefined`). The fix writes the strict operator; it is `suggest`, as the result changes when the operands' types differ.

**Why:** `==` converts types before comparing, so `"0" == 0` and `[] == false` are true.

### How to fix

1. Write `===` for `==` and `!==` for `!=`; check that both sides have the same type first.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (count == limit || state != "done") {
  stop();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (count === limit || state !== "done") {
  stop();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (count == limit) {
  stop();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (count === limit) {
  stop();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (count == limit) {
  stop();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (count === limit) {
  stop();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (count == limit) {
  stop();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (count === limit) {
  stop();
}
```

## `js/escape-case` — Upper-case hex digits in escapes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/escape-case.md

### What it checks

Hexadecimal digits in `\x`, `\u` and `\u{…}` escapes are upper case.

**Why:** Mixed case makes the same character look like two; one case is easier to search for.

### How to fix

1. Upper-case the letters a–f in the escape (`\u00a0` → `\u00A0`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const nbsp = "\u00a0";
```

##### Do

```js
const nbsp = "\u00A0";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const nbsp = "\u00a0";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const nbsp = "\u00A0";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const nbsp = "\u00a0";
```

##### Do


## `js/explicit-length-check` — Compare length explicitly

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an object whose `length` is not a number (a custom class) compares differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/explicit-length-check.md

### What it checks

A `.length` used as the whole condition of an `if` or `while` is compared with 0 explicitly. Upstream also covers `!x.length`, `.size` and other boolean positions; this port covers the plain condition.

**Why:** An explicit comparison says that the count is being checked, not the truthiness of some value.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (items.length) {
  render(items);
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (items.length > 0) {
  render(items);
}
```

#### JSX

```jsx
if (items.length) {
  render(items);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (items.length > 0) {
  render(items);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (items.length) {
  render(items);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (items.length > 0) {
  render(items);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (items.length) {
  render(items);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (items.length > 0) {
  render(items);
}
```

## `js/exports-at-end` — Exports are gathered at the end of the file

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/exports-at-end.md

### What it checks

Declarations are written without `export`, and the module's exports are listed in one `export { … }`
(and `export type { … }`) block at the end of the file.

**Why:** A reader or an agent sees the module's whole public API in one place.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const zero = 0;
```

##### Do

```js
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
const zero = 0;
export { add, zero };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const zero = 0;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
const zero = 0;
export { add, zero };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
export interface Point {
  x: number;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
interface Point {
  x: number;
}
export { add };
export type { Point };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
export interface Point {
  x: number;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
interface Point {
  x: number;
}
export { add };
export type { Point };
```

### Differences from the source

`export default`, namespaces and `declare` blocks are left alone.

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Do

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

## `js/flag-expiry` — Every feature flag read is registered, with an owner and a date it goes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (Keeping one branch of a flag removes the other branch's code; a person or agent accepts the diff.)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/flag-expiry.md

### What it checks

Each call that reads a feature flag names a flag that is registered — in `.codelaw/flags.toml` or by an inline `codelaw-flag` marker — and that has not expired on the as-of date. The rule is on when the root config has a `[flags]` table (SR-PROJECT-GRAPH decision 11), and reads nothing until `[flags]` names a preset or an accessor.

```toml
[flags]
presets   = ["launchdarkly"]                 # launchdarkly, unleash, split, openfeature, growthbook, flagsmith
accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)", "flags.get($NAME, $$$)", "useFeature({ key: $NAME })"]
inline    = "allow"                          # or "registry-only"
warn_days = 14
```

A function whose parameter flows unchanged into an accessor's `$NAME` is an accessor too — a team's wrapper over LaunchDarkly, Unleash or Split, and a wrapper of that wrapper — found through the project graph, across files and imports; `codelaw flags accessors` lists them all. A flag's name is a string literal, or a constant, enum member or object key the graph resolves; a name computed at run time is reported as `info`, uncertain, never an error.

| at a read of a flag that is | finding |
|---|---|
| not registered | `error` |
| registered, expiring within `warn_days` of the as-of date | `warn` |
| registered, past its `expires` on the as-of date | `error` |
| registered with `keep = "on"` or `"off"` (decided) | `warn`, with the fix |
| registered with `expires = "never"` and a `reason` | nothing |
| read with a computed name | `info`, uncertain |

Dates are judged on the as-of date (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date), never the clock; with no as-of date only unregistered and decided flags are reported. codelaw never asks a flag service whether a flag is live (L5): the registry is the truth.

**Why:** a flag left in the code after its rollout is a branch nobody tests, and every one makes the next change slower. A flag with an owner and a date is one someone removes.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `presets` | `string[]` | *none* | `[flags] presets`, for this rule only: the SDKs whose reads codelaw knows (launchdarkly, unleash, split, openfeature, growthbook, flagsmith) |
| `accessors` | `string[]` | *none* | `[flags] accessors`, for this rule only: calls with one `$NAME` slot that read a flag |
| `inline` | `string` | *none* | `[flags] inline`, for this rule only: `allow` or `registry-only` |
| `warn_days` | `integer` | *none* | `[flags] warn_days`, for this rule only: how many days before `expires` a read warns |

### How to fix

1. Unregistered: add the flag to `.codelaw/flags.toml` (`[[flag]] name, owner, ticket, expires`), or mark it inline above the read: `// codelaw-flag <name> expires YYYY-MM-DD owner @team`.
2. Expiring or expired: decide which branch stays. Set `keep = "on"` or `keep = "off"` on its registry entry and run `codelaw fix --unsafe`: an `if` or a conditional whose whole condition is the read keeps that branch. Where the read is anything else (`&&`, `!`, a variable), keep the branch by hand.
3. When the flag has no read left, `codelaw fix` removes its registry entry (`data/flag-registry`).
4. A flag meant to stay (a kill switch): `expires = "never"` with a `reason`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```js files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "new-checkout"
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.js
if (isFeatureOn("new-checkout")) {
  renderNew();
} else {
  renderOld();
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```js files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "new-checkout"
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.js
renderNew();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```jsx files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "new-checkout"
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.jsx
export const Checkout = () => (isFeatureOn("new-checkout") ? <NewCheckout /> : <OldCheckout />);
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```jsx files

owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.jsx
export const Checkout = () => (<NewCheckout />);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```ts files

owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.ts

  if (isFeatureOn("new-checkout")) {
    return newTotal(cart);
  } else {
    return oldTotal(cart);
  }

```

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```ts files
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"

  return newTotal(cart);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```tsx files

name = "new-checkout"
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.tsx
export const Checkout = (): JSX.Element => (isFeatureOn("new-checkout") ? <NewCheckout /> : <OldCheckout />);
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```tsx files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "new-checkout"
owner = "@payments"
expires = "2026-12-31"
keep = "on"
// src/checkout.tsx
export const Checkout = (): JSX.Element => (<NewCheckout />);
```

## `js/flag-marker` — An inline flag marker agrees with the registry

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/flag-marker.md

### What it checks

An inline marker registers a flag where it is read, when no `.codelaw/flags.toml` entry does:

```text
// codelaw-flag new-checkout expires 2027-02-28 owner @payments ticket PAY-12 keep on reason <the rest of the line>
```

`expires` is a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`) or `never`, which needs a `reason`; `keep` is `on` or `off`. The rule is on when the root config has a `[flags]` table (SR-PROJECT-GRAPH decision 11). It reports:

| the marker | finding | fix |
|---|---|---|
| disagrees with the flag's registry entry | `warn` | `auto`: the marker is rewritten to the registry's values — the registry wins |
| marks a flag also marked elsewhere with other values | `error` | by hand: register the flag once in `.codelaw/flags.toml` |
| cannot be read, has no `expires`, or `never` without a `reason` | `error` | by hand |
| marks a flag with no read left | `info` | `auto`: the marker is removed |
| any marker, under `[flags] inline = "registry-only"` | `error` | `auto` when the registry has the flag: the marker is removed |

**Why:** two places saying when a flag goes will disagree, and the one nobody reads wins by accident. The registry is the one place; a marker is a convenience that must say the same.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `presets` | `string[]` | *none* | `[flags] presets`, for this rule only: the SDKs whose reads codelaw knows (launchdarkly, unleash, split, openfeature, growthbook, flagsmith) |
| `accessors` | `string[]` | *none* | `[flags] accessors`, for this rule only: calls with one `$NAME` slot that read a flag |
| `inline` | `string` | *none* | `[flags] inline`, for this rule only: `allow` or `registry-only` |
| `warn_days` | `integer` | *none* | `[flags] warn_days`, for this rule only: how many days before `expires` a read warns |

### How to fix

1. Run `codelaw fix`: a marker that disagrees with the registry is rewritten to match it, and a marker of a flag with no read left is removed.
2. A flag marked in several places with different values: add one `[[flag]]` entry for it to `.codelaw/flags.toml` with the values that are right, and delete the markers (or let `codelaw fix` rewrite them).
3. An unreadable marker: write it as `codelaw-flag <name> expires YYYY-MM-DD [owner …] [ticket …] [keep on|off] [reason …]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```js files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "beta"
owner = "@web"
expires = "2027-02-28"
// src/beta.js
// codelaw-flag beta expires 2027-01-31 owner @web
export const on = isFeatureOn("beta");
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```js files
// .codelaw/flags.toml
[[flag]]
name = "beta"
owner = "@web"
expires = "2027-02-28"
// src/beta.js
// codelaw-flag beta expires 2027-02-28 owner @web
export const on = isFeatureOn("beta");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`

```jsx files
// .codelaw/flags.toml

name = "beta"
owner = "@web"
expires = "2027-02-28"
// src/beta.jsx
// codelaw-flag beta expires 2027-01-31 owner @web

```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ accessors = ["isFeatureOn($NAME)"] }`


#### TypeScript

## `js/for-direction` — A for loop's counter moves toward its end condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (whether the update or the comparison is the wrong half needs the author; both flips are offered)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/for-direction.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop whose condition tests `i < n` counts up, and one that tests `i > n` counts down.

**Why:** A counter that moves the wrong way never meets its end condition, so the loop never ends.

### How to fix

1. Decide which way the loop should count.
2. Fix the update (`i++` or `i--`) or the comparison to match.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the update)

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the comparison)

```js
for (let i = 0; i > 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the update)

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the comparison)

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i > 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the update)

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the comparison)

```ts
for (let i = 0; i > 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the update)

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Fixed (flip the comparison)

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i > 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

## `js/for-loop-increment-sign` — A for loop counts towards its end

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the condition or the update is wrong is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/for-loop-increment-sign.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop's update moves the counter towards the bound its condition tests.

**Why:** Counting the wrong way makes the loop run forever or not at all.

### How to fix

1. Flip the update (`i++`/`i--`) or the comparison so they agree.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (let i = 0; i < n; i--) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < n; i--) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < n; i--) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < n; i--) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  use(i);
}
```

## `js/func-name-matching` — A named function expression has the name it is assigned to

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two names is right is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/func-name-matching.md

### What it checks

A function expression with a name, assigned to a variable, a property or an object key, has that same name: `const save = function save() {}`, not `function store() {}`.

**Why:** Stack traces show the function's own name; when it differs from the binding, the trace points nowhere a reader can search.

### How to fix

1. Give the function expression the name it is assigned to, or drop its own name so it takes that one.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const save = function store(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

##### Do

```js
const save = function save(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const save = function store(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const save = function save(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const save = function store(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

##### Do

```ts
const save = function save(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const save = function store(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
const save = function save(record) {
  db.put(record);
};
```

## `js/func-style` — Functions as expressions, not declarations

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a declaration is hoisted and an expression is not, so callers above it may break; the author moves it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/taste` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/func-style.md

### What it checks

A function is written as a `const` assigned a function expression or arrow, not as a `function` declaration (ESLint's default, `expression`). Exported declarations are left alone.

**Why:** An expression is defined where it is written, never before. A matter of taste, so in the opt-in `js/taste` preset.

### How to fix

1. Write `const name = function (…) { … };` or an arrow, and check nothing calls it before that line.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```js
const double = function (n) {
  return n * 2;
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
const double = function (n) {
  return n * 2;
};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
const double = function (n) {
  return n * 2;
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
const double = function (n) {
  return n * 2;
};
```

## `js/getter-return` — A getter returns a value on every path

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the path that falls off the end gets `return undefined;`, which it already returns; the reviewer confirms that is the value meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/getter-return.md

### What it checks

Every path through a getter ends in `return <value>` or a `throw`.

**Why:** A getter that falls off its end returns `undefined`, which is almost always a forgotten
`return`.

### How to fix

1. Find the path that ends without a `return`.
2. Return the value the property should have there, or throw.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
  },
};
```

##### Fixed

```js
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
    return undefined;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const box = {
  get size() {
    return this.items ? this.items.length : 0;
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
  },
};
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
    return undefined;
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const box = {
  get size() {
    return this.items ? this.items.length : 0;
  },
};
```

## `js/guard-for-in` — for-in is filtered

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (looping over the own keys or guarding with `Object.hasOwn` both drop inherited keys; the author picks the form)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/guard-for-in.md

### What it checks

The body of a `for…in` loop starts with an `if` that filters the keys.

**Why:** `for…in` also visits inherited enumerable properties.

### How to fix

1. Loop over `Object.keys(obj)` instead, or start the body with `if (!Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) continue;`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (const key in obj) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (loop over the own keys)

```js
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (guard with hasOwn)

```js
for (const key in obj) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (const key in obj) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (loop over the own keys)

```jsx
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (guard with hasOwn)

```jsx
for (const key in obj) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (const key in obj) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (loop over the own keys)

```ts
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (guard with hasOwn)

```ts
for (const key in obj) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (const key in obj) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (loop over the own keys)

```tsx
for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) {
  use(obj[key]);
}
```

##### Fixed (guard with hasOwn)

```tsx

  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
  use(obj[key]);
```

##### Do

## `js/hashing` — No MD5 or SHA-1

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (changing the algorithm changes every stored digest)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/hashing.md

### What it checks

`createHash` and `createHmac` are not called with a weak algorithm (`md2`, `md4`, `md5`, `sha1`, `ripemd160`).

**Why:** Collisions for these can be computed, so a signature or integrity check based on them can be forged.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the code as the message says.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const digest = crypto.createHash("md5").update(data).digest("hex");
```

##### Do

```js
const digest = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const digest = crypto.createHash("md5").update(data).digest("hex");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const digest = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex");
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const digest = crypto.createHash("md5").update(data).digest("hex");
```

##### Do

```ts
const digest = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const digest = crypto.createHash("md5").update(data).digest("hex");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const digest = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex");
```

## `js/hooks-before-test-cases` — Test hooks come before the tests

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving the hook is simple but the author checks the order it implies)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/hooks-before-test-cases.md

### What it checks

`beforeEach`, `beforeAll`, `afterEach`, `afterAll`, `before` and `after` are written before the tests of their block, not after one.

**Why:** Hooks run around every test of the block whatever their position, so one written after a test misleads the reader about what that test sees.

### How to fix

1. Move the hook to the top of its `describe` block, before the first test.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("cart", () => {
  it("adds", () => {});
  beforeEach(() => reset());
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("cart", () => {
  beforeEach(() => reset());
  it("adds", () => {});
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
describe("cart", () => {
  it("adds", () => {});
  beforeEach(() => reset());
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
describe("cart", () => {
  beforeEach(() => reset());
  it("adds", () => {});
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe("cart", () => {
  it("adds", () => {});
  beforeEach(() => reset());
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("cart", () => {
  beforeEach(() => reset());
  it("adds", () => {});
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
describe("cart", () => {
  it("adds", () => {});
  beforeEach(() => reset());
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
describe("cart", () => {
  beforeEach(() => reset());
  it("adds", () => {});
});
```

## `js/import-consistent-type-specifier-style` — import type rather than a type marker on every specifier

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-consistent-type-specifier-style.md

### What it checks

An import whose every named specifier is marked `type` is written as one `import type { … }` (the plugin's default, `prefer-top-level`).

**Why:** One marker at the top says the whole import goes away at compile time.

##### Don't

```ts
import type { User, Role } from "./model";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

