
##### Do

```tsx
import type { User, Role } from "./model";
```

## `js/import-dynamic-import-chunkname` — Dynamic imports name their webpack chunk

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the chunk name becomes the file name of the bundle, which the author may want shorter)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-dynamic-import-chunkname.md

### What it checks

Each `import()` of a string path carries a leading `/* webpackChunkName: "…" */` comment. The fix names the chunk after the path; it is offered only for a path that is already a valid chunk name (letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `/`, `.`). An `import()` of a computed path is not reported.

**Why:** Without a name webpack numbers the chunk, so bundle reports, network panels and cache keys show `123.js` instead of what was loaded.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const page = import("./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

##### Do

```js
const page = import(/* webpackChunkName: "./pages/settings" */ "./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const page = import("./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const page = import(/* webpackChunkName: "./pages/settings" */ "./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const page = import("./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

##### Do

```ts
const page = import(/* webpackChunkName: "./pages/settings" */ "./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const page = import("./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const page = import(/* webpackChunkName: "./pages/settings" */ "./pages/settings");
use(page);
```

## `js/import-enforce-node-protocol-usage` — Node.js built-ins are imported with node:

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-enforce-node-protocol-usage.md

### What it checks

A Node.js built-in module is imported by its `node:` name (`node:fs`, `node:path`), in `import`, `export … from`, `import()` and `require()`. This is upstream's `always` setting; the rule takes no option.

**Why:** The prefix says at a glance that the module is part of Node.js, and no package of the same name in `node_modules` can stand in for it.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
const path = require("path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

##### Do

```js
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const path = require("node:path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
const path = require("path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const path = require("node:path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
const path = require("path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

##### Do

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const path = require("node:path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
const path = require("path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const path = require("node:path");
readFile(path.join("a", "b"));
```

## `js/import-first` — Imports come before other statements

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-first.md

### What it checks

Every `import` sits at the top of the module, before any other statement (directives such as `"use strict"` and comments may come first).

**Why:** Imports run before the module body wherever they are written, so an import placed after code misleads the reader about what runs first.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { a } from "./a";
a();
import { b } from "./b";
b();
```

##### Do

```js
import { a } from "./a";
import { b } from "./b";
a();
b();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { a } from "./a";
a();
import { b } from "./b";
b();
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { a } from "./a";
import { b } from "./b";
a();
b();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { a } from "./a";
a();
import { b } from "./b";
b();
```

##### Do

```ts
import { a } from "./a";
import { b } from "./b";
a();
b();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { a } from "./a";
a();
import { b } from "./b";
b();
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { a } from "./a";
import { b } from "./b";
a();
b();
```

## `js/import-group-exports` — Named exports in one export statement

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (gathering the exports moves declarations; the author arranges them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-group-exports.md

### What it checks

A module's named exports are gathered in one `export { … }` statement rather than spread over several.

**Why:** One list shows the module's interface in one place. Off unless a project opts in.

### How to fix

1. Declare the values without `export`, and list them in one `export { a, b }` at the end of the file.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export const a = 1;
export const b = 2;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
export { a, b };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export const a = 1;
export const b = 2;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
export { a, b };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const a = 1;
export const b = 2;
```

##### Do

```ts
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
export { a, b };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const a = 1;
export const b = 2;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
export { a, b };
```

## `js/import-groups` — Imports are grouped builtin, external, internal, relative

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-groups.md

### What it checks

The file's leading imports come in four groups, in order — Node.js built-ins, packages, internal
aliases (the `internal` option, `@/` and `~/` by default), relative paths — with a blank line
between groups.

**Why:** Grouped imports show at a glance what a module depends on, and keep diffs of the import
block small.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `internal` | `string[]` | `["@/", "~/"]` | prefixes of internal imports |

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```js
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```ts
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

### Differences from the source

A block of imports with a comment inside is left alone, so no comment is moved away from the import
it describes. A side-effect import (`import './polyfills'`, a stylesheet) stays where it is, since moving it
changes what runs first; only the imports between two of them are ordered.

## `js/import-max-dependencies` — At most ten imports in a module

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting the module is a design decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-max-dependencies.md

### What it checks

A module has at most ten `import` statements; the eleventh is reported. The limit is upstream's default and is fixed; upstream also counts `require()` calls and counts each module once, this rule counts `import` statements.

**Why:** A module that depends on many others usually does several jobs: it is hard to test, and a change anywhere it imports from can break it.

### How to fix

1. Group the imports by the job each serves in this module.
2. Move each job into its own module with the imports it needs, and import the new modules here.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
import a from "a";
import b from "b";
import c from "c";
import d from "d";
import e from "e";
import f from "f";
import g from "g";
import h from "h";
import i from "i";
import j from "j";
import k from "k";
use(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k);
```

##### Do

```js
import a from "a";
import b from "b";
import c from "c";
import d from "d";
import e from "e";
import f from "f";
import g from "g";
import h from "h";
import i from "i";
import j from "j";
use(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import a from "a";
import b from "b";
import c from "c";
import d from "d";
import e from "e";
import f from "f";
import g from "g";
import h from "h";
import i from "i";
import j from "j";
import k from "k";
use(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import a from "a";
import b from "b";
import c from "c";
import d from "d";
import e from "e";
import f from "f";
import g from "g";
import h from "h";
import i from "i";
import j from "j";
use(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import a from "a";
import b from "b";
import c from "c";
import d from "d";
import e from "e";
import f from "f";
import g from "g";
import h from "h";
import i from "i";
import j from "j";
import k from "k";
use(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k);
```

##### Do

```ts

import c from "c";
```


## `js/import-no-absolute-path` — Imports use relative paths, not absolute ones

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the absolute path names a place on the machine it was written on; which project file it means, and so the relative path, is the author's to say)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-absolute-path.md

### What it checks

An `import`, `export … from`, `import()` or `require()` names a module by a package name or a path relative to the file, never by an absolute file-system path.

**Why:** An absolute path works only on the machine where it was written; on any other checkout the module is not found.

### How to fix

1. Work out the path from this file to the module (`../lib/util` rather than `/home/me/app/lib/util`).
2. Write that relative path, or the package name when the module is a dependency.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { helper } from "/home/me/app/lib/helper";
helper();
```

##### Do

```js
import { helper } from "../lib/helper";
helper();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { helper } from "/home/me/app/lib/helper";
helper();
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { helper } from "../lib/helper";
helper();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { helper } from "/home/me/app/lib/helper";
helper();
```

##### Do

```ts
import { helper } from "../lib/helper";
helper();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { helper } from "/home/me/app/lib/helper";
helper();
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { helper } from "../lib/helper";
helper();
```

## `js/import-no-amd` — No AMD define or require

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (turning an AMD module into an ES module rewrites its whole body and every loader config that names it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-amd.md

### What it checks

Modules use `import` and `export`, not AMD's `define([deps], factory)` or `require([deps], callback)` at the top level of the file.

**Why:** AMD needs a loader such as RequireJS at run time, and bundlers and type checkers cannot see its dependencies statically.

### How to fix

1. Turn each dependency in the array into an `import` of the same path, named as the factory's parameter.
2. Move the factory's body to the top level, and turn its `return` into `export default`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
define(["./dep"], function (dep) {
  return dep.make();
});
```

##### Do

```js
import dep from "./dep";
export default dep.make();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
define(["./dep"], function (dep) {
  return dep.make();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
import dep from "./dep";
export default dep.make();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
define(["./dep"], function (dep) {
  return dep.make();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
import dep from "./dep";
export default dep.make();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
define(["./dep"], function (dep) {
  return dep.make();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
import dep from "./dep";
export default dep.make();
```

## `js/import-no-anonymous-default-export` — Default exports have a name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the name to give the value is the author's choice, and no code holds it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-anonymous-default-export.md

### What it checks

`export default` exports a named function or class, or a name declared earlier; not an arrow function, an anonymous function or class, an object, an array, a literal or a `new` expression. A call is allowed, as upstream allows it by default.

**Why:** An anonymous default export has no name to search for, auto-import guesses one, and stack traces and dev tools show it as `default` or `anonymous`.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a name that says what it is: `const routes = [...]` or `function createStore() {}`.
2. Export that name: `export default routes;`, or write `export default function createStore() {}`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export default () => {
  return 1;
};
```

##### Do

```js
export default function one() {
  return 1;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export default () => {
  return 1;
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
export default function one() {
  return 1;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export default () => {
  return 1;
};
```

##### Do

```ts
export default function one() {
  return 1;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export default () => {
  return 1;
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
export default function one() {
  return 1;
}
```

## `js/import-no-commonjs` — No CommonJS require or exports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving to ES modules changes how the file is loaded; the author converts it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-commonjs.md

### What it checks

A module uses `import` and `export`, not `require()` at its top level, `module.exports` or `exports.x`. A `require` inside a function or a condition is left alone, as upstream's default allows.

**Why:** ES modules are statically analysable, and one module system per project avoids interop surprises.

### How to fix

1. Replace `require` with `import` and `module.exports`/`exports.x` with `export`, and set the package's module type.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const fs = require("node:fs");
module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

```js
import fs from "node:fs";
export default load;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const fs = require("node:fs");
module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

```jsx
import fs from "node:fs";
export default load;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const fs = require("node:fs");
module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

```ts
import fs from "node:fs";
export default load;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const fs = require("node:fs");
module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

```tsx
import fs from "node:fs";
export default load;
```

## `js/import-no-dynamic-require` — No require() of a computed path

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (listing the modules that can be loaded is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-dynamic-require.md

### What it checks

`require()` is given a string literal, not a value computed at run time.

**Why:** A computed path hides the dependency from bundlers and readers, and can load a file the author never meant.

### How to fix

1. Require each possible module by its literal path (for example from an object of loaders), or use a dynamic `import()` with a known set.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const plugin = require(`./plugins/${name}`);
```

##### Do

```js
const plugins = { csv: require("./plugins/csv"), json: require("./plugins/json") };
const plugin = plugins[name];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const plugin = require(`./plugins/${name}`);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const plugins = { csv: require("./plugins/csv"), json: require("./plugins/json") };
const plugin = plugins[name];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const plugin = require(`./plugins/${name}`);
```

##### Do

```ts
const plugins = { csv: require("./plugins/csv"), json: require("./plugins/json") };
const plugin = plugins[name];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const plugin = require(`./plugins/${name}`);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const plugins = { csv: require("./plugins/csv"), json: require("./plugins/json") };
const plugin = plugins[name];
```

## `js/import-no-import-module-exports` — No module.exports in a file that imports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which module system the file should use is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-import-module-exports.md

### What it checks

A file with `import` declarations does not also assign `module.exports` or `exports.x`.

**Why:** Mixing the two systems in one file breaks under bundlers that treat it as an ES module, where `module` is not defined.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
import { load } from "./load";
module.exports = load;
```

```js
import { load } from "./load";
export default load;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { load } from "./load";
module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

```jsx

export default load;
```

##### Don't

```ts

module.exports = load;
```

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do

## `js/import-no-internal-modules` — Imports stop at a module's entry point

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the module has to export the name from its entry point first, which is another file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-internal-modules.md

### What it checks

An import names a package or a folder (`lodash`, `./widgets`), not a file inside one (`lodash/fp/map`, `./widgets/button/style`). The path is read as written, with `./` and `../` steps folded; upstream also skips a path its resolver cannot find, which this rule does not check.

**Why:** Reaching inside a module couples the importer to its internal layout, so the module cannot reorganise its files without breaking callers.

### How to fix

1. Export what you need from the module's entry point (its `index` file, or `exports` in its `package.json`).
2. Import it from there: `./widgets` rather than `./widgets/button/style`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { Button } from "./widgets/button/Button";
use(Button);
```

##### Do

```js
import { Button } from "./widgets";
use(Button);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { Button } from "./widgets/button/Button";
use(Button);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { Button } from "./widgets";
use(Button);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { Button } from "./widgets/button/Button";
use(Button);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { Button } from "./widgets";
use(Button);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { Button } from "./widgets/button/Button";
use(Button);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { Button } from "./widgets";
use(Button);
```

## `js/import-no-mutable-exports` — No exported let or var

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether importers should see later changes is the author's design)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-mutable-exports.md

### What it checks

A module exports `const` bindings, functions and classes, not `let` or `var`.

**Why:** An exported `let` changes under every importer when the module reassigns it, which is rarely what they expect.

##### Do

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/import-no-namespace` — No namespace import

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which names are used is read through the file; the author lists them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-namespace.md

### What it checks

A module is imported by the names used (`import { a, b } from "m"`), not as a namespace (`import * as m from "m"`).

**Why:** Named imports say what the file depends on and let bundlers drop the rest.

### How to fix

1. List the names the file uses from the module in braces, and drop the namespace prefix at each use.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
import * as path from "node:path";
const file = path.join(dir, name);
```

##### Do

```js
import { join } from "node:path";
const file = join(dir, name);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import * as path from "node:path";
const file = path.join(dir, name);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { join } from "node:path";
const file = join(dir, name);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import * as path from "node:path";
const file = path.join(dir, name);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { join } from "node:path";
const file = join(dir, name);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import * as path from "node:path";
const file = path.join(dir, name);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { join } from "node:path";
const file = join(dir, name);
```

## `js/import-no-nodejs-modules` — No Node.js built-in modules

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what replaces the built-in (a browser API, a package, an injected dependency) is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-nodejs-modules.md

### What it checks

Code meant to run outside Node.js (a browser bundle, an edge function) does not import Node.js built-in modules such as `fs`, `path` or `node:crypto`.

**Why:** A built-in module does not exist in the browser: the bundle fails to build, or ships a polyfill nobody asked for.

### How to fix

1. Find what the module is used for here (`path.join`, `crypto.randomUUID`, `events.EventEmitter`).
2. Replace it with the platform API (`crypto.randomUUID()` on `globalThis`, `URL`, `EventTarget`) or a package built for the browser, or move the code into a Node-only module.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { join } from "path";
join("a", "b");
```

##### Do

```js
const joined = ["a", "b"].join("/");
use(joined);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { join } from "path";
join("a", "b");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const joined = ["a", "b"].join("/");
use(joined);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { join } from "path";
join("a", "b");
```

##### Do

```ts
const joined = ["a", "b"].join("/");
use(joined);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { join } from "path";
join("a", "b");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const joined = ["a", "b"].join("/");
use(joined);
```

## `js/import-no-relative-parent-imports` — No imports from a parent folder

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the module has to move, or be published as a package, which reaches beyond this file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-relative-parent-imports.md

### What it checks

An `import`, `export … from` or `import()` path does not climb to a parent folder (`../`); modules depend on what sits beside or below them, or on packages.

**Why:** Imports that reach up the tree tie a folder to its surroundings, so it cannot be moved or extracted, and the dependency graph stops following the folder structure.

### How to fix

1. Decide where the shared code belongs: move the imported module into this folder (or below it), or move this module up beside it.
2. If several folders share it, make it a package of the workspace and import it by name, or pass it in as an argument.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { format } from "../utils/format";
format(1);
```

##### Do

```js
import { format } from "./format";
format(1);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { format } from "../utils/format";
format(1);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { format } from "./format";
format(1);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { format } from "../utils/format";
format(1);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { format } from "./format";
format(1);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { format } from "../utils/format";
format(1);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { format } from "./format";
format(1);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/import-no-webpack-loader-syntax` — No webpack loaders in import paths

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the loaders move to the bundler config, which is another file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-no-webpack-loader-syntax.md

### What it checks

A module path names only the module (`./styles.css`), never a chain of webpack loaders (`style-loader!css-loader!./styles.css`).

**Why:** Inline loaders tie the code to webpack: another bundler, a test runner or a type checker cannot resolve the path, and the loaders are configured in two places.

### How to fix

1. Add a rule for the file type to the bundler config (`module.rules` in `webpack.config.js`) with the loaders named in the path.
2. Import the plain path: drop everything up to and including the last `!`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import styles from "style-loader!css-loader!./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

##### Do

```js
import styles from "./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import styles from "style-loader!css-loader!./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import styles from "./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import styles from "style-loader!css-loader!./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

##### Do

```ts
import styles from "./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import styles from "style-loader!css-loader!./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import styles from "./styles.css";
use(styles);
```

## `js/jsdoc-check-access` — @access takes a known level, once

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (which access level was meant is the author's choice, so each of the four is offered for an unknown `@access` value; a block with two access tags keeps the one the author means, by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`

### What it checks

A JSDoc block's `@access` names `package`, `private`, `protected` or `public`, and a block carries at most one access tag (`@access`, `@package`, `@private`, `@protected`, `@public`).

## `js/jsdoc-check-syntax` — No Closure optional syntax in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`[name]` also tells readers the parameter is optional, which the author confirms is what `=` meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-check-syntax.md

### What it checks

An optional `@param` or `@property` is written `{Type} [name]`, not with Closure's trailing `=` in the type (`{Type=} name`).

**Why:** `{Type=}` is Google Closure syntax; JSDoc and TypeScript tooling read the bracketed name, so the trailing `=` is either ignored or misread.

### How to fix

1. Remove the trailing `=` from the type.
2. Wrap the parameter or property name in brackets: `@param {string} [label]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string=} name who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string=} name who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string=} name who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string=} name who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-check-types` — Primitive type names in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a type written `String` may mean the wrapper object on purpose; the author confirms the primitive is meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-check-types.md

### What it checks

JSDoc types use the primitive names `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `bigint` and `object`, and the generic form `Array<T>`, not the wrapper objects (`String`, `Object`) or the dotted `Array.<T>`. `Object<K, V>` is left alone.

**Why:** `String` is the wrapper object, not the primitive a function takes; TypeScript reads `{String}` as that object type, so checked JavaScript types come out wrong.

### How to fix

1. Lower-case the wrapper type: `String` → `string`, `Number` → `number`, `Boolean` → `boolean`, `Symbol` → `symbol`, `BigInt` → `bigint`, `Object` → `object`.
2. Drop the dot of a dotted generic: `Array.<string>` → `Array<string>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {String} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {string} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {String} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {string} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {String} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {string} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {String} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Shouts.
 * @param {string} text what to shout
 */
function shout(text) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-check-values` — @version, @since and @kind take valid values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right version or kind is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-check-values.md

### What it checks

`@version` and `@since` carry a semver version (`1.4.0`), and `@kind` one of JSDoc's kinds (`class`, `constant`, `event`, `external`, `file`, `function`, `member`, `mixin`, `module`, `namespace`, `typedef`). The upstream `@license` check against the SPDX list is left out.

**Why:** Documentation generators sort and filter by these values; one that is not a version or a kind is dropped or mis-sorted.

### How to fix

1. Write the version as `major.minor.patch` (`@since 2.1.0`).
2. For `@kind`, use one of: class, constant, event, external, file, function, member, mixin, module, namespace, typedef.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since two
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since 2.1.0
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since two
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since 2.1.0
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since two
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since 2.1.0
 */

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Parses a date.
 * @since two
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

##### Do

```tsx

 * Parses a date.
 * @since 2.1.0
 */
function parseDate() {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-convert-to-jsdoc-comments` — Functions documented in JSDoc, not // comments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a plain comment above a function may be a note to the maintainer rather than its documentation; the author confirms it is meant for readers of the API)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-convert-to-jsdoc-comments.md

### What it checks

A plain `//` or `/* */` comment directly above a function, method or function-valued `const` is written as a `/** */` JSDoc block. Directive comments (`// eslint-…`, `// @ts-…`, `// prettier-…`, coverage pragmas, `///` references) are left alone. Upstream's variable and property contexts are left out: this port covers functions only, and a comment separated by a blank line still counts.

**Why:** Editors, TypeScript and documentation tools show a JSDoc block on hover and in generated docs; a line comment above a function is invisible to all of them.

### How to fix

1. Turn the comment into a JSDoc block: `// Adds two numbers.` becomes `/** Adds two numbers. */`, and several `//` lines become the lines of one `/** … */` block.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// Adds two numbers.
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
/** Adds two numbers. */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
// Adds two numbers.
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/** Adds two numbers. */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  return a + b;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/** Adds two numbers. */

  return a + b;
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-empty-tags` — Flag tags like @private carry no text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the text after the tag is prose; where it belongs in the description, and how it reads there, is the author's writing)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-empty-tags.md

### What it checks

Tags that are flags — `@abstract`, `@async`, `@generator`, `@global`, `@hideconstructor`, `@ignore`, `@inheritdoc`, `@inner`, `@instance`, `@internal`, `@overload`, `@override`, `@package`, `@private`, `@protected`, `@public`, `@readonly`, `@static` — have nothing after them on their line.

**Why:** Documentation tools discard text after a flag tag, so whatever the author wrote there never reaches a reader.

## `js/jsdoc-escape-inline-tags` — A bare @word in a description is escaped

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the word may be a tag the author meant TypeScript to read; they confirm it is text)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-escape-inline-tags.md

### What it checks

In a JSDoc description line, an `@` word after a space (`see @types/node`) is wrapped in backticks or escaped as `\@`. `{@link …}` and other braced inline tags, e-mail addresses and text already inside backticks are left alone; lines that start with a tag are not checked.

```js
 * Needs the types from `@types/node` to build.
```

#### TSX

## `js/jsdoc-implements-on-classes` — @implements only on classes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

### What it checks

```js
function makeShape() {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-match-description` — A function's description is a sentence

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (rewording the description is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-match-description.md

### What it checks

The description of a function's JSDoc block, when it has one, starts with a capital letter, a digit, `_` or a backtick, and ends with `.`, `?`, `!` or a backtick — upstream's default pattern. Only the main description is checked, not `@description` tags.

**Why:** Descriptions are rendered as prose in hovers and generated docs; a consistent sentence form reads as finished documentation rather than a note.

### How to fix

2. End it with `.`, `?` or `!`.

### Examples

```js
 * returns the total
```

##### Do

```jsx

 * Returns the total.
 */
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

 * returns the total
 */

```

##### Do

```ts

 * Returns the total.
 */

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
 * returns the total
 */
```

##### Do

```tsx
 * Returns the total.
 */

```

## `js/jsdoc-multiline-blocks` — /** and */ on their own lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-multiline-blocks.md

### What it checks

In a JSDoc block that spans lines, nothing follows `/**` on the first line and nothing precedes `*/` on the last. Single-line blocks (`/** @type {number} */`) are fine.

**Why:** Text on the delimiter lines is easy to miss and is parsed inconsistently by documentation tools.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
/** Adds two numbers.

 * @param {number} b the second */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/** Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second */

  return a + b;

```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/** Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second */

  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/** Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second */

  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a the first
 * @param {number} b the second
 */

  return a + b;
```

## `js/jsdoc-no-defaults` — Defaults in the signature, not in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the default leaves the documentation; the author checks the signature carries the same one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-no-defaults.md

### What it checks

A `@param` is not given a default in JSDoc (`[name=value]`); the default is written in the function signature and the tag says `[name]`.

**Why:** A default written only in the comment can drift from the one the code applies, and TypeScript ignores it.

```js
function greet(name = "you") {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
 * @param {string} [name="you"] who to greet
 */

```

##### Do

```jsx

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name="you"] who to greet
 */

```

##### Do

```ts

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name] who to greet
 */

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} [name="you"] who to greet
```

##### Do

```tsx

 * Greets someone.
```

## `js/jsdoc-no-types` — No JSDoc types in TypeScript

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the JSDoc type may say more than the signature (a narrower type, a union the code checks); the author confirms it can go)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-no-types.md

### What it checks

In TypeScript, `@param` and `@returns` carry no `{type}`: the signature already states it. This port runs on TypeScript files only; in JavaScript the JSDoc type is the only type there is.

**Why:** A type in the comment duplicates the signature, and when one changes the other is left saying something false.

### How to fix

1. Remove the `{type}` from each `@param` and `@returns` tag; keep the name and description.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @param {number} n the number
 */
function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @param n the number
 */
function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @param {number} n the number
 */
function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @param n the number
 */
function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-prefer-import-tag` — @import a type instead of inline import()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type comes in once by a new file-level `@import` block, whose place among the file's imports, and whose name against the names the file already binds, are the author's to decide)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-prefer-import-tag.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc type does not write `import("module").Name` inline; the type is brought in once with `@import { Name } from "module"` and used by name. `@typedef` tags are exempt, as upstream exempts them by default.

**Why:** Inline `import()` types repeat the module path at every use, are hard to read, and must each be edited when the module moves.

### How to fix

1. Add a block `/** @import { Name } from "module" */` near the top of the file.
2. Replace each `import("module").Name` in the JSDoc types with `Name`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {import("./config").Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/** @import { Config } from "./config" */

/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {import("./config").Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/** @import { Config } from "./config" */

/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {import("./config").Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

##### Do

```ts
/** @import { Config } from "./config" */

/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {import("./config").Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/** @import { Config } from "./config" */

/**
 * Starts the app.
 * @param {Config} config the settings
 */
function start(config) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-reject-any-type` — No any or * types in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the real type is the author's to name)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-reject-any-type.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc type is not `any` or `*`, alone or inside a union or generic.

**Why:** `any` switches type checking off for the value and everything it flows into, so the documented API promises nothing.

### How to fix

1. Write the type the value actually has, or `unknown` if it really can be anything and is checked before use.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {*} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {string} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {*} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {string} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {*} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {string} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {*} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Logs a value.
 * @param {string} value the value
 */
function log(value) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-reject-function-type` — No bare Function type in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the function's signature is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-reject-function-type.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc type is not the bare `Function`; it states the signature, `(a: string) => void`, or names a `@callback`.

**Why:** `Function` accepts any callable and returns `any`, so neither the arguments nor the result are checked.

### How to fix

1. Replace `Function` with the signature the code calls it with, e.g. `{(err: Error) => void}`, or define a `@callback` and use its name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {Function} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {(err: Error) => void} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {Function} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {(err: Error) => void} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {Function} done called when finished
 */

```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {(err: Error) => void} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {Function} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Runs a job.
 * @param {(err: Error) => void} done called when finished
 */
function run(done) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-description` — A function's JSDoc has a description

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the description is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a function, method or function-valued `const` has description text before its first tag. A block with `@inheritdoc` is exempt.

**Why:** Tags say what the parameters are; only the description says what the function is for, and that is what a reader looks for first.

##### Do

```jsx

 * @param {number} n the number
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/jsdoc-require-description-complete-sentence` — A JSDoc description is complete sentences

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the sentence is the author's to finish)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-description-complete-sentence.md

### What it checks

The description of a function's JSDoc block starts with a capital letter and ends with `.`, `?` or `!`. Only the main description is checked; upstream also checks tag descriptions.

**Why:** A description in fragments reads as an unfinished note in hovers and generated docs.

### How to fix

2. End the description with `.`, `?` or `!`.

### Examples

```js
 */

```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Fetches the user.
 */
function fetchUser() {}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * fetches the user
 */
function fetchUser() {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Fetches the user.
 */

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * fetches the user
 */

```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Fetches the user.
 */
function fetchUser() {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * fetches the user
 */

```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Fetches the user.
 */
function fetchUser() {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-example` — A function's JSDoc has an @example

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the example is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-example.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a function, method or function-valued `const` includes an `@example`. A block with `@inheritdoc` is exempt; a function with no JSDoc block is not reported here.

**Why:** An example shows how to call the function faster than any description, and is what readers copy.

```js
}
```

```js
 */
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 */
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx

 * Doubles a number.
 * @example
 * double(2); // 4
 */

  return n * 2;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 */

  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @example
 * double(2); // 4
 */

  return n * 2;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 */

  return n * 2;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Doubles a number.
 * @example
 * double(2); // 4
 */
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-file-overview` — Each file starts with an @file block

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the file overview is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-file-overview.md

### What it checks

Every file has a top-level JSDoc block with `@file` (or its aliases `@fileoverview`, `@overview`). Only the missing case is reported; upstream also reports a duplicate or a misplaced overview.

**Why:** A file overview tells a reader what the module is for before they read its code, and documentation tools group files by it.

### How to fix

1. Add a JSDoc block at the top of the file: `/** @file What this module does. */`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export const answer = 42;
```

##### Do

```js
/** @file The answer to everything. */
export const answer = 42;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export const answer = 42;
```

##### Do

```jsx
/** @file The answer to everything. */
export const answer = 42;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do


## `js/jsdoc-require-next-description` — @next says what is sent in

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

#### TypeScript

## `js/jsdoc-require-param` — A documented function documents its parameters

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each parameter needs its own @param line with the author's description)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-param.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a function that takes parameters has `@param` tags. Ported in part: a block with no `@param` at all is reported; one that names some parameters and misses others is not (that needs the parameter list compared with the tags). Blocks with `@inheritdoc`, `@override`, `@type` or a file-level tag are skipped.

**Why:** A comment that documents a function but not what it takes leaves the reader guessing at its inputs.

### How to fix

1. Add a `@param` line for each parameter, in order, with its name and what it means.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a The first.
 * @param b The second.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a The first.
 * @param b The second.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a The first.
 * @param b The second.
 */

  return a + b;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 */

  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a The first.
 * @param b The second.
 */
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-param-name` — @param names its parameter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which parameter the tag is for is the author's to say)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-param-name.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc `@param` tag names the parameter it documents.

**Why:** A `@param` with only a type cannot be matched to a parameter, so tools ignore it.

### How to fix

1. Write the parameter's name after the `@param` type.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
 * @param {string}
```

##### Do

```js
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

##### Don't

```jsx

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string}
 */
```

##### Do

```jsx

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} name Who to greet.
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string}
 */

```

##### Do

```ts

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} name Who to greet.
 */

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string}
 */

```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Greets someone.
 * @param {string} name Who to greet.
 */
function greet(name) {}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-param-type` — @param has a type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-property.md

## `js/jsdoc-require-rejects` — A function that rejects documents @rejects

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (when and why the promise rejects is the author's to describe)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-rejects.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on an async function that throws, or on a function that returns `Promise.reject(...)`, has a `@rejects` tag. A throw or rejection inside a nested function does not count.

**Why:** Callers of a promise-returning function need to know which failures to `catch`.

### How to fix

1. Add `@rejects {ErrorType} When ...` describing when the returned promise rejects.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 */
async function load(id) {
  if (!id) throw new Error("no id");
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 * @rejects {Error} When the id is empty.
 */
async function load(id) {
  if (!id) throw new Error("no id");
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 */
async function load(id) {
  if (!id) throw new Error("no id");
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 * @rejects {Error} When the id is empty.
 */
async function load(id) {
  if (!id) throw new Error("no id");
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 */

  if (!id) throw new Error("no id");
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

##### Do

```ts

 * Loads a user.
 * @param {string} id The user.
 * @rejects {Error} When the id is empty.
 */

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


## `js/jsdoc-require-returns` — A function that returns a value documents @returns

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a function that returns a value (a `return` with an expression, or an arrow with an expression body) has a `@returns` tag. Generators, and blocks with `@inheritdoc`, `@override`, `@type` or a file-level tag, are skipped.

```js
 * Adds two numbers.

  return a + b;
```


#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a The first.

  return a + b;
```

##### Do

```ts

 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param {number} a The first.
 * @param {number} b The second.

  return a + b;

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


## `js/jsdoc-require-returns-check` — @returns only where a value is returned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to return the documented value or drop the tag is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-returns-check.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc `@returns` tag (other than `{void}`, `{undefined}`, `{never}` or `{Promise<void>}`) sits on a function whose body returns a value. Async functions, generators, functions that throw, and blocks with `@abstract`, `@virtual` or `@interface` are skipped.

**Why:** A `@returns` on a function that returns nothing promises callers a value they never get.

### How to fix

1. Return the documented value, or remove the `@returns` tag (or make it `@returns {void}`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js

 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */
function log(m) {
  console.log(m);
}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */
function log(m) {
  console.log(m);
  return m;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */

  console.log(m);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */
function log(m) {
  console.log(m);
  return m;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */
function log(m) {
  console.log(m);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */

  console.log(m);
  return m;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */

  console.log(m);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

 * Logs a message.
 * @param {string} m The message.
 * @returns {string} The message.
 */

  return m;
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-template` — Type parameters are documented with @template

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each type parameter needs its own @template line with the author's description)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-template.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a generic function, class, interface or type alias has `@template` tags. Ported in part: a block with no `@template` at all is reported; one that documents some type parameters and misses others is not. JavaScript `@typedef` generics are not checked.

**Why:** A generic's type parameters are part of its contract, and readers look for them next to `@param`.

### How to fix

1. Add `@template T description` for each type parameter, in order.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @param value The value.
 * @returns The box.
 */
export function box<T>(value: T): T[] {
  return [value];
}
```

##### Do

```ts
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @template T The value's type.
 * @param value The value.
 * @returns The box.
 */
export function box<T>(value: T): T[] {
  return [value];
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @param value The value.
 * @returns The box.
 */
export function box<T>(value: T): T[] {
  return [value];
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @template T The value's type.
 * @param value The value.
 * @returns The box.
 */
export function box<T>(value: T): T[] {
  return [value];
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-template-description` — @template says what the type parameter is

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the description is the author's words)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-template-description.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc `@template` tag carries a description after the type parameter's name.

**Why:** A bare type-parameter name says nothing about what the type stands for or what it is constrained to.

### How to fix

1. After the type parameter's name, write what it stands for.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @template T
 * @param {T} value The value.
 * @returns {T[]} The box.
 */
function box(value) {
  return [value];
}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Wraps a value.
 * @template T The value's type.
 * @param {T} value The value.
 * @returns {T[]} The box.
 */
function box(value) {
  return [value];
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

##### Do

```jsx

  return [value];

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do


## `js/jsdoc-require-throws` — A function that throws documents @throws

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (when and why the function throws is the author's to describe)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-throws.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a non-async function whose body has a `throw` has a `@throws` tag. A throw inside a nested function does not count; async functions are `jsdoc-require-rejects`'s.

**Why:** Callers need to know which errors to expect and when, and the signature does not say.

### How to fix

1. Add `@throws {ErrorType} When ...` describing when the function throws.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
/**
 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 */
function port(s) {
  const n = Number(s);
  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 * @throws {RangeError} When the text is not a number.
 */
function port(s) {
  const n = Number(s);
  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 */
function port(s) {
  const n = Number(s);
  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
/**
 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 * @throws {RangeError} When the text is not a number.
 */
function port(s) {
  const n = Number(s);
  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/**
 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 */

  const n = Number(s);
  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

##### Do

```ts

 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 * @throws {RangeError} When the text is not a number.
 */

  if (!n) throw new RangeError(s);
  return n;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * Parses a port.
 * @param {string} s The text.
 * @returns {number} The port.
 */
```


## `js/jsdoc-require-yields` — A generator that yields documents @yields

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the yielded values mean is the author's to describe)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-yields.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc block on a generator that yields a value has a `@yields` tag. A `yield` inside a nested function does not count; blocks with `@inheritdoc`, `@override` or `@type` are skipped.

**Why:** What a generator yields is its output; without `@yields` its consumers must read the body to find out.

### How to fix

```js
  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

##### Do

```js
 * Counts from zero.
 * @yields {number} The next id.
 */
function* ids() {
  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
/**
 * Counts from zero.
 */

  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
```

##### Do

```jsx
  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
 * Counts from zero.
 */

  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

 * Counts from zero.
 */

  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
```

## `js/jsdoc-require-yields-check` — @yields only where a value is yielded

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to yield the documented value or drop the tag is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-require-yields-check.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc `@yields` tag sits on a generator whose body yields a value. A `yield` inside a nested function does not count.

**Why:** A `@yields` on a generator that yields nothing promises its consumers values they never get.

## `js/jsdoc-ts-ban-ts-comment` — No @ts-ignore or @ts-nocheck in JavaScript

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the reason the error is expected has to come from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-ts-ban-ts-comment.md

### What it checks

In a JavaScript file checked by TypeScript, type-checking is not switched off with `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck` (in a line, block or JSDoc comment), and a `@ts-expect-error` says why. TypeScript files are `ts/ban-ts-comment`'s.

**Why:** `@ts-ignore` hides an error for good, even after the code it excused changes; `@ts-expect-error` fails as soon as the error is gone.

### How to fix

1. Fix the type error if you can.
2. Otherwise replace the comment with `// @ts-expect-error: <why>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// @ts-ignore
const n = Math.max("1");
```

##### Do

```js
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the checker's message
const n = Math.max("1");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
// @ts-ignore
const n = Math.max("1");
```

##### Do

```jsx
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the checker's message
const n = Math.max("1");
```

## `js/jsdoc-ts-no-empty-object-type` — No {} type in JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (whether `object`, `unknown` or a real shape is meant is the author's call, so `object` and `unknown` are offered; a shape is written by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/jsdoc` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/jsdoc-ts-no-empty-object-type.md

### What it checks

A JSDoc type does not use the empty object type `{}` (as `{{}}` or inside a generic such as `{Array<{}>}`); `object`, `unknown` or a written-out shape is used instead.

**Why:** `{}` does not mean "an empty object": it accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, so it checks nothing.

### How to fix

1. Replace `{}` with `object` for any non-primitive, `unknown` for any value, or the object's real shape.

### Examples

```js
/**
 * Merges options.
 * @param {{}} opts The options.
 */
function merge(opts) {}
```

##### Do

```js
/**
 * Merges options.
 * @param {object} opts The options.
 */
function merge(opts) {}
```

##### Fixed (object)

```js
/**
 * Merges options.
 * @param {object} opts The options.
 */
function merge(opts) {}
```

##### Fixed (unknown)

```js
/**
 * Merges options.
 * @param {unknown} opts The options.
 */
function merge(opts) {}
```

#### JSX

## `js/label-position` — Only loops and switches are labelled

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the label was for, and how to write it without one, is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/label-position.md

### What it checks

A label is put only on a loop or a `switch`, where `break` and `continue` can use it.

**Why:** A label on any other statement is almost always a leftover, or an object literal's key mistaken for a statement.

### How to fix

1. Remove the label, or move it onto the loop it was meant to name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
found: {
  if (ready) break found;
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```js
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell) continue outer;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
found: {
  if (ready) break found;
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell) continue outer;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  run();
```

##### Do

```ts

  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell) continue outer;
  }

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  if (ready) break found;
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  }

```
