## `js/max-depth` — Blocks nest no deeper than a maximum

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (flattening nested blocks changes the function's structure; which guard to invert or which block to extract is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-depth.md

### What it checks

Blocks nest at most `max` deep (4 by default). A block is a statement that opens its own scope of control: `if`, `switch`, `try`, `for`, `for…in`, `for…of`, `while`, `do…while` and `with`. An `else if` continues its chain and adds no depth. Each function starts again at zero, so a callback is not charged for the blocks around it. The rule reports on each statement that sits too deep: `Blocks are nested 5 deep (max 4)`.

**Why:** Every level of nesting is another condition a reader must keep in mind to know when a line runs. Deep nesting is also where the bug lives: the `else` that belongs to the wrong `if`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `4` | the most blocks that may nest inside one another in a function |

### How to fix

1. Turn a guard into an early `return`, `continue` or `throw`, so the rest of the function sits one level up.
2. Extract the body of the innermost block into a well-named function.
3. Replace a nested pair of `if`s with one condition joined by `&&`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```js
function f(a) {
  if (a) {
    for (const x of a) {
      if (x) {
        x();
      }
    }
  }
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```js
function f(a) {
  if (!a) return;
  for (const x of a) {
    if (x) x();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 1 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  if (items) {
    if (items.length) {
      return <ul />;
    }
  }
  return null;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 1 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  if (!items?.length) return null;
  return <ul />;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```ts
function f(a?: Array<() => void>) {
  if (a) {
    for (const x of a) {
      if (x) {
        x();
      }
    }
  }
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```ts
function f(a?: Array<() => void>) {
  if (!a) return;
  for (const x of a) {
    if (x) x();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 1 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items?: string[] }) {
  if (items) {
    if (items.length) {
      return <ul />;
    }
  }
  return null;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 1 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items?: string[] }) {
  if (!items?.length) return null;
  return <ul />;
}
```

## `js/max-lines` — A file stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting a file changes its structure; which exports belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-lines.md

### What it checks

A file has at most `max` lines (300 by default). Blank lines and lines that hold only a comment (a `{/* … */}`
in JSX is one) are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`; a line that holds code and a
comment counts as code. `skip_imports` leaves the import block out too. The rule reports once, on the first line over
the limit, with the measured count: `412 lines (max 300; blank lines and comments not counted)`.

**Why:** A long file is hard to hold in your head, slow to review and the usual place a second responsibility hides. The
limit is a prompt to split, not a goal in itself: raise `max` for a file that is long on purpose, or put
a generated file where `[files] lint_generated = false` skips it. Only the host file is measured, never a `<script>` in
HTML or a code block in Markdown.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `300` | the most lines a file may have |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_imports` | `boolean` | `false` | the import block does not count |

### How to fix

1. Find a cohesive group of exports (a component and its helpers, one feature's types) and move it to a new module next to the file.
2. Import it back where it is used, or re-export it from the old file so callers do not change.
3. If the file is long on purpose, raise `max` for it in an `[[overrides]]` entry, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule js/max-lines`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
const c = 3;
const d = 4;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
import { d } from "./more.js";
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
const a = <i />;
const b = <b />;
const c = <u />;
const d = <s />;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
import { d } from "./more.jsx";
const a = <i />;
const b = <b />;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
const a: number = 1;
const b: number = 2;
const c: number = 3;
const d: number = 4;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
import { d } from "./more";
const a: number = 1;
const b: number = 2;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
const a: JSX.Element = <i />;
const b: JSX.Element = <b />;
const c: JSX.Element = <u />;
const d: JSX.Element = <s />;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
import { d } from "./more";
const a: JSX.Element = <i />;
const b: JSX.Element = <b />;
```

## `js/max-lines-per-function` — A function stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (extracting part of a function changes its structure; where to cut and what to call the piece is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-lines-per-function.md

### What it checks

A function spans at most `max` lines (50 by default), from its first line to its last. Every function form counts:
declarations, expressions, arrows, methods, getters and setters, and class `static` blocks. Blank lines and comment-only
lines are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`. With `include_nested` (the default) an
inner function's lines count toward the outer function as well; with `include_nested = false` they do not, from the
inner function's first line to its last. An immediately invoked function is not measured on its own unless
`include_iife` is `true`; its lines belong to the function around it. `ignore_names` is a regular expression for names
to exempt, such as `"^(test|it|describe)"`. The rule reports on the function's name: `renderOrders is 84 lines (max 50)`.

**Why:** A function that long does several jobs, and its name can say only one. The limit is a prompt to extract, not a goal in
itself: a test suite's `describe` callback is long on purpose, so exempt it with `ignore_names`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `50` | the most lines one function may span |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `include_nested` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of an inner function count toward the outer one too |
| `include_iife` | `boolean` | `false` | measure an immediately invoked function, `(() => { … })()`, as a function of its own |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; functions named like this are exempt, e.g. "^(test\|it\|describe)" |

### How to fix

1. Find a block inside the function that does one thing (a loop body, a branch, a run of statements that build one value).
2. Extract it into a well-named function, and pass in what it reads.
3. Repeat until each piece fits `max`. If the function is long on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule js/max-lines-per-function`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  for (const item of items) sum += item;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  const rows = items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>);
  const empty = <p>none</p>;
  return rows.length ? <ul>{rows}</ul> : empty;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>)}</ul>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
function total(items: number[]): number {
  let sum = 0;
  for (const item of items) sum += item;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
function total(items: number[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item, 0);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const rows = items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>);
  const empty = <p>none</p>;
  return rows.length ? <ul>{rows}</ul> : empty;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>)}</ul>;
}
```

## `js/max-nested-callbacks` — No callbacks nested more than ten deep

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which callbacks become named functions or awaits is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-nested-callbacks.md

### What it checks

A function passed as an argument is not nested inside more than ten others (ESLint's default `max: 10`).

**Why:** Past that depth the code is a pyramid no reader can hold; promises, `async`/`await` or named functions flatten it.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => k(() => {})))))))))));
```

##### Do

```js
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => {}))))))))));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => k(() => {})))))))))));
```

##### Do

```jsx
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => {}))))))))));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => k(() => {})))))))))));
```

##### Do

```ts
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => {}))))))))));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => k(() => {})))))))))));
```

##### Do

```tsx
a(() => b(() => c(() => d(() => e(() => f(() => g(() => h(() => i(() => j(() => {}))))))))));
```

## `js/max-params` — A function takes at most a maximum number of parameters

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (grouping parameters changes the function's signature and every call to it; which belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-params.md

### What it checks

A function takes at most `max` parameters (3 by default). A destructured object or array parameter counts as one, which
is the usual way out. A rest parameter and a TypeScript `this:` parameter are not counted unless `count_varargs` or
`count_this` is `true`, and neither is a parameter whose name matches `ignore_names` (`"^_"` by default: a
parameter named `_unused` is already said to be unused). A TypeScript `override` method, an overload signature, a
`declare` function, an abstract method and anything in a `.d.ts` file are skipped, since you do not own that
signature; set `ignore_overrides` or `ignore_declarations` to `false` to count them. A constructor that only
declares parameter properties (`constructor(private a: A, private b: B)`) can be skipped with
`ignore_constructor_injection`. The rule reports on the function's name: `createOrder takes 6 parameters (max 3)`.

**Why:** A call with many positional arguments is easy to get in the wrong order, and every added parameter is a change to every
caller. Grouping related parameters in one object names them at the call site.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `3` | the most parameters a function may take |
| `count_this` | `boolean` | `false` | TypeScript: count a `this:` parameter |
| `count_varargs` | `boolean` | `false` | count a rest parameter, `...rest` |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | `"^_"` | a regular expression; parameters named like this do not count |
| `ignore_overrides` | `boolean` | `true` | skip a TypeScript `override` method: its signature is not yours |
| `ignore_declarations` | `boolean` | `true` | skip an overload signature, a `declare` function, an abstract method and a `.d.ts` file |
| `ignore_constructor_injection` | `boolean` | `false` | TypeScript: skip a constructor whose parameters are all parameter properties (Angular, NestJS) |

### How to fix

1. Group the parameters that belong together into one options object: `createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address })`.
2. Update the callers to pass the object, and give the destructured parameter a type in TypeScript.
3. If the signature is not yours to change, exempt it: an `override`, an overload and a `declare` function already are.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function createOrder(customer, items, coupon, address) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

##### Do

```js
function createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address }) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Card(title, body, footer, onClose) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Card({ title, body, footer, onClose }) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function createOrder(customer: string, items: string[], coupon: string, address: string) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address }: Order) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Card(title: string, body: string, footer: string, onClose: () => void) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Card({ title, body, footer, onClose }: CardProps) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

## `js/max-statements` — No function with more than ten statements

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

#### TypeScript

```ts
  k();
```

##### Do

#### TSX

```tsx
  a(); b(); c(); d(); e();
```

##### Do


## `js/max-switch-cases` — No switch with more than 30 cases

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the table that replaces it is the author's design)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-switch-cases.md

### What it checks

A `switch` has at most 30 `case` clauses (SonarJS's default).

**Why:** A switch that long is a lookup table written as code; a map or an object says so and is easier to extend.

### How to fix

1. Replace the cases with an object or a `Map` from each value to its result, and look the value up.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (code) {
  case 1: return "a"; case 2: return "b"; case 3: return "c"; case 4: return "d"; case 5: return "e";

  case 11: return "k"; case 12: return "l"; case 13: return "m"; case 14: return "n"; case 15: return "o";
  case 16: return "p"; case 17: return "q"; case 18: return "r"; case 19: return "s"; case 20: return "t";
  case 21: return "u"; case 22: return "v"; case 23: return "w"; case 24: return "x"; case 25: return "y";
  case 26: return "z"; case 27: return "A"; case 28: return "B"; case 29: return "C"; case 30: return "D";
  case 31: return "E";
}
```

```js
return LETTERS[code];
```

```jsx
  case 26: return "z"; case 27: return "A"; case 28: return "B"; case 29: return "C"; case 30: return "D";

}
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


## `js/max-union-size` — No union of more than three types outside an alias

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the alias's name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-union-size.md

### What it checks

A union written in place has at most three members (SonarJS's default); a longer one is given a name with a type alias. Unions that are an alias's own value are left alone.

**Why:** A long union repeated at each use is hard to read and easy to let drift.

### How to fix

1. Declare `type <Name> = …` with the union and use the name here.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function pick(mode: "a" | "b" | "c" | "d") {}
```

##### Do

```ts
type Mode = "a" | "b" | "c" | "d";
function pick(mode: Mode) {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function pick(mode: "a" | "b" | "c" | "d") {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Mode = "a" | "b" | "c" | "d";
function pick(mode: Mode) {}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/no-accessor-recursion` — A getter or setter does not use itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the backing field name (`#name`, `_name`) is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-accessor-recursion.md

### What it checks

A getter or setter does not read or write the property it defines through `this`.

**Why:** It calls itself recursively and throws a stack overflow.

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class User {
  get name() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class User {
  get name() {
    return this._name;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class User {
  get name() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class User {
  get name() {
    return this._name;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class User {
  get name() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class User {
  get name() {
    return this._name;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class User {
  get name() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class User {
  get name() {
    return this._name;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-accidental-bitwise-operator` — No & or | in a condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`&&` short-circuits and yields an operand, while the bitwise test stays as is with an explicit nonzero check; the author picks)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-accidental-bitwise-operator.md

### What it checks

The whole condition of an `if`, `while` or `do … while` is not a bitwise `&` or `|`.

**Why:** In a condition `&` and `|` are almost always a typo for `&&` and `||`; they evaluate both sides and give a number.

### How to fix

1. Use `&&` for `&` and `||` for `|`; if a bit test was meant, compare it: `(flags & MASK) !== 0`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (ready & visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (logical operator)

```js
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (test the bits against zero)

```js
if ((ready & visible) !== 0) {
  show();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (ready & visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (logical operator)

```jsx
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (test the bits against zero)

```jsx
if ((ready & visible) !== 0) {
  show();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (ready & visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (logical operator)

```ts
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (test the bits against zero)

```ts
if ((ready & visible) !== 0) {
  show();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (ready & visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (logical operator)

```tsx
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

##### Fixed (test the bits against zero)

```tsx
if ((ready & visible) !== 0) {
  show();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (ready && visible) {
  show();
}
```

## `js/no-accumulating-spread` — No spread of the accumulator in reduce

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a push onto an array-literal start value nothing else holds is auto; any other start value, a nested function in the elements, or the object form is a suggestion)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-accumulating-spread.md

### What it checks

A `reduce` callback does not build a new array or object by spreading its accumulator on every step.

**Why:** Each step copies everything accumulated so far, which turns a linear pass into a quadratic one.

### How to fix

1. Mutate the accumulator (`acc.push(x); return acc;` or `acc[k] = v; return acc;`), or build the result with a loop.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => [...acc, r.id], []);
```

##### Fixed

```js
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

##### Do

```js
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => [...acc, r.id], []);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => [...acc, r.id], []);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

##### Do

```ts
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => [...acc, r.id], []);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const ids = rows.reduce((acc, r) => {
  acc.push(r.id);
  return acc;
}, []);
```

## `js/no-array-callback-reference` — Wrap function references passed to array methods

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the wrapped function no longer receives the index and the array, which it may have used)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-callback-reference.md

### What it checks

A bare function name is not passed as the callback of an array method (built-in converters like `Boolean` are allowed).

**Why:** Array methods pass `(element, index, array)`; a function with optional parameters, like `parseInt`, silently takes the index too.

```js
const n = inputs.map(parseInt);
```

```js
const n = inputs.map((x) => parseInt(x));
```

#### JSX

```jsx

```

##### Do


## `js/no-array-concat-in-loop` — No concat() in a loop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`push` mutates the array in place, which other holders of the old array would see, and `concat` of a non-array adds the value while a spread throws)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-concat-in-loop.md

### What it checks

An array is not rebuilt with `a = a.concat(...)` inside a loop.

**Why:** Each `concat` copies the whole array, so the loop is quadratic.

### How to fix

1. Use `a.push(...items)`, or build a list of parts in the loop and `.flat()` it once after.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (const page of pages) {
  rows = rows.concat(page.rows);
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
for (const page of pages) {
  rows.push(...page.rows);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (const page of pages) {
  rows.push(...page.rows);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (const page of pages) {
  rows = rows.concat(page.rows);
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
for (const page of pages) {
  rows.push(...page.rows);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (const page of pages) {
  rows.push(...page.rows);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (const page of pages) {
  rows = rows.concat(page.rows);
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
for (const page of pages) {

```

##### Do

```ts
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  rows = rows.concat(page.rows);
}
```

##### Fixed


## `js/no-array-fill-with-reference-type` — No fill() with an object

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (each element gets its own value, which is the point, but code that relied on the elements being one shared object changes; a `fill` whose length is not in a `new Array(n)` or `Array(n)` before it is rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-fill-with-reference-type.md

### What it checks

`.fill()` is not given an object, array, function or `new` value.

**Why:** Every slot gets the same reference, so changing one row changes them all.

### How to fix

1. Use `Array.from({ length: n }, () => value)`, which creates a new value for each slot.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const grid = new Array(3).fill([]);
```

##### Do

```js
const grid = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const grid = new Array(3).fill([]);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const grid = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const grid = new Array(3).fill([]);
```

##### Do

```ts
const grid = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const grid = new Array(3).fill([]);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const grid = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []);
```

## `js/no-array-from-fill` — Array.from with a mapper rather than fill()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`fill` evaluates its value once and the mapper once per element: a call or an object literal there gives each element its own value; a `fill` with a start or end, or an `Array.from` with a mapper already, is rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-from-fill.md

### What it checks

`Array.from(…).fill(…)` is written as `Array.from(…, () => value)`.

**Why:** It makes one array instead of two passes, and the mapper creates a fresh value each time.

### How to fix

1. Move the fill value into a mapper: `Array.from({ length: n }, () => value)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }).fill(0);
```

##### Do

```js
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }).fill(0);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }).fill(0);
```

##### Do

```ts
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }).fill(0);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const zeros = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0);
```

## `js/no-array-front-mutation` — No unshift() or shift()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (switching ends changes the order the rest of the code reads)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-front-mutation.md

### What it checks

Elements are not added to the front of an array with `unshift`.

**Why:** Adding to the front shifts every element, so it is O(n), and the order logic is easy to get backwards.

### How to fix

1. Push at the end and read from the end, or build a new array `[item, ...queue]` where a copy is wanted.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
queue.unshift(job);
```

##### Do

```js
queue.push(job);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
queue.unshift(job);
```

##### Do

```jsx
queue.push(job);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
queue.unshift(job);
```

##### Do

```ts
queue.push(job);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
queue.unshift(job);
```

##### Do

```tsx
queue.push(job);
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/no-array-reduce` — No reduce()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the loop needs a variable for the accumulator)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-reduce.md

### What it checks

`reduce` and `reduceRight` are not given a callback with a block body; a one-expression reducer (`(a, b) => a + b`) is allowed, as upstream allows simple ones.

**Why:** A reducer with statements hides a loop and its accumulator in a call; a `for … of` loop says the same plainly.

### How to fix

1. Declare the accumulator with `let`, loop over the array with `for … of`, and update it in the body.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
const total = items.reduce((sum, x) => {
  return sum + x.price;
}, 0);
```

##### Do

```js
let total = 0;
for (const x of items) {
  total += x.price;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = items.reduce((sum, x) => {
  return sum + x.price;
}, 0);
```

##### Do

```jsx
let total = 0;
for (const x of items) {
  total += x.price;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const total = items.reduce((sum, x) => {
  return sum + x.price;
}, 0);
```

##### Do

```ts
let total = 0;
for (const x of items) {
  total += x.price;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const total = items.reduce((sum, x) => {
  return sum + x.price;
}, 0);
```

##### Do

```tsx
let total = 0;
for (const x of items) {
  total += x.price;
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toReversed()` leaves the original untouched, which code later reading it may rely on either way)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-reverse.md

### What it checks

The result of `.reverse()` is not used as a value; `.toReversed()` returns a reversed copy. A `.reverse()` call on its own line, used for its effect, is left alone.

**Why:** `.reverse()` reverses the array in place and returns it, so code that uses the result also changes the original.


#### TypeScript

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-array-sort-for-min-max` — Math.min/max rather than sorting for one value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Math.min` of an empty array is `Infinity` where the sort gave `undefined`, `sort` no longer reorders the array in place, and a value that is not a number compares differently; only a `(a, b) => a - b` or `b - a` comparator is rewritten)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-array-sort-for-min-max.md

### What it checks

The first element of a sorted copy is not read just to find the smallest or largest value.

**Why:** Sorting does far more work than a single pass, and `.sort()` also reorders the original.

### How to fix

1. If the comparator sorts ascending, use `Math.min(...values)`; descending, `Math.max(...values)`. For objects, find the extreme with a `reduce` or a loop.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const first = values.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)[0];
```

##### Do

```js
const first = Math.min(...values);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const first = values.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)[0];
```

##### Do

```jsx
const first = Math.min(...values);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const first = values.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)[0];
```

##### Do

```ts
const first = Math.min(...values);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const first = values.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)[0];
```

##### Do

```tsx
const first = Math.min(...values);
```

## `js/no-async-iterator-callback` — No async callback to forEach, filter, some, every or find

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a loop with await or Promise.all over map changes how the work runs; which one is right is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-async-iterator-callback.md

### What it checks

`forEach`, `filter`, `some`, `every`, `find` and their kin are not given an `async` callback: they do not wait for its promise, so `forEach` returns before the work ends and `filter` keeps every element (a promise is truthy).

**Why:** The array method treats the returned promise as the answer, which it never is.

### How to fix

1. Use a `for … of` loop with `await` inside, or `await Promise.all(items.map(async …))` and work on the results.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
items.forEach(async (item) => {
  await save(item);
});
```

##### Do

```js
for (const item of items) {
  await save(item);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
items.forEach(async (item) => {
  await save(item);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (const item of items) {
  await save(item);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
items.forEach(async (item) => {
  await save(item);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
for (const item of items) {
  await save(item);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
items.forEach(async (item) => {
  await save(item);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (const item of items) {
  await save(item);
}
```

## `js/no-async-promise-executor` — A Promise executor is not an async function

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (dropping `async` sends a thrown error to the promise instead of an unhandled rejection, which the author confirms; offered only when the executor has no `await`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-async-promise-executor.md

### What it checks

The function passed to `new Promise(...)` is not `async`.

**Why:** An error thrown in an async executor doesn't reject the promise, and an executor that needs
`await` doesn't need the `Promise` wrapper.

### How to fix

1. If the executor only awaits and resolves, use the awaited promise directly.
2. Otherwise make the executor a plain function and handle errors with `reject`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Fixed

```js
const data = new Promise((resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Do

```js
const data = load();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const data = new Promise((resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const data = load();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const data = new Promise((resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const data = load();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const data = new Promise((resolve) => {
  resolve(load());
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const data = load();
```

## `js/no-async-promise-finally` — No async callback in finally

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the cleanup must finish first decides the rewrite)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

```js
  await close();
```

```jsx

  close();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  await close();
```

##### Do

```ts
  close();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  await close();
```

##### Do


## `js/no-await-expression-member` — No member access on an await expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the destructuring depends on how the value is used next)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

##### Do

```jsx
const { name } = await getUser();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const name = (await getUser()).name;
```

##### Do

```ts
const { name } = await getUser();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-await-in-loop` — No await inside a loop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Promise.all` runs the iterations together, which changes ordering and failure handling; the reviewer confirms they are independent)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-await-in-loop.md

### What it checks

`await` is not used directly inside a loop body.

**Why:** Each iteration waits for the last; independent work runs far faster with `Promise.all`.

### How to fix

1. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` after the loop, if the iterations are independent.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
async function f(ids) {
  for (const id of ids) {
    await load(id);
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
async function f(ids) {
  await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => load(id)));
}
```

##### Do

```js
async function f(ids) {
  await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => load(id)));
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
async function f(ids) {
  for (const id of ids) {
    await load(id);
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
async function f(ids) {
  await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => load(id)));
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
async function f(ids) {
  await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => load(id)));
}
```

#### TypeScript

## `js/no-await-in-promise-methods` — No await inside Promise.all([...])

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the awaited promise no longer finishes before the others start)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

### What it checks

An element of the array given to `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `any` or `race` is not `await`ed.

```jsx
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([await loadA(), loadB()]);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([loadA(), loadB()]);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([await loadA(), loadB()]);
```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do


## `js/no-boolean-sort-comparator` — A sort comparator returns a number

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a numeric difference or a string comparison suits different values; the author picks by what is sorted)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

### What it checks


##### Fixed (string comparison)

```js
items.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

##### Do

```js
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
items.sort((a, b) => a > b);
```

##### Fixed (numeric difference)

```jsx
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (string comparison)

```jsx
items.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

##### Do

```jsx
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
items.sort((a, b) => a > b);
```

##### Fixed (numeric difference)

```ts
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (string comparison)

```ts
items.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

##### Do

```ts
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
items.sort((a, b) => a > b);
```

##### Fixed (numeric difference)

```tsx
items.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (string comparison)

```tsx
items.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-case-declarations` — No let, const, function or class directly in a case

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the braces end the declaration's scope at the case, so another case that reads it no longer can, which the fix does not check)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-case-declarations.md

### What it checks

A `let`, `const`, `function` or `class` inside a `case` sits in a block `{ … }` of its own.

**Why:** Declarations in a case are scoped to the whole `switch`, so another case can see them
uninitialised.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the case's statements in `{ … }`.
2. If another case uses the declaration, move it above the `switch`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-chained-comparison` — No a < b < c

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the middle operand is evaluated twice in the rewrite, and the comparison the author meant may not be the range; where `&&` would bind differently with what surrounds it, the rewrite is by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-chained-comparison.md

### What it checks

A comparison is not chained (`a < b < c`).

**Why:** JavaScript evaluates `a < b` to `true` or `false` first and compares that with `c`, so the range check is always wrong.

### How to fix

1. Split it into two comparisons joined by `&&`: `a < b && b < c`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (0 <= x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (0 <= x && x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (0 <= x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (0 <= x && x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (0 <= x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (0 <= x && x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (0 <= x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (0 <= x && x <= 10) {
  ok();
}
```

## `js/no-char-at-multichar-compare` — charAt() compared with a longer string

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`startsWith` is one reading of the comparison; a `slice` or a one-character string is another, so the author confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-char-at-multichar-compare.md

### What it checks

The result of `charAt()` is compared only with one-character strings. A comparison with `""` (the out-of-range check) is fine.

**Why:** `charAt()` returns one character, so comparing it with a longer string is always false (or always true with `!==`).

### How to fix

1. To test a prefix at a position, use `$S.startsWith(str, i)`.
2. To compare one character, compare with that one character.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (line.charAt(0) === "//") {
  skip();
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (line.charAt(0) === "//") {
  skip();
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (line.charAt(0) === "//") {
  skip();
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (line.startsWith("//", 0)) {
  skip();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (line.charAt(0) === "//") {
  skip();
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

  skip();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  skip();
}
```

## `js/no-collapsible-if` — Merge nested ifs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

```ts
    grant();
  }
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  if (user.admin) {
    grant();
  }
```

##### Do

```tsx
    grant();
  }
```

## `js/no-compare-neg-zero` — No comparisons against -0

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`0` keeps what the code does today, `Object.is` tests for -0 as the code seems to intend; the author picks)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-compare-neg-zero.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't compare a value with `-0` using `==`, `===`, `<` or the other comparison operators.

**Why:** These operators treat `-0` and `0` as equal, so the comparison doesn't test what it says.

### How to fix

1. To test for negative zero, use `Object.is(x, -0)`.
2. To test for zero of either sign, compare with `0`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare with 0)

```js
if (x === 0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (use Object.is)

```js
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare with 0)

```jsx
if (x === 0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (use Object.is)

```jsx
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare with 0)

```ts
if (x === 0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (use Object.is)

```ts
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare with 0)

```tsx
if (x === 0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Fixed (use Object.is)

```tsx
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  flip();
}
```

## `js/no-cond-assign` — No assignment in a condition, unless doubly parenthesised

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a mistyped `=` or an intended assignment look alike; the author picks `===` or the doubled parentheses)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-cond-assign.md

### What it checks

The condition of an `if`, `while`, `do … while` or `for` is not an assignment, unless it is wrapped
in a second pair of parentheses to say it's meant.

**Why:** `if (a = b)` assigns and tests the result, which is almost always a mistyped `===`.

### How to fix

1. If a comparison was meant, use `===`.
2. If the assignment is meant, wrap it in a second pair of parentheses.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare)

```js
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (mark the assignment intended)

```js
if ((user = admin)) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```js
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare)

```jsx
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (mark the assignment intended)

```jsx
if ((user = admin)) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```jsx
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare)

```ts
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (mark the assignment intended)

```ts
if ((user = admin)) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```ts
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (compare)

```tsx

  grant();
}
```

##### Fixed (mark the assignment intended)

```tsx

  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  grant();
}
```

```tsx

  visit(node);
}
```

## `js/no-console` — No console calls left in the code

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (deleting the call also drops its arguments, which may have side effects; and a call whose value is used needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-console.md

### What it checks

Code makes no calls on the global `console` (`console.log(…)`, `console["debug"](…)`), except the
methods the `allow` option names. A local variable named `console` is not the global one.

**Why:** `console` output is debugging left behind: it clutters the browser console and the server
logs, and it can leak data. A team that wants it on a laptop and not in CI sets the rule to `warn`
in `[profiles.local]` and `error` in `[profiles.ci]`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `string[]` | `[]` | console methods that may stay, e.g. ["warn", "error"] |

### How to fix

1. Delete the call (`codelaw fix --unsafe` does when the call is a whole statement).
2. If the output is wanted, report through the project's logger instead.
3. If the method should stay everywhere, add it to the rule's `allow` option.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load(items) {
  console.log(items);
  return items.length;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  console.log(items);
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load(items: string[]): number {
  console.log(items);
  return items.length;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load(items: string[]): number {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  console.log(items);
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

## `js/no-console-spaces` — No leading or trailing space in console arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the space may be deliberate (two spaces for alignment); the author confirms the output)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-console-spaces.md

### What it checks

A string argument of a `console.log` (or `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) call with more than one argument does not start or end with a space.

**Why:** `console` joins arguments with a space, so the extra one prints two.

### How to fix

1. Remove the leading or trailing space from the string.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
console.log("total:", n, " items");
```

##### Do

```js
console.log("total:", n, "items");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
console.log("total:", n, " items");
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
console.log("total:", n, " items");
```

##### Do

```tsx
console.log("total:", n, "items");
```

## `js/no-const-assign` — A const is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the variable should be `let` or the assignment should go is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-const-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to a `const`.

**Why:** Assigning to a `const` throws a TypeError at run time.

### How to fix

1. If the value is meant to change, declare it with `let`.
2. Otherwise assign to a new variable.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = 0;
total = 1;
```

##### Do

```js
let total = 0;
total = 1;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = 0;
total = 1;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let total = 0;
total = 1;
```

## `js/no-constant-binary-expression` — No binary expression whose result is fixed

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are dropping the operand that never decides the result (the default, behaviour-preserving) or regrouping, `a + b ?? c` as `a + (b ?? c)`; a constant comparison is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-constant-binary-expression.md

### What it checks

The left side of `??`, `||` and `&&` is not a value whose nullishness or truthiness is fixed, and
nothing is compared with a newly created object or with `null` when it can never be `null`.

**Why:** Such an expression always gives the same answer, which usually means the author misread
operator precedence.

### How to fix

1. Add the parentheses the expression was meant to have.
2. Or compare with the value that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const total = price + tax;
```

##### Do

```js
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const total = price + tax;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const total = price + tax;
```

##### Do

```ts
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const total = price + tax;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

## `js/no-constant-condition` — No conditions that are always true or always false

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to remove the branch or fix the condition needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-constant-condition.md

### What it checks

The condition of an `if`, `while` or `do … while` is not a literal or another value that is always
truthy or always falsy; `while (true)` is allowed.

**Why:** A constant condition is usually leftover debugging or a typo, and hides dead code.

### How to fix

1. If the branch is dead, remove it.
2. Otherwise replace the constant with the condition that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```js
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```jsx
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```ts
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```tsx
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only literal conditions are checked; ESLint also folds some expressions such as `typeof x` and `!1`.

## `js/no-constant-math-min-max-clamp` — No clamp with its bounds swapped

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (swapping the bounds makes the clamp work, which changes the value it returns)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-constant-math-min-max-clamp.md

### What it checks

`Math.min(lo, Math.max(hi, x))` with `lo` below `hi` (or the mirror form) always returns a bound.

**Why:** The clamp is constant: its bounds are the wrong way round.

### How to fix

1. Swap the two bounds.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const v = Math.min(0, Math.max(100, x));
```

##### Do

```js
const v = Math.min(100, Math.max(0, x));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const v = Math.min(0, Math.max(100, x));
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const v = Math.min(0, Math.max(100, x));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const v = Math.min(100, Math.max(0, x));
```

## `js/no-constructor-return` — A constructor returns no value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

#### TSX

## `js/no-continue` — No continue

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (an unlabelled `continue` guarding the rest of a loop body is rewritten to a negated `if` around that rest; a body that declares a function, or any other `continue`, is not auto)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/taste` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-continue.md

### What it checks

Loops do not use `continue`.

**Why:** A `continue` jumps over the rest of the loop body; an `if` around it states the condition where it applies.

### How to fix

1. Invert the condition and wrap the rest of the body in an `if`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!x) continue;
  use(x);
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!(!x)) {
    use(x);
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (const x of xs) {
  if (x) use(x);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!x) continue;
  use(x);
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!(!x)) {
    use(x);
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (x) use(x);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!x) continue;
  use(x);
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!(!x)) {
    use(x);
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (const x of xs) {
  if (x) use(x);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!x) continue;
  use(x);
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (!(!x)) {
    use(x);
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (const x of xs) {
  if (x) use(x);
}
```

```js
  debugger;

```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {
  return fetchAll();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  debugger;
  return fetchAll();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
  return fetchAll();
```

## `js/no-default-export` — No default exports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (every importer of the default export must change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-default-export.md

### What it checks

Modules export by name; `export default` is not used.

**Why:** A named export has one name everywhere, so it can be found, renamed and auto-imported
reliably.

### How to fix

1. Give the exported value a name and export it with `export { name }`.
2. Change every `import x from` of this module to `import { name } from`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load() {}
export { load };
```

## `js/no-default-import` — Import by name, not the default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the module's named export for this value is not written in this file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-default-import.md

### What it checks

An `import` names the binding it takes (`import { parse } from ...`), not the module's default export. The import-side twin of `js/no-default-export`.

**Why:** A default import can be given any local name, so the same thing is called different names across the codebase, and renaming the export doesn't reach its importers.

### How to fix

1. Find the named export the module offers for this value (export it by name if it has none).
2. Import it by that name: `import { name } from "module"`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import parse from "./parse";
```

##### Do

```js
import { parse } from "./parse";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import parse from "./parse";
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { parse } from "./parse";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import parse from "./parse";
```

##### Do

```ts
import { parse } from "./parse";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import parse from "./parse";
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { parse } from "./parse";
```

## `js/no-default-utility-imports` — No default import of lodash or underscore

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the functions the file uses are listed by the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-default-utility-imports.md

### What it checks

`lodash`, `lodash-es` and `underscore` are imported by the functions used (`import { debounce } from "lodash-es"`), not as a default.

**Why:** The default import pulls in the whole library, which bundlers can't trim.

### How to fix

1. List the functions in braces and drop the `_.` prefix at each use.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import _ from "lodash";
const run = _.debounce(save, 300);
```

##### Do

```js
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
const run = debounce(save, 300);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import _ from "lodash";
const run = _.debounce(save, 300);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
const run = debounce(save, 300);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import _ from "lodash";
const run = _.debounce(save, 300);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
const run = debounce(save, 300);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import _ from "lodash";
const run = _.debounce(save, 300);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
const run = debounce(save, 300);
```

## `js/no-delete-var` — No delete on a variable

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`delete x` does nothing on a binding; resetting it to `undefined` is the closest live meaning, which the reviewer confirms (the author may have meant another value or to drop the line))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-delete-var.md

### What it checks

`delete` is applied to object properties, never to a variable.

**Why:** Deleting a variable does nothing in sloppy mode and is a syntax error in strict mode.

### How to fix

```js
let cache = {};
cache = undefined;
```

##### Do

```js
cache = {};
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
cache = undefined;
```

##### Do

```jsx

cache = {};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Fixed

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Fixed

```tsx
cache = undefined;
```

##### Do


## `js/no-document-cookie` — No document.cookie

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the replacement is async and its arguments come from parsing the string)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-document-cookie.md

### What it checks

`document.cookie` is not assigned to.

**Why:** Its string format is easy to get wrong (encoding, attributes), and each assignment silently sets one cookie.


#### JSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
await cookieStore.set("theme", "dark");
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
if (n >= limit) {

  stop();
```

```jsx
  stop();
```

##### Do

```ts
  stop();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  stop();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  stop();
```

## `js/no-dupe-args` — No two parameters share a name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which parameter was meant can't be known from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-args.md

### What it checks

A function's parameters, destructured ones included, all have different names.

**Why:** The later parameter silently hides the earlier one, so one argument can never be read.

### How to fix

1. Rename the duplicate parameter.
2. Update the body to read the parameter it meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function add(a, b, a) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function add(a, b, c) {
  return a + b + c;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function add(a, b, a) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function add(a, b, c) {
  return a + b + c;
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-class-members` — No two class members share a name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the later member is the one the class keeps, so the choices are deleting the earlier (the default, which keeps behaviour) or the later)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-class-members.md

### What it checks

A class declares each method and field name once, separately for static and instance members; a
getter and a setter may share a name.

**Why:** The later declaration replaces the earlier one, so one of them is dead code.

### How to fix

1. Decide which declaration is right.
2. Remove or rename the other.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  subtotal() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  subtotal() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-else-if` — No two conditions in an if/else-if chain are the same

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the second condition should have been is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-else-if.md

### What it checks

Each condition in an `if … else if …` chain is different from the ones before it.

**Why:** A repeated condition's branch can never run, because the earlier one already took it.

```js
  audit();

```

##### Do

```js
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-keys` — No two keys in an object literal are the same

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the later key is the one the object keeps, so the choices are deleting the earlier (the default, which keeps the value; its own evaluation goes with it) or the later)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-keys.md

### What it checks

An object literal names each key once; `a`, `'a'` and `["a"]` are the same key, as are `1` and
`0x1`.

**Why:** The later value silently replaces the earlier one.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Remove the other entry, or give it its own key.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  name: "Grace",
};
```

```js

  name: "Grace",
};
```

##### Do

```js
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  nickname: "Grace",
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  name: "Grace",
};
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const user = {
  name: "Grace",
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  nickname: "Grace",
};
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`

### What it checks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
  allow();
}
```

```js
  allow();
```

##### Do

```jsx
  allow();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  allow();
```

##### Do

## `js/no-duplicate-imports` — One import per module

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (two imports of `{ … }` names only are merged automatically, a name both hold kept once; an import with a default or namespace binding is merged by hand, since the two can't always share one statement)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-duplicate-imports.md

### What it checks

A module is imported by one `import` statement; type-only imports are counted apart.

**Why:** Two imports of the same module are noise and make it easy to import a name twice.

### How to fix

1. Move the second import's names into the first, and delete the second.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { a } from "./util";
import { b } from "./util";
```

##### Do

```js
import { a, b } from "./util";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { a } from "./util";
import { b } from "./util";
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { a, b } from "./util";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { a } from "./util";
import { b } from "./util";
```

##### Do

```ts
import { a, b } from "./util";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { a } from "./util";
import { b } from "./util";
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { a, b } from "./util";
```

## `js/no-duplicate-in-composite` — No type written twice in a union or intersection

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-duplicate-in-composite.md

### What it checks

A union or intersection does not name the same type twice side by side: `A | A` is `A`.

**Why:** The repeat adds nothing and usually hides the type that was meant.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
type Id = string | string;
```

##### Do

```ts
type Id = string;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
type Id = string | string;
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Id = string;
```

## `js/no-duplicate-logical-operands` — No a && a

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-duplicate-logical-operands.md

### What it checks

The two operands of `&&`, `||` or `??` are not the same expression. Operands that call a function are left alone, since a call can return something different each time.

**Why:** The repeat is redundant at best and usually a typo for a different operand.

##### Do

```js
if (ready) {
  go();
}
```

#### JSX

```jsx
if (ready && ready) {
  go();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (ready) {
  go();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (ready && ready) {
  go();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (ready) {
  go();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (ready && ready) {
  go();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (ready) {
  go();
}
```
