## `js/no-dynamic-namespace-import-access` — No computed access on a namespace import

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (naming the exports used means the author choosing them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dynamic-namespace-import-access.md

### What it checks

A namespace import (`import * as ns`) is not read with a computed key (`ns[key]`).

**Why:** A computed access makes the bundler keep every export of the module, defeating tree shaking.

### How to fix

1. Import the names you need and pick between them explicitly (a `switch` or an object of the imports).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import * as icons from './icons';
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

##### Do

```js
import { add, remove } from './icons';
const icons = { add, remove };
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import * as icons from './icons';
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { add, remove } from './icons';
const icons = { add, remove };
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import * as icons from './icons';
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

##### Do

```ts
import { add, remove } from './icons';
const icons = { add, remove };
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import * as icons from './icons';
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { add, remove } from './icons';
const icons = { add, remove };
export const icon = (name) => icons[name];
```

## `js/no-element-overwrite` — No element written twice in a row

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two values was meant is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-element-overwrite.md

### What it checks

An array element or a `Map` entry is not written and then, in the very next statement, written again at the same index or key: the first write is lost.

**Why:** Two writes in a row to one place mean one of them is a slip, usually a wrong index or key.

### How to fix

1. Fix the index or key of one of the two writes, or delete the one that is not wanted.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[0] = sum(b);
```

##### Do

```js
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[1] = sum(b);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[0] = sum(b);
```

##### Do

```jsx
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[1] = sum(b);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[0] = sum(b);
```

##### Do

```ts
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[1] = sum(b);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[0] = sum(b);
```

##### Do

```tsx
totals[0] = sum(a);
totals[1] = sum(b);
```

## `js/no-else-return` — No else after return

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a declaration in the `else` block moves into the enclosing scope, where it could clash with one of the same name)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-else-return.md

### What it checks

An `else` block does not follow an `if` block that ends in `return`.

**Why:** The `else` only adds nesting; the code after the `if` runs exactly when the condition is false.

### How to fix

1. Delete `else {` and its closing `}`, and move its statements up one level.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  } else {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  }
  return 1;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  } else {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  }
  return 1;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  } else {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  }
  return 1;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  } else {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  }
  return 1;
}
```

- **Fix:** `auto` (an empty block standing alone as a statement has no effect and is removed; an empty catch, if, loop or switch body carries no edit (it needs a reason or a body))

#### TSX

## `js/no-empty-character-class` — No empty character classes in regular expressions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which characters the class should hold needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-empty-character-class.md

### What it checks

A regular expression contains no empty character class `[]`; `[^]`, which matches any character, is
fine.

**Why:** `[]` matches no character at all, so the whole pattern can never match.

### How to fix

1. Put the characters the class should match inside it.
2. If `[]` was meant literally, escape it: `\[\]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```js
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```jsx
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```ts
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```tsx
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Fixed (default to an empty object)

```jsx

```

##### Fixed (bind the value by name)

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const { a: {} } = options;
```

##### Fixed (default to an empty object)

```ts
const { a = {} } = options;
```

##### Fixed (bind the value by name)

```ts
const { a } = options;
```

##### Do

```ts
const { a = {} } = options;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const { a: {} } = options;
```

##### Fixed (default to an empty object)

```tsx
const { a = {} } = options;
```

##### Fixed (bind the value by name)

##### Do

```tsx

  check();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
it("rejects an empty name", () => {
  check();
});
```

## `js/no-eq-null` — No == null

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a plain identifier compared with `null` through `==` or `!=`: the explicit two-way check is exact; other operands are reported as suggest)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-eq-null.md

### What it checks

Comparisons with `null` use `===` or `!==`.

**Why:** `== null` also matches `undefined`, which is either a hidden intention or a bug.

### How to fix

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
if (value == null) reset();
```

##### Fixed

```js
if ((value === null || value === undefined)) reset();
```

##### Do

```js
if (value === null) reset();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (value == null) reset();
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
if ((value === null || value === undefined)) reset();
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (value === null) reset();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (value == null) reset();
```

##### Fixed

```ts
if ((value === null || value === undefined)) reset();
```

##### Do

```ts
if (value === null) reset();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Fixed

```tsx
if ((value === null || value === undefined)) reset();
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-equals-in-for-termination` — No == or != as a for loop end test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which relational operator is right depends on the direction)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-equals-in-for-termination.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop that steps its counter by more than one does not end on `!=` or `==`. `i++` and `i--` are left alone.

**Why:** A step can jump over the exact value, so the loop never ends.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
for (let i = 0; i != 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i != 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (let i = 0; i != 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i != 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) {
  use(i);
}
```

## `js/no-ex-assign` — A caught error is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the original error should go is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-ex-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to the parameter of a `catch` clause.

**Why:** Reassigning the caught error discards it, so nothing can report or rethrow it.

##### Do

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx

  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  load();

  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

## `js/no-fallthrough` — A switch case does not fall through into the next by accident

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are `break;` ending the case, which stops the fall-through, or a `// falls through` comment saying it is meant, which keeps behaviour; only the author knows which)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-fallthrough.md

### What it checks

A `case` with statements ends in `break`, `return`, `throw` or `continue`, or says `// falls
through` before the next case.

**Why:** Falling through is easy to do by accident and hard to see in review.

### How to fix

1. If the case should stop, end it with `break` (or `return`).
2. If it should fall through, say so with a `// falls through` comment before the next case.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Fixed (break)

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Fixed (falls through)

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
```

##### Fixed (break)

```jsx
switch (kind) {
```

##### Fixed (falls through)


##### Do

```jsx

    break;

```

```jsx

  case "b":
    second();
    break;
```

## `js/no-fixed-wait-in-tests` — No fixed wait in a UI test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what to wait for is the author's to name)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-fixed-wait-in-tests.md

### What it checks

A Cypress or Playwright test does not wait a fixed time — `cy.wait(1000)`, `page.waitForTimeout(1000)` — but for the condition it needs.

**Why:** A fixed wait is too long on a fast machine and too short on a slow one, so the suite is slow and flaky at once.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
cy.wait(2000);
```

##### Do

```js
cy.wait("@loadUsers");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx
cy.wait("@loadUsers");
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
cy.wait("@loadUsers");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
cy.wait(2000);
```

##### Do

```tsx
cy.wait("@loadUsers");
```

```js
const all = groups.flat();
```

## `js/no-focused-tests` — No focused tests left in the suite

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (dropping the focus puts every other test in the file back in the run, and tests that were hidden behind it may fail; the author should see that)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/markers` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-focused-tests.md

### What it checks

A test file has no `.only` (`it.only`, `test.only`, `describe.only`, `test.describe.only`, `it.only.each(…)`) and no Jasmine `fit`, `fdescribe` or `ftest`. A call on something else that happens to have an `only` method is not a test and is not reported. The suggested fix drops the focus: `.only` is removed, `fit` becomes `it` and `fdescribe` becomes `describe`.

**Why:** A focused test makes the runner skip every other test in the run, and the run still passes. It is meant as a debugging aid for one minute on a laptop and it reaches the main branch as a suite that checks almost nothing.

### How to fix

1. Remove the focus: `it.only(…)` becomes `it(…)`, `fit` becomes `it`, `fdescribe` becomes `describe` (`codelaw fix --unsafe` does).
2. Run the whole suite once; tests that were hidden may now fail, and that is the point.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("cart", () => {
  it.only("totals the items", () => {
    expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("cart", () => {
  it("totals the items", () => {
    expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3);
  });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test.only("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
fdescribe("cart", () => {
  it("totals the items", () => expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3));
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("cart", () => {
  it("totals the items", () => expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3));
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
fit("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
it("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

## `js/no-for-each` — for…of rather than forEach

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`for … of` iterates what the value's iterator gives, where `forEach` visits an array's indices: a sparse array, or a `Map` (whose `forEach` passes the value and `for … of` the entry), changes; a callback with a `return`, an index parameter, `async`, or a block-less body is rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-for-each.md

### What it checks

A statement calling `.forEach` with an arrow function is written as a `for … of` loop.

**Why:** A loop can `break`, `continue`, `return` and `await`; a `forEach` callback can do none of them.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite as `for (const item of items) { … }`; turn `return` into `continue`; for an index parameter use `for (const [i, item] of items.entries())`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
items.forEach((item) => {
  send(item);
});
```

##### Do

```js
for (const item of items) {
```

## `js/no-forced-browser-interaction` — No forced click or type in a UI test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what makes the element actionable is the author's to find)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-forced-browser-interaction.md

### What it checks

A Cypress or Playwright interaction (`click`, `type`, `check`, `fill`, `hover`, …) is not passed `{ force: true }`.

**Why:** Forcing skips the checks that the element is visible and enabled, so the test passes where a user could not act.


#### JSX


##### Do



##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-func-assign` — A function declaration is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the assignment was for is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-func-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to the name a function declaration binds.

**Why:** Overwriting a declared function is almost always a mistake, and every later call means
something else.


##### Do

```js
function save() {}
const saveHandler = null;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function save() {}
save = null;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function save() {}
const saveHandler = null;
```

## `js/no-hook-setter-in-body` — No state setter called in a component's body

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the update belongs — an effect, a handler, the initial state — is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-hook-setter-in-body.md

### What it checks

A `useState` setter is not called as a statement of the component's own body: each render sets state, which renders again, without end.

**Why:** Setting state while rendering loops until React stops it with an error.

### How to fix

1. Set the value as the initial state, or move the call into an event handler or a `useEffect`.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(0);
  setNow(Date.now());
  return <time>{now}</time>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(() => Date.now());
  return <time>{now}</time>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(0);
  setNow(Date.now());
  return <time>{now}</time>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(() => Date.now());
  return <time>{now}</time>;
}
```

## `js/no-identical-conditions` — No repeated condition in an if chain

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which condition was meant is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-identical-conditions.md

### What it checks

An `if … else if` chain does not test the same condition twice (checked for the next two links).

**Why:** The second branch is dead code: the first one always takes its cases.

### How to fix

1. Correct the repeated condition, or remove the dead branch.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 1) {
  b();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 2) {
  b();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 1) {
  b();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 2) {
  b();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 1) {
  b();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 2) {
  b();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 1) {
  b();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (x === 1) {
  a();
} else if (x === 2) {
  b();
}
```

## `js/no-identical-expressions` — No identical operands

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which operand was meant is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-identical-expressions.md

### What it checks

The two operands of a comparison, logical, subtraction, division or xor operator are not the same expression. Operands containing a call are left alone, and `x !== x` is left to `js/use-isnan`'s NaN idiom only when the operand is a number literal.

**Why:** The result is constant (`a - a` is 0, `a === a` is true but for NaN), so one operand is almost certainly a typo.

### How to fix

1. Correct the operand that was meant to be different, or replace the expression with its constant result.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (a.x === a.x) {
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (a.x === b.x) {
  run();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (a.x === a.x) {
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (a.x === b.x) {
  run();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (a.x === a.x) {
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (a.x === b.x) {
  run();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (a.x === a.x) {
  run();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (a.x === b.x) {
  run();
}
```

## `js/no-implicit-coercion` — Explicit conversions, not !!x or +x

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Number(x)` and `+x` differ for a BigInt (`+1n` throws, `Number(1n)` is `1`), so the author confirms what the value holds)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-implicit-coercion.md

### What it checks

`!!x` is written `Boolean(x)` and `+x` is written `Number(x)` (the upstream defaults; `"" + x` is left alone).

**Why:** The explicit call says which conversion is meant; `+x` in particular is easy to misread.

```js
const has = !!items.length;
```

##### Do

```js
const has = Boolean(items.length);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-import-assign` — An imported binding is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new value needs a variable of its own)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-import-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to a name bound by `import`.

**Why:** Imported bindings are read-only: assigning to one throws a TypeError.

### How to fix

### Examples


##### Do

```js

```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

config = {};
```

##### Do


## `js/no-invalid-property-descriptor` — No property descriptor with both a value and an accessor

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the property holds a value or is computed is the author's to say)

### What it checks

A descriptor passed to `Object.defineProperty` or `Reflect.defineProperty` does not have both a data part (`value`, `writable`) and an accessor (`get`, `set`): defining it throws a `TypeError`.

##### Don't

```jsx
Object.defineProperty(config, "port", { value: 80, get() { return 80; } });
```

##### Do

```jsx
Object.defineProperty(config, "port", { get() { return 80; } });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
Object.defineProperty(config, "port", { value: 80, get() { return 80; } });
```

##### Do

```ts
Object.defineProperty(config, "port", { get() { return 80; } });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
Object.defineProperty(config, "port", { value: 80, get() { return 80; } });
```

##### Do

```tsx

```


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

### Differences from the source

Only structural problems are found: unbalanced brackets and groups, misplaced quantifiers, out-of-

## `js/no-irregular-whitespace` — No irregular whitespace in templates, regular expressions, JSX text or comments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the escape keeps a template's cooked value but changes the raw string a tagged template such as `String.raw` sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-irregular-whitespace.md

### What it checks

Templates, regular expressions and JSX text spell a no-break space, zero-width space or other
irregular whitespace as an escape (`\u00A0`, `&#x00A0;`), and comments use ordinary spaces.

**Why:** Irregular whitespace is invisible in most editors. In a template, regular expression or JSX
text it silently becomes part of the value, so the text looks right and compares wrong.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const label = `Total: 1`;
```

##### Do

```js
const label = `Total:\u00A01`;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const label = <p>Total: 1</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const label = <p>Total:&#x00A0;1</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const label = `Total: 1`;
```

##### Do

```ts
const label = `Total:\u00A01`;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const label = <p>Total: 1</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const label = <p>Total:&#x00A0;1</p>;
```

### Differences from the source

- **Between tokens the formatter owns it.** ESLint also reports irregular whitespace between tokens;
  here that is layout, and `codelaw format` replaces it with a space (SR-FORMATTER decision 3), so
  this rule does not report it.
- **Strings are skipped**, as ESLint's `skipStrings` default does.
- **The fix escapes, it doesn't delete:** `\uXXXX` in a template or regular expression, `&#xXXXX;`
  in JSX text, so the value is unchanged; a comment gets an ordinary space.

## `js/no-iterator` — No __iterator__

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the edit activates the standard iteration protocol in place of the dead SpiderMonkey one, which the reviewer confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-iterator.md

### What it checks


##### Fixed

```jsx
Foo.prototype[Symbol.iterator] = function () { return items(this); };
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
Foo.prototype.__iterator__ = function () { return items(this); };
```

##### Fixed

```ts
Foo.prototype[Symbol.iterator] = function () { return items(this); };
```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Fixed

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the replacement handler is code the author writes)


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do


## `js/no-labels` — No labels

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (replacing a labelled jump means restructuring the loops, often into a function with a `return`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-labels.md

### What it checks

Statements are not labelled, and `break`/`continue` take no label.

**Why:** Labels are rare enough that readers misread them, and they are mostly a `goto` in disguise.

### How to fix

1. Move the nested loops into a function and `return` from it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
outer: for (const a of as) {
  for (const b of bs) {
    if (a === b) break outer;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
function find() {
  for (const a of as) {
    for (const b of bs) {
      if (a === b) return;
    }
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
outer: for (const a of as) {
  for (const b of bs) {
    if (a === b) break outer;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function find() {

    for (const b of bs) {
      if (a === b) return;
    }
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  for (const b of bs) {
    if (a === b) break outer;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function find() {
  for (const a of as) {
    for (const b of bs) {
      if (a === b) return;
    }
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  for (const b of bs) {
    if (a === b) break outer;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  for (const a of as) {
    for (const b of bs) {
      if (a === b) return;
    }
  }
```
```tsx
}
```

## `js/no-loss-of-precision` — Number literals keep their value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are the literal the engine already stores (behaviour-preserving) or, for an integer, a BigInt, which keeps every digit but is another type)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-loss-of-precision.md

### What it checks

A number literal can be represented exactly as a JavaScript number.

**Why:** A literal with more precision than a double holds is silently rounded, so the code doesn't

### How to fix

##### Fixed (the value it holds)


```js
const id = 9007199254740993n;
```

##### Do


#### JSX

##### Don't


##### Fixed (the value it holds)

```jsx

```

##### Fixed (BigInt)

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Fixed (the value it holds)

```ts

```

##### Fixed (BigInt)

```ts

```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

## `js/no-magic-numbers` — No unnamed number in an expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the constant's name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-magic-numbers.md

### What it checks

A number literal is not used in an expression where its meaning is unnamed; it is given a name with a variable first. A number that initialises a variable, is an object property's value or a property assignment, is `parseInt`'s radix, or is a TypeScript literal type or enum value is left alone, as ESLint's defaults leave them.

**Why:** `timeout * 60000` makes the reader guess; `timeout * MS_PER_MINUTE` doesn't.

### How to fix

1. Declare a `const` with a name that says what the number means, and use the name here.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const ms = minutes * 60000;
```

##### Do

```js
const MS_PER_MINUTE = 60000;
const ms = minutes * MS_PER_MINUTE;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const ms = minutes * 60000;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const MS_PER_MINUTE = 60000;
const ms = minutes * MS_PER_MINUTE;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const ms = minutes * 60000;
```

##### Do

```ts
const MS_PER_MINUTE = 60000;
const ms = minutes * MS_PER_MINUTE;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const ms = minutes * 60000;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const MS_PER_MINUTE = 60000;
const ms = minutes * MS_PER_MINUTE;
```

## `js/no-map-spread` — No object spread of each item in map()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Object.assign` changes each item in place, so code still holding the original items sees the new properties)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-map-spread.md

### What it checks

A `map()` or `flatMap()` callback that adds properties to its item does so without copying the whole item with `{ ...item }`, when the original items are not used again. Only an arrow returning an object literal that starts with a spread of its parameter is reported.

**Why:** Spreading copies every property of every item, allocating a whole new object per element: on large arrays it is a measurable cost.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const rows = users.map((u) => ({ ...u, label: u.name }));
```

##### Do

```js
const rows = users.map((u) => Object.assign(u, { label: u.name }));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const rows = users.map((u) => ({ ...u, label: u.name }));
```

##### Do

```jsx
const rows = users.map((u) => Object.assign(u, { label: u.name }));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const rows = users.map((u) => ({ ...u, label: u.name }));
```

##### Do

```ts
const rows = users.map((u) => Object.assign(u, { label: u.name }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const rows = users.map((u) => ({ ...u, label: u.name }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const rows = users.map((u) => Object.assign(u, { label: u.name }));
```

## `js/no-misleading-character-class` — No character class holding a character made of several code points

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are writing each several-code-point character as an alternative beside the class (the default), or the `u` flag when the class holds astral characters; either changes what the pattern matches, to what it shows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-misleading-character-class.md

### What it checks

A character class contains no character built from several code points — an emoji with a skin-tone
modifier, a flag, a letter with a combining mark — and no astral character without the `u` flag.

**Why:** A class matches one code point at a time, so `[👍🏻]` matches the thumb or the tone, never
the pair.

### How to fix

1. Use an alternation such as `(?:👍🏻|👍)` for multi-code-point characters.
2. Add the `u` flag for astral characters.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

## `js/no-misrefactored-shorthand-assign` — No compound assignment that repeats its target

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the target is repeated on the right, so either the compound form or the long form was meant: both are offered and the reviewer picks)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-misrefactored-shorthand-assign.md

### What it checks

A compound assignment does not repeat its target on the right: `a += a + b` is `a += b` (or `a = a + b`).

**Why:** It adds the target twice — almost always a half-finished refactor from `a = a + b`.

### How to fix

1. Drop the repeated target (`a += b`), or write the plain assignment you meant (`a = a + b`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
total += total + step;
```

##### Fixed (compound assignment)

```js
total += step;
```

##### Fixed (long form)

```js
total = total + step;
```

##### Do

```js
total += step;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
total += total + step;
```

##### Fixed (compound assignment)

```jsx
total += step;
```

##### Fixed (long form)

```jsx
total = total + step;
```

##### Do

```jsx
total += step;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
total += total + step;
```

##### Fixed (compound assignment)

```ts
total += step;
```

##### Fixed (long form)

```ts
total = total + step;
```

##### Do

```ts
total += step;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
total += total + step;
```

##### Fixed (compound assignment)

```tsx
total += step;
```

##### Fixed (long form)

```tsx
total = total + step;
```

##### Do

```tsx
total += step;
```

## `js/no-multi-assign` — No chained assignment

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a chain of identifier targets written as a whole expression statement splits right to left with the same evaluation order; member targets, declarators and chains inside larger expressions carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-multi-assign.md

### What it checks

An assignment's value is not itself an assignment (`a = b = c`).

**Why:** Chained assignments read left to right but run right to left, and with `const a = b = 1` create an implicit global.

### How to fix

1. Write one assignment per statement.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
a = b = 0;
```

##### Fixed

```js
b = 0;
a = b;
```

##### Do

```js
a = 0;
b = 0;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
a = b = 0;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
b = 0;
a = b;
```

##### Do

```jsx
a = 0;
b = 0;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
a = b = 0;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
b = 0;
a = b;
```

##### Do

```ts
a = 0;
b = 0;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
a = b = 0;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
b = 0;
a = b;
```

##### Do

```tsx
a = 0;
b = 0;
```

## `js/no-negated-comparison` — No negated equality comparison

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-negated-comparison.md

### What it checks

An equality comparison is not negated as a whole: `!(a === b)` is `a !== b`, and `!(a !== b)` is `a === b`.

**Why:** The operator says it directly; the negation and its parentheses make the reader invert it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (!(status === "done")) retry();
```

##### Do

```js
if (status !== "done") retry();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (!(status === "done")) retry();
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (status !== "done") retry();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (!(status === "done")) retry();
```

##### Do

```ts
if (status !== "done") retry();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (!(status === "done")) retry();
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (status !== "done") retry();
```

## `js/no-negated-condition` — No negated condition with an else

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (`!a` and `a` are exact complements, so dropping the negation (or flipping `!==` and `!=`) and swapping the two branches keeps the behaviour)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-negated-condition.md

### What it checks

An `if` with an `else`, or a conditional expression, does not test a negated condition.

**Why:** `if (!a) x else y` reads as a double negative; `if (a) y else x` says the same directly.

### How to fix

1. Remove the negation and swap the two branches.

```js
if (!ok) {
  fail();
} else {
  pass();
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
if (ok) {
  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (ok) {
  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  fail();
} else {
  pass();
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
if (ok) {
  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (ok) {
  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (!ok) {
  fail();
} else {
  pass();
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
if (ok) {
  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  fail();
} else {
  pass();
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  pass();
} else {
  fail();
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

## `js/no-nested-assignment` — No assignment inside an expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

## `js/no-nested-functions` — No function nested more than four deep

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which function to pull out and what to name it is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-nested-functions.md

### What it checks

A function is not nested inside more than four others (SonarJS's default threshold).

**Why:** Each level adds a scope a reader has to hold in mind; past four, the code is hard to follow and to test.

### How to fix

1. Move the inner function out to the top level of the module (or a method), passing what it needs as arguments.

### Examples

```js
      return function d() {
        return function e() {};
      };
    };
  };
}
```

##### Do

```js
function e() {}
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return e;
      };
    };
  };
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return function e() {};
      };
    };
  };
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function e() {}
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return e;
      };
    };
  };
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return function e() {};
      };
    };
  };
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function e() {}
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return e;
      };
    };
  };
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return function e() {};
      };
    };
  };
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function e() {}
function a() {
  return function b() {
    return function c() {
      return function d() {
        return e;
      };
    };
  };
}
```

```js
    handleB(b);

    }
```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
    }
```

##### Do


## `js/no-nested-ternary` — No nested conditional expressions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a nested conditional that is the whole value of a `return` or an arrow's concise body becomes an exact if/return chain; nesting elsewhere (declarations, arguments, parentheses) carries no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`

```js
function size(n) {
  if (n > 100) return 'large';
  if (n > 10) return 'medium';
  return 'small';
```

#### JSX

##### Fixed


##### Do

```jsx

  return 'small';
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Fixed


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Don't

##### Do


## `js/no-new-array` — No new Array(n)

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a length and a single element give different arrays: both rewrites are offered and the reviewer picks the one that was meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-new-array.md

### What it checks

`new Array` is not called with one argument.

**Why:** `new Array(3)` makes three empty slots but `new Array("3")` an array holding "3": one call, two meanings.

### How to fix

1. For a length, write `Array.from({ length: n })`; for one element, `[x]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const slots = new Array(size);
```

##### Fixed (a length)

```js
const slots = Array.from({ length: size });
```

##### Fixed (one element)

```js
const slots = [size];
```

##### Do

```js
const slots = Array.from({ length: size });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const slots = new Array(size);
```

##### Fixed (a length)

```jsx
const slots = Array.from({ length: size });
```

##### Fixed (one element)

```jsx
const slots = [size];
```

##### Do

```jsx
const slots = Array.from({ length: size });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const slots = new Array(size);
```

##### Fixed (a length)

```ts
const slots = Array.from({ length: size });
```

##### Fixed (one element)

```ts
const slots = [size];
```

##### Do


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a function expression with the literal parameters and body is the closest equivalent; it closes over local scope instead of global scope, which the reviewer confirms (calls with computed or escaped strings carry no edit))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-new-func.md

### What it checks

##### Fixed


#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Fixed


##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

#### TSX


##### Do

```tsx

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (either the listener should not be passive or the call should go; making it not passive is offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

### What it checks

A listener added with `{ passive: true }` does not call `preventDefault()`: the browser ignores the call and warns.

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
el.addEventListener("touchmove", (e) => { e.preventDefault(); }, { passive: true });
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
el.addEventListener("touchmove", (e) => { e.preventDefault(); }, { passive: true });
```

##### Do

```tsx
el.addEventListener("touchmove", (e) => { e.preventDefault(); }, { passive: false });
```

## `js/no-promise-executor-return` — A promise executor returns nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (dropping an ignored return value is exact; a call to `resolve` or `reject`, or a call taking one of them, is auto, and any other returned value (it may have been meant for `resolve`) reports suggest)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-promise-executor-return.md

### What it checks

The function passed to `new Promise` does not return a value.

**Why:** The executor's return value is ignored; returning one usually means `resolve` was forgotten.

### How to fix


##### Do

```js
  setTimeout(resolve, 10);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

##### Fixed

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

  setTimeout(resolve, 10);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Fixed

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
new Promise((resolve) => {
  setTimeout(resolve, 10);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, 10); });
```

##### Do

```tsx

  setTimeout(resolve, 10);
```

## `js/no-proto` — No __proto__

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Object.getPrototypeOf` and `Object.setPrototypeOf` differ from `__proto__` for null-prototype objects and own `__proto__` properties, which the reviewer confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-proto.md

### What it checks

`__proto__` is not read or written.

**Why:** It is a legacy accessor; `Object.getPrototypeOf` and `Object.setPrototypeOf` are the standard.

### How to fix

1. Use `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` to read and `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto)` to write.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const p = obj.__proto__;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

##### Do

```js
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const p = obj.__proto__;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const p = obj.__proto__;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

##### Do

```ts
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const p = obj.__proto__;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj);
```

## `js/no-prototype-builtins` — No calling Object.prototype methods on the object itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an object whose own method is meant would change behaviour)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-prototype-builtins.md

### What it checks

`hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf` and `propertyIsEnumerable` are called through `Object.prototype`,
not on the object being tested.

**Why:** An object can shadow these methods, or have no prototype at all, and then the call breaks
or lies.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

## `js/no-redeclare` — No variable is declared twice

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a `var` redeclaration of a name already declared in the scope is just an assignment, so `var x = e;` becomes `x = e;` and a bare `var x;` is dropped; other redeclarations (let, function, destructured, multi-declarator) carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-redeclare.md

### What it checks

A name is declared once per scope: a second `var` or `function` with the same name is not allowed.

**Why:** Redeclaring silently merges two declarations, so one of them is usually a mistake.

### How to fix

1. If it's the same variable, drop the second `var` and assign.
2. If it's a different one, rename it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
var count = 1;
var count = 2;
```

##### Do

```js
var count = 1;
count = 2;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
var count = 1;
var count = 2;
```

##### Do

```jsx
var count = 1;
count = 2;
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (for a non-boolean operand the comparison and the bare value differ)

```js
  go();
```

```js
  go();
```

```jsx
  go();
```

## `js/no-redundant-use-strict` — No redundant "use strict"

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-redundant-use-strict.md

### What it checks

A `"use strict"` directive is not written where the code is already strict: in a module, in a class, or inside a function in a file that is strict already.

**Why:** Modules and classes are always strict; the directive there is noise that suggests the code around it is not.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
import { run } from './run';
'use strict';
run();
```

##### Do

```js
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

##### Fixed

```js
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { run } from './run';
'use strict';
run();
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { run } from './run';
'use strict';
run();
```

##### Do

```ts
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

##### Fixed

```ts
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { run } from './run';
'use strict';
run();
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { run } from './run';
run();
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

run();
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (analytics that read the referrer may change; the change closes access that something may rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-referrer-policy.md

### What it checks

helmet is not configured with `referrerPolicy: false` or a leaking policy (`unsafe-url`, `no-referrer-when-downgrade`).

**Why:** Full URLs, with tokens in their query strings, reach every linked site.

```js

```

##### Fixed

```js
app.use(helmet({  }));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(helmet({ referrerPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```jsx
app.use(helmet());
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
app.use(helmet({  }));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(helmet({ referrerPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```ts
app.use(helmet());
```

##### Fixed

```ts
app.use(helmet({  }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(helmet({ referrerPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.use(helmet());
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
app.use(helmet({  }));
```

## `js/no-regex-spaces` — No runs of spaces in a regular expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-regex-spaces.md

### What it checks

A regular expression writes several spaces as ` {n}`, not as a run of spaces.

**Why:** A run of spaces is impossible to count by eye.


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-restricted-exports` — No export named default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the statement is rewritten as `export default`; the reviewer confirms (a clause with several specifiers or a `from` source carries no edit))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-restricted-exports.md

### What it checks

A named export is not called `default` (`export { x as default }`). The upstream rule takes a list of restricted names; this port checks the one every project shares.

**Why:** `export { x as default }` is a default export written as a named one, which hides it from readers looking for `export default`.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the code as the message says.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export { main as default };
```

##### Do

```js
export default main;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export { main as default };
```

##### Do

```jsx
export default main;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export { main as default };
```

##### Do

```ts
export default main;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export { main as default };
```

##### Do

```tsx
export default main;
```

## `js/no-return-assign` — No assignment in a return

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (re-reading a plain identifier after assigning it gives the assigned value, so `return x = e` becomes `x = e; return x;` with the same behaviour; member targets (a getter may run) report suggest)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-return-assign.md

### What it checks

A `return` or an arrow's body is not an assignment, unless wrapped in parentheses.

**Why:** `return a = b` is usually a typo for `return a === b`.

### How to fix

1. Use `===` if a comparison was meant; otherwise assign on its own line and return the value.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
function set(v) {
  return value = v;
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
function set(v) {
  value = v; return value;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function set(v) {
  value = v;
  return value;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function set(v) {
  return value = v;
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
function set(v) {
  value = v; return value;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function set(v) {
  value = v;
  return value;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function set(v) {
  return value = v;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function set(v) {
  value = v; return value;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function set(v) {
  value = v;
  return value;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function set(v) {
  return value = v;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
function set(v) {
  value = v; return value;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  value = v;
  return value;
}
```

## `js/no-selector-as-dom-name` — No selector syntax where a DOM name is expected

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-selector-as-dom-name.md

### What it checks

An id or a class name is passed without its selector prefix: `getElementById("#app")` is `getElementById("app")`, and `classList.add(".open")` is `classList.add("open")`.

**Why:** These APIs take the name itself; with `#` or `.` they look for an id or class that has that character, and find nothing.

### Examples

##### Don't


##### Do

```js
const app = document.getElementById("app");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const app = document.getElementById("#app");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const app = document.getElementById("app");
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const app = document.getElementById("app");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const app = document.getElementById("app");
```

## `js/no-self-assign` — No assigning a variable to itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the statement is exact for a local identifier but hides what was meant to be assigned, which the reviewer confirms; a property or other target carries no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-self-assign.md

### What it checks

An assignment's left and right sides are not the same expression.

**Why:** `a = a` has no effect; it is usually a typo for another name.

### How to fix

##### Fixed

```js

```

##### Do

```js

x = y;
```

#### JSX

```jsx

x = x;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Fixed

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
let x = 1;
x = y;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

x = x;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

```

##### Do


## `js/no-self-compare` — No comparing a value with itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (an identifier compared with itself by equality is a NaN test, so `x !== x` becomes `Number.isNaN(x)` and `x === x` becomes `!Number.isNaN(x)` with the same result; member operands and relational forms carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-self-compare.md

### What it checks

An expression is not compared with itself.

**Why:** `x === x` is true except for `NaN` — use `Number.isNaN` for that — and is otherwise a typo.

### How to fix

1. Compare with the value meant, or use `Number.isNaN(x)` to test for `NaN`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (x !== x) skip();
```

##### Do

```js
if (Number.isNaN(x)) skip();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (x !== x) skip();
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Number.isNaN(x)) skip();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (x !== x) skip();
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Number.isNaN(x)) skip();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (x !== x) skip();
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (Number.isNaN(x)) skip();
```

## `js/no-sequences` — No comma operator

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a comma sequence that is a whole expression statement or a return value splits into statements with the same evaluation order (two expressions); longer sequences and sequences elsewhere carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-sequences.md

### What it checks

The comma operator is used only in a `for` loop's header or inside its own parentheses.

**Why:** `a, b` evaluates and discards `a`: easy to write by mistake and hard to spot.

### How to fix

1. Write each expression as its own statement.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
a = 1, b = 2;
```

##### Fixed

```js
a = 1; b = 2;
```

##### Do


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Fixed

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

b = 2;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
a = 1, b = 2;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
a = 1; b = 2;
```

##### Do

```tsx
a = 1;
b = 2;
```

## `js/no-setter-return` — A setter does not return a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a setter's return value is thrown away, so `return e;` becomes `e; return;`, a last `return` goes, and a value that can do nothing goes with it; behaviour is unchanged)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-setter-return.md

### What it checks

A setter body contains no `return <value>`; a bare `return;` to leave early is fine.

**Why:** The value a setter returns is discarded, so returning one hides a mistake.

### How to fix

1. Keep the expression's side effect as a statement.
2. Remove the value from the `return`, or the `return`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    return (this.n = n);
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    this.n = n;
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    return (this.n = n);
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    this.n = n;
  },
};
```

## `js/no-shadow` — No declaration that shadows an outer one

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-shadow.md

### What it checks

A name declared in an inner scope is not one already declared in a scope around it.

**Why:** Inside the inner scope the outer value can't be reached, and a reader may think it is being used.

### How to fix

1. Rename the inner declaration, or reuse the outer one if that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const user = guest();
  return user.name;
}
```

##### Do

```js
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const visitor = guest();
  return visitor.name;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const user = guest();
  return user.name;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const visitor = guest();
  return visitor.name;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const user = guest();
  return user.name;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const visitor = guest();
  return visitor.name;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const user = load();

  const user = guest();
  return user.name;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
const user = load();
function greet() {
  const visitor = guest();
  return visitor.name;
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Fixed (delete the extra comma)


##### Fixed (fill with undefined)

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

##### Fixed (delete the extra comma)


##### Fixed (fill with undefined)


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Fixed (delete the extra comma)

##### Fixed (fill with undefined)

## `js/no-static-only-class` — No class with only static members

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (callers of `MathUtil.double` become callers of `double`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-static-only-class.md

### What it checks

```js
  return x * 2;
}
```

```jsx
  static double(x) {
    return x * 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
export function double(x) {
  return x * 2;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  static double(x) {
    return x * 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  return x * 2;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  return x * 2;
}
```

## `js/no-string-case-mismatch` — No comparison that case conversion makes impossible

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

##### Do

```js
  swap();
}
```

#### TSX

```tsx
  swap();
```

##### Do

## `js/no-this-assignment` — No this alias

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the functions reading the alias become arrow functions)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-this-assignment.md

### What it checks

`this` is not assigned to a variable (`const self = this`).

**Why:** Arrow functions keep `this`, so an alias is a leftover that hides which object is meant.

```js
items.forEach((x) => {
  this.add(x);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const self = this;
items.forEach(function (x) {
  self.add(x);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
items.forEach((x) => {
  this.add(x);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const self = this;
items.forEach(function (x) {
  self.add(x);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
items.forEach((x) => {
  this.add(x);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const self = this;
items.forEach(function (x) {
  self.add(x);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
items.forEach((x) => {
  this.add(x);
});
```

## `js/no-this-before-super` — this is not used before super() in a derived constructor

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the `super(…)` call moves above the first statement using `this` when its arguments read neither `this` nor anything declared in between; the parent's constructor then runs earlier, which is the fix but is a change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-this-before-super.md

### What it checks

In the constructor of a class that extends another, `this` and `super.x` are used only after
`super()` has been called.

**Why:** Before `super()` runs, `this` is not initialised and touching it throws a ReferenceError.

### How to fix

1. Move the `super(...)` call above the first use of `this`.
2. If the base class needs a value computed from `this`, compute it into a local first.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
    super();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
    super();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-this-in-exported-function` — No this in an exported function

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (replacing `this` with a parameter changes the function's signature and every caller)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-this-in-exported-function.md

### What it checks

An exported function declaration does not use `this`. Arrow functions inside it are checked as part of it; a TypeScript function that declares a `this` parameter is left alone.

**Why:** An imported function is called as `f()`, not as a method, so `this` is `undefined` (or the global object) and the code fails at its first property read.

### How to fix

1. Add a parameter for the object the function reads, and pass it at each call site.
2. If the function is meant to be a method, move it into the class or object it belongs to.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export function fullName() {
  return this.first + " " + this.last;
}
```

##### Do

```js
export function fullName(person) {
  return person.first + " " + person.last;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export function fullName() {
  return this.first + " " + this.last;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
export function fullName(person) {
  return person.first + " " + person.last;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export function fullName() {
  return this.first + " " + this.last;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export function fullName(person) {
  return person.first + " " + person.last;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export function fullName() {
  return this.first + " " + this.last;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export function fullName(person) {
  return person.first + " " + person.last;
}
```

## `js/no-this-in-static` — The class name, not this, in a static method

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (naming the class is not the same as `this` when a subclass calls the method; review it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-this-in-static.md

### What it checks

A static method of a named class refers to the class by its name, not by `this`.

**Why:** `this` in a static method is the class only when called on it; called on a subclass or detached it is something else, which is rarely what the code means.

```js
    return Config.defaults;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Config {
  static load() {
    return this.defaults;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Config {
  static load() {
    return Config.defaults;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Config {
  static load() {
    return this.defaults;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Config {
  static load() {
    return Config.defaults;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do


## `js/no-typeof-undefined` — x === undefined rather than typeof x === "undefined"

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (for an undeclared global, `typeof` does not throw and the comparison does)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-typeof-undefined.md

### What it checks

```js
    reset();
  }

  }
```

##### Do

## `js/no-undef` — No references to undeclared names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right declaration — an import, a local, or an environment — is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-undef.md

### What it checks

Every name the code reads or writes is declared in the file, built into JavaScript, or a global of
an environment the rule's `env` option names. As in ESLint, a `/* global a, b:writable */` comment
declares names for that file (`name:off` declares nothing), and a `/* eslint-env node */` comment
adds environments.

**Why:** An undeclared name is usually a typo or a missing import, and throws a ReferenceError when
that line runs.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` | `string[]` | `["shared-node-browser"]` | environments whose globals are declared: browser, node, commonjs, worker, serviceworker, shared-node-browser, jest, mocha, vitest |
| `globals` | `string[]` | `[]` | more names to treat as declared |
| `typeof` | `boolean` | `false` | also report names used only as `typeof x` |

### How to fix

1. If it's a typo, correct the name.
2. If it comes from another module, import it.
3. If it's a global of the runtime (browser, Node), add that environment to the rule's `env` option.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
const prices = [1, 2];
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
const prices = [1, 2];
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

## `js/no-unexpected-multiline` — A line break doesn't silently join two lines into one expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are a `;` ending the first line, splitting the two, or joining them, keeping what JavaScript parses today; only the author knows which was meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unexpected-multiline.md

### What it checks

A line that starts with `(`, `[` or a template literal does not continue the expression on the line
before it without a semicolon.

**Why:** Without semicolons, JavaScript joins such lines: `a\n(b)` is the call `a(b)`, which is
rarely what was written.

### How to fix

1. If the lines are separate statements, end the first with a semicolon.
2. If they are one expression, move the `(` or `[` onto the first line.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (split)

```js
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (join)

```js
const total = sum(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```js
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (split)

```jsx
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (join)

```jsx
const total = sum(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (split)

```ts
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (join)

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (split)

```tsx

(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Fixed (join)

