
##### Do

```tsx

(items).forEach(log);
```

## `js/no-uninvoked-array-callback` — map() over new Array(n) never runs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the callback starts running, once per index, where today it never runs)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-uninvoked-array-callback.md

### What it checks

Code builds an array of `n` items with `Array.from({ length: n }, ...)`, not by calling `map`, `forEach` or another iterating method on `new Array(n)`.

**Why:** `new Array(n)` has `n` empty slots, not `n` undefined values, and the iterating methods skip empty slots: the callback is never called.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const ids = new Array(5).map((_, i) => i);
```

##### Do

```js
const ids = Array.from({ length: 5 }).map((_, i) => i);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const ids = new Array(5).map((_, i) => i);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const ids = Array.from({ length: 5 }).map((_, i) => i);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const ids = new Array(5).map((_, i) => i);
```

##### Do

```ts
const ids = Array.from({ length: 5 }).map((_, i) => i);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const ids = new Array(5).map((_, i) => i);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const ids = Array.from({ length: 5 }).map((_, i) => i);
```

## `js/no-uniq-key` — No React key made fresh on each render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a stable key comes from the data, which the author knows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-uniq-key.md

### What it checks

A JSX `key` is not computed by `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, `uuid…()`, `nanoid()` or `uniqueId()`: a new key each render makes React drop and rebuild the element.

**Why:** Keys tell React which element is which across renders; a key that changes every time destroys state and costs a rebuild.

### How to fix

1. Use an id the item already has (a database id, a slug), or one assigned once when the item is created.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const list = items.map((item) => <Row key={Math.random()} item={item} />);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const list = items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const list = items.map((item) => <Row key={Math.random()} item={item} />);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const list = items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />);
```

## `js/no-unnecessary-boolean-comparison` — No comparison of a boolean expression with true or false

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unnecessary-boolean-comparison.md

### What it checks

An expression that is already a boolean — a comparison, a negation, or a call such as `includes`, `some`, `every`, `has`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `Array.isArray` — is not compared with `true` or `false`: `x.includes(y) === true` is `x.includes(y)`, and `=== false` is its negation.

**Why:** The comparison repeats the value it compares.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (list.includes(item) === true) add(item);
if (Array.isArray(value) === false) wrap(value);
```

##### Do

```js
if (list.includes(item)) add(item);
if (!Array.isArray(value)) wrap(value);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (list.includes(item) === true) add(item);
if (Array.isArray(value) === false) wrap(value);
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (list.includes(item)) add(item);
if (!Array.isArray(value)) wrap(value);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (list.includes(item) === true) add(item);
if (Array.isArray(value) === false) wrap(value);
```

##### Do

```ts
if (list.includes(item)) add(item);
if (!Array.isArray(value)) wrap(value);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (list.includes(item) === true) add(item);
if (Array.isArray(value) === false) wrap(value);
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (list.includes(item)) add(item);
if (!Array.isArray(value)) wrap(value);
```

## `js/no-unnecessary-callback-wrapper` — Pass the function, not a wrapper

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (unwrapping `x => f(x)` to `f` passes every argument the caller supplies (`map` passes the index too) and loses the receiver of `obj.f`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unnecessary-callback-wrapper.md

### What it checks

An arrow function that only forwards its own parameters, in order, to another function is replaced by that function.

**Why:** The wrapper is a closure allocated on every evaluation and one more layer to read through for no behaviour.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

```js

```

##### Do

```js

```

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
items.forEach(render);
```

## `js/no-unnecessary-nested-ternary` — No nested ternary that repeats a branch

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unnecessary-nested-ternary.md

### What it checks

A ternary nested in another that shares one of its results is one ternary with a combined condition: `a ? (b ? x : y) : y` is `a && b ? x : y`, and `a ? x : (b ? x : y)` is `a || b ? x : y`.

**Why:** The repeated branch and the nesting hide a plain `&&` or `||`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const label = signedIn ? (isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest") : "guest";
```

##### Do

```js
const label = signedIn && isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const label = signedIn ? (isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest") : "guest";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const label = signedIn && isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const label = signedIn ? (isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest") : "guest";
```

##### Do

```ts
const label = signedIn && isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const label = signedIn ? (isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest") : "guest";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const label = signedIn && isAdmin ? "admin" : "guest";
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/no-unreachable` — No code after a return, throw, break or continue

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (deleting the code is right only when it was really dead, not misplaced)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unreachable.md

### What it checks

Statements after an unconditional `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue` in the same block are
removed or moved; hoisted function declarations and uninitialised `var`s are allowed.

**Why:** Unreachable code never runs, so it misleads every reader who assumes it does.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
  log(items);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
  log(items);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

## `js/no-unreachable-loop` — A loop that always exits on its first pass

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the rewrite (an `if`, or moving the exit into a condition) depends on intent)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

A loop body does not end, at its top level, with an unconditional `return`, `throw` or `break` and contain no `continue`.

##### Do

#### TSX

```tsx
  return user;
```

##### Do


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

## `js/no-unreadable-iife` — No arrow IIFE with a parenthesized body

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (naming the function or the value is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unreadable-iife.md

### What it checks

An arrow function that is called at once does not return a parenthesized expression: `(x => (x ? a : b))(value)` hides its argument behind two layers of parentheses.

```js
const user = getUser();
```

##### Do

```jsx

const name = user ? user.name : "guest";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

const name = user ? user.name : "guest";
```

## `js/no-unsafe-finally` — No return, throw, break or continue in finally

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the control statement lets the try or catch result through, and a value it carried is dropped; the reviewer confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-finally.md

### What it checks

A `finally` block doesn't end the function or loop with `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`.

**Why:** Control flow in `finally` silently replaces whatever the `try` or `catch` block returned or
threw.

### How to fix

1. Check the statement removed was not carrying a value the function needs; if it was, move it into the `try` or `catch` block.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

## `js/no-unsafe-negation` — No negating the left side of in or instanceof

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (code that really meant `(!a) in b` would change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-negation.md

### What it checks

`!` before `a in b` or `a instanceof B` wraps the whole test in parentheses.

**Why:** `!a in b` means `(!a) in b`, which tests whether `true` or `false` is a key — never what
was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (!key in cache) {
  load(key);
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (!(key in cache)) {
  load(key);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (!key in cache) {
  load(key);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (!(key in cache)) {
  load(key);
}
```

## `js/no-unsafe-optional-chaining` — No ?. chain used where undefined throws

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are a fallback (`?? {}` for destructuring, `?? []` for spreading, `?.` carried through a call or access), the default, or plain `.` when the value is always there)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-optional-chaining.md

### What it checks

A `?.` chain, which can evaluate to `undefined`, is not called through parentheses, constructed,
spread into an array or call, destructured, iterated with `for … of`, used on the right of `in` or
`instanceof`, or extended.

**Why:** In those places `undefined` throws a TypeError, which defeats the point of `?.`.

### How to fix

1. Give the chain a fallback with `??`.
2. Or move the `?.` so that it covers the operation that can fail.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```js
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```ts
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

## `js/no-unsafe-sqlite-interpolation` — No values interpolated into an SQL statement

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the parameters and their binding are the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-sqlite-interpolation.md

### What it checks

An SQL statement passed to `prepare()` or `exec()` (`node:sqlite`, better-sqlite3 and kin) is not a template literal with `${…}` in it; values are bound as parameters.

**Why:** An interpolated value becomes SQL, so a quote in it changes the statement: SQL injection.

### How to fix

1. Write `?` (or `:name`) where each value goes and pass the values to `run`, `get` or `all`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const row = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`).get();
```

##### Do

```js
const row = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?").get(id);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const row = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`).get();
```

##### Do

```jsx
const row = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?").get(id);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const row = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`).get();
```

##### Do

```ts
const row = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?").get(id);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const row = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`).get();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const row = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?").get(id);
```

## `js/no-unused-function-parameters` — No unused trailing parameter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (renaming the parameter to `_name` marks it unused; removing it instead may change the signature callers rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-function-parameters.md

### What it checks

A function's last parameter is used in its body, or named with a leading underscore.

**Why:** An unused parameter suggests a forgotten use, or a signature that promises more than it does.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function greet(name, punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function greet(name, _punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function greet(name, punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function greet(name, _punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function greet(name, punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function greet(name, _punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function greet(name, punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function greet(name, _punctuation) {
  return 'Hi ' + name;
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only the last parameter is checked — earlier unused ones are kept by the parameters after them; destructured parameters are not checked.

## `js/no-unused-imports` — No unused imports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing an import can drop a module's side effects only when the whole statement goes; review before accepting)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-imports.md

### What it checks

Every name an `import` brings in is used in the file.

**Why:** An unused import is dead code that still loads the module, and hides what the file really depends on.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs';
writeFile('a', 'b');
```

##### Do

##### Do

```ts
writeFile('a', 'b');
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs';
writeFile('a', 'b');
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs';
writeFile('a', 'b');
```

### Differences from the source

A default import or namespace import is reported on its name, and the fix removes only that name.

## `js/no-unused-private-class-members` — Every private class member is read

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing a member may also remove writes that matter, so it's a reader's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-private-class-members.md

### What it checks

A private field, method or accessor (`#name`) is read somewhere in its class; only being written
doesn't count.

**Why:** A private member nothing reads is dead code, since nothing outside the class can reach it.

### How to fix

1. Check that nothing needs the member's value.
2. Remove the member and the writes to it, or read it where it was meant to be used.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-unused-vars` — Every declared name is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing a declaration can drop the side effects of its initialiser)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-vars.md

### What it checks

Every variable, function, class, import, parameter and caught error is read somewhere. Parameters
before the last used one are allowed (`args: after-used`).

**Why:** An unused declaration is either dead code or a sign the code doesn't do what it was meant
to.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vars` | `string` | `"all"` | all, or local to skip module-level names |
| `args` | `string` | `"after-used"` | after-used, all or none |
| `caughtErrors` | `string` | `"all"` | all or none |
| `ignoreRestSiblings` | `boolean` | `false` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `varsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression of names to skip |
| `argsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrorsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `destructuredArrayIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Check the initialiser has no side effect that matters.
2. Remove the declaration, or use it where it was meant to be used.
3. For a parameter that must stay for its position, prefix it with `_` and set `argsIgnorePattern: "^_"`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```js
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

## `js/no-useless-assignment` — No value is stored that nothing reads

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto for a literal initialiser overwritten before anything reads it: `let sum = 0;` becomes `let sum;`, and the overwrite still sets it; any other dead store is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-assignment.md

### What it checks

A variable is not assigned a value that is overwritten before anything reads it, or that nothing
reads after the assignment.

**Why:** A dead store is wasted work and usually means the code reads the wrong variable.

### How to fix

1. If the value is not needed, remove the assignment.
2. If it should be read, read it where it was meant to be used.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
function total(items) {
  let sum;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
function total(items) {
  let sum;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function total(items) {
  let sum;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
function total(items) {
  let sum;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only stores a straight-line reading proves dead are reported: an overwrite in the same block, or a
last assignment outside any loop. A variable a nested function touches is skipped.

## `js/no-useless-backreference` — No backreference that can only match the empty string

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the backreference, with its quantifier, always matches the empty string, so it goes; the reviewer confirms the pattern was not meant to match more)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-backreference.md

### What it checks

A backreference such as `\1` or `\k<name>` appears after its group closes, in the same alternative,
and not into a negative lookaround.

**Why:** A backreference that comes first, sits inside its own group or in another alternative
always matches the empty string.

### How to fix

1. Move the backreference after the group it refers to.
2. Or remove it if it was meant to be literal text.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const re = /(a)/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const re = /(a)/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const re = /(a)/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const re = /(a)/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

## `js/no-useless-call` — No needless call or apply

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a call on a plain identifier with `undefined`, or on `o.m` with `o` as the receiver, is the plain call exactly; a `null` this or a complex callee stays a suggestion)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-call.md

### What it checks

`.call()` and `.apply()` are not used where a plain call does the same.

**Why:** `f.call(undefined, a)` is `f(a)` and `obj.m.call(obj, a)` is `obj.m(a)`; the long form hides that.

### How to fix

1. Call the function directly. The fix does it for a plain identifier called with `undefined`, and for `o.m.call(o, ...)`; any other callee is offered for a reviewer to confirm.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
greet.call(undefined, 'Ada');
```

##### Fixed

```js
greet('Ada');
```

##### Do

```js
greet('Ada');
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
greet.call(undefined, 'Ada');
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
greet('Ada');
```

##### Do

```jsx
greet('Ada');
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
greet.call(undefined, 'Ada');
```

##### Fixed

```ts
greet('Ada');
```

##### Do

```ts
greet('Ada');
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
greet.call(undefined, 'Ada');
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
greet('Ada');
```

##### Do

```tsx
greet('Ada');
```

## `js/no-useless-catch` — No catch that only rethrows

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (the try block stays as a block, keeping its declarations scoped, and the same error rethrows; with a `finally` only the catch clause goes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-catch.md

### What it checks

A `catch` clause does more than rethrow the error it caught.

**Why:** `catch (e) { throw e; }` does nothing but add noise and a level of nesting.

### How to fix

1. If there is no `finally`, replace the `try` statement with the statements of its block (the fix keeps them in a block).
2. If there is a `finally`, remove only the `catch` clause.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
{
  load();
}
```

##### Do

```js
load();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
{
  load();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
load();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
{
  load();
}
```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

  load();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/no-useless-constructor` — No constructor that only calls super

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an empty constructor in a derived class is not equivalent: removing it starts calling the parent constructor)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-constructor.md

### What it checks

A constructor does not only pass its parameters on to `super`; the TypeScript forms (parameter properties, overloads) are left to a TypeScript rule.

**Why:** The language supplies exactly that constructor, so writing it out adds lines and nothing else.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name);
  }
  ban() {}
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Admin extends User {
  ban() {}
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name);
  }
  ban() {}
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Admin extends User {
  ban() {}
}
```

## `js/no-useless-continue` — No continue at the end of a loop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-continue.md

### What it checks

A `continue` is not the last statement of a loop body.

**Why:** The loop continues there anyway.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (const x of xs) {
  use(x);
  continue;
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (const x of xs) {
  use(x);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  use(x);
  continue;
```
```tsx
}
```

## `js/no-useless-delete-check` — No existence check before a delete

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-delete-check.md

### What it checks

A key is deleted without first checking it is there: `if (map.has(k)) map.delete(k)` is `map.delete(k)`, and `if (k in obj) delete obj[k]` is `delete obj[k]`.

**Why:** Deleting a missing key already does nothing; the check only repeats the lookup.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (cache.has(key)) cache.delete(key);
```

##### Do

```js
cache.delete(key);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (cache.has(key)) cache.delete(key);
```

##### Do

```jsx
cache.delete(key);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (cache.has(key)) cache.delete(key);
```

##### Do

```ts
cache.delete(key);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (cache.has(key)) cache.delete(key);
```

##### Do

```tsx
cache.delete(key);
```

## `js/no-useless-escape` — No backslash that changes nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-escape.md

### What it checks

A string or template literal escapes only characters that need it: quotes that match the delimiter,
`\\`, line breaks and the escape letters.

**Why:** A useless escape suggests the author meant something else, and makes the string harder to
read.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```js
const path = "a.b";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const path = "a.b";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```ts
const path = "a.b";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const path = "a.b";
```

### Differences from the source

Escapes inside regular expressions are not checked yet. A tagged template (`String.raw`, `html`) is not checked: its tag sees the raw text, backslashes included, as in ESLint.

## `js/no-useless-length-check` — No length check before every() or some()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-length-check.md

### What it checks

An array's length is not checked before `every()` or `some()` when the check changes nothing: `arr.length === 0 || arr.every(f)` is `arr.every(f)` (true for an empty array), and `arr.length > 0 && arr.some(f)` is `arr.some(f)` (false for one).

**Why:** The check repeats what the method already returns for an empty array.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const ok = items.length === 0 || items.every(isValid);
const any = items.length > 0 && items.some(isValid);
```

##### Do

```js
const ok = items.every(isValid);
const any = items.some(isValid);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const ok = items.length === 0 || items.every(isValid);
const any = items.length > 0 && items.some(isValid);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const ok = items.every(isValid);
const any = items.some(isValid);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const ok = items.length === 0 || items.every(isValid);
const any = items.length > 0 && items.some(isValid);
```

##### Do

```ts
const ok = items.every(isValid);
const any = items.some(isValid);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const ok = items.length === 0 || items.every(isValid);
const any = items.length > 0 && items.some(isValid);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const ok = items.every(isValid);
const any = items.some(isValid);
```

## `js/no-useless-react-setstate` — No state setter called with its own state

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the value the setter was meant to get is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-react-setstate.md

### What it checks

A `useState` setter is not called with the state variable it sets: `setCount(count)` changes nothing.

**Why:** React bails out when the value is the same, so the call is a slip for another value.

### How to fix

1. Pass the value the state should become, often computed from the current one: `$SET(c => c + 1)`.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

## `js/no-useless-template-literals` — No template literal without substitutions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (changing the quotes may need re-escaping the text)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-template-literals.md

### What it checks

A one-line template literal without substitutions, not used as a tag's argument, is a plain string.

**Why:** Backticks signal interpolation that is not there.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the code as the message says.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const title = `Settings`;
```

##### Do

```js
const title = "Settings";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const title = `Settings`;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const title = "Settings";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const title = `Settings`;
```

##### Do

```ts
const title = "Settings";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const title = `Settings`;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const title = "Settings";
```

## `js/no-useless-undefined` — No return undefined

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-undefined.md

### What it checks

`return undefined;` is written `return;`. Upstream also covers `let x = undefined` and `undefined` arguments; this port covers the return.

**Why:** A bare `return` already returns `undefined`.

### Examples

```js
function find() {
  return undefined;

```

##### Do

```js
function find() {
  return;
}
```

```jsx
  return undefined;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function find() {
  return;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
  return undefined;
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  return;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function find() {
  return undefined;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function find() {
  return;
}
```

## `js/no-var` — let or const instead of var

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`let` is block-scoped, so a `var` used outside its block or before its declaration changes meaning)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-var.md

### What it checks

Variables are declared with `let` or `const`, never `var`.

**Why:** `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, which causes bugs `let` and `const` rule out.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```js
let total = 0;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let total = 0;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```ts
let total = 0;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let total = 0;
```

## `js/no-void` — No void operator

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (`void <literal>` is `undefined` exactly; `void e;` as a statement stays a suggestion, as the `void` may mark a promise left unhandled on purpose)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-void.md

### What it checks

The `void` operator is not used.

**Why:** `void 0` is `undefined` written obscurely; `void promise` hides an unhandled promise.

### How to fix

1. Write `undefined`, or handle the promise with `await` or `.catch()`; the fix writes `undefined` for `void` of a literal and offers the bare expression for a `void e;` statement.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const nothing = void 0;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const nothing = undefined;
```

##### Do

```js
const nothing = undefined;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const nothing = void 0;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const nothing = undefined;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const nothing = undefined;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const nothing = void 0;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const nothing = undefined;
```

##### Do

```ts
const nothing = undefined;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const nothing = void 0;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const nothing = undefined;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const nothing = undefined;
```

## `js/no-void-type-return` — A void function returns no value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (either the return type or the returned value is wrong; the author decides which)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-void-type-return.md

### What it checks

A function whose return type is `void` does not `return` a value.

**Why:** The caller has been told nothing comes back, so the value is silently thrown away.

### How to fix

1. Remove the value from the `return`, or change the return type.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function log(msg: string): void {
  return console.log(msg);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function log(msg: string): void {
  console.log(msg);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function log(msg: string): void {
  return console.log(msg);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function log(msg: string): void {
  console.log(msg);
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (changing the cipher changes the key size and the data format)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`

### What it checks

A cipher is not created with DES, 3DES, RC2, RC4 or Blowfish.

**Why:** These ciphers have short keys or known attacks.

### How to fix

```js
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("des-cbc", key, iv);
```

```js
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
```

```jsx
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("des-cbc", key, iv);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
```

##### Don't

```ts
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("des-cbc", key, iv);
```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("des-cbc", key, iv);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const c = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
```

## `js/no-weak-keys` — No RSA or DSA key shorter than 2048 bits

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a longer key changes what the other side must accept; the owner decides)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-weak-keys.md

### What it checks

A key pair made with Node's `crypto.generateKeyPair` or `generateKeyPairSync` has a `modulusLength` of at least 2048 bits.

**Why:** Keys shorter than 2048 bits can be factored with resources that are within reach today.

### How to fix

1. Set `modulusLength` to 2048 or more (3072 for keys meant to last), and rotate keys already issued.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 1024 });
```

##### Do

```js
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 3072 });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 1024 });
```

##### Do

```jsx
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 3072 });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 1024 });
```

##### Do

```ts
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 3072 });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 1024 });
```

##### Do

```tsx
crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 3072 });
```

## `js/no-with` — No with statements

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each name inside needs to be qualified by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-with.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't use `with`.

**Why:** `with` makes it impossible to tell which names are properties and which are variables, and
is an error in strict code.

### How to fix

1. Replace each property used inside `with` by `object.property`.
2. Remove the `with`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
with (Math) {
  area = PI * r * r;
}
```

##### Do

```js
area = Math.PI * r * r;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
with (Math) {
  area = PI * r * r;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
area = Math.PI * r * r;
```

## `js/no-xor-as-exponentiation` — No ^ where a power was meant

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`^` is bitwise XOR; whether a power was meant is the author's to confirm)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-xor-as-exponentiation.md

### What it checks

`2 ^ 8` and `10 ^ 3` are not written to mean a power: `^` is bitwise XOR in JavaScript (`2 ^ 8` is 10), and a power is `2 ** 8`.

**Why:** The XOR of two small constants is almost never wanted; the power almost always is.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const max = 2 ^ 16;
```

##### Do

```js
const max = 2 ** 16;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const max = 2 ^ 16;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const max = 2 ** 16;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const max = 2 ^ 16;
```

##### Do

```ts
const max = 2 ** 16;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const max = 2 ^ 16;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const max = 2 ** 16;
```

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/non-existent-operator` — No =+, =- or =!

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which operator was meant is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/non-existent-operator.md

### What it checks

An assignment is not written `x =+ y`, `x =- y` or `x =! y` with no space after `=`.

**Why:** These are a typo for a compound operator or a comparison, and assign the wrong value without an error.

### How to fix

1. Write `+=`, `-=` or `!==`, or put a space after `=` if the unary operator is meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
total =+ price;
```

##### Do

```js
total += price;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
total =+ price;
```

##### Do

```jsx
total += price;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
total =+ price;
```

##### Do

```ts
total += price;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
total =+ price;
```

##### Do

```tsx
total += price;
```

## `js/number-arg-out-of-range` — Number method argument out of range

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the radix or digit count that was meant is not in the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/number-arg-out-of-range.md

### What it checks

A literal passed to `toString()` is a radix from 2 to 36; to `toFixed()` and `toExponential()`, 0 to 100 digits; to `toPrecision()`, 1 to 100.

**Why:** An argument outside the range throws a RangeError when the line runs.

### How to fix

1. Pass the radix (2–36) or number of digits (0–100; 1–100 for `toPrecision`) you meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const hex = n.toString(160);
```

##### Do

```js
const hex = n.toString(16);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const hex = n.toString(160);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const hex = n.toString(16);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const hex = n.toString(160);
```

##### Do

```ts
const hex = n.toString(16);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const hex = n.toString(160);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const hex = n.toString(16);
```

## `js/object-alt-content` — object elements have fallback content

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the text is human-written)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/object-alt-content.md

### What it checks

A JSX `<object>` element has content (fallback text).

**Why:** Screen readers announce the fallback content; an empty object is skipped or announced as unlabelled.

### How to fix

1. Write a short description of the embedded content between the tags.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx
const v = <object data="chart.svg">Sales by month</object>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const v = <object data="chart.svg" />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const v = <object data="chart.svg">Sales by month</object>;
```

## `js/operator-assignment` — x += 1 rather than x = x + 1

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/operator-assignment.md

### What it checks

An assignment of the form `x = x op y` uses `x op= y`.

**Why:** The shorter form names `x` once, so the two names cannot drift apart.

1. Rewrite `x = x + y` as `x += y` (and likewise for the other operators).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js

```

##### Do

```js
total += price;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
total = total + price;
```

##### Do

```jsx
total += price;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
total += price;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
total += price;
```

## `js/prefer-add-event-listener` — addEventListener rather than an on-property

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the listener can no longer be replaced by a later assignment, which other code may rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-add-event-listener.md

### What it checks

Event handlers are added with `addEventListener`, not by assigning an `on…` property.

**Why:** An assignment replaces whatever handler was there before; listeners stack.

### How to fix

1. Write `el.addEventListener("click", handler)`; to remove it later keep the handler and call `removeEventListener`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
button.onclick = save;
```

##### Do

```js
button.addEventListener("click", save);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
button.onclick = save;
```

##### Do

```jsx
button.addEventListener("click", save);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
button.onclick = save;
```

##### Do

```ts
button.addEventListener("click", save);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
button.onclick = save;
```

##### Do

```tsx
button.addEventListener("click", save);
```

## `js/prefer-add-event-listener-options` — An options object rather than a capture boolean

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-add-event-listener-options.md

### What it checks

`addEventListener` and `removeEventListener` take `{ capture: true }`, not a bare `true`, as their third argument; a bare `false` is the default and is dropped.

**Why:** A bare boolean doesn't say what it switches on.

### Examples


##### Do

```js
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, { capture: true });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, true);
```

##### Do

```jsx
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, { capture: true });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, true);
```

##### Do

```ts
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, { capture: true });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, true);
```

##### Do

```tsx
document.addEventListener("click", onClick, { capture: true });
```

## `js/prefer-array-find` — find() rather than filter()[0]

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-find.md

### What it checks

`.filter(f)[0]` is written `.find(f)`.

**Why:** `find` stops at the first match.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js

```

##### Do

```js
const admin = users.find((u) => u.admin);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const admin = users.filter((u) => u.admin)[0];
```

##### Do

```jsx
const admin = users.find((u) => u.admin);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const admin = users.filter((u) => u.admin)[0];
```

##### Do

```ts
const admin = users.find((u) => u.admin);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const admin = users.filter((u) => u.admin)[0];
```

##### Do

```tsx
const admin = users.find((u) => u.admin);
```

## `js/prefer-array-flat` — flat() rather than concat spreading

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-flat.md

### What it checks

`[].concat(...a)` is written `a.flat()`. Upstream also covers `reduce` and `_.flatten`; this port covers the concat form.

**Why:** `flat()` names the operation.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const flat = [].concat(...rows);
```

##### Do

```js
const flat = rows.flat();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const flat = [].concat(...rows);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const flat = rows.flat();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const flat = [].concat(...rows);
```

##### Do

```ts
const flat = rows.flat();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const flat = [].concat(...rows);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const flat = rows.flat();
```

## `js/prefer-array-flat-map` — flatMap() rather than map().flat()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-flat-map.md

### What it checks

`.map(f).flat()` is written `.flatMap(f)`.

**Why:** One pass instead of two, and no intermediate array.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const tags = posts.map((p) => p.tags).flat();
```

##### Do

```js
const tags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const tags = posts.map((p) => p.tags).flat();
```

##### Do

```jsx
const tags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const tags = posts.map((p) => p.tags).flat();
```

##### Do

```ts
const tags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const tags = posts.map((p) => p.tags).flat();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const tags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags);
```

## `js/prefer-array-from-map` — Array.from(x, f) rather than Array.from(x).map(f)

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the mapper receives `(value, index)` but not the array as its third argument)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-from-map.md

### What it checks

`Array.from(x).map(f)` is written `Array.from(x, f)`.

**Why:** One array instead of two.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const ids = Array.from(nodes).map((n) => n.id);
```

##### Do

```js
const ids = Array.from(nodes, (n) => n.id);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const ids = Array.from(nodes).map((n) => n.id);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const ids = Array.from(nodes, (n) => n.id);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const ids = Array.from(nodes).map((n) => n.id);
```

##### Do

```ts
const ids = Array.from(nodes, (n) => n.id);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const ids = Array.from(nodes).map((n) => n.id);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const ids = Array.from(nodes, (n) => n.id);
```

## `js/prefer-array-index-of` — indexOf() rather than findIndex(x => x === v)

## `js/prefer-array-last-methods` — findLast() rather than reversing a copy to find

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the callback's index argument counts from the other end after the rewrite; offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-last-methods.md

### What it checks

The last element that matches is found with `arr.findLast(fn)`, not by reversing a copy and calling `find`.

**Why:** `findLast` walks from the end without copying the array.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const last = [...events].reverse().find((e) => e.ok);
```

##### Do

```js
const last = events.findLast((e) => e.ok);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const last = [...events].reverse().find((e) => e.ok);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const last = events.findLast((e) => e.ok);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const last = [...events].reverse().find((e) => e.ok);
```

##### Do

```ts
const last = events.findLast((e) => e.ok);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const last = [...events].reverse().find((e) => e.ok);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const last = events.findLast((e) => e.ok);
```

## `js/prefer-array-some` — some() rather than find() in a boolean test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-array-some.md

### What it checks

`.filter(f).length > 0` is written `.some(f)`. Upstream also covers `find` in boolean positions; this port covers the filter-length form.

**Why:** `.some()` stops at the first match and returns a boolean.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (users.filter((u) => u.admin).length > 0) {
  warn();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (users.some((u) => u.admin)) {
  warn();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (users.filter((u) => u.admin).length > 0) {
  warn();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (users.some((u) => u.admin)) {
  warn();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (users.filter((u) => u.admin).length > 0) {
  warn();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (users.some((u) => u.admin)) {
  warn();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (users.filter((u) => u.admin).length > 0) {
  warn();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (users.some((u) => u.admin)) {
  warn();
}
```

## `js/prefer-arrow-callback` — Arrow functions for callbacks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an arrow function cannot be called with `new` and has no `prototype`, which a callee could rely on; a function with type parameters is rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-arrow-callback.md

### What it checks

An anonymous function expression passed as an argument, that does not use `this`, `arguments`, `super` or `new.target`, is an arrow function.

**Why:** An arrow function is shorter and cannot be called with a surprising `this`.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite `function (a, b) { … }` as `(a, b) => { … }`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
items.map(function (x) {
  return x * 2;
});
```

##### Do

```js
items.map((x) => {
  return x * 2;
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
items.map(function (x) {
  return x * 2;
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
items.map((x) => {
  return x * 2;
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
items.map(function (x) {
  return x * 2;
});
```

##### Do

```ts
items.map((x) => {
  return x * 2;
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
items.map(function (x) {
  return x * 2;
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
items.map((x) => {
  return x * 2;
});
```

## `js/prefer-at` — at(-1) rather than [a.length - 1]

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/prefer-bigint-literals` — BigInt literal rather than BigInt() of a constant

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-bigint-literals.md

### What it checks

A `BigInt` of an integer literal, or of a string of decimal digits, is written as a BigInt literal: `10n`, not `BigInt(10)` or `BigInt("10")`.

**Why:** The literal is shorter and is a constant the reader sees at once; the call does the same work at run time.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const big = BigInt(9007199254740993);
const id = BigInt("42");
```

##### Do

```js
const big = 9007199254740993n;
const id = 42n;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const big = BigInt(9007199254740993);
const id = BigInt("42");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const big = 9007199254740993n;
const id = 42n;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const big = BigInt(9007199254740993);
const id = BigInt("42");
```

##### Do

```ts
const big = 9007199254740993n;
const id = 42n;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const big = BigInt(9007199254740993);
const id = BigInt("42");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const big = 9007199254740993n;
const id = 42n;
```

## `js/prefer-blob-reading-methods` — blob.text() rather than FileReader

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the event handlers become an `await`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

### What it checks

`FileReader#readAsText` and `#readAsArrayBuffer` are not used.

**Why:** The `Blob` methods return a promise directly, without the event dance.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the code as the message says.

### Examples

```js
reader.readAsText(file);
```

##### Do

```js
const text = await file.text();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
reader.readAsText(file);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const text = await file.text();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const text = await file.text();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const text = await file.text();
```

## `js/prefer-block-statement-over-iife` — A block rather than an arrow IIFE used only for scope

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-block-statement-over-iife.md

### What it checks

An arrow function written and called at once as a statement, only to scope its `let` and `const`, is a plain block: `{ … }` scopes them the same.

**Why:** The block says the same thing without a function and a call.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
(() => {
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
})();
```

##### Do

```js
{
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
}
```

##### Don't

```jsx
(() => {
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
})();
```

##### Do

```jsx
{
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
(() => {
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
})();
```

##### Do

```ts
{
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
(() => {
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
})();
```

##### Do

```tsx
{
  const tmp = load();
  use(tmp);
}
```

## `js/prefer-classlist-toggle` — classList.toggle() rather than add or remove by a condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-classlist-toggle.md

### What it checks

A class added when a condition holds and removed otherwise is set with `el.classList.toggle(name, condition)`, not an `if`-`else` of `add` and `remove` or a computed `classList[c ? "add" : "remove"]`.

**Why:** `toggle`'s second argument does exactly this in one call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (open) {
  menu.classList.add("is-open");
} else {
  menu.classList.remove("is-open");
}
```

##### Do

```js
menu.classList.toggle("is-open", open);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (open) {
  menu.classList.add("is-open");
} else {
  menu.classList.remove("is-open");
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
menu.classList.toggle("is-open", open);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (open) {
  menu.classList.add("is-open");
} else {
  menu.classList.remove("is-open");
}
```

##### Do

```ts
menu.classList.toggle("is-open", open);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (open) {
  menu.classList.add("is-open");
} else {
  menu.classList.remove("is-open");
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
menu.classList.toggle("is-open", open);
```

## `js/prefer-code-point` — codePointAt rather than charCodeAt

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (for an astral character the result differs)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

`charCodeAt` and `String.fromCharCode` are written `codePointAt` and `String.fromCodePoint`.

##### Do

```jsx

```


##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/prefer-combined-guards` — One guard for two that exit the same way

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-combined-guards.md

### What it checks

Two `if` statements in a row that each only `return;` (or only `continue;`) are one `if` with their conditions joined by `||`.

**Why:** The two guards do the same thing; one says so in a line.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function save(user) {
  if (!user) return;
  if (user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function save(user) {
  if (!user || user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function save(user) {
  if (!user) return;
  if (user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function save(user) {
  if (!user || user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function save(user) {
  if (!user) return;
  if (user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function save(user) {
  if (!user || user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function save(user) {
  if (!user) return;
  if (user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function save(user) {
  if (!user || user.locked) return;
  store(user);
}
```

## `js/prefer-const` — const for variables that are never reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-const.md

### What it checks

A `let` whose names all get their value in the declaration and are never reassigned is a `const`.

**Why:** `const` tells the reader the binding won't change, and the engine enforces it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript


##### Do

```js
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

use(limit);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

use(limit);
```

##### Do

```ts

use(limit);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

use(limit);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

## `js/prefer-default-parameters` — A default parameter rather than reassigning it

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`||` replaces every falsy argument while a default replaces only `undefined`; offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-default-parameters.md

### What it checks

A function whose first statement gives its one parameter a fallback (`name = name || "guest"`) declares it as a default parameter (`name = "guest"`).

**Why:** The default is in the signature, where callers and readers look for it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function greet(name) {
  name = name || "guest";
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function greet(name = "guest") {
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function greet(name) {
  name = name || "guest";
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function greet(name = "guest") {
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function greet(name) {
  name = name || "guest";
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function greet(name = "guest") {
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  name = name || "guest";
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function greet(name = "guest") {
  return `Hi ${name}`;
}
```

##### Do

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do


##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do


- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do


## `js/prefer-group-by` — Object.groupBy() rather than reducing into arrays

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`Object.groupBy` returns an object with no prototype; code that calls `hasOwnProperty` on the result needs review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-group-by.md

### What it checks

Grouping elements by a key is `Object.groupBy(items, (item) => key)`, not a `reduce` that pushes each element into `acc[key] ??= []` (or `||=`).

**Why:** The built-in names the operation; the reduce makes the reader work it out.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const byRole = users.reduce((acc, user) => { (acc[user.role] ??= []).push(user); return acc; }, {});
```

##### Do

```js
const byRole = Object.groupBy(users, (user) => user.role);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const byRole = users.reduce((acc, user) => { (acc[user.role] ??= []).push(user); return acc; }, {});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const byRole = Object.groupBy(users, (user) => user.role);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const byRole = users.reduce((acc, user) => { (acc[user.role] ??= []).push(user); return acc; }, {});
```

##### Do

```ts
const byRole = Object.groupBy(users, (user) => user.role);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const byRole = users.reduce((acc, user) => { (acc[user.role] ??= []).push(user); return acc; }, {});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const byRole = Object.groupBy(users, (user) => user.role);
```

## `js/prefer-includes-over-repeated-comparisons` — includes() rather than three or more === tests of one value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`includes` evaluates every candidate and treats `NaN` as equal to itself; the rewrite is offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-includes-over-repeated-comparisons.md

### What it checks

A value compared with `===` against three candidates joined by `||` is tested with `[a, b, c].includes(value)`.

**Why:** The list names the candidates once and the value once.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (key === "a" || key === "d" || key === "w") move(key);
```

##### Do

```js
if (["a", "d", "w"].includes(key)) move(key);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (key === "a" || key === "d" || key === "w") move(key);
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (["a", "d", "w"].includes(key)) move(key);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (key === "a" || key === "d" || key === "w") move(key);
```

##### Do

```ts
if (["a", "d", "w"].includes(key)) move(key);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (key === "a" || key === "d" || key === "w") move(key);
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (["a", "d", "w"].includes(key)) move(key);
```

## `js/prefer-iterable-in-constructor` — new Set(x) rather than new Set([...x])

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

### What it checks

A `Set` or `Map` is built from an iterable directly, not from a spread of it.

**Why:** The constructors take any iterable; the spread copies it once more.

#### JSX

##### Don't

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
  submit();
```

```js
  submit();
```

##### Do

## `js/prefer-named-capture-group` — Name capture groups

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the group name is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-named-capture-group.md

### What it checks

A capture group in a regular-expression literal is named (`(?<year>…)`) or non-capturing (`(?:…)`).

##### Do

```jsx
const m = /(?<from>\d+)-(?<to>\d+)/.exec(s);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const m = /(\d+)-(\d+)/.exec(s);
```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const m = /(\d+)-(\d+)/.exec(s);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const m = /(?<from>\d+)-(?<to>\d+)/.exec(s);
```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


## `js/prefer-object-from-entries` — Object.fromEntries() rather than reducing pairs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-object-from-entries.md

### What it checks

An object built from a list of key-value pairs is built with `Object.fromEntries(pairs)`, not by reducing the pairs into a spread object or with lodash's `_.fromPairs`.

**Why:** `Object.fromEntries` names the operation, and does not copy the object once per pair as the spread form does.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do


```js
const failed = Promise.reject(error);
```

## `js/prefer-reflect-apply` — Reflect.apply() rather than Function#apply with no receiver

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-reflect-apply.md

### What it checks

A function called with an argument list and no receiver is called with `Reflect.apply(fn, null, args)`, not `fn.apply(null, args)` or `Function.prototype.apply.call(fn, null, args)`.


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/prefer-regexp-escape` — RegExp.escape() rather than a hand-written escape

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-regexp-escape.md

### What it checks

Text is made safe for a regular expression with `RegExp.escape(text)`, not with a `replace` of the special characters by `\\$&`.

**Why:** The built-in covers every special character and every position; a hand-written class is easy to get subtly wrong.


#### JSX

```jsx
const safe = input.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const safe = RegExp.escape(input);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const safe = input.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
```

##### Do

```ts
const safe = RegExp.escape(input);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const safe = input.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const safe = RegExp.escape(input);
```
