- **Fix:** `suggest` (the response gains a `Content-Type: application/json` header)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-response-static-json.md

### What it checks

`new Response(JSON.stringify(x))` is written `Response.json(x)`.

**Why:** `Response.json` also sets the `Content-Type` header.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
return new Response(JSON.stringify(body));
```

##### Do

```js
return Response.json(body);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
return new Response(JSON.stringify(body));
```

##### Do

```jsx
return Response.json(body);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
return new Response(JSON.stringify(body));
```

##### Do

```ts
return Response.json(body);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
return new Response(JSON.stringify(body));
```

##### Do

```tsx
return Response.json(body);
```

## `js/prefer-rest-params` — Rest parameters instead of arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the parameter list has to be rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-rest-params.md

### What it checks

Functions take a rest parameter `...args` instead of reading `arguments`.

**Why:** `arguments` is not a real array, isn't available in arrow functions, and hides how many
arguments a function takes.

### How to fix

1. Add a rest parameter `...args` to the function.
2. Replace each use of `arguments` with it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

## `js/prefer-set-methods` — Set methods rather than filtering a spread

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the methods exist only on a `Set`; whether the left-hand value is one is not known here, so the edit is offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-set-methods.md

### What it checks

The intersection, difference or union of two sets is computed with `a.intersection(b)`, `a.difference(b)` or `a.union(b)`, not by spreading into an array and filtering or concatenating.

**Why:** The methods name the operation and skip the intermediate array.

### Examples


##### Do

```js

```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx
const both = mine.intersection(theirs);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-short-escape-sequences.md

##### Don't

```js
const cell = "a\u0009b";
```

##### Do

```ts

const cell = "a\tb";
```

#### TSX

##### Do


## `js/prefer-single-boolean-return` — Return the condition, not true/false

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a non-boolean condition needs `Boolean(…)` or `!`, decided per pattern)

- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-single-boolean-return.md

### What it checks

An `if … else` that only returns `true` in one branch and `false` in the other is a single `return`.

```js
    return true;
  } else {
    return false;
  }
```

##### Do

## `js/prefer-single-call` — One push() with several items

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the receiver is evaluated once instead of twice, and a value the first push's arguments read is now computed before the second's: a getter or a call with effects can tell)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-single-call.md

### What it checks

Consecutive `push` calls on the same array are merged. Upstream also covers `classList.add` and others; this port covers `push`.

**Why:** One call says the same in one statement.

### How to fix

1. Move the second call's arguments into the first call, after its own, and delete the second statement.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
list.push(a);
list.push(b);
```

##### Do

```js
list.push(a, b);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
list.push(a);
list.push(b);
```

##### Do

```jsx
list.push(a, b);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

list.push(b);
```

##### Do

```ts
list.push(a, b);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
list.push(a);
list.push(b);
```

##### Do

```tsx
list.push(a, b);
```

## `js/prefer-single-object-destructuring` — One destructuring of an object, not two in a row

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`

Two `const` destructurings of the same variable in a row are one: `const { a } = o; const { b } = o;` is `const { a, b } = o;`.

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/prefer-split-limit` — A limit on split() when only the first parts are read

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-split-limit.md

### What it checks

A `split` whose result is read at one small index, or destructured into one name, passes the limit it needs: `s.split(",")[0]` is `s.split(",", 1)[0]`.

**Why:** Without a limit `split` cuts the whole string, however long, to return parts nobody reads.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

```js
const scheme = url.split(":")[0];
```

##### Do

```js
const scheme = url.split(":", 1)[0];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const scheme = url.split(":")[0];
```

##### Do

```jsx
const scheme = url.split(":", 1)[0];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const scheme = url.split(":")[0];
```

##### Do

```ts
const scheme = url.split(":", 1)[0];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const scheme = url.split(":", 1)[0];
```

## `js/prefer-spread` — Spread instead of .apply()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-spread.md

### What it checks

A function is called with spread arguments, `f(...args)`, instead of `f.apply(null, args)`.

**Why:** Spread says the same thing more directly, and doesn't need a `this` value.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```js
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```ts
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

### Differences from the source

Only `f.apply(null, args)` and `f.apply(undefined, args)` on a plain function name are checked;
method calls are left alone.

## `js/prefer-string-starts-ends-with` — startsWith() rather than a ^ regex test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`.startsWith()` is a string method: a value that is not a string (`null`, a number) threw nothing with `.test()` and throws now)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-string-starts-ends-with.md

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
if (/^http/.test(url)) {

}
```

##### Do

```js
if (url.startsWith("http")) {
  fetchIt();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  fetchIt();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx

  fetchIt();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  fetchIt();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (url.startsWith("http")) {
  fetchIt();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (/^http/.test(url)) {
  fetchIt();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  fetchIt();
}
```

## `js/prefer-switch` — A switch rather than an if-else chain on one value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the switch needs a break or return per case, which the author writes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-switch.md

### What it checks

An `if`-`else if` chain that compares the same value with `===` three or more times is a `switch` (unicorn's default `minimumCases: 3`).

**Why:** The switch names the value once and lines up the cases.

### How to fix

1. Write `switch (value)` with one `case` per compared value, each ending in `break` or `return`, and the final `else` as `default`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (key === "a") {
  left();
} else if (key === "d") {
  right();
} else if (key === "w") {
  up();
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (key) {
  case "a":
    left();
    break;
  case "d":
    right();
    break;
  case "w":
    up();
    break;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (key === "a") {
  left();
} else if (key === "d") {
  right();
} else if (key === "w") {
  up();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (key) {
  case "a":
    left();
    break;
  case "d":
    right();
    break;
  case "w":
    up();
    break;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (key === "a") {
  left();
} else if (key === "d") {
  right();
} else if (key === "w") {
  up();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (key) {
  case "a":
    left();
    break;
  case "d":
    right();
    break;
  case "w":
    up();
    break;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (key === "a") {
  left();
} else if (key === "d") {
  right();
} else if (key === "w") {
  up();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (key) {
  case "a":
    left();
    break;
  case "d":
    right();
    break;
  case "w":
    up();
    break;
}
```

## `js/prefer-template` — Template literal rather than string concatenation

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a value joined with `+` is read through its `valueOf` and in a template through its `toString`, which differ for some objects; a join holding a comment, or a line continuation in a string, is rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-template.md

### What it checks

#### JSX

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do

## `js/prefer-ternary` — A ternary for an if-else that only returns or assigns

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-ternary.md

### What it checks

An `if`-`else` whose two branches each only return a value, or each only assign to the same target, is written as one `return` or one assignment with a ternary.

**Why:** The ternary says once what both branches do, and leaves only the difference.

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  } else {
    return "positive";
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  return n < 0 ? "negative" : "positive";
```

- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-type-error.md

An `if` whose whole condition is a type check (`typeof`, `instanceof`, `Array.isArray`) and whose branch throws, throws a `TypeError`, not a plain `Error`.

```jsx
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (typeof name !== "string") {
  throw new Error("name must be a string");
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  throw new TypeError("name must be a string");
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

  throw new TypeError("name must be a string");
```

## `js/prefer-uint8array-base64` — Uint8Array base64 methods rather than btoa and atob

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (only a `Uint8Array` has `toBase64()`; whether the bytes are one is not known here, so the edit is offered for review)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-uint8array-base64.md

### What it checks

Bytes are encoded with `bytes.toBase64()` and decoded with `Uint8Array.fromBase64(text)`, not through `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))` and `Uint8Array.from(atob(text), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0))`.

**Why:** The built-ins skip the binary string in between, and spreading a large array into `fromCharCode` can overflow the stack.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const text = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes));
const back = Uint8Array.from(atob(text), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
```

##### Do

```js
const text = bytes.toBase64();
const back = Uint8Array.fromBase64(text);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const text = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes));
const back = Uint8Array.from(atob(text), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
```

##### Do

```jsx
const text = bytes.toBase64();
const back = Uint8Array.fromBase64(text);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const text = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes));
const back = Uint8Array.from(atob(text), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
```

##### Do

```ts
const text = bytes.toBase64();
const back = Uint8Array.fromBase64(text);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const text = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes));
const back = Uint8Array.from(atob(text), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const text = bytes.toBase64();
const back = Uint8Array.fromBase64(text);
```

## `js/prefer-while-loop-condition` — The loop condition in the while, not a break at the top

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-while-loop-condition.md

### What it checks

**Why:** The loop's exit is then where a reader looks for it.

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the new error class must accept an options argument)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/preserve-caught-error.md

### What it checks

A built-in error (`Error`, `TypeError` and the rest) thrown from a `catch` block passes the caught
error as `{ cause }`.

**Why:** Without the cause, the original error and its stack are lost.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```ts

  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

## `js/production-debug` — No error-handler middleware that shows stack traces, unguarded

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which environments get the debug handler is the owner's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/production-debug.md

### What it checks

Express's `errorhandler` middleware, which sends stack traces to the client, is installed only behind a development check — not with a bare `app.use(errorhandler())`.

**Why:** Stack traces in production tell an attacker the code's structure, paths and versions.

### How to fix

1. Wrap it in `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development")`, and use a handler that hides details elsewhere.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.use(errorhandler());
```

##### Do

```js
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development") {
  app.use(errorhandler());
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(errorhandler());
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development") {
  app.use(errorhandler());
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(errorhandler());
```

##### Do

```ts
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development") {
  app.use(errorhandler());
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(errorhandler());
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development") {
  app.use(errorhandler());
}
```

## `js/promise-always-return` — A then callback returns or throws

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (returning the last expression passes a new value downstream and `return undefined;` only silences the rule, so the reviewer picks)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-always-return.md

### What it checks

A `.then()` callback with a block body returns a value or throws.

**Why:** The next link of the chain receives what the callback returns; a callback that returns nothing passes `undefined` on, which is almost always a forgotten `return` before an inner promise.

### How to fix

1. Return the value the next step needs, or throw if the callback found an error; the fix offers `return` of the last expression, or `return undefined;` when nothing is meant to pass on.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
load().then((data) => {
  store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return the value)

```js
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return undefined)

```js
load().then((data) => {
  store(data); return undefined;
}).catch(report);
```

##### Do

```js
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
load().then((data) => {
  store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return the value)

```jsx
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return undefined)

```jsx
load().then((data) => {
  store(data); return undefined;
}).catch(report);
```

##### Do

```jsx
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
load().then((data) => {
  store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return the value)

```ts
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return undefined)

```ts
load().then((data) => {
  store(data); return undefined;
}).catch(report);
```

##### Do

```ts
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
load().then((data) => {
  store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return the value)

```tsx
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

##### Fixed (return undefined)

```tsx
load().then((data) => {
  store(data); return undefined;
}).catch(report);
```

##### Do

```tsx
load().then((data) => {
  return store(data);
}).catch(report);
```

### Differences from the source

The source follows each code path; this rule asks only whether the body has a `return` or `throw` anywhere, so a callback that returns on one branch and falls off the end of another is not reported.

## `js/promise-avoid-new` — No new Promise

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (replacing an executor means choosing an `async` function or a promisified API)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-avoid-new.md

### What it checks

Promises are made with `Promise.resolve`, `Promise.reject`, an `async` function or a promisified API, not with `new Promise`.

**Why:** A hand-written executor is where resolve-twice and forgotten-reject bugs live; most code that writes one is wrapping a callback API `util.promisify` already wraps.

### How to fix

1. Write the function as `async`, or wrap the callback API with `util.promisify`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
```

##### Do

```js
const wait = promisify(setTimeout);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const wait = promisify(setTimeout);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const wait = promisify(setTimeout);
```

## `js/promise-catch-or-return` — A promise chain is returned, awaited or ends in catch

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (returning or awaiting the chain changes the function's result and timing, and a `.catch()` is a decision about the error; the reviewer picks)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-catch-or-return.md

### What it checks

A promise chain used as a statement on its own ends with `.catch()`; otherwise it is returned or awaited so its caller handles a rejection.

**Why:** A rejection in a chain nobody returns, awaits or catches becomes an unhandled rejection — in Node, a crash.

### How to fix

1. Add a `.catch()` at the end of the chain that handles or reports the error, or `return` / `await` the chain so the caller does; the fix offers the last two.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (return the chain)

```js
async function run(doc) {
  return save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (await the chain)

```js
async function run(doc) {
  await save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Do

```js
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc)
    .then(() => notify())
    .catch((err) => report(err));
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (return the chain)

```jsx
async function run(doc) {
  return save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (await the chain)

```jsx
async function run(doc) {
  await save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc)
    .then(() => notify())
    .catch((err) => report(err));
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (return the chain)

```ts
async function run(doc) {
  return save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (await the chain)

```ts
async function run(doc) {
  await save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Do

```ts
async function run(doc) {
  save(doc)
    .then(() => notify())
    .catch((err) => report(err));
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (return the chain)

```tsx
async function run(doc) {
  return save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Fixed (await the chain)

```tsx

  await save(doc).then(() => notify());
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  save(doc)
    .then(() => notify())
    .catch((err) => report(err));
}
```

## `js/promise-no-callback-in-promise` — No node-style callback is called inside a then or catch

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (any edit leaves the callback call inside the promise chain; the call has to move out, which restructures the caller)
- **Severity when named:** `warn` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-callback-in-promise.md

### What it checks

A `.then()` or `.catch()` callback does not call `callback`, `cb`, `next` or `done`.

**Why:** Calling a callback from inside a promise runs it inside the promise's error handling: if it throws, the throw becomes a rejection the callback's caller never sees, and the callback may run twice.

### How to fix

1. Return the promise to the caller, or call the callback outside the chain (for example in `setImmediate`) so an error it throws is not swallowed.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load(cb) {
  read().then((data) => cb(null, data));
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {
  return read();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function load(cb) {
  read().then((data) => cb(null, data));
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {
  return read();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load(cb) {
  read().then((data) => cb(null, data));
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {
  return read();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function load(cb) {
  read().then((data) => cb(null, data));
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load() {
  return read();
}
```

## `js/promise-no-multiple-resolved` — A promise executor settles once on each path

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (early `return` also skips the later statements and deleting the late call hides the bug; the reviewer picks which call is the right one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-multiple-resolved.md

### What it checks

A promise executor does not call `resolve` or `reject` twice in a row in the same block.

**Why:** Only the first call settles the promise; the second is silently ignored, which is almost always a missing `return`.

### How to fix

1. Add the missing `return` after the first call, or delete the call that should not run; the fix offers both.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (return from the earlier call)

```js
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  return resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (drop the later call)

```js
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

##### Do

```js
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) return reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (return from the earlier call)

```jsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  return resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (drop the later call)

```jsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) return reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (return from the earlier call)

```ts
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  return resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (drop the later call)

```ts
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) return reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (return from the earlier call)

```tsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  return resolve(value);
  reject(late);
});
```

##### Fixed (drop the later call)

```tsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (bad) return reject(err);
  resolve(value);
});
```

### Differences from the source

The source follows each code path through branches; this rule reports two settling calls written one after the other in the same block.

## `js/promise-no-native` — Promise is imported, not the global

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which promise library to import is the project's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

`Promise` is used only where it is declared or imported in the file, for code that must run where there is no native `Promise`.

**Why:** In an environment without a native `Promise`, the global one is `undefined` and the code fails at the first use.

##### Do

```jsx

const p = Promise.resolve(1);
```

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `js/promise-no-nesting` — Promise chains are flattened, not nested

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (hoisting the inner `.then` onto the outer chain is only equivalent when its callback uses nothing the outer callback declared, which the reviewer confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `warn` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-nesting.md

### What it checks

A `.then()` or `.catch()` is not called inside another `.then()` or `.catch()` callback: return the inner promise and chain on it.

**Why:** Nested chains rebuild the callback pyramid promises were meant to remove, and a rejection inside one is easy to lose.

### How to fix

1. Return the inner promise from the outer callback and move its `.then()` up to the outer chain; the fix does this for a single-argument `.then` that is the arrow callback's whole body, and the reviewer checks the moved callback uses nothing the outer callback declared.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user).then((posts) => show(posts)),
);
```

##### Fixed

```js
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user),
).then((posts) => show(posts));
```

##### Do

```js
getUser()
  .then((user) => getPosts(user))
  .then((posts) => show(posts));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user).then((posts) => show(posts)),
);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user),
).then((posts) => show(posts));
```

##### Do

```jsx
getUser()
  .then((user) => getPosts(user))
  .then((posts) => show(posts));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user).then((posts) => show(posts)),
);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user),
).then((posts) => show(posts));
```

##### Do

```ts
getUser()
  .then((user) => getPosts(user))
  .then((posts) => show(posts));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user).then((posts) => show(posts)),
);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
getUser().then((user) =>
  getPosts(user),
).then((posts) => show(posts));
```

##### Do

```tsx
getUser()
  .then((user) => getPosts(user))
  .then((posts) => show(posts));
```

### Differences from the source

The source allows a nested chain whose callback uses the outer callback's parameters; this rule reports every nested chain.

## `js/promise-no-new-statics` — Promise's static methods are called without new

## `js/promise-no-promise-in-callback` — No promise chain inside a node-style callback

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (converting the callback API to promises (for example with `util.promisify`) is a refactor of the caller)
- **Severity when named:** `warn` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-promise-in-callback.md

### What it checks

A callback whose first parameter is `err` or `error` does not start a `.then()` or `.catch()` chain.

**Why:** Mixing the two styles splits error handling in two places, and a rejection inside the callback goes nowhere.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the callback API with `util.promisify` (or write a promise version) and chain or `await` it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
fs.readFile(path, (err, text) => {
  parse(text).then(show);
});
```

##### Do

```js
const text = await readFile(path);
show(await parse(text));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
fs.readFile(path, (err, text) => {
  parse(text).then(show);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const text = await readFile(path);
show(await parse(text));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
fs.readFile(path, (err, text) => {
  parse(text).then(show);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const text = await readFile(path);
show(await parse(text));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
fs.readFile(path, (err, text) => {
  parse(text).then(show);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const text = await readFile(path);
show(await parse(text));
```

## `js/promise-no-return-in-finally` — A finally callback returns nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the returned value is dropped from the result either way; the reviewer confirms it should not move to a `.then()`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-return-in-finally.md

### What it checks

The callback passed to `.finally()` does not `return` a value.

**Why:** Whatever `.finally()`'s callback returns is thrown away — the chain keeps the value before it — so a `return x` there reads as if it changed the result and never does.

### How to fix

1. Move the value into a `.then()` before the `.finally()`, or delete the `return` value if it was not meant to change the result.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
load().finally(() => {
  return cleanup();
});
```

##### Fixed

```js
load().finally(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

##### Do

```js
load().finally(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
load().finally(() => {
  return cleanup();
});
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
load().finally(() => {
```

## `js/promise-no-return-wrap` — A then or catch callback returns the value, not Promise.resolve or Promise.reject

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (`return Promise.resolve(x)` is `return x` and `return Promise.reject(e)` is `throw e`; only a callback with a try around the return, where the new throw would be caught, stays a suggestion)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-no-return-wrap.md

### What it checks

Inside a `.then()` or `.catch()` callback, return the value itself rather than `Promise.resolve(value)`, and `throw` the error rather than return `Promise.reject(error)`.

**Why:** The callback's return value is already wrapped in a promise, so the extra wrapping is noise, and a returned rejection hides a `throw` the reader would see at once.

### How to fix

1. Replace `return Promise.resolve(x)` with `return x`, and `return Promise.reject(e)` with `throw e`; the fix does both, and reports a suggestion where a `try` in the callback would catch the new `throw`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return Promise.resolve(user.name);
});
```

##### Fixed

```js
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

##### Do

```js
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return Promise.resolve(user.name);
});
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return Promise.resolve(user.name);
});
```

##### Fixed

```ts
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

##### Do

```ts
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return Promise.resolve(user.name);
});
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
fetchUser().then((user) => {
  return user.name;
});
```

## `js/promise-param-names` — A promise executor names its parameters resolve and reject

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming a parameter is safe only when every use in the executor is renamed with it; rename it by hand or with the editor)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-param-names.md

### What it checks

The function passed to `new Promise` calls its first parameter `resolve` and its second `reject` (an underscore in front is allowed for one that is unused).

**Why:** Every reader expects those two names; `new Promise((ok, fail) => …)`, or the two swapped, makes each call site a puzzle and hides a resolve that should have been a reject.

### How to fix

1. Rename the first parameter to `resolve` and the second to `reject`, and every use of each in the executor.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const p = new Promise((ok, fail) => setTimeout(ok, 10));
```

##### Do

```js
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const p = new Promise((ok, fail) => setTimeout(ok, 10));
```

##### Do

```jsx
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const p = new Promise((ok, fail) => setTimeout(ok, 10));
```

##### Do

```ts
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const p = new Promise((ok, fail) => setTimeout(ok, 10));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
```

## `js/promise-prefer-await-to-callbacks` — async and await, not callbacks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (turning a callback API into a promise changes every caller)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-prefer-await-to-callbacks.md

### What it checks

A function does not take or call a `callback` or `cb` parameter: it returns a promise and its callers `await` it.

**Why:** Callbacks spread error handling across every call site and do not compose with `try`/`catch`.

### How to fix

1. Make the function `async` (or return a promise), drop the callback parameter, and `await` it at each call site.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load(path, cb) {
  read(path, cb);
}
```

##### Do

```js
async function load(path) {
  return read(path);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function load(path, cb) {
  read(path, cb);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
async function load(path) {
  return read(path);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load(path, cb) {
  read(path, cb);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
async function load(path) {
  return read(path);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function load(path, cb) {
  read(path, cb);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
async function load(path) {
  return read(path);
}
```

## `js/promise-prefer-await-to-then` — await, not then

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a chain to `await` needs an `async` function and may restructure the error handling)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-prefer-await-to-then.md

### What it checks

A promise's result is taken with `await`, not `.then()`.

**Why:** `await` reads top to bottom, keeps values in scope without nesting, and works with `try`/`catch`.

### How to fix

1. Make the enclosing function `async` and replace `p.then((x) => …)` with `const x = await p;`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function show() {
  return load().then((data) => render(data));
}
```

##### Do

```js
async function show() {
  const data = await load();
  return render(data);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function show() {
  return load().then((data) => render(data));
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
async function show() {
  const data = await load();
  return render(data);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function show() {
  return load().then((data) => render(data));
}
```

##### Do

```ts
async function show() {
  const data = await load();
  return render(data);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function show() {
  return load().then((data) => render(data));
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
async function show() {
  const data = await load();
  return render(data);
}
```

## `js/promise-prefer-catch` — catch, not a second then argument

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`.catch(b).then(a)` passes the handler's result on to `a` where `.then(a, b)` did not; review the order before accepting)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-prefer-catch.md

### What it checks

Rejections are handled with `.catch()`, not with `.then()`'s second argument.

**Why:** A reader looking for error handling looks for `.catch`; the second argument of `.then` is easy to miss.

### Examples

```js
load().then(show, report);
```

##### Do

```js
load().catch(report).then(show);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
load().then(show, report);
```

##### Do

```jsx
load().catch(report).then(show);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
load().then(show, report);
```

##### Do

```ts
load().catch(report).then(show);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
load().then(show, report);
```

##### Do

```tsx
load().catch(report).then(show);
```

## `js/promise-spec-only` — Only standard Promise methods

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (library methods differ in concurrency and callback arguments from the standard ones, so the reviewer confirms the rewrite; a method with no standard equivalent has no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-spec-only.md

### What it checks

Only the static methods the language defines are called on `Promise`.

**Why:** A method a promise library adds to the global (`Promise.map`, `Promise.delay`) breaks when that library is not loaded first, or is swapped out.

### How to fix

1. Replace the library method with the standard ones (`Promise.all(items.map(f))` for `Promise.map`, a `setTimeout` promise for `Promise.delay`) or import the library explicitly; the fix writes those two.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const out = Promise.map(items, load);
```

##### Do

```js
const out = Promise.all(items.map(load));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const out = Promise.map(items, load);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const out = Promise.all(items.map(load));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const out = Promise.map(items, load);
```

##### Do

```ts
const out = Promise.all(items.map(load));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const out = Promise.map(items, load);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const out = Promise.all(items.map(load));
```

## `js/promise-valid-params` — Promise methods get the number of arguments they take

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which argument is the intended one cannot be known from the call)
- **Severity when named:** `warn` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/promise-valid-params.md

### What it checks

`Promise.resolve` and `Promise.reject` take at most one argument; `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `race` and `any` exactly one; `.then()` one or two; `.catch()` and `.finally()` exactly one.

**Why:** An extra argument is silently ignored and a missing one makes the call do nothing useful — either way the code does not do what it says.

### How to fix

1. Pass the arguments the method takes: one value to `resolve`/`reject`, one iterable to `all`/`race`, one or two handlers to `then`, one to `catch`/`finally`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
Promise.all(a, b);
```

##### Do

```js
Promise.all([a, b]);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
Promise.all(a, b);
```

##### Do

```jsx
Promise.all([a, b]);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
Promise.all(a, b);
```

##### Do

```ts
Promise.all([a, b]);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
Promise.all(a, b);
```

##### Do

```tsx
Promise.all([a, b]);
```

## `js/publicly-writable-directories` — No files in /tmp

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the private directory's lifetime is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/publicly-writable-directories.md

### What it checks

A string does not name a file directly in `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm` or `/usr/tmp`.

**Why:** Other users can predict the name, read the file, or plant a symlink there first.

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const out = "/tmp/report.json";
```

##### Do

```js
const dir = await fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "report-"));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const out = "/tmp/report.json";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const dir = await fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "report-"));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const out = "/tmp/report.json";
```

##### Do

```ts
const dir = await fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "report-"));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const out = "/tmp/report.json";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const dir = await fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "report-"));
```

## `js/redundant-type-aliases` — No type alias that only renames a built-in type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the alias's uses are replaced by hand, file by file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/redundant-type-aliases.md

### What it checks

A type alias does not only rename a built-in type: `type Name = string` adds a name, not a type.

**Why:** The alias makes a reader look it up to find a plain `string`, and checks nothing a `string` wouldn't.

### How to fix

1. Use the built-in type where the alias is used, and delete the alias — or make the alias a real type (a branded type, a union).

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
type UserId = string;
```

##### Do

```ts
type UserId = string & { readonly brand: "UserId" };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
type UserId = string;
```

##### Do

```tsx
type UserId = string & { readonly brand: "UserId" };
```

## `js/regexp-confusing-quantifier` — No quantifier whose minimum is misleading

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (lowering the minimum to 0 says what the pattern does, but the author may have meant the element to be required)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-confusing-quantifier.md

### What it checks

A quantifier with a minimum above zero doesn't repeat something that can match the empty string: `(a?){2}` reads as two at least, but matches nothing too.

**Why:** The minimum promises characters the pattern doesn't require.

### How to fix

1. Write the minimum as 0 if empty is meant.
2. Otherwise make what is repeated require a character.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /(a?){2}/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /(a?){0,2}/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /(a?){2}/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(a?){0,2}/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /(a?){2}/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(a?){0,2}/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /(a?){2}/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(a?){0,2}/;
```

## `js/regexp-grapheme-string-literal` — String literals in a class hold one character each

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a string out of the class into an alternation changes the pattern's structure, which the author decides)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-grapheme-string-literal.md

### What it checks

Under the `v` flag, each string of a `\q{…}` class string literal is a single character (one grapheme); longer strings are written as an alternation outside the class.

**Why:** A class reads as a set of characters; a word inside it is easy to miss.

##### Do

```js
const re = /(?:abc|[x])/v;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /[\q{abc}x]/v;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(?:abc|[x])/v;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(?:abc|[x])/v;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(?:abc|[x])/v;
```

## `js/regexp-no-contradiction-with-assertion` — No element the assertion before it contradicts

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the element or its quantifier says what the pattern does, which may not be what was meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-contradiction-with-assertion.md

### What it checks

An optional element right after a `\b` or `\B` either can never match there or must always match: `a\b-?a` always takes the `-`.

**Why:** The quantifier claims a choice the assertion has already made.


#### TSX

##### Do


## `js/regexp-no-dupe-disjunctions` — No alternative that repeats or is covered by an earlier one

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the alternative changes the pattern's text; check it wasn't a typo for a different one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-dupe-disjunctions.md

### What it checks

An alternative doesn't repeat an earlier one, and a single-character alternative isn't inside an earlier single-character one: `(?:a|b|a)`, `(?:\w|a)`.

**Why:** It can never match, and it slows the backtracking down.

### How to fix

1. Remove the alternative, or fix the one that was meant.

### Examples

##### Do

```js
const re = /(?:ab|cd)/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /(?:ab|cd|ab)/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(?:ab|cd)/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /(?:ab|cd|ab)/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(?:ab|cd)/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /(?:ab|cd|ab)/;
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/regexp-no-empty-alternative` — No empty alternative

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (making the group optional matches the same strings, but a capturing group then captures nothing instead of the empty string)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-empty-alternative.md

### What it checks

A disjunction has no empty alternative: `(?:a|b|)` is written `(?:a|b)?`.

**Why:** An empty alternative is easy to miss and is often a stray `|`.

### How to fix


##### Do

```js

```

#### JSX

```jsx
const re = /(?:a|b|)c/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(?:a|b)?c/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/regexp-no-legacy-features` — No legacy `RegExp` static properties

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (reading the match result instead of the global properties moves code to where the match is made)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-legacy-features.md

### What it checks

`RegExp.$1`–`$9`, `RegExp.lastMatch`, `RegExp.input`, `RegExp.leftContext` and the other legacy statics are not read.

**Why:** They are a global record of the last match anywhere: any other match overwrites them.

### How to fix

1. Keep the match result (`const m = re.exec(s)`) and read `m[1]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const first = RegExp.$1;
```

##### Do

```js
const first = match[1];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const first = RegExp.$1;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const first = match[1];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const first = RegExp.$1;
```

##### Do

```ts
const first = match[1];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const first = RegExp.$1;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const first = match[1];
```

## `js/regexp-no-misleading-capturing-group` — No capturing group whose start the quantifier before it always takes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (making the quantifier before the group lazy changes what it matches; it is offered for an agent or a person to accept)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-misleading-capturing-group.md

### What it checks

A capturing group whose first element is optional isn't right after a greedy quantifier that matches the same characters: in `^\w+(\d*)$` the group always captures nothing.

**Why:** The group looks like it captures digits; it never does.

### How to fix

1. Make the quantifier before it lazy, or narrow what it matches.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js

```

##### Do

```js
const re = /^\w+?(\d*)$/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /^\w+(\d*)$/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /^\w+?(\d*)$/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /^\w+(\d*)$/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /^\w+?(\d*)$/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /^\w+(\d*)$/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /^\w+?(\d*)$/;
```

### What it checks



##### Do

## `js/regexp-no-super-linear-backtracking` — No exponential backtracking

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when one alternative of a repeated alternation matches a subset of another (it is removed, the language is the same); a repeated sequence with an unbounded quantifier is reported without an edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:js/regexp` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-no-super-linear-backtracking.md

### What it checks

A repeated group can't match the same text in many ways: `(?:\w|\d)*` (alternatives overlap) or `(?:a+b?)*` (one run splits many ways).

**Why:** A failing match on a long input can take exponential time — a denial of service.

### How to fix

1. Remove the overlap between the alternatives, or make the parts of the repeated sequence exclusive.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /(?:\w|\d)*x/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /(?:\w)*x/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /(?:\w|\d)*x/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(?:\w)*x/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /(?:\w|\d)*x/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(?:\w)*x/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /(?:\w|\d)*x/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(?:\w)*x/;
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (an anchor or a different quantifier changes what the pattern finds; the author decides)

A pattern that isn't anchored or sticky doesn't start with an unbounded quantifier followed by more: `/\s+$/` retries the quantifier at every position.

##### Do

## `js/regexp-no-zero-quantifier` — No quantifier that repeats zero times

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the element keeps what the pattern matches, but it was probably meant to be there)

##### Don't

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `js/regexp-prefer-lookaround` — A captured text put back unchanged is matched with a lookaround

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (matching with a lookaround changes which text a global replacement consumes, so overlapping matches can differ)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-prefer-lookaround.md

### What it checks

A replacement that starts or ends with `$1`, where group 1 is the pattern's first or last element, uses a lookbehind or lookahead instead: `s.replace(/(a)b/, '$1c')` is `s.replace(/(?<=a)b/, 'c')`.

**Why:** The capture and the reinsertion say less than a lookaround.

### How to fix

1. Turn the group into a lookbehind (or lookahead) and drop the `$1`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
s.replace(/(a)b/g, '$1c');
```

##### Do

```js
s.replace(/(?<=a)b/g, 'c');
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
s.replace(/(a)b/g, '$1c');
```

##### Do

```jsx
s.replace(/(?<=a)b/g, 'c');
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
s.replace(/(a)b/g, '$1c');
```

##### Do

```ts
s.replace(/(?<=a)b/g, 'c');
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
s.replace(/(a)b/g, '$1c');
```

##### Do

```tsx
s.replace(/(?<=a)b/g, 'c');
```

## `js/regexp-prefer-named-capture-group` — Capturing groups are named

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the group's name is the author's to choose)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-prefer-named-capture-group.md

### What it checks

A capturing group has a name: `(?<year>\d{4})`, not `(\d{4})`.


#### JSX


##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(?<year>\d{4})/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /(\d{4})/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(?<year>\d{4})/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(?<year>\d{4})/;
```

- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-prefer-predefined-assertion.md

### What it checks

A lookaround equal to `^`, `$`, `\b` or `\B` is written as that assertion: `a(?!\w)` is `a\b`; `(?![\s\S])` is `$` without `m`.

**Why:** The assertion is shorter and plainer.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /a(?!\w)/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /a\b/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /a(?!\w)/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /a\b/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /a(?!\w)/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /a\b/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /a(?!\w)/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /a\b/;
```

## `js/regexp-prefer-quantifier` — A repeated element is written with a quantifier

## `js/regexp-prefer-regexp-exec` — `RegExp#exec` over `String#match` without `g`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`String#match` on a receiver that isn't a string may behave differently; the edit is for an agent or a person to accept)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-prefer-regexp-exec.md

### What it checks

`s.match(/re/)` with a regular expression without `g` is written `/re/.exec(s)`.

**Why:** `exec` says the regular expression drives the match, and is what `match` calls.

### How to fix

1. Call `exec` on the regular expression with the string.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const m = s.match(/a/);
```

##### Do

```js
const m = /a/.exec(s);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const m = s.match(/a/);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const m = /a/.exec(s);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const m = s.match(/a/);
```

##### Do

```ts
const m = /a/.exec(s);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const m = s.match(/a/);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const m = /a/.exec(s);
```

## `js/regexp-prefer-regexp-test` — `RegExp#test` when only whether it matches is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

## `js/regexp-prefer-result-array-groups` — A named group is read from `groups`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/regexp-prefer-result-array-groups.md

### What it checks

A match result's named group is read as `m.groups.name`, not `m[n]`.

**Why:** The name survives a reordering of the groups.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const m = /(?<y>\d+)/.exec(s);
use(m[1]);
```

##### Do

```js
const m = /(?<y>\d+)/.exec(s);
use(m.groups.y);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const m = /(?<y>\d+)/.exec(s);
use(m[1]);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const m = /(?<y>\d+)/.exec(s);
use(m.groups.y);
```

## `js/regexp-simplify-set-operations` — Set operations in their simplest form

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`


##### Do

```jsx
const re = /[\w--[\d]]/v;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /[\w&&[^\d]]/v;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /[\w--[\d]]/v;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /[\w&&[^\d]]/v;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /[\w--[\d]]/v;
```

##### Don't

##### Do

```ts
const re = /a\]/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /a\]/;
```

## `js/require-array-sort-compare` — A compare function for sort()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the order wanted — numeric, by locale, or the default code-unit order — is the author's; the two common compare functions are offered)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/require-array-sort-compare.md

### What it checks

`sort()` and `toSorted()` are called with a compare function. Without one they compare the elements as strings, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` is `[1, 10, 9]`.

**Why:** The default order is right only for strings of code units, and is a common source of wrong numeric sorts.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
scores.sort();
```

##### Do

```js
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (numbers)

```js
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (text)

```js
scores.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
scores.sort();
```

##### Do

```jsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (numbers)

```jsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (text)

```jsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
scores.sort();
```

##### Do

```ts
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (numbers)

```ts
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (text)

```ts
scores.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
scores.sort();
```

##### Do

```tsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (numbers)

```tsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
```

##### Fixed (text)

```tsx
scores.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
  return fetch(url);
```

```js
  return fetch(url);
```

```js
  return fetch(url);
```

```jsx
  return fetch(url);
```

```jsx
  return fetch(url);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
  return fetch(url);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
  return fetch(url);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
  return fetch(url);
}
```

#### TSX

```tsx
  return fetch(url);
```

```js
import React, {} from "react";
```

##### Do

```ts
import "./polyfills.js";
import React from "react";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import {} from "./polyfills.js";
import React, {} from "react";
```

##### Do


## `js/require-proxy-trap-boolean-return` — A Proxy set or deleteProperty trap returns a boolean

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`return true` is offered; a trap that forwards may mean to return `Reflect.set`'s result)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/require-proxy-trap-boolean-return.md

### What it checks

A `set`, `deleteProperty` or `defineProperty` trap of a `new Proxy` handler returns whether it succeeded.

```js
  },
});
```

##### Do

```js
const p = new Proxy(target, {
  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
    return true;
  },
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const p = new Proxy(target, {
  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
  },
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
    return true;
  },
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
  },
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
    return true;
  },
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  set(obj, key, value) {
    obj[key] = value;
  },
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  },
```

## `js/shorthand-property-grouping` — Shorthand properties grouped at the start or the end

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the order is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/shorthand-property-grouping.md

### What it checks

In an object literal, shorthand properties (`{ a }`) are all at the start or all at the end, not between `key: value` pairs.

**Why:** Grouped, a reader sees at once which values come from variables of the same name.

### How to fix

1. Move the shorthand properties together, before or after the `key: value` pairs.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```js
const user = { name, email, id: 1, role: "admin" };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const user = { id: 1, name, role: "admin", email };
```

##### Do

```jsx
const user = { name, email, id: 1, role: "admin" };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const user = { id: 1, name, role: "admin", email };
```

##### Do

```ts
const user = { name, email, id: 1, role: "admin" };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const user = { id: 1, name, role: "admin", email };
```

##### Do

```tsx
const user = { name, email, id: 1, role: "admin" };
```

## `js/skipped-test` — A skipped test has a reason and an expiry

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (why a test is off, and until when, is a fact only the author knows; the engine can't write it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/markers` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/skipped-test.md

### What it checks

A test turned off with `.skip` (`it.skip`, `test.skip`, `describe.skip`, `test.describe.skip`, `it.skip.each(…)`) or with Jasmine's and Mocha's `xit`, `xdescribe`, `xtest`, `xcontext`, `xspecify` says why and until when. Playwright's `test.skip(condition, "reason")` already carries its reason in the call; the expiry still goes in a `SKIP` comment.

The reason comes from the framework's own argument where it has one, else from the text of a **`SKIP` comment** on the line directly above the test (or at the end of its first line): `// SKIP(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): reason`. The ticket and the date are in the parentheses, in either order. The expiry is the date the skip stops being allowed: it is **expired** from the as-of date on (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date, never the clock: [SR-BASELINE](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md) decision 9) and is a **warning** for the `warn_days` before it. A skip whose `SKIP` comment names a date that has come is an error at the skipped test.

**Why:** A skipped test is a check that is switched off, and nothing shows it. A reason says why, an expiry makes it come back for review on a day somebody agreed to, and a failing skip on that day is how it gets turned on again instead of staying off for years.

**Configuration** is the `[tests.skip]` table of `codelaw.toml` ([SR-CONFIG](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0110_config.md) decision 11a), shared by `js/skipped-test` and `py/skipped-test`:

```toml
[tests.skip]
require_reason = true    # a reason is required (default)
require_expiry = true    # a SKIP(…, date) expiry is required (default)
require_ticket = false   # a ticket is required (default: no)
ticket_pattern = "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\\d+"
warn_days      = 14      # warn this many days before the expiry
```

### How to fix

1. Write the reason, the ticket that tracks the fix and the date you will look again, on the line above: `// SKIP(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): reason`.
2. For an expired skip: fix the test and remove the skip; or, if it really must stay off, move the date and say why in the reason.
3. If the test is not needed, delete it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
it.skip("totals the items", () => {
  expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3);
});
```

##### Do

```js
// SKIP(SHOP-77, 2027-01-31): flaky on the CI clock
it.skip("totals the items", () => {
  expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
xtest("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
// SKIP(UI-8, 2027-02-15): waits for the new icon font
xtest("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe.skip("cart", () => {
  it("totals the items", () => expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3));
});
```

##### Do

```ts
// SKIP(SHOP-90, 2027-03-01): rewritten in the checkout rework
describe.skip("cart", () => {
  it("totals the items", () => expect(total([1, 2])).toBe(3));
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test.skip("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
// SKIP(UI-8, 2027-02-15): waits for the new icon font
test.skip("renders the badge", () => {
  render(<Badge />);
});
```

## `js/todo-marker` — JavaScript and TypeScript TODO comments carry a ticket and, when asked, a date

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a ticket and a date are facts about the work that only the author knows; the engine can't invent them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/markers` at `error` · `codelaw:js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:js/sonarjs` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/todo-marker.md

### What it checks

A comment line that opens with a marker tag (`TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` by default) in a `//` or `/* … */` comment carries a ticket, and a date when the project asks for one: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): text`. The ticket and the date go in the parentheses, in either order, either one optional unless required; any other item in them (an owner's name) is ignored. The tag must start the comment line, so a sentence that merely mentions a TODO is not a marker.

A date that is written is always enforced, whether or not `require_date` is set: it is **expired** from the as-of date on (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date, never the clock: [SR-BASELINE](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md) decision 9) and is a **warning** for the `warn_days` before it. A date that is not a calendar day is reported too. With no as-of date, only the missing and the malformed are reported.

**Why:** A TODO with no ticket has no owner and no place to be tracked, and one with no date never comes due; both outlive the people who wrote them. Naming a ticket ties the comment to the work, and a date makes the comment fail loudly the day it is overdue instead of rotting quietly.

**Configuration** is the `[todo]` table of `codelaw.toml` ([SR-CONFIG](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0110_config.md) decision 11a), one for every language:

```toml
[todo]
tags           = ["TODO", "FIXME", "HACK"]   # the words that open a marker
require_ticket = true                         # a ticket is required (default)
require_date   = false                        # a date is required (default: only a written date is enforced)
ticket_pattern = "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\\d+"        # a whole ticket must match this regular expression
warn_days      = 14                           # warn this many days before the date
```

**A repo full of bare TODOs** gets every one of them at once. Take them into the baseline (`codelaw baseline`) and pay them down, or set `require_ticket = false` and let the rule enforce only the dates that are written.

### How to fix

1. Open or find the ticket for the work and write it in the parentheses: `TODO(ABC-123): …`.
2. When the project asks for a date (`require_date`), or the work has a deadline, add it: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): …`.
3. For an expired marker: do the work and delete the comment; or, if the work really moves, change the date and say why in the text.
4. If the comment is not a to-do, rewrite it so it does not open with the tag.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// TODO: handle the empty cart
function total(cart) {
  return cart.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```js
// TODO(SHOP-214): handle the empty cart
function total(cart) {
  return cart.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
// FIXME: the badge flickers
const Badge = () => <span>new</span>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
// FIXME(UI-87): the badge flickers
const Badge = () => <span>new</span>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/* HACK: widen until the API is typed */
export const load = (id: string): any => fetch(id);
```

##### Do

```ts
/* HACK(API-9): widen until the API is typed */
export const load = (id: string): any => fetch(id);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
// TODO: use the design-system button
export const Save = () => <button>Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
// TODO(UI-31): use the design-system button
export const Save = () => <button>Save</button>;
```
