## `py/literal-membership` — Test membership in a set literal

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a set needs hashable items, which a list did not)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/literal-membership.md

### What it checks

`x in [a, b, c]` and `x in (a, b, c)` with literal items are written `x in {a, b, c}`. The fix covers lists.

**Why:** A set tests membership in constant time and says order does not matter.

## `py/logging-eager-conversion` — No str() on a logging argument

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`%s` already calls `str`; it differs only if the format uses another conversion for that argument)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/logging-eager-conversion.md

### What it checks

An argument after a logging call's format string is not wrapped in `str()` when the format uses only `%s`.

**Why:** Logging formats lazily with `%s`; the call converts eagerly even when the message is not emitted.

### Examples

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python

```

## `py/logging-exc-info` — logger.exception, not error(exc_info=True)

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`exception` must be called from an exception handler, which this keyword implied)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/logging-exc-info.md

### What it checks

Inside an `except` block, `logger.error(..., exc_info=True)` is written `logger.exception(...)`.

**Why:** `exception` says the traceback is attached.

## `py/logging-extra-attr-clash` — A logging extra does not reuse a LogRecord attribute

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the key's new name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/logging-extra-attr-clash.md

### What it checks

A key in a logging call's `extra={...}` (or `extra=dict(...)`) is not one of `LogRecord`'s own attributes — `name`, `msg`, `args`, `module`, `lineno`, `message`, `asctime` and the rest.

**Why:** `logging` raises `KeyError` when an extra key would overwrite a record attribute, so the log call itself fails.

### How to fix

1. Rename the key (`name` → `user_name`) so it no longer collides with a `LogRecord` attribute.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
log.info("login", extra={"name": user})
```

##### Do

```python
log.info("login", extra={"user_name": user})
```

## `py/logging-f-string` — No f-string in a logging call

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (turning `{}` fields into `%s` with arguments rewrites the string)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/logging-f-string.md

### What it checks

A logging call's message is not an f-string.

**Why:** Logging formats lazily, only when the message is emitted; an f-string formats every time, and loses the message template log tools group by.

### How to fix

1. Replace each `{value}` with `%s` and pass the values as arguments after the message.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python
logger.info("user %s", name)
```

## `py/loop-iterator-mutation` — No changing a list while looping over it

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to loop over a copy or build a new list is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/loop-iterator-mutation.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop's iterable is not appended to, removed from or cleared inside the loop.

**Why:** Changing a list while iterating skips or repeats items.

### How to fix

1. Loop over a copy (`for x in list($L):`) or build a new list.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
for item in items:
    if item < 0:
        items.remove(item)
```

##### Do

```python
items = [item for item in items if item >= 0]
```

## `py/loop-variable-overrides-iterator` — A loop variable doesn't replace what it iterates

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/loop-variable-overrides-iterator.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop's target doesn't reuse a name read in the iterable expression.

**Why:** After the loop the name holds the last item, not the collection, which breaks later uses.

### How to fix

1. Give the loop variable its own name.
2. Update its uses in the loop body.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
for items in items:
    print(items)
```

##### Do

```py
for item in items:
    print(item)
```

## `py/lowercase-imported-as-non-lowercase` — A lowercase name is not imported under a capitalised alias

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which alias to give the import is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset


## `py/manual-dict-comprehension` — A loop that only sets keys is a dict comprehension

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the loop becomes `update` with a comprehension; the loop variable is no longer bound after it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/manual-dict-comprehension.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop whose body is only `d[key] = value`, or one `if` holding only that, is written `d.update({key: value for x in items})`.

**Why:** The comprehension says what the loop builds, and runs faster.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
for u in users:
    by_id[u.id] = u
```

##### Do

```python
by_id.update({u.id: u for u in users})
```

### What it checks

`import a.b as b` is written `from a import b`.

**Why:** The `from` form says the same with no alias.


##### Do

## `py/manual-list-comprehension` — A loop that only appends is a comprehension

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the loop becomes `extend` over a generator; the loop variable is no longer bound after it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/manual-list-comprehension.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop whose body is only `result.append(expr)`, or one `if` holding only that, is written `result.extend(expr for x in items)` (with the `if` as the generator's condition). A loop that appends the loop variable itself is `py/manual-list-copy`'s.

**Why:** The comprehension says what the loop builds, and runs faster.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def names(users):
    out = []
    for u in users:
        out.append(u.name)
    return out
```

##### Do

```python
def names(users):
    out = []
    out.extend(u.name for u in users)
    return out
```

## `py/manual-list-copy` — A loop that appends every item is extend

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the loop becomes one `extend` call; the loop variable is no longer bound after it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/manual-list-copy.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop whose body is only `result.append(x)`, `x` being the loop variable, is written `result.extend(items)`.

**Why:** `extend` (or `list(items)`) copies in one call and says so.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
for u in users:
    out.append(u)
```

##### Do

```python
out.extend(users)
```

## `py/map-int-version-parsing` — No map(int, version.split('.'))

- **Fix:** `manual` (the right parser (packaging.version, or a tuple the library exposes) is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/map-int-version-parsing.md

### What it checks

A version string is not parsed with `map(int, v.split("."))`.

**Why:** Versions like `1.2.0rc1` or `2.0.post1` raise ValueError; a version parser handles them.

### How to fix

1. Use `packaging.version.Version(v)`, or a tuple attribute the library already exposes (`version_info`).

## `py/map-without-explicit-strict` — `map()` over several iterables says `strict=`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`strict=` exists only from Python 3.14, and codelaw cannot tell which Python the code runs on: on an older one the added keyword raises `TypeError`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/map-without-explicit-strict.md

### What it checks

`map()` with two or more iterables is called with `strict=True` or `strict=False`.

**Why:** Without it, `map` silently stops at the shortest input. The keyword exists from Python 3.14.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target_version` | `string` | *none* | the oldest Python the code supports; below 3.14 the rule is off |

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys)
```

##### Do

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys, strict=True)
```

##### Fixed

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys, strict=False)
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is `suggest` (`codelaw fix --unsafe`), not `auto`: the `target_version` option may be unset, and on Python before 3.14 the keyword raises `TypeError`.

A literal that approximates π, τ or e to at least two decimals (`3.14`, `6.28`, `2.71`) is written `math.pi`, `math.tau` or `math.e`. The fix covers π.

**Why:** The constant is exact to double precision and says what the number is.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

## `py/max-depth` — Blocks nest no deeper than a maximum

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (flattening nested blocks changes the function's structure; which guard to invert or which block to extract is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-depth.md

### What it checks

Blocks nest at most `max` deep (4 by default; Pylint's `too-many-nested-blocks` allows 5). A block is `if`, `for`, `while`, `try`, `with` or `match`. `elif` and `else` continue their `if` and add no depth. Each `def` starts again at zero, and so does the module's own code. The rule reports on each statement that sits too deep: `Blocks are nested 5 deep (max 4)`.

**Why:** Every level of nesting is another condition a reader must keep in mind to know when a line runs. Deep nesting is also where the bug lives: the `else` that belongs to the wrong `if`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `4` | the most blocks that may nest inside one another in a function |

### How to fix

1. Turn a guard into an early `return`, `continue` or `raise`, so the rest of the function sits one level up.
2. Extract the body of the innermost block into a well-named function.
3. Join a nested pair of `if`s with `and`, or flatten a `with` pair into one `with a, b:`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```py
def f(a):
    if a:
        for x in a:
            if x:
                x()
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```py
def f(a):
    if not a:
        return
    for x in a:
        if x:
            x()
```

## `py/max-lines` — A module stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting a module changes its structure; which names belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-lines.md

### What it checks

A module has at most `max` lines (1000 by default, as Pylint's `too-many-lines`). Blank lines and lines that hold
only a comment are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`; a line that holds code and a
comment counts as code. `skip_docstrings` leaves out the lines of module, class and function docstrings, and
`skip_imports` the top-level import block. The rule reports once, on the first line over the limit, with the measured
count: `1204 lines (max 1000; blank lines and comments not counted)`.

**Why:** A module that long is usually several modules: it is slow to review, and every import of it pays for all of it. The
limit is a prompt to split, not a goal in itself: raise `max` for a module that is long on purpose, or leave generated
code to `[files] lint_generated = false`. Only the host file is measured, never a code block in Markdown.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `1000` | the most lines a module may have |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_docstrings` | `boolean` | `false` | the lines of docstrings do not count |
| `skip_imports` | `boolean` | `false` | the import block does not count |

### How to fix

1. Find a cohesive group of names (one class and its helpers, one feature's functions) and move it to a new module in the same package.
2. Import it back in the old module, or re-export it from the package's `__init__.py`, so callers do not change.
3. If the module is long on purpose, raise `max` for it in an `[[overrides]]` entry, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule py/max-lines`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
a = 1
b = 2
c = 3
d = 4
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
from more import d

a = 1
b = 2
```

## `py/max-lines-per-function` — A function stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (extracting part of a function changes its structure; where to cut and what to call the piece is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-lines-per-function.md

### What it checks

A function (`def` or `async def`, a method included) spans at most `max` lines (50 by default), from its `def` line to
its last. Blank lines, comment-only lines and docstring lines are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines`,
`skip_comments` or `skip_docstrings` is `false`. With `include_nested` (the default) an inner function's lines count
toward the outer function as well; with `include_nested = false` they do not, from the inner `def` to its last
line. `ignore_names` is a regular expression for names to exempt, such as `"^test_"`. The rule reports on the
function's name: `render_orders is 84 lines (max 50)`. A `lambda` is an expression, not a function here.

**Why:** A function that long does several jobs, and its name can say only one. The limit is a prompt to extract, not a goal in
itself: a long table of test data is long on purpose, so exempt it with `ignore_names`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `50` | the most lines one function may span |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_docstrings` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of the function's docstring (and of a nested one's) do not count |
| `include_nested` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of an inner function count toward the outer one too |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; functions named like this are exempt, e.g. "^test_" |

### How to fix

1. Find a block inside the function that does one thing (a loop body, a branch, a run of statements that build one value).
2. Extract it into a well-named function, and pass in what it reads.
3. Repeat until each piece fits `max`. If the function is long on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule py/max-lines-per-function`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
def total(items):
    result = 0
    for item in items:
        result += item
    return result
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
def total(items):
    return sum(items)
```

## `py/max-params` — A function takes at most a maximum number of parameters

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (grouping parameters changes the function's signature and every call to it; which belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-params.md

### What it checks

A function (`def` or `async def`, a method included) takes at most `max` parameters (5 by default, as Pylint and
Ruff). `self` and `cls` are not counted, nor are `*args` and `**kwargs` unless `count_varargs` is `true`, nor a
parameter whose name matches `ignore_names` (`"^_"` by default). A keyword-only parameter counts. `max_positional`
adds a second cap on the parameters a caller can pass by position, those before `*` or `*args`. A method decorated
`@override` and an `@overload` stub are skipped, since you do not own that signature; set `ignore_overrides` or
`ignore_declarations` to `false` to count them. The rule reports on the function's name:
`create_order takes 6 parameters (max 5)`.

**Why:** A call with many positional arguments is easy to get in the wrong order, and every added parameter is a change to every
caller. Grouping related parameters in one object, or making them keyword-only, names them at the call site.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `5` | the most parameters a function may take |
| `max_positional` | `integer` | *none* | a separate cap on positional parameters, those before `*` or `*args` (Ruff PLR0917); none by default |
| `count_varargs` | `boolean` | `false` | count `*args` and `**kwargs` |
| `ignore_self_cls` | `boolean` | `true` | `self` and `cls`, the first parameter of a method, do not count |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | `"^_"` | a regular expression; parameters named like this do not count |
| `ignore_overrides` | `boolean` | `true` | skip a method decorated `@override` or `@typing.override`: its signature is not yours |
| `ignore_declarations` | `boolean` | `true` | skip an `@overload` stub |

### How to fix

1. Group the parameters that belong together into a dataclass or a `TypedDict`: `create_order(Order(customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift))`.
2. Or make the rarely used ones keyword-only with a bare `*`, and set `max_positional` to cap how many a caller passes by position.
3. If the signature is not yours to change, exempt it: an `@override` and an `@overload` stub already are.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def create_order(customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift):
    return (customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift)
```

##### Do

```py
def create_order(order):
    return order
```

## `py/missing-return-type-class-method` — A class method annotates its return type

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (suggest when the function returns no value, annotated `-> None`; one that returns a value is manual: its type is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/missing-return-type-class-method.md

### What it checks

A method marked `@classmethod` has a return annotation.

**Why:** An annotated return type lets a type checker check every caller, and tells the reader what comes back.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

    @classmethod
    def clear(cls):
        cls.store.clear()
```

##### Do

```python

    @classmethod
    def clear(cls) -> None:
        cls.store.clear()
```

## `py/missing-return-type-special-method` — A special method annotates its return type

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (suggest when the function returns no value, annotated `-> None`; one that returns a value is manual: its type is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/missing-return-type-special-method.md

### What it checks

A dunder method (`__init__`, `__enter__`, `__eq__`, …) has a return annotation; `__init__` and the others that return nothing take `-> None`.

**Why:** An annotated return type lets a type checker check every caller, and tells the reader what comes back.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class Store:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path
```

##### Do

```python
class Store:
    def __init__(self, path) -> None:
        self.path = path
```

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

## `py/missing-terminal-punctuation` — A docstring's summary ends with punctuation

```python
def get(user_id):
```
```python
    """Return the user with this id."""
```

## `py/mixed-case-variable-in-class-scope` — Class attributes are not mixedCase

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the attribute is read through instances and the class, here and in other files)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mixed-case-variable-in-class-scope.md

### What it checks

A name assigned in a class body is not mixedCase: `maxRetries = 3` is reported; `max_retries` and `MAX_RETRIES` are not.

**Why:** PEP 8 names attributes in lowercase with underscores; mixedCase is the style of neither a variable nor a constant.

### How to fix

1. Rename the attribute in snake_case and update every place that reads it, in this file and others.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class Client:
    maxRetries = 3
```

##### Do

```python
class Client:
    max_retries = 3
```

## `py/mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope` — Module variables are not mixedCase

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (a module variable can be imported elsewhere, so the rename is a change across files)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope.md

### What it checks

A name assigned at module level is not mixedCase: `defaultTimeout = 5` is reported; `default_timeout` and `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` are not.

**Why:** PEP 8 names module variables in lowercase and constants in capitals; mixedCase is neither.

### How to fix

1. Rename the variable in snake_case (or in capitals for a constant) and update every module that imports it.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
defaultTimeout = 5
```

##### Do

```python
DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5
```

## `py/modified-iterating-dict` — A dict is not resized while it is iterated

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the loop iterates a copy, or collects the keys and changes the dict after)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/modified-iterating-dict.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop over a dict (`d`, `d.keys()`, `d.values()`, `d.items()`) does not add or delete keys of that dict in its body.

**Why:** Python raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`.

### How to fix

1. Iterate over a copy (`list(d)`), or collect the keys and change the dict after the loop.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
for k in cache:
    if stale(k):
        del cache[k]
```

##### Do

```python
for k in list(cache):
    if stale(k):
        del cache[k]
```

## `py/modified-iterating-list` — A list is not changed while it is iterated

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the loop builds a new list, or iterates a copy)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/modified-iterating-list.md

### What it checks

A `for x in items:` loop does not `append`, `remove`, `insert`, `extend` or `pop` on `items` in its body.

**Why:** The loop then skips or repeats items; with `append`, it may never end.

### How to fix

1. Build a new list (a comprehension) or iterate over a copy (`items[:]`).

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
for x in items:
    if not x:
        items.remove(x)
```

##### Do

```python
items = [x for x in items if x]
```

## `py/module-import-not-at-top` — Module-level imports come first

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving an import above other code changes the order the module runs in)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/module-import-not-at-top.md

### What it checks

Module-level imports come before other code. A docstring, `__future__` imports, dunder assignments (`__all__`, `__version__`), `if`/`try`/`with` blocks and changes to `sys.path` or `os.environ` may come before them.

**Why:** Imports scattered through a module hide its dependencies, and code that runs before them can change what they load.

### How to fix

1. Move the import up to the module's import section.
2. If it must run after the code above it, keep it and suppress the finding with a comment saying why.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os

print(os.name)

import sys
```

##### Do

```py
import os
import sys

print(os.name)
```

## `py/multi-line-summary-first-line` — A multi-line docstring's summary starts on the first line

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multi-line-summary-first-line.md

### What it checks

A docstring of more than one line starts its summary right after the opening quotes, not on the next line. It is the opposite convention to `py/multi-line-summary-second-line`; a project turns on one of the two.

**Why:** One place for the summary keeps docstrings consistent; `inspect.getdoc` reads both the same.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def get(user_id):
    """
    Return the user with this id.

    Raises KeyError when there is none.
    """
```

##### Do

```python
def get(user_id):
    """Return the user with this id.

    Raises KeyError when there is none.
    """
```

A docstring of more than one line, whose closing quotes are on their own line, starts its summary on the line after the opening quotes. It is the opposite convention to `py/multi-line-summary-first-line`; a project turns on one of the two.

**Why:** One place for the summary keeps docstrings consistent; `inspect.getdoc` reads both the same.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

    """Return the user with this id.
```

```python
    """
    Return the user with this id.

    Raises KeyError when there is none.
```

## `py/multiple-imports-on-one-line` — One module per `import` statement

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-imports-on-one-line.md

### What it checks

Each `import` statement imports one module; `import os, sys` is split into one line per module.

**Why:** One import per line keeps diffs and merges clean and lets import sorting work line by line.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os, sys
```

##### Do

```py
import os
import sys
```

### Differences from the source

`from module import a, b` is not affected; it imports from one module.

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which target should collect the rest has to be chosen)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-starred-expressions.md

### What it checks

An unpacking assignment has at most one starred target.



## `py/multiple-starts-ends-with` — One startswith with a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the receiver is a plain name, so evaluating it once changes nothing)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-starts-ends-with.md

### What it checks

`s.startswith(a) or s.startswith(b)` is written `s.startswith((a, b))` (and the same for `endswith`).

**Why:** One call takes the tuple of prefixes.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
if name.startswith("a") or name.startswith("b"):
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
if name.startswith(("a", "b")):
    pass
```

## `py/multiple-with-statements` — One with statement, not nested ones

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (merging re-indents the inner body, which a template edit cannot do)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-with-statements.md

### What it checks

A `with` whose whole body is another `with` is written as one `with a, b:`.

**Why:** One statement says the resources are held together, with one level less of indentation.

### How to fix

1. Write both context managers in one `with`, separated by a comma, and dedent the inner body one level.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
with open(a) as src:
    with open(b, "w") as dst:
        dst.write(src.read())
```

##### Do

```python
with open(a) as src, open(b, "w") as dst:
    dst.write(src.read())
```

## `py/mutable-class-default` — Mutable class attribute is ClassVar

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the fix needs `ClassVar` imported, and whether sharing was meant is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mutable-class-default.md

### What it checks

A class attribute whose default is a list, dict or set literal and whose annotation is not `ClassVar` is reported (outside dataclasses, which RUF008 covers).

**Why:** The one value is shared by every instance; annotating it `ClassVar` makes that visible to readers and type checkers.

### How to fix

1. Annotate it `ClassVar[<type>]`, or make it immutable (a tuple or `frozenset`).

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class Registry:
    names: list[str] = []
```

##### Do

```python
class Registry:
    names: ClassVar[list[str]] = []
```

## `py/mutable-contextvar-default` — No mutable `ContextVar` defaults

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to use an immutable value or set a fresh one per context is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mutable-contextvar-default.md

### What it checks

A `ContextVar`'s `default=` isn't a list, dict, set or the result of a call.

**Why:** The default is one object shared by every context, so mutating it leaks state between them.

### How to fix

1. Use an immutable default, or no default and set a fresh value in each context.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from contextvars import ContextVar

items = ContextVar("items", default=[])
```

##### Do

```py
from contextvars import ContextVar

items = ContextVar("items", default=())
```

## `py/mutable-dataclass-default` — No mutable default in a dataclass field

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the fix needs `field` imported, which the file may not do)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mutable-dataclass-default.md

### What it checks

A dataclass field defaults to a fresh list, dict or set through `field(default_factory=…)`, not a literal.

**Why:** A literal default is shared by every instance; dataclasses refuse `list`, `dict` and `set` literals at runtime.

### How to fix

1. Replace the literal with `field(default_factory=list)` (or `dict`, `set`, or a lambda returning the literal).

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
@dataclass
class Cart:
    items: list = []
```

##### Do

```python
@dataclass
class Cart:
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)
```

## `py/mutable-fromkeys-value` — No mutable value in dict.fromkeys

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the comprehension gives each key its own value, which changes behaviour if sharing was relied on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mutable-fromkeys-value.md

### What it checks

`dict.fromkeys(keys, [])` is written as a comprehension, so each key gets its own list.

**Why:** `fromkeys` stores the one value under every key; appending to one appends to all.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
groups = dict.fromkeys(names, [])
```

##### Do

```python
groups = {key: [] for key in names}
```

## `py/named-expr-without-context` — No walrus as a statement

A bare `(x := value)` statement is written `x = value`.

## `py/nan-comparison` — math.isnan, not == nan

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the result changes from always False to the NaN test that was meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/nan-comparison.md

### What it checks

`x == math.nan` is written `math.isnan(x)` (Ruff also reports `!=`, `float("nan")` and `numpy.nan`; those are left out).

**Why:** NaN is not equal to anything, itself included: `==` is always False.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
if x == math.nan:
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
if math.isnan(x):
    pass
```

## `py/native-literals` — Literals, not str() or int() of a literal

- **Fix:** `auto`

### What it checks

`str("x")`, `int(1)`, `float(1.0)`, `bool(True)` and `bytes(b"x")` are written as the literal; `str()` as `""`.

**Why:** The call converts a value to the type it already has.

### Examples

## `py/needless-bool` — Return the condition, not True or False

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`bool(...)` calls `__bool__`, just as the `if` did; the text changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/needless-bool.md

### What it checks

`if cond: return True else: return False` is written `return bool(cond)`.

**Why:** The branches restate the condition.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def ok(x):
    if x > 0:
        return True
    else:
        return False
```

##### Do

```python
def ok(x):
    return bool(x > 0)
```

## `py/needless-else` — No empty else

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/needless-else.md

### What it checks

An `else:` whose body is only `pass` or `...` is removed.

**Why:** It says nothing and makes the reader look for a missing branch.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
    go()

```

##### Do

```python
    go()
```

## `py/negate-equal-op` — a != b, not not a == b

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a class may define `__ne__` differently from `not __eq__`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/negate-equal-op.md

### What it checks

`not a == b` is written `a != b`.

**Why:** The operator says it directly.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
if not x == 1:
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
if x != 1:
    pass
```

## `py/nested-star-import` — `import *` only at module level

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the names to import must be chosen by reading the function)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/nested-star-import.md

### What it checks

`from module import *` appears only at the top level of a module.

**Why:** Inside a function or class a star import is a `SyntaxError` in Python 3.

### How to fix

1. Replace the star with the names the function uses.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def paths():
    from os.path import *
    return join("a", "b")
```

##### Do

```py
def paths():
    from os.path import join
    return join("a", "b")
```

## `py/never-union` — No Never or NoReturn in a union

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the member keeps the type equal; the annotation text changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/never-union.md

### What it checks

`Never` and `NoReturn` are not members of a union; they add nothing to it.

**Why:** `T | Never` is `T`; the extra member suggests a meaning it does not have.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def f(x: int | Never) -> None:
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
def f(x: int) -> None:
    pass
```

## `py/no-bare-except` — No bare `except:`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`except Exception:` no longer catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-bare-except.md

### What it checks

Every `except` clause names the exceptions it handles.

**Why:** A bare `except:` also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, so Ctrl-C and `sys.exit()` stop working inside it.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except:
    log()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except Exception:
    log()
```

### Differences from the source

As in Ruff, a handler whose body re-raises with a bare `raise` is allowed: it doesn't swallow anything.

## `py/no-explicit-stacklevel` — `warnings.warn` sets `stacklevel`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`stacklevel=2` is right for a warning about the caller; deeper helpers need a higher value)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-explicit-stacklevel.md

### What it checks

`warnings.warn()` is called with `stacklevel=` (or `skip_file_prefixes=`).

**Why:** The default `stacklevel=1` points the warning at the line inside your library, not at the caller who needs to change.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import warnings

warnings.warn("old API")
```

##### Do

```py
import warnings

warnings.warn("old API", stacklevel=2)
```

## `py/no-method-argument` — A method takes self

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`self` is added, so the method can be called on an instance; a method meant to be static should say `@staticmethod`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-method-argument.md

### What it checks

A plain method (no `@staticmethod`) has at least one parameter.

**Why:** Calling it on an instance passes the instance, and the call raises TypeError.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class A:
    def ping():
        return 1
```

##### Do

```python
class A:
    def ping(self):
        return 1
```

## `py/no-mutable-default` — No mutable default arguments

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (callers that relied on the shared object, or passed `None` on purpose, behave differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-mutable-default.md

### What it checks

A parameter's default isn't a list, dict or set (literal, comprehension or constructor call).

**Why:** The default is created once, when the function is defined, and every call shares and mutates the same object.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def append(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items
```

##### Do

```py
def append(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is offered only for unannotated parameters whose default doesn't read the parameter's own name; Ruff also rewrites an annotation to `T | None`.

## `py/no-print` — No `print()` in library code

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the log level, and whether the output was meant for the user, need a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-print.md

### What it checks

Code under `src/` reports through `logging`, not `print()`.

**Why:** `print` writes to standard output whether or not the caller wants it; a logger can be filtered, redirected and silenced.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py path=src/app.py
import logging

def run():
    print("started")
```

##### Do

```py path=src/app.py
import logging

def run():
    logging.getLogger(__name__).info("%s", "started")
```

## `py/no-self-argument` — A method's first parameter is self

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the parameter and its uses in the method are renamed)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-self-argument.md

### What it checks

The first parameter of a plain method (no `@staticmethod` or `@classmethod`) is named `self`.

**Why:** Python passes the instance there; another name hides that.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class A:
    def size(this):
        return this.n
```

##### Do

```python
class A:
    def size(self):
        return self.n
```

## `py/no-slots-in-namedtuple-subclass` — namedtuple subclasses define __slots__

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (instances can no longer take attributes of their own; review code that set any)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-slots-in-namedtuple-subclass.md

### What it checks

A class that subclasses a `namedtuple(...)` call defines `__slots__`.

**Why:** Without it every instance carries a `__dict__`, losing the namedtuple's compactness.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class Point(namedtuple("Point", "x y")):
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
class Point(namedtuple("Point", "x y")):
    __slots__ = ()
    pass
```

## `py/no-star-import` — No `from module import *`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which names the module needs can only be found by reading its uses)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-star-import.md

### What it checks

Modules import the names they use explicitly instead of `from module import *`.

**Why:** A star import hides where names come from, can silently replace local names, and stops a linter from finding undefined names.

### How to fix

1. List the names the module uses from the star-imported module.
2. Replace the star with those names.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from os.path import *

print(join("a", "b"))
```

##### Do

```py
from os.path import join

print(join("a", "b"))
```

### Differences from the source

Relative star imports (`from .sub import *`) are not reported: that is how a package re-exports its submodules' API, and Ruff leaves them alone in `__init__.py`.

## `py/no-tunable-literals` — No hard-coded timeouts, limits or thresholds

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which configuration key holds the value is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-tunable-literals.md

### What it checks

A number passed as, defaulted to or assigned to a setting whose name says it is tunable (`timeout`, `retries`, `max_*`, `limit`, `threshold`, `interval`, `delay`, `ttl`, `backoff`, `deadline`, …) comes from configuration, not a literal in the code. `0` and `1` are allowed, and so are module-level `UPPER_CASE` constants, the one place such a value may be written down.

**Why:** Tunable values buried in code can't be changed per environment without a release, and the same number drifts apart in several places.

### How to fix

1. Pick or add a configuration key for the value.
2. Read the value from configuration where it is used.
3. For a fixed protocol constant, name it as a module-level `UPPER_CASE` constant instead.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def fetch(url):
    return get(url, timeout=30)
```

##### Do

```py
from config import settings

def fetch(url):
    return get(url, timeout=settings.http_timeout)
```

## `py/non-ascii-import-name` — Imported names are ASCII

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the ASCII alias is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/non-ascii-import-name.md

### What it checks

An imported module or name, or its alias, is spelt in ASCII.

**Why:** A non-ASCII name may look like another name, and is hard to type for anyone without that keyboard.

### How to fix

1. Import it under an ASCII alias (`as size`).

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python
from shapes import größe as size
```

### What it checks

A name a statement binds — a variable, function, class or parameter — is spelt in ASCII.

## `py/non-augmented-assignment` — x += 1, not x = x + 1

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python

- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/non-augmented-assignment.md

### What it checks

`x = x + y` (and `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `**`, `|`, `&`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`) is written `x += y`. The fix covers `+`.

```python
count += 1
```

## `py/non-empty-init-module` — __init__.py holds imports only

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the code moves (a submodule) is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/non-empty-init-module.md

### What it checks

A package's `__init__.py` defines no functions or classes.

**Why:** Code in `__init__.py` runs on every import of the package and is hard to find; a submodule is clearer.

### How to fix

1. Move the definition to a submodule.
2. Import it in `__init__.py` (and list it in `__all__`).

### Examples


##### Do

## `py/non-lowercase-variable-in-function` — Variables in a function are lowercase

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the local and its uses in the function are renamed; code that reads it through `locals()` or `eval` would not follow)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/non-lowercase-variable-in-function.md

### What it checks

A variable assigned inside a function has no capital letter: `total`, not `Total` or `TOTAL`. An assignment of a `TypeVar`, `ParamSpec`, `TypeVarTuple`, `NewType`, `NamedTuple` or `TypedDict` call, which names a type, is not reported.

**Why:** PEP 8 names variables in lowercase; capitals in a function read as a class or a module constant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def area(w, h):
    Total = w * h
    return Total
```

##### Do

```python
def area(w, h):
    total = w * h
    return total
```

## `py/non-octal-permissions` — File modes are octal

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the decimal literal is rewritten as the octal one it was probably meant to be; review that it was)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/non-octal-permissions.md

### What it checks

A file mode passed to `os.chmod`, `os.mkdir`, `os.makedirs`, `os.open`, `Path.chmod` or `Path.mkdir` is an octal literal (`0o644`), not a decimal one (`644`).

**Why:** `644` in decimal is `0o1204`: a different, usually wrong, set of permissions.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
os.chmod(path, 644)
```

##### Do

```python
os.chmod(path, 0o644)
```

## `py/non-pep646-unpack` — *Ts, not Unpack[Ts]

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python

`*args: Unpack[Ts]` is written `*args: *Ts`, and `tuple[int, Unpack[Ts]]` `tuple[int, *Ts]` (Python 3.11+, PEP 646). `**kwargs: Unpack[Options]` (PEP 692) is not touched, nor `typing.Unpack[...]` written with its module.

## `py/none-comparison` — Compare with `None` using `is`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an object whose `__eq__` treats itself as equal to `None` would compare differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/none-comparison.md

### What it checks

Comparisons with `None` use `is` / `is not`, not `==` / `!=`.

**Why:** `None` is a singleton; `==` calls the other object's `__eq__`, which may not return what you expect.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if user == None:
    login()
```

##### Do

```py
if user is None:
    login()
```

## `py/none-not-at-end-of-union` — None goes last in a union

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a union's order is what `typing.get_args` returns at run time, which code may read; a `None` inside a member (`list[None] | int`) is moved by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/none-not-at-end-of-union.md

### What it checks

In a `|` union, `None` is the last member: `int | str | None`.

**Why:** One place for `None` makes optional types read the same everywhere.

### How to fix

1. Move `None` to the end of the union.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def f(x: None | int) -> None:
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
def f(x: int | None) -> None:
    pass
```

## `py/nonlocal-and-global` — No name both nonlocal and global

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which scope was meant is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/nonlocal-and-global.md

### What it checks

A function does not declare the same name `nonlocal` and `global`.

**Why:** That is a SyntaxError.

### How to fix

1. Keep the declaration for the scope you mean and remove the other.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def outer():
    x = 1
    def inner():
        global x
        nonlocal x
```

##### Do

```python
def outer():
    x = 1
    def inner():
        nonlocal x
```

## `py/not-in-test` — Write `x not in y`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/not-in-test.md

### What it checks

A membership test is negated as `x not in y`, not `not x in y`.

**Why:** `not x in y` reads as `(not x) in y`; `not in` says what is meant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if not item in seen:
    keep(item)
```

##### Do

```py
if item not in seen:
    keep(item)
```

## `py/not-is-test` — Write `x is not y`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/not-is-test.md

### What it checks

An identity test is negated as `x is not y`, not `not x is y`.

**Why:** `not x is y` reads as `(not x) is y`; `is not` says what is meant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if not value is None:
    use(value)
```

##### Do

```py
if value is not None:
    use(value)
```

- **Fix:** `auto`

## `py/open-alias` — open(), not io.open()

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/open-alias.md

### What it checks

`io.open` is written `open`.

**Why:** In Python 3 they are the same function.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python

```

## `py/open-file-with-context-handler` — Open files in a with statement

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the code that uses the file moves into the `with` block)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/open-file-with-context-handler.md

### What it checks

A file opened with `open()` and assigned to a name is opened in a `with` statement instead.

**Why:** `with` closes the file even when an exception is raised; a bare `open` leaks it until garbage collection.

### How to fix

1. Write `with open(...) as f:` and move the code that uses `f` into the block.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
f = open("data.txt")
data = f.read()
```

##### Do

```python
with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()
```

## `py/os-chmod` — pathlib, not os.chmod

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the result is a `Path` (or uses one), and `pathlib` must be imported; review code that expects a string)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/os-chmod.md

### What it checks

`os.chmod()` is written with `pathlib`: `Path.chmod`.

**Why:** `pathlib` keeps paths as objects, and its methods compose; mixing the two styles makes path code harder to read.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
x = os.chmod("data/a.txt", 0o644)
```

##### Do

```python
x = pathlib.Path("data/a.txt").chmod(0o644)
```

## `py/os-error-alias` — OSError, not its aliases

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/os-error-alias.md

### What it checks

`IOError`, `EnvironmentError`, `WindowsError`, `socket.error`, `select.error` and `mmap.error` are written `OSError`.

**Why:** They are all aliases of `OSError` since Python 3.3.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
try:
    load()
except IOError:
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
try:
    load()
except OSError:
    pass
```

## `py/os-path-commonprefix` — os.path.commonpath, not commonprefix

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`commonpath` compares whole path components and raises on mixed absolute and relative paths)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/os-path-commonprefix.md

```python

```

## `py/os-path-splitext` — pathlib, not os.path.splitext

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the code moves to `pathlib`, whose objects and methods differ from the strings it used)

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python
ext = Path(path).suffix
```

**Why:** `pathlib` keeps paths as objects, and its methods compose; mixing the two styles makes path code harder to read.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python

```

##### Do

```python
x = pathlib.Path("data/a.txt").unlink()
```

## `py/overlapping-except` — An except tuple does not list an exception twice over

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the broad or the narrow name was meant is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/overlapping-except.md

### What it checks

An `except (A, B)` tuple does not list `Exception` (or `BaseException`) beside another exception it already covers.

**Why:** The narrower name is dead; the tuple reads as if it were handled separately.

### How to fix

1. Keep the exceptions the handler is meant for, and drop the ones another already covers.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
try:
    run()
except (ValueError, Exception):
    pass
```

##### Do

```python
try:
    run()
except Exception:
    pass
```

```python
    ...
```

## `py/parenthesize-chained-operators` — Parenthesize `and` inside `or`

## `py/patch-version-comparison` — A version check in a stub compares major and minor only

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which minor version the declaration belongs to is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/patch-version-comparison.md

### What it checks

A stub compares `sys.version_info` with a tuple of at most two numbers: `(3, 10)`, not `(3, 10, 2)`.

**Why:** Type checkers ignore the patch level, so a three-part check does not mean what it says.

### How to fix

1. Compare with `(major, minor)` only, picking the first minor version the declaration holds for.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python path=api.pyi
if sys.version_info >= (3, 10, 2):
    def f() -> None: ...
```

##### Do

```python path=api.pyi
if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
    def f() -> None: ...
```

## `py/pep484-style-positional-only-parameter` — Positional-only parameters use /

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the parameter is renamed and a `/` placed after the last positional-only one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pep484-style-positional-only-parameter.md

### What it checks

A stub marks positional-only parameters with `/`, not with PEP 484's double-underscore prefix (`def f(__x)`).

**Why:** `/` is the syntax for it since Python 3.8; the prefix is a convention only type checkers understand.

### How to fix

1. Rename the parameters without the `__` prefix and put `/` after the last positional-only one.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python path=api.pyi

```

##### Do

```python path=api.pyi

```

## `py/percent-format-count-mismatch` — A `%` format string gets one value per placeholder

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value is missing, or extra, can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-count-mismatch.md

### What it checks

The tuple (or single literal) formatted into a `%` string has as many values as the string has positional placeholders.

**Why:** Too few values raise `TypeError: not enough arguments`; too many raise `TypeError: not all arguments converted`.

### How to fix

1. Add or remove values, or placeholders, until they match.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%s is %s" % ("Ada",)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s is %s" % ("Ada", 36)
```

## `py/percent-format-expected-mapping` — Named `%` placeholders get a mapping

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the key each value belongs to isn't written anywhere)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-expected-mapping.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string with named placeholders (`%(name)s`) is applied to a mapping, not a tuple.

**Why:** Python raises `TypeError: format requires a mapping`.

### How to fix

1. Pass a dict whose keys are the placeholder names.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s" % ("Ada",)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

## `py/percent-format-expected-sequence` — Positional `%` placeholders get a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the order of the values isn't written anywhere)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-expected-sequence.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string with two or more positional placeholders is applied to a tuple, not a dict.

**Why:** A dict is a single value, so Python raises `TypeError: not enough arguments`.

### How to fix

1. Pass a tuple with one value per placeholder, or switch to named placeholders.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%s and %s" % {"a": 1, "b": 2}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s and %s" % (1, 2)
```

## `py/percent-format-invalid` — A `%` format string is complete

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended placeholder can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-invalid.md

### What it checks

A string formatted with `%` has no unfinished placeholder such as `%(name` or a trailing `%`.

**Why:** Python raises `ValueError` when the string is formatted.

### How to fix

1. Finish the placeholder (`%(name)s`) or escape a literal percent as `%%`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

## `py/percent-format-missing-argument` — Every named `%` placeholder has a value

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the value for the missing key has to be supplied)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-missing-argument.md

### What it checks

A dict literal formatted into a `%` string has a key for every named placeholder.

**Why:** A missing key raises `KeyError` when the string is formatted.

1. Add the missing key to the dict, or remove the placeholder.

### Examples

#### Python

## `py/percent-format-mixed-placeholders` — A `%` format string doesn't mix positional and named placeholders

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which style the string should use is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-mixed-placeholders.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string uses either positional placeholders (`%s`) or named ones (`%(name)s`), not both.

**Why:** Python can't fill both from one right-hand side and raises `TypeError`.

### How to fix

1. Name every placeholder, or make every placeholder positional.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s is %s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s is %(age)s" % {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
```

## `py/percent-format-star-requires-sequence` — A `*` width in a `%` format takes a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the order of the values has to be decided)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-star-requires-sequence.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string using `*` for a width or precision is applied to a tuple.

**Why:** The `*` takes its value from the next positional argument, which a mapping doesn't have.

### How to fix

1. Pass a tuple with the width before the value.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py

```

##### Do

```py
message = "%*d" % (5, 1)
```

## `py/percent-format-unsupported-character` — A `%` format uses known conversions

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended conversion can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-unsupported-character.md

### What it checks

Each `%` placeholder ends with a conversion Python knows (`s`, `r`, `a`, `d`, `f`, `x`, …).

**Why:** An unknown conversion raises `ValueError: unsupported format character`.

### How to fix

1. Use the conversion you meant, or escape a literal percent as `%%`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py

```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s" % (1,)
```

## `py/post-init-default` — No defaults on __post_init__ parameters

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the default belongs on the `InitVar` field, which moves it to the class body)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/post-init-default.md

### What it checks

A dataclass's `__post_init__` gives its parameters no default value.

**Why:** `__post_init__` is called with every `InitVar`, so the default is never used; the default belongs on the field.

### How to fix

1. Remove the default here and give the matching `InitVar` field the default: `x: InitVar[int] = 1`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
@dataclass
class A:
    x: InitVar[int]
    def __post_init__(self, x=1):
        pass
```

##### Do

```python
@dataclass
class A:
    x: InitVar[int] = 1
    def __post_init__(self, x):
        pass
```

## `py/printf-in-get-text-func-call` — No % formatting inside a gettext call

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`%` moves outside the call; a catalogue entry under the old filled-in text, if any, no longer matches)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/printf-in-get-text-func-call.md

### What it checks

`_("…" % args)` is written `_("…") % args`, so the template is translated, then filled in.

**Why:** Translators translate the template; formatting first hands the catalogue a different string every time.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
msg = _("Hello, %s" % name)
```

##### Do

```python
msg = _("Hello, %s") % name
```

## `py/private-member-access` — No access to another object's private members

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the owner should expose instead is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/private-member-access.md

### What it checks

An attribute whose name starts with one underscore is read or written only on `self`, `cls` or `mcs`, or through `super()`. Dunder names, and the names in `ignore_names` (namedtuple's and enum's public `_make`, `_asdict`, `_replace`, `_fields`, `_field_defaults`, `_name_`, `_value_` by default), are not reported.

**Why:** A leading underscore marks a member as the class's own; code outside it that relies on one breaks when the class changes.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignore_names` | `string[]` | `["_make", "_asdict", "_replace", "_fields", "_field_defaults", "_name_", "_value_"]` | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Use the object's public interface, or give its class a public method or property for what the code needs.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def total(cart):
    return cart._items_total()
```

##### Do

```python
def total(cart):
    return cart.items_total()
```

## `py/property-with-parameters` — A property takes only self

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the property becomes a method, and every read of it a call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/property-with-parameters.md

### What it checks

A method marked `@property` takes no parameter besides `self`.

**Why:** A property is read as `obj.name`; there is no way to pass it an argument.

### How to fix

1. Make it a plain method and call it, or move the parameter onto the object.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class A:
    @property
    def size(self, unit):
        return self.n
```

##### Do

```python
class A:
    def size(self, unit):
        return self.n
```

## `py/property-without-return` — A property returns a value

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the property returns is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/property-without-return.md

### What it checks

A function decorated `@property` contains a `return` with a value, a `raise` or a `yield` (stubs whose body is `...` or `pass` are left alone).

**Why:** Without one, every read of the attribute gives `None`.

### How to fix

1. Return the value the attribute should have.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
class A:
    @property
    def size(self):
        self._size
```

##### Do

```python
class A:
    @property
    def size(self):
        return self._size
```

## `py/py-path` — pathlib, not py.path

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the code moves to `pathlib`, whose objects and methods differ from the strings it used)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/py-path.md

### What it checks

`py.path.local(...)`, from the `py` library, is written with `pathlib.Path`.

**Why:** `pathlib` keeps paths as objects with their own operations, one API instead of several string functions.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite it with `pathlib.Path`, importing `pathlib.Path`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
p = py.path.local(tmpdir)
```

##### Do

```python
p = Path(tmpdir)
```

## `py/pytest-assert-always-false` — pytest.fail, not assert False

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the message that says why the test fails is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-assert-always-false.md

### What it checks

A test does not fail with an assertion that is always false — `assert False`, `assert 0`, `assert None`, `assert ""`, an empty list, tuple or dict — but with `pytest.fail("why")`.

**Why:** An always-false assert reads like a check, and Python drops it under `-O`.

### How to fix

1. Replace the assert with `pytest.fail("<why the test fails>")`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def test_x():
    assert False
```

##### Do

```python
def test_x():
    pytest.fail("the parser accepted an empty file")
```

## `py/pytest-assert-in-except` — No assert on the exception inside except

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the test is rewritten around `pytest.raises`, which holds the exception)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-assert-in-except.md

### What it checks

An `assert` inside an `except` block does not check the caught exception: use `pytest.raises` and assert on `excinfo` after the block.

**Why:** If nothing is raised, the `except` block never runs and the test passes.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the call in `with pytest.raises(Error) as excinfo:` and assert on `excinfo.value` after the block.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def test_parse():
    try:
        parse("")
    except ValueError as e:
        assert "empty" in str(e)
```

##### Do

```python
def test_parse():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError) as excinfo:
        parse("")
    assert "empty" in str(excinfo.value)
```

## `py/pytest-composite-assertion` — One condition per assert

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the assert is split into one per condition, each on its own line at the assert's indentation)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-composite-assertion.md

### What it checks

An `assert a and b` is written as two asserts, `assert a` and `assert b`, and `assert not (a or b)` as `assert not a` and `assert not b`.

**Why:** A failing composite assert does not say which part failed.

### How to fix

1. Split the assert into one assert per condition.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def test_user():
    assert user.active and user.admin
```

##### Do

```python
def test_user():
    assert user.active
    assert user.admin
```

## `py/pytest-duplicate-parametrize-test-cases` — No duplicate parametrize cases

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the repeated case is removed; it ran the same test twice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-duplicate-parametrize-test-cases.md

### What it checks

A `pytest.mark.parametrize` list holds each case once.

```python
    assert n
```

`pytest.fail()` is given a message saying why: not no argument, and not an empty string.

## `py/pytest-fixture-finalizer-callback` — A fixture tears down after yield, not with addfinalizer

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the fixture's body is rewritten around a `yield`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-fixture-finalizer-callback.md

### What it checks

A fixture cleans up after `yield`, not by registering a callback with `request.addfinalizer`.

**Why:** A yield fixture reads in order — set up, hand over, tear down — and its cleanup runs only if the setup succeeded.

### How to fix

1. Replace `return value` with `yield value`, and move the finalizer's body after the `yield`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
@pytest.fixture
def db(request):
    conn = connect()
    request.addfinalizer(conn.close)
    return conn
```

##### Do

```python
@pytest.fixture
def db():
    conn = connect()
    yield conn
    conn.close()
```

A fixture with no arguments is decorated `@pytest.fixture`, without empty parentheses.

## `py/pytest-fixture-param-without-value` — A fixture used only for its effect is in usefixtures

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the parameter moves into a `@pytest.mark.usefixtures` decorator)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/pytest-fixture-param-without-value.md

### What it checks

A test's parameter whose name starts with `_` — a fixture the test needs only for its side effect — is requested with `@pytest.mark.usefixtures("_name")` instead.

**Why:** A parameter the test never reads looks like a mistake; `usefixtures` says it is wanted for its effect.

### How to fix

1. Remove the parameter and add `@pytest.mark.usefixtures("<name>")` above the test.

```python

```

##### Do

```python
@pytest.mark.usefixtures("_db")
def test_query(user):
    assert user.name
```

## `py/pytest-incorrect-pytest-import` — pytest is imported as pytest
