
##### Do

```tsx
Card.propTypes = { size: sizeShape };
```

## `react/forbid-prop-types` — No PropTypes.any, array or object

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the precise type — `arrayOf(…)`, `shape({…})` — is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/forbid-prop-types.md

### What it checks

`propTypes` don't use the vague `PropTypes.any`, `PropTypes.array` or `PropTypes.object`.

**Why:** A vague prop type validates almost nothing; `arrayOf` and `shape` say what's expected.

### How to fix

1. Use `PropTypes.arrayOf(…)`, `PropTypes.shape({…})` or `PropTypes.objectOf(…)` with the real element type.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.array };
```

##### Do

```js
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.arrayOf(PropTypes.string) };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.array };
```

##### Do

```jsx
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.arrayOf(PropTypes.string) };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.array };
```

##### Do

```tsx
List.propTypes = { items: PropTypes.arrayOf(PropTypes.string) };
```

## `react/forward-ref-uses-ref` — A forwardRef callback takes the ref

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (adding the `ref` parameter is what the wrapper is for, but the author still has to attach it, or drop `forwardRef` instead)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/forward-ref-uses-ref.md

### What it checks

The function passed to `forwardRef` takes a second parameter, the ref.

**Why:** `forwardRef` around a function that ignores the ref forwards nothing; either use the ref or drop the wrapper.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const Input = forwardRef((props) => <input {...props} />);
```

##### Do

```js
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input ref={ref} {...props} />);
```

##### Fixed

```js
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input {...props} />);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const Input = forwardRef((props) => <input {...props} />);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input ref={ref} {...props} />);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input {...props} />);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const Input = forwardRef((props) => <input {...props} />);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input ref={ref} {...props} />);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => <input {...props} />);
```

## `react/function-component-definition` — Named components are function declarations

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the arrow is rewritten as a declaration, with its body, its type annotation and its export)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/function-component-definition.md

### What it checks

A named component is written as a function declaration (`function Card() {…}`), not as an arrow function or function expression assigned to a constant.

**Why:** One shape for components; a declaration is hoisted and shows its name in stack traces without inference.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite `const $N = (props) => …` as `function $N(props) { return …; }`, keeping the export.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const Card = ({ title }) => <h2>{title}</h2>;
```

##### Do

```js
function Card({ title }) {
  return <h2>{title}</h2>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const Card = ({ title }) => <h2>{title}</h2>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Card({ title }) {
  return <h2>{title}</h2>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const Card = ({ title }) => <h2>{title}</h2>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Card({ title }) {
  return <h2>{title}</h2>;
}
```

## `react/globals` — Render doesn't change module-level or global values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the change belongs — state, a ref, an effect, an event — depends on what the value is for)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/globals.md

### What it checks

A component or hook doesn't assign, increment or set a property of a value declared outside
it — a module-level variable or a global such as `window` — in its own body. Changes made in
effects, event handlers and other callbacks are fine.

**Why:** React may render a component any number of times, in any order, and throw renders away; a module-level value changed during render changes a different number of times than the component appears to render, and leaks between components and requests.

### How to fix

1. If the value belongs to the component, keep it in state or a ref.
2. If it must change outside React, change it in an effect or an event handler.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
let renders = 0;

function useRenderCount() {
  renders += 1;
  return renders;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useRenderCount() {
  const renders = useRef(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    renders.current += 1;
  });
  return renders;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Page({ title }) {
  window.pageTitle = title;
  return <h1>{title}</h1>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Page({ title }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    window.pageTitle = title;
  }, [title]);
  return <h1>{title}</h1>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const seen: Record<string, boolean> = {};

function useSeen(id: string) {
  seen[id] = true;
  return Object.keys(seen).length;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
const seen: Record<string, boolean> = {};

function useSeen(id: string) {
  useEffect(() => {
    seen[id] = true;
  }, [id]);
  return id in seen;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Page({ title }: { title: string }) {
  window.pageTitle = title;
  return <h1>{title}</h1>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Page({ title }: { title: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    window.pageTitle = title;
  }, [title]);
  return <h1>{title}</h1>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- Only assignments, `+=`-style updates and `++` / `--` are reported; upstream also reports mutating method calls on a global array (`list.push(x)`), which needs to know the value is an array.
- Changes in a function the component calls during render are not followed.

## `react/hook-prefix` — Functions that call hooks are named use…

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (every caller of the function must be renamed too)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/hook-prefix.md

### What it checks

A function that isn't a component (PascalCase) and calls a hook is a custom hook, and is named
`use…`.

**Why:** React and its tools recognise hooks by the `use` prefix; without it the Rules of Hooks
can't be checked for the function's callers.

### How to fix

1. Rename the function to start with `use` (e.g. `loadUser` → `useUser`).
2. Rename its callers.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function currentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useCurrentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function currentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function useCurrentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function currentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useCurrentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function currentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function useCurrentUser() {
  return useContext(UserContext);
}
```

## `react/hook-use-state` — useState is destructured as [value, setValue]

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the names are the author's; a template cannot recase the value's name into the setter's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/hook-use-state.md

### What it checks

The result of `useState` is destructured into exactly two names, the second starting with `set` (`const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)`). That the setter repeats the value's name is not checked yet.

**Why:** The pair naming makes the setter findable from the value, and the reverse.

### How to fix

1. Write `const [thing, setThing] = useState(…)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function T() {
  const state = useState(false);
  return state[0];
}
```

##### Do

```js
function T() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return open;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function T() {
  const state = useState(false);
  return state[0];
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function T() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return open;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function T() {
  const state = useState(false);
  return state[0];
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function T() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return open;
}
```

## `react/iframe-missing-sandbox` — An <iframe> has a sandbox

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an empty `sandbox` blocks scripts, forms and same-origin access in the frame, which a page that needs them must loosen by name)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/iframe-missing-sandbox.md

### What it checks

Every `<iframe>` has a `sandbox` attribute.

**Why:** An unsandboxed frame runs its scripts with the full rights the browser gives its origin.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const f = <iframe src={url} title="Map" />;
```

##### Do

```js
const f = <iframe sandbox="" src={url} title="Map" />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const f = <iframe src={url} title="Map" />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const f = <iframe sandbox="" src={url} title="Map" />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const f = <iframe src={url} title="Map" />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const f = <iframe sandbox="" src={url} title="Map" />;
```

## `react/immutability` — Props and state are never mutated

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the change becomes a new value — a copy passed to the state setter, or a callback to the parent that owns the prop)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/immutability.md

### What it checks

A component or hook does not assign to, or call a mutating method (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, …) on, its props or a value it got from `useState` or `useReducer`.

**Why:** React compares by reference: a mutated value looks unchanged, so the screen doesn't update, and memoised values go stale.

### How to fix

1. Build a new value (`[...items, item]`, `{ ...user, name }`) and pass it to the state setter.
2. For a prop, call a callback the parent passes so the owner makes the change.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function List({ items }) {
  items.push("x");
  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function List({ items }) {
  const all = [...items, "x"];
  return <ul>{all.length}</ul>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  items.push("x");
  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  const all = [...items, "x"];
  return <ul>{all.length}</ul>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function List({ items }) {
  items.push("x");
  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function List({ items }) {
  const all = [...items, "x"];
  return <ul>{all.length}</ul>;
}
```

## `react/incompatible-library` — No library API that defeats memoisation

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the component either opts out of compilation or reads the value through the library's memo-safe API)
- **Severity when named:** `warn` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/incompatible-library.md

### What it checks

A component does not use library APIs that return functions or objects whose results change without their identity changing, which automatic memoisation cannot follow: TanStack Table's `useReactTable`, TanStack Virtual's `useVirtualizer` and `useWindowVirtualizer`, and React Hook Form's `watch` taken from `useForm`.

**Why:** The React Compiler memoises by identity; these APIs mutate in place, so memoised output goes stale.

### How to fix

1. Add the `"use no memo"` directive to the component, or use the library's memo-safe API (`useWatch` for React Hook Form).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { watch } = useForm();
  return watch("name");
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useForm, useWatch } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { control } = useForm();
  return useWatch({ control, name: "name" });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { watch } = useForm();
  return watch("name");
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useForm, useWatch } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { control } = useForm();
  return useWatch({ control, name: "name" });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { watch } = useForm();
  return watch("name");
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useForm, useWatch } from "react-hook-form";
function F() {
  const { control } = useForm();
  return useWatch({ control, name: "name" });
}
```

## `react/jsx-boolean-value` — A true prop is written bare

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`

A prop set to `{true}` is written as the bare prop name: `<Input disabled />`.

**Why:** `disabled` and `disabled={true}` mean the same; one spelling reads faster.

```js
const i = <Input disabled />;
```



## `react/jsx-child-element-spacing` — No inline element glued to text across a line break

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: whether the words were meant to run together is the author's; a `{" "}` changes the rendered text)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-child-element-spacing.md

### What it checks

An inline element (`<a>`, `<strong>`, …) is not separated from neighbouring text only by a line break: JSX drops that whitespace, so the two render glued together.

**Why:** `<b>Hi</b>` on one line and `there` on the next renders `Hithere`, which the source does not show.

### How to fix

1. Put `{" "}` where a space is meant, or join the lines if no space is.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>
    there
  </p>
);
```

##### Do

```js
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>{" "}
    there
  </p>
);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>
    there
  </p>
);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>{" "}
    there
  </p>
);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>
    there
  </p>
);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const t = (
  <p>
    <b>Hi</b>{" "}
    there
  </p>
);
```

## `react/jsx-curly-brace-presence` — No braces around a plain string prop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-curly-brace-presence.md

### What it checks

A prop whose value is a string literal in braces (`title={"Save"}`) is written as a plain attribute string (`title="Save"`). Strings with a backslash or a newline are left alone, since an attribute string reads them differently.

**Why:** The braces add nothing to a fixed string, and the plain form is what the rest of the markup uses.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const b = <Button title={"Save"} />;
```

##### Do

```js
const b = <Button title="Save" />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const b = <Button title={"Save"} />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const b = <Button title="Save" />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const b = <Button title={"Save"} />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const b = <Button title="Save" />;
```

## `react/jsx-filename-extension` — JSX lives in .jsx and .tsx files

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the file is renamed, and every import of it follows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-filename-extension.md

### What it checks

A `.js` file contains no JSX; JSX goes in a `.jsx` file (or `.tsx`). The rule reports the file once.

**Why:** The extension tells tools and readers that the file needs a JSX transform.

### How to fix

1. Rename the file to `.jsx`.
2. Update the imports that name the extension.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js path=src/Button.js
export const Button = () => <button type="button" />;
```

##### Do

```js path=src/Button.js
export const label = "Save";
```

## `react/jsx-fragments` — <>…</> rather than <React.Fragment>

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-fragments.md

### What it checks

A fragment with no `key` is written with the short syntax `<>…</>`, not `<React.Fragment>…</React.Fragment>` or `<Fragment>…</Fragment>`.

**Why:** The short syntax is the same fragment with less to read.

```js
const l = <><A /><B /></>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const l = <React.Fragment><A /><B /></React.Fragment>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const l = <><A /><B /></>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const l = <React.Fragment><A /><B /></React.Fragment>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const l = <><A /><B /></>;
```

## `react/jsx-handler-names` — Handlers are named handle…, handler props on…

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the new method name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-handler-names.md

### What it checks

A prop named `on…` is given a method named `handle…` (`onClick={this.handleClick}`), and a `handle…` method is passed only to a prop named `on…`. Handlers passed through from props (`this.props.onClick`) are fine.

**Why:** The two prefixes say at a glance which side of an event a name is on: the prop that receives it, the method that handles it.

### How to fix

1. Rename the method to `handle<Event>`, or the prop to `on<Event>`, so the two prefixes match.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.save}>Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```js
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.handleSave}>Save</button>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.save}>Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.handleSave}>Save</button>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.save}>Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const b = <button type="button" onClick={this.handleSave}>Save</button>;
```

## `react/jsx-key` — Elements in an array or a map() callback have a key

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the key must be a stable identity of the item, which only the author knows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-key.md

### What it checks

An element written in an array literal, or returned by a `.map()` callback, has a `key` prop.

**Why:** Without keys, React can't match list items between renders, which loses state and re-
renders more than it must.

### How to fix

1. Give the element a `key` that identifies the item, such as its id.
2. Avoid the array index if items can be reordered or removed.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li>{todo.text}</li>);
```

##### Do

```js
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li key={todo.id}>{todo.text}</li>);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li>{todo.text}</li>);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li key={todo.id}>{todo.text}</li>);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li>{todo.text}</li>);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const items = todos.map((todo) => <li key={todo.id}>{todo.text}</li>);
```

### Differences from the source

Elements returned from a `.map()` callback's block body (`return <li/>`) are not checked yet.

## `react/jsx-no-bind` — No new function in a JSX prop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the function moves out of render, into a method or a `useCallback` with its dependencies)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-bind.md

### What it checks

A JSX prop is not given a function created in place: an arrow function, a function expression, or a `.bind(…)` call.

**Why:** A new function on every render gives a memoised child a new prop each time, so it re-renders anyway.

### How to fix

1. Define the handler once: a class method, or a `useCallback` in a function component.
2. Pass it by name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const r = <Row onClick={() => select(id)} />;
```

##### Do

```js
const r = <Row onClick={handleSelect} />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const r = <Row onClick={() => select(id)} />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const r = <Row onClick={handleSelect} />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const r = <Row onClick={() => select(id)} />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const r = <Row onClick={handleSelect} />;
```

## `react/jsx-no-comment-textnodes` — No comment syntax as text inside JSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (whether the text is a comment or content needs the author, so both are offered: wrapped as a JSX comment, or kept as text in a string)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-comment-textnodes.md

### What it checks

**Why:** In JSX, `// note` is text that ends up on the page.

```js
const a = <div>

  <h1>Hi</h1>
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <div>

</div>;
```

##### Fixed (comment)

```js
const a = <div>
  {/* the title */}
  <h1>Hi</h1>
</div>;
```

##### Fixed (text)

```js
const a = <div>
  {"// the title"}
  <h1>Hi</h1>
</div>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <div>
  // the title
  <h1>Hi</h1>
</div>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <div>
  {/* the title */}
  <h1>Hi</h1>
</div>;
```

##### Fixed (comment)

```jsx
const a = <div>

</div>;
```

##### Fixed (text)

```jsx

  {"// the title"}
  <h1>Hi</h1>
</div>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
</div>;
```

##### Do

##### Fixed (comment)

##### Fixed (text)

## `react/jsx-no-constructed-context-values` — A context value is not rebuilt on every render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the value is memoised with `useMemo` (or hoisted), and its dependencies are the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-constructed-context-values.md

### What it checks

The `value` of a `<Context.Provider>` is not an object, array, function or `new` expression written in place.

**Why:** A new value on every render re-renders every consumer of the context, changed or not.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the value in `useMemo` with its dependencies, or hoist it out of the component if it never changes.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const p = <Theme.Provider value={{ mode, toggle }}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

##### Do

```js
const p = <Theme.Provider value={theme}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const p = <Theme.Provider value={{ mode, toggle }}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const p = <Theme.Provider value={theme}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const p = <Theme.Provider value={{ mode, toggle }}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const p = <Theme.Provider value={theme}>{children}</Theme.Provider>;
```

## `react/jsx-no-duplicate-props` — No prop given twice on one element

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (the earlier of two props never takes effect, since the last one wins; it goes, automatically, when its value is a literal or a name, which nothing evaluates to any effect. An earlier value that calls something is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-duplicate-props.md

### What it checks

A JSX element gives each prop once.

**Why:** The last value silently wins, so the first is dead code or a mistake.

### How to fix

1. Keep the value that is right and remove the other.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <input type="text" type="email" />;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <input type="email" />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <input type="text" type="email" />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <input type="email" />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <input type="text" type="email" />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <input type="email" />;
```

## `react/jsx-no-jsx-as-prop` — No JSX element built in a component's prop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (hoisting or memoising the element moves code out of the render)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-jsx-as-prop.md

### What it checks

A component's prop isn't a JSX element written in place: `<Card icon={<Star />} />`.

## `react/jsx-no-leaked-render` — No && that can render 0 or ""

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a ternary renders nothing where `&&` rendered `0` or `""`, which is the intent but is a visible change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-leaked-render.md

### What it checks

A JSX child is not written `{x && <El />}` with a left side that may be a number or a string: `0 && …` renders `0`. A left side that is already a boolean — `!x`, a comparison, `Boolean(x)` — is fine.

**Why:** `{count && <Badge />}` shows a stray `0` when the count is zero, and on React Native it crashes.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const l = <ul>{count && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Do

```js
const l = <ul>{count > 0 && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const l = <ul>{count ? <Badge n={count} /> : null}</ul>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const l = <ul>{count && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const l = <ul>{count > 0 && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const l = <ul>{count ? <Badge n={count} /> : null}</ul>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const l = <ul>{count && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const l = <ul>{count > 0 && <Badge n={count} />}</ul>;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const l = <ul>{count ? <Badge n={count} /> : null}</ul>;
```

## `react/jsx-no-literals` — No bare text in JSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the text moves into the project's message catalogue under a key the author chooses)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-literals.md

### What it checks

JSX holds no literal text between tags; text comes from an expression, such as a translation call.

**Why:** Bare strings in markup are what makes a UI hard to translate later; this rule is for projects that translate.

### How to fix

1. Add the text to the project's message catalogue under a key.
2. Render it with the project's translation call, e.g. `{t("save")}`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const b = <button type="button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```js
const b = <button type="button">{t("save")}</button>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const b = <button type="button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const b = <button type="button">{t("save")}</button>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const b = <button type="button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const b = <button type="button">{t("save")}</button>;
```

## `react/jsx-no-script-url` — No javascript: URLs in JSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (security: the code the URL runs has to become a real handler)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-script-url.md

### What it checks

No JSX attribute is set to a `javascript:` URL.

**Why:** React 19 blocks these URLs, and before that they were an injection path; a click handler does the same job safely.

### How to fix

1. Move the code into an `onClick` handler.
2. Give the link a real `href`, or make it a `<button type="button">`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <a href="javascript:void(0)">Open</a>;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <button type="button" onClick={open}>Open</button>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <a href="javascript:void(0)">Open</a>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <button type="button" onClick={open}>Open</button>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <a href="javascript:void(0)">Open</a>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <button type="button" onClick={open}>Open</button>;
```

## `react/jsx-no-target-blank` — Links that open a new tab set rel="noreferrer"

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-no-target-blank.md

### What it checks

An `<a target="_blank">` with an `href` also has `rel="noreferrer"`.

**Why:** Without it, older browsers give the opened page a handle on this one (`window.opener`), and
the referrer leaks.

### Examples

```js
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank">Docs</a>;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Docs</a>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank">Docs</a>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Docs</a>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank">Docs</a>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <a href={url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Docs</a>;
```

### Differences from the source

A link that already has a `rel` is not checked.

## `react/jsx-no-undef` — Components used in JSX are declared

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right import is the author's to choose)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`

```js
import { Header } from "./header";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export const App = () => <Header />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { Header } from "./header";
export const App = () => <Header />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX

##### Do

```tsx

```

## `react/jsx-pascal-case` — Component names are PascalCase

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the new name is the author's, and every import of the component follows it)

A component named in JSX is PascalCase: no underscores (`<User_Card>`) and not all capitals (`<USERCARD>`).

**Why:** JSX reads a capitalised name as a component; one casing for all of them keeps imports and file names predictable.

##### Do

```js

```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx
const c = <UserCard />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const c = <UserCard />;
```

## `react/jsx-props-no-spread-multi` — One object is not spread twice into a JSX element

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the later spread wins for every key it sets, so removing it can change a prop set between the two)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

An element does not spread the same expression twice (`<A {...p} {...p} />`).

### Examples


##### Fixed

```js
const c = <Card {...props} title="x"  />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

```jsx

```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const c = <Card {...props} title="x"  />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const c = <Card {...props} title="x" {...props} />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const c = <Card {...props} title="x" />;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const c = <Card {...props} title="x"  />;
```

## `react/jsx-props-no-spreading` — No spread props in JSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: each prop the spread carried is named, which needs the set the author means to pass)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-props-no-spreading.md

### What it checks

JSX passes props by name, never by spreading an object (`<Input {...props} />`).

**Why:** A spread hides which props reach the element, and passes along ones it should not see.

```js
const i = <Input value={props.value} onChange={props.onChange} />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const i = <Input {...props} />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const i = <Input value={props.value} onChange={props.onChange} />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
const i = <Input value={props.value} onChange={props.onChange} />;
```

## `react/jsx-sort-props` — JSX props are in alphabetical order

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (reordering props reorders the evaluation of their values, and a later duplicate prop wins, so the order can matter)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/jsx-sort-props.md

### What it checks

An element's props are in alphabetical order; a spread starts a new run.

**Why:** A sorted list is easy to scan and to diff.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignore_case` | `boolean` | `false` | compare names without case |

### How to fix

1. Sort the props.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const e = <a title="t" href="/" />;
```

##### Do

```js
const e = <a href="/" title="t" />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const e = <a title="t" href="/" />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const e = <a href="/" title="t" />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const e = <a title="t" href="/" />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const e = <a href="/" title="t" />;
```

## `react/max-jsx-depth` — JSX elements nest no deeper than a maximum

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a nested part into a component means choosing its name and its props; that is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/max-jsx-depth.md

### What it checks

JSX elements nest at most `max` deep (6 by default). Every element and fragment counts, a self-closing one too, and nesting goes through `{…}` — an element returned from a `.map()` callback inside `<ul>` is one level below the `<ul>`. A callback does not reset the count. The rule reports once for each branch that passes the limit, on the first element past it: `JSX is nested 8 deep (max 6)`, the number being how deep that branch goes.

**Why:** Deep markup hides what is a component and what is just layout, and an indent at that depth leaves little room for the content. Naming a subtree makes it testable and reusable.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `6` | the most JSX elements that may nest inside one another |

### How to fix

1. Take the subtree that starts at the reported element and move it into a component with a name that says what it is (`<ProfileMenu />`).
2. Pass in what the subtree reads as props.
3. A wrapper `<div>` that only carries a class can often be a prop on its child, or go away.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```jsx
const Page = () => (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ul>
        <li>one</li>
      </ul>
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```jsx
const Items = () => (
  <ul>
    <li>one</li>
  </ul>
);
const Page = () => (
  <main>
    <Items />
  </main>
);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```tsx
const Page = (): JSX.Element => (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ul>
        <li>one</li>
      </ul>
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 2 }`

```tsx
const Items = (): JSX.Element => (
  <ul>
    <li>one</li>
  </ul>
);
const Page = (): JSX.Element => (
  <main>
    <Items />
  </main>
);
```

## `react/max-props` — A React component takes at most a maximum number of props

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (grouping props changes the component's interface and every place that renders it; which props belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/max-props.md

### What it checks

A function component takes at most `max` props (8 by default). The props are counted from the first parameter: the keys it destructures (`({ a, b = 1, c: d })`; a `...rest` is not counted), or the members of its declared type — an inline `{ a: string; b: number }`, or an `interface` or `type` of the same file (`props: RowProps`) — whichever is larger. A class component and a type declared in another file are not counted. The rule reports on the component's name: `Component Row takes 11 props (max 8)`.

**Why:** Every prop is a decision made at each place the component is rendered, and a component with a dozen has no single job. Props that always travel together are one thing with a name.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `8` | the most props one component may take |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; components named like this are exempt |

### How to fix

1. Group props that always travel together into one object prop (`user={user}` instead of `id`, `name`, `email`).
2. Pass children instead of a prop per slot (`<Card><Header /></Card>`).
3. Split the component if its props fall into two sets used by different parts.
4. If the component is wide on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule react/max-props`.

### Examples

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function Row({ id, name, email, phone }) {
  return <tr>{id}{name}{email}{phone}</tr>;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function Row({ user }) {
  return <tr>{user.id}{user.name}{user.email}{user.phone}</tr>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
interface RowProps {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  phone: string;
}
function Row(props: RowProps) {
  return <tr>{props.id}</tr>;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
interface RowProps {
  user: User;
}
function Row(props: RowProps) {
  return <tr>{props.user.id}</tr>;
}
```

## `react/memoized-effect-dependencies` — Effect dependencies are stable values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the value is wrapped in `useMemo` or `useCallback`, or moved inside the effect, with its own dependencies)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/memoized-effect-dependencies.md

### What it checks

A value listed in an effect's dependency array is not an object, array or function created fresh in the component body.

**Why:** A value made on every render is a new dependency on every render, so the effect runs every time.

### How to fix

1. Move `$D` inside the effect, or wrap it in `useMemo` / `useCallback` with its dependencies.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function Chat({ room }) {
  const options = { room };
  useEffect(() => connect(options), [options]);
  return null;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => connect({ room }), [room]);
  return null;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Chat({ room }) {
  const options = { room };
  useEffect(() => connect(options), [options]);
  return null;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => connect({ room }), [room]);
  return null;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Chat({ room }) {
  const options = { room };
  useEffect(() => connect(options), [options]);
  return null;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => connect({ room }), [room]);
  return null;
}
```

## `react/no-access-state-in-setstate` — setState does not read this.state

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the update becomes an updater function, `setState((state) => …)`, which reads its own state)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-access-state-in-setstate.md

### What it checks

An object passed to `this.setState` is not built from `this.state`.

**Why:** State updates are batched, so `this.state` may already be stale: two quick clicks of `count: this.state.count + 1` add one.

### How to fix

1. Pass a function: `this.setState((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 }))`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 }));
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 }));
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class C extends Component {
  inc() {
    this.setState((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 }));
  }
}
```

## `react/no-adjacent-inline-elements` — No inline elements that touch

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a space between the elements changes what is rendered)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-adjacent-inline-elements.md

### What it checks

Two inline elements (`<a>`, `<span>`, `<b>`, …) that are siblings have something between them.

**Why:** With nothing between them, the rendered words run together.

### How to fix

1. Add the space or text that was meant between them.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const e = <div><a>x</a><a>y</a></div>;
```

##### Do

```js
const e = <div><a>x</a> <a>y</a></div>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const e = <div><a>x</a><a>y</a></div>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const e = <div><a>x</a> <a>y</a></div>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const e = <div><a>x</a><a>y</a></div>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const e = <div><a>x</a> <a>y</a></div>;
```

## `react/no-array-index-key` — No array index as a key

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: a stable key comes from the item's data (an id), which only the author knows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-array-index-key.md

### What it checks

A `key` is not the index a `map`, `forEach`, `filter`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex`, `flatMap` or `reduce` callback receives — alone, in a template literal, or through `String(i)` or `i.toString()`.

**Why:** An index key moves with position, so inserting or reordering items makes React reuse the wrong element and its state.

### How to fix

1. Use a stable id from the item as the key: `key={item.id}`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const l = items.map((item, i) => <li key={i}>{item.name}</li>);
```

##### Do

```js
const l = items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const l = items.map((item, i) => <li key={i}>{item.name}</li>);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const l = items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const l = items.map((item, i) => <li key={i}>{item.name}</li>);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const l = items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>);
```

## `react/no-arrow-function-lifecycle` — Lifecycle methods are methods, not arrow fields

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-arrow-function-lifecycle.md

### What it checks

A lifecycle method (`render`, `componentDidMount`, …) of a class component is a method, not a class field holding an arrow function. Arrow fields with an expression body, or `async`, are reported but left alone by the fix's pattern.

**Why:** React calls lifecycle methods on the instance, so the arrow's bound `this` buys nothing, and a field is created again for every instance.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount = () => {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount = () => {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount = () => {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
class Clock extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.start();
  };
}
```

## `react/no-children-prop` — Children are passed as children, not as a prop

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (a self-closing element whose last attribute is children={...} moves it into the body with identical output; the createElement form and other placements stay suggest)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-children-prop.md

### What it checks

Children go between an element's tags (or as the third argument of `createElement`), not in a
`children` prop.

**Why:** Passing `children` as a prop works, but hides the element's content where readers don't
look for it.

### How to fix

1. Move the value between the opening and closing tags.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <Panel children={<p>Hi</p>} />;
```

##### Fixed

```js
const a = <Panel >{<p>Hi</p>}</Panel>;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <Panel>
  <p>Hi</p>
</Panel>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <Panel children={<p>Hi</p>} />;
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const a = <Panel >{<p>Hi</p>}</Panel>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <Panel>
  <p>Hi</p>
</Panel>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <Panel children={<p>Hi</p>} />;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const a = <Panel >{<p>Hi</p>}</Panel>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <Panel>
  <p>Hi</p>
</Panel>;
```

## `react/no-clone-element` — No `cloneElement`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (replacing a clone with props or a render function changes the component's API)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-clone-element.md

### What it checks

`React.cloneElement` isn't called.

**Why:** Cloning hides which props a child really gets, and breaks when the child is wrapped.

### How to fix

1. Pass the props explicitly, or take a render function.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const b = React.cloneElement(child, { size: 2 });
```

##### Do

```js
const b = <Button size={2} />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const b = React.cloneElement(child, { size: 2 });
```

##### Do

```jsx
const b = <Button size={2} />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const b = React.cloneElement(child, { size: 2 });
```

##### Do

```tsx
const b = <Button size={2} />;
```

## `react/no-context` — No React context: no createContext, no useContext

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what replaces the context — props, a store, a module — is the team's design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-context.md

### What it checks

No code calls `createContext` or `useContext` from `react`: the named import under any alias, or
`React.createContext` / `React.useContext` on the default or namespace import. A function of your
own that happens to be named `useContext` is not flagged. The rule is a team's choice, so it is not
in `react/recommended`; turn it on in `codelaw.toml`, and name what the team uses instead in the
`use_instead` option. To keep today's context as warnings while new context fails, grandfather it
with a baseline: `codelaw baseline add --rule react/no-context --warn-from <today> --on-touch keep
--reason "legacy context, grandfathered"`.

**Why:** Context hides where a value comes from and re-renders every consumer when it changes; a
team that has settled on props or a store keeps one way of passing data.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `use_instead` | `string` | `"props or the app's state store"` | what the codebase uses instead of context, named in the message |

### How to fix

1. Pass the value another way — props, or the app's state store (the `use_instead` option names the team's choice) — and delete the `createContext` / `useContext` call.
2. If the use predates the rule, grandfather it instead: `codelaw baseline add --rule react/no-context --warn-from <today> --on-touch keep --reason "legacy context, grandfathered"` — today's uses then warn and new ones fail.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { createContext } from 'react';

export const ThemeContext = createContext('light');
```

##### Do

```js
export const defaultTheme = 'light';
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useContext } from 'react';
import { ThemeContext } from './theme';

export function Button() {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <button className={theme}>OK</button>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
export function Button({ theme }) {
  return <button className={theme}>OK</button>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import * as React from 'react';

export const UserContext = React.createContext<string | null>(null);
```

##### Do

```ts
export type User = string | null;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import { UserContext } from './user';

export function Name() {
  const user = React.useContext(UserContext);
  return <span>{user}</span>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export function Name({ user }: { user: string }) {
  return <span>{user}</span>;
}
```

### Adopting it in a codebase that uses context

Old context warns, new context fails — no engine feature beyond the baseline
(SR-BASELINE decisions 1–2):

```toml
# codelaw.toml
[rules]
"react/no-context" = "error"
```

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule react/no-context \
  --warn-from 2026-10-25 --on-touch keep --reason "legacy context, grandfathered"
```

| what changes | what `codelaw check` says |
|---|---|
| nothing: each file that used context when the baseline was written | a **warning** per use, with no deadline (exit 0) |
| a **new file** calls `createContext` or `useContext` | an **error** — the file has no baseline entry (exit 1) |
| **one more** use in an old file | **every** use in that file is an error: "2 in this file; the baseline allows 1" (exit 1) |
| an old file edited for other reasons | nothing: `--on-touch keep` leaves its uses as warnings |

Add `--expires <date>` to give the old uses a deadline: from that day they are errors too, with a warning `warn_days` before it.
`fixtures/react-no-context/` is this recipe as a repo, run by `crates/codelaw-cli/tests/react_no_context.rs`.

### What is not flagged

- React 19's `use(SomeContext)`: without types, `use` reading a context can't be told from `use` reading a promise.
- `<Ctx.Provider>` and `<Ctx>` in JSX: the context they provide was made by a `createContext` the rule already reports.
- The count hole: with `--on-touch keep`, removing one `useContext` from an old file and adding another in the same file nets out, and the run passes. The baseline counts uses per file; it does not tell one use from another.

## `react/no-danger-with-children` — No dangerouslySetInnerHTML together with children

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the element keeps either its children or its injected HTML; the reviewer picks which to drop)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-danger-with-children.md

### What it checks

An element with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` has no children.

**Why:** React throws when an element has both, since it can't know which content wins.

### How to fix

1. Keep either the HTML or the children, not both: drop the children, or drop `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }}>Fallback</div>;
```

##### Fixed (remove the children)

```js
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

##### Fixed (remove the HTML)

```js
const a = <div >Fallback</div>;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }}>Fallback</div>;
```

##### Fixed (remove the children)

```jsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

##### Fixed (remove the HTML)

```jsx
const a = <div >Fallback</div>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }}>Fallback</div>;
```

##### Fixed (remove the children)

```tsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

##### Fixed (remove the HTML)

```tsx
const a = <div >Fallback</div>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />;
```

## `react/no-deprecated` — No deprecated React APIs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the UNSAFE_ alias is exact for a legacy lifecycle, but the reviewer confirms React is 16.3 or later and nothing calls the method by name; the other APIs carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-deprecated.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't use React APIs that are deprecated: the legacy `componentWill…` lifecycles,
`React.createClass`, `React.PropTypes`, `ReactDOM.render`, `hydrate` and `unmountComponentAtNode`.

**Why:** Deprecated APIs are removed in later versions, and the legacy lifecycles misbehave with
concurrent rendering.

### How to fix

1. A legacy lifecycle takes its `UNSAFE_` name from the fix; the others are by hand. Replace `ReactDOM.render` with `createRoot(el).render(…)` and `hydrate` with `hydrateRoot`.
2. Rename legacy lifecycles to their `UNSAFE_` names, or move their work to `componentDidMount`/`componentDidUpdate`.
3. Use the `prop-types` package instead of `React.PropTypes`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
class Card extends React.Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Card extends React.Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

### Differences from the source

The React version setting is not read: every listed API is reported.

## `react/no-deriving-state-in-effects` — No effect that only copies a value into state

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the derived value is computed during render and the state and the effect are deleted)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-deriving-state-in-effects.md

### What it checks

A `useEffect` whose body does nothing but call setters — at least one of them from this component's `useState` — with plain values (not updater functions) (`setFullName(first + " " + last)`) is replaced by a value computed during render.

**Why:** Deriving state in an effect renders twice, once with the stale value, and keeps two sources of truth in step by hand.

### How to fix

1. Delete the state and the effect.
2. Compute the value in the component body: `const fullName = first + " " + last;` (with `useMemo` if it is expensive).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + " " + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return full;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const full = first + " " + last;
  return full;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + " " + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return full;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const full = first + " " + last;
  return full;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + " " + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return full;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const full = first + " " + last;
  return full;
}
```

## `react/no-did-mount-set-state` — No setState in componentDidMount

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the state is derived in render, or the update moves to a handler)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-did-mount-set-state.md

### What it checks

A class component does not call `this.setState` directly in `componentDidMount`. A call inside a callback defined there (a subscription, a timer) is fine.

**Why:** A state update in `componentDidMount` triggers a second render before the browser paints, and is usually state that could be computed.

### How to fix

1. Compute the value in `render` from props and state instead of storing it, or move the update into an event handler.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Panel extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Panel extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  componentDidMount() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
```
```tsx
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

## `react/no-direct-mutation-state` — No assigning to this.state outside the constructor

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a plain `this.state.k = e` becomes `this.setState({ k: e })`, which is batched; the reviewer confirms nothing reads the value on the next line; updater-form and nested writes carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-direct-mutation-state.md

### What it checks

A class component changes its state with `this.setState`, never by assigning to `this.state` outside
the constructor.

**Why:** A direct assignment doesn't trigger a re-render, and a later `setState` may overwrite it.

### How to fix

1. Replace the assignment with `this.setState(…)`; use the updater form when the new state depends on the old.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Menu extends React.Component {
  open() {
    this.state.open = true;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Menu extends React.Component {
  open() {
    this.setState({ open: true });
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Menu extends React.Component {
  open() {
    this.state.open = true;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Menu extends React.Component {
  open() {
    this.setState({ open: true });
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  open() {
    this.state.open = true;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  open() {
    this.setState({ open: true });
  }
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a ref has to be attached to the right element by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`


##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

```

## `react/no-is-mounted` — No this.isMounted()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a guard with only a block of statements and no else is dropped, keeping the block (a setState after unmount is a no-op); the reviewer confirms the callback needs no cancellation instead)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-is-mounted.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't call `this.isMounted()`.

**Why:** `isMounted` hides leaks: a callback that outlives the component should be cancelled
instead.

### How to fix

1. Cancel pending work in `componentWillUnmount`.
2. Remove the `isMounted` check.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class A extends React.Component {
  done() {
    if (this.isMounted()) {
      this.setState({ ok: true });
    }
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
class A extends React.Component {
  done() {
    this.setState({ ok: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class A extends React.Component {
  componentWillUnmount() {
    this.request.cancel();
  }
  done() {
    this.setState({ ok: true });
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class A extends React.Component {
  done() {
    if (this.isMounted()) {
      this.setState({ ok: true });
    }
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class A extends React.Component {
  done() {
    this.setState({ ok: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class A extends React.Component {
  componentWillUnmount() {
    this.request.cancel();
  }
  done() {
    this.setState({ ok: true });
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  done() {
    if (this.isMounted()) {
      this.setState({ ok: true });
    }
  }
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx

    this.setState({ ok: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  }
```

## `react/no-nested-components` — Components are not defined inside other components

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a nested component that reads nothing its parent declares moves above the parent's top-level statement; its state then survives the parent's renders, which is the fix but is a change. One that reads the parent's props or locals is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-nested-components.md

### What it checks

A PascalCase function that renders JSX is not defined inside another component — a function
component, or a class component's `render()`. Lower-case helpers that return JSX
(`const renderRow = () => <tr />`) are not components and are fine.

**Why:** A component defined during render is a new component type on every render: React unmounts the old one and mounts the new one, so its state and its DOM are thrown away each time.

### How to fix

1. Move the component to the top level of the module.
2. Pass the values it read from the outer component as props.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function List({ items }) {
  const Item = ({ text }) => <li>{text}</li>;
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
const Item = ({ text }) => <li>{text}</li>;
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```js
const Item = ({ text }) => <li>{text}</li>;

function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  function Item({ text }) {
    return <li>{text}</li>;
  }
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
function Item({ text }) {
    return <li>{text}</li>;
  }
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Item({ text }) {
  return <li>{text}</li>;
}

function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const Item = ({ text }: { text: string }) => <li>{text}</li>;
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const Item = ({ text }: { text: string }) => <li>{text}</li>;
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
const Item = ({ text }: { text: string }) => <li>{text}</li>;

function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((t) => <Item key={t} text={t} />)}</ul>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- The React Compiler's `static-components` reports a component made during render only where it is used as JSX; @eslint-react's `no-nested-component-definitions` reports the definition. codelaw reports the definition, like @eslint-react.
- A component made by a call (`const C = styled(…)`, `const C = memo(…)` with no function written there) or passed inline as a JSX prop is not reported.

## `react/no-object-type-as-default-prop` — No object or function literal as a prop default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the default is hoisted to a module-level constant, whose name is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

A component's destructured props have no default that is a new object, array or function (`function List({ items = [] })`).

**Why:** The default is a new value on every render, so a memoised child or an effect dependency sees a change each time.

```js
const NO_ITEMS = [];

  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx

function List({ items = NO_ITEMS }) {
  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
const NO_ITEMS = [];
function List({ items = NO_ITEMS }) {
  return <ul>{items.length}</ul>;
}
```
