## `react/no-ref-in-render` — A ref's current value is not read or written during render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a body-level `ref.current = …` moves into `useLayoutEffect(() => { … })`, run after every render before paint, the hook added to the `react` import; a ref read during render is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-ref-in-render.md

### What it checks

A component or hook doesn't read or write `ref.current` in its own body, for a ref made by
`useRef` in that body. Reads and writes in effects, event handlers and other callbacks are fine,
and so is the one lazy initialisation React documents: `if (ref.current === null) { ref.current
= … }` (or `== null`, `=== undefined`, `!ref.current`).

**Why:** React doesn't re-render when a ref changes, so a value read during render can be stale, and a write during render runs again — or not at all — when React renders a component more than once or throws a render away.

### How to fix

1. Move the read or write into an effect, an event handler or another callback.
2. If the value is shown on screen, keep it in state instead of a ref.
3. If the ref is created lazily, initialise it inside `if (ref.current === null) { … }`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  ref.current = value;
  return ref;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    ref.current = value;
  });
  return ref;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  ref.current = value;
  return ref;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    ref.current = value;
  });
  return ref;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useLatest<T>(value: T) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  ref.current = value;
  return ref;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function useLatest<T>(value: T) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    ref.current = value;
  });
  return ref;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useStore() {
  const store = useRef<Store | null>(null);
  if (store.current === null) {
    store.current = createStore();
  }
  return store;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  ref.current = value;
  return ref;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    ref.current = value;
  });
  return ref;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- Only refs made by `useRef` in the same function are checked; upstream also tracks refs passed in as props or returned by other hooks, and reports a ref passed to a function called during render.
- A second lazy initialisation of the same ref, which upstream reports, is not reported.

## `react/no-render-return-value` — The return value of ReactDOM.render is not used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a `const x = ReactDOM.render(…)` statement drops the binding and keeps the call; the reviewer confirms the binding is never read (otherwise a ref must be threaded in); other uses carry no edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-render-return-value.md

### What it checks

The value `ReactDOM.render` returns is not stored, returned or passed on.

**Why:** It's a legacy handle that is `null` in some cases and gone in newer APIs.

### How to fix

1. Pass a ref to the root element and use it instead of the return value.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const app = ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Fixed

```js
ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Do

```js
ReactDOM.render(<App ref={appRef} />, root);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const app = ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Do

```jsx
ReactDOM.render(<App ref={appRef} />, root);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const app = ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
ReactDOM.render(<App />, root);
```

##### Do

```tsx
ReactDOM.render(<App ref={appRef} />, root);
```

## `react/no-set-state` — No this.setState

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the state moves to a store or to a parent, which is an architecture choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-set-state.md

### What it checks

Components do not call `this.setState`; state lives in a store or a parent.

**Why:** For projects whose state is kept outside components (Redux, a state machine), a local `setState` is state that escaped.

### How to fix

1. Move the state to the project's store (or a parent component) and pass it in as props.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.setState({ on: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.props.onFlip();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.setState({ on: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.props.onFlip();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.setState({ on: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Toggle extends Component {
  flip() {
    this.props.onFlip();
  }
}
```

## `react/no-set-state-in-effect` — An effect doesn't set state synchronously

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an effect that only sets one state from its dependencies becomes a value computed during render, the state and the effect gone; the first render then shows the value at once. Any other effect is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-set-state-in-effect.md

### What it checks

The callback of `useEffect`, `useLayoutEffect` or `useInsertionEffect` doesn't call a `useState`
setter directly — conditionally or not. A setter called in a callback the effect sets up (a
subscription, a timer, a promise's `then`) is fine, and so is one given a value read from a ref
(`setX(ref.current)`).

**Why:** An effect runs after React has committed a render; setting state there commits a second render at once, so every change costs two renders, and the first one shows stale values.

### How to fix

1. If the value can be computed from props or state, compute it during render and drop the state and the effect.
2. If it depends on a change of a prop, handle the event that changed the prop instead.
3. If it comes from an outside source, subscribe in the effect and set the state in the subscription's callback, or use `useSyncExternalStore`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useFullName(first, last) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState('');
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + ' ' + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return full;
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
function useFullName(first, last) {
  const full = first + ' ' + last;
  return full;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useWidth() {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
  }, []);
  return width;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState('');
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + ' ' + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return <p>{full}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Name({ first, last }) {
  const full = first + ' ' + last;
  return <p>{full}</p>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useFullName(first: string, last: string) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState('');
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + ' ' + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return full;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function useFullName(first: string, last: string) {
  const full = first + ' ' + last;
  return full;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useWidth(): number {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
  }, []);
  return width;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Name({ first, last }: { first: string; last: string }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState('');
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + ' ' + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return <p>{full}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Name({ first, last }: { first: string; last: string }) {
  const full = first + ' ' + last;
  return <p>{full}</p>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- Upstream follows the setter through local functions the effect calls; codelaw reports only a direct call of the setter in the effect's own body.
- Upstream exempts a value derived from a ref by data flow; codelaw exempts a call whose arguments mention `.current`.

## `react/no-set-state-in-render` — State is not set on every render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the state should be instead — derived during render, or set in an event — is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-set-state-in-render.md

### What it checks

A component or hook doesn't call a `useState` setter unconditionally in its own body: not inside a
condition, a loop, a callback or after an early `return`. The setter is recognised by its
declaration — the second element of `const [value, setValue] = useState(…)` in the same function.

**Why:** Setting state during render schedules another render, which sets the state again: the component renders forever, or React stops it with an error.

### How to fix

1. If the value can be computed from props or other state, compute it during render instead of storing it.
2. If the state must follow a prop, set it only when the prop changes: keep the previous prop in state and compare, inside an `if`.
3. Otherwise set it where the change happens: an event handler, or an effect's subscription callback.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useCounter(start) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(start);
  return count;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useCounter(start) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start);
  return [count, setCount];
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Counter({ start }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(start);
  return <p>{count}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Counter({ start }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useCounter(start: number) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(start);
  return count;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useCounter(start: number) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start);
  return [count, setCount] as const;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Counter({ start }: { start: number }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(start);
  return <p>{count}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Counter({ start }: { start: number }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- The React Compiler follows a setter through aliases and helper functions called during render; codelaw sees only a direct call of the setter's own name in the body of the function that declared it.
- A call inside `useMemo`'s callback (which upstream also reports) is not reported: it is in a nested function.

## `react/no-string-refs` — No string refs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the ref object has to be created where the component can reach it)

### What it checks

Refs are objects or callbacks, never strings (`ref="input"`, `this.refs.input`).

**Why:** String refs are legacy, slow, and removed in React 19.

##### Do

```jsx

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <input ref="name" />;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <input ref={nameRef} />;
```

## `react/no-svg-without-title` — An SVG has a title or is hidden

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (adds aria-hidden="true", which is right only when the SVG is decorative; the reviewer confirms that, or writes a title instead)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-svg-without-title.md

### What it checks

An inline `<svg>` has a `<title>` inside it, an `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, or is hidden with `aria-hidden="true"` or `role="presentation"`.

**Why:** Screen readers announce an unlabelled SVG as "image" with no name, or read out its raw contents.

```js
const icon = <svg viewBox="0 0 8 8"><title>Stop</title><path d="M0 0h8v8H0z" /></svg>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

##### Fixed

```jsx

```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Fixed


- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: what `this` was meant to reach — props, state, a ref — is passed in or held in a hook)

```js
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{this.props.name}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{this.props.name}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

  return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}
```

## `react/no-typos` — No miscased React class members

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (each miscased name has one spelling in React's own list; the reviewer confirms the member was meant to be that lifecycle or static)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-typos.md

### What it checks

A component's static properties and lifecycle methods are spelled as React spells them: `propTypes`, not `PropTypes` or `proptypes`; `componentDidMount`, not `componentdidmount`.

**Why:** React silently ignores a miscased name, so the validation or the lifecycle code never runs.

### How to fix

1. Spell the name as React does: `propTypes`, `defaultProps`, `contextTypes`, `componentDidMount`, …

### Examples

#### JavaScript

```js
class A extends Component {
  componentdidmount() {}
}
A.PropTypes = {};
```

##### Fixed

```js
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

##### Do

```js
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class A extends Component {
  componentdidmount() {}
}
A.PropTypes = {};
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

##### Do

```jsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class A extends Component {
  componentdidmount() {}
}
A.PropTypes = {};
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

##### Do

```tsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {}
}
A.propTypes = {};
```

## `react/no-unescaped-entities` — No unescaped >, ", ' or } in JSX text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-unescaped-entities.md

### What it checks

JSX text doesn't contain `>`, `"`, `'` or `}` unescaped.

**Why:** These characters are easy to misread as markup or code, and a stray `}` is usually a typo.

### How to fix

1. Use an HTML entity (`&apos;`, `&quot;`, `&gt;`) or a string expression (`{"'"}`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <p>Don't stop</p>;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <p>Don&apos;t stop</p>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <p>Don't stop</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <p>Don&apos;t stop</p>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <p>Don't stop</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <p>Don&apos;t stop</p>;
```

## `react/no-unknown-property` — DOM elements use React's prop names, not HTML attribute names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-unknown-property.md

### What it checks

A DOM element in JSX uses React's names for attributes: `className` not `class`, `htmlFor` not
`for`, `onClick` not `onclick`, `tabIndex` not `tabindex`.

**Why:** React ignores or warns about the HTML spellings, so the attribute silently does nothing.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const a = <input tabindex="1" onclick={go} />;
```

##### Do

```js
const a = <input tabIndex="1" onClick={go} />;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const a = <input tabindex="1" onclick={go} />;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const a = <input tabIndex="1" onClick={go} />;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const a = <label class="x" for="name" onclick={go}>Name</label>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const a = <label className="x" htmlFor="name" onClick={go}>Name</label>;
```

### Differences from the source

Only HTML spellings React renames are checked (the pack's `react/dom-property-aliases` data table);
unknown attributes in general are not. In `.js` and `.jsx` files the JavaScript grammar can't parse
`class=` and `for=` as JSX attributes (they are reserved words), so those two are found only in
`.tsx`.

## `react/no-unnecessary-use-prefix` — A use… function calls a hook

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming the function means renaming every caller, in other files too)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-unnecessary-use-prefix.md

### What it checks

A function named `use…` calls at least one hook somewhere in its body. Not reported: an empty
function, `use` and `useMDXComponents`, a function whose comments name a hook call (`// useX()`
later), and functions passed to a test mock (`vi.mock`, `jest.mock`, `mock.module`).

**Why:** The `use` prefix tells React's tools — and readers — that the Rules of Hooks apply; on a plain function it forbids calling it in a condition or a loop for no reason.

### How to fix

1. Rename the function without the `use` prefix (`useFormat` → `format`), and rename its callers.
2. If it is meant to become a hook, leave a comment naming the hook it will call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useFormatDate(date) {
  return date.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function formatDate(date) {
  return date.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const useGreeting = (name) => <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const greeting = (name) => <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useTotal(items: number[]): number {
  return items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useTotal(items: number[]): number {
  return useMemo(() => items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0), [items]);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const useGreeting = (name: string) => <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const greeting = (name: string) => <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
```

### Differences from the source

- A hook call anywhere in the body counts, nested callbacks included; upstream counts the hook calls its collector attributes to the function.

## `react/no-unsafe` — No UNSAFE_ lifecycle methods

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: each legacy method has a different modern replacement)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-unsafe.md

### What it checks

Class components do not define `UNSAFE_componentWillMount`, `UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps` or `UNSAFE_componentWillUpdate`.

**Why:** These methods misbehave under concurrent rendering, which is why React renamed them.

### How to fix

1. `UNSAFE_componentWillMount`: move the code to the constructor or `componentDidMount`.
2. `UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps`: use `getDerivedStateFromProps` or a key.
3. `UNSAFE_componentWillUpdate`: use `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate` with `componentDidUpdate`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class A extends Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class A extends Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class A extends Component {
  UNSAFE_componentWillMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class A extends Component {
  componentDidMount() {
    this.load();
  }
}
```

## `react/no-will-update-set-state` — No setState in componentWillUpdate

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the state is derived in render, or the update moves to a handler)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/no-will-update-set-state.md

### What it checks

A class component does not call `this.setState` directly in `componentWillUpdate`. A call inside a callback defined there (a subscription, a timer) is fine.

**Why:** `componentWillUpdate` runs just before a render; updating state there loops or is lost.

### How to fix

1. Compute the value in `render` from props and state instead of storing it, or move the update into an event handler.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.setState({ ready: true });
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Panel extends Component {
  componentWillUpdate() {
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.setState({ ready: true }), 100);
  }
}
```

## `react/prefer-lazy-state-init` — useState's initial value is not computed on every render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (wrapping changes behaviour when the value is itself a function, and moves the call's side effects to the first render only)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/prefer-lazy-state-init.md

### What it checks

`useState`'s argument doesn't call a function or construct an object on every render:
`useState(load())` and `useState(new Map())` compute a value that React uses only on the first
render. Pass a function instead — `useState(() => load())` — and React calls it once. Calls of
hooks, of `Boolean`, `String` and `Number`, of a method (`JSON.parse(…)`), and calls inside
`use(…)` or inside a function are not reported.

**Why:** The argument is evaluated on every render even though React ignores it after the first, so an expensive call runs for nothing each time.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useTodos() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState(loadTodos());
  return [todos, setTodos];
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useTodos() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState(() => loadTodos());
  return [todos, setTodos];
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Cart() {
  const [items] = useState(new Map());
  return <p>{items.size}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Cart() {
  const [items] = useState(() => new Map());
  return <p>{items.size}</p>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useFilters() {
  const [filters, setFilters] = useState({ tags: readTags() });
  return [filters, setFilters] as const;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useFilters() {
  const [filters, setFilters] = useState(() => ({ tags: readTags() }));
  return [filters, setFilters] as const;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Editor() {
  const [doc] = useState(createDocument());
  return <article>{doc.title}</article>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Editor() {
  const [doc] = useState(() => createDocument());
  return <article>{doc.title}</article>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- This is the lazy-initialisation part of @eslint-react's `use-state`; its other two checks — that the call is destructured, and that the setter is named `set` + the value's name — are naming conventions, not ported here.
- Upstream reports each call in the argument; codelaw reports the argument once, naming the first call, and offers one fix for it.

## `react/prefer-read-only-props` — Props types are readonly

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`

### What it checks

Each member of a component's props type is `readonly`: the inline type of a component's first parameter, and any interface or type alias whose name ends in `Props`.

**Why:** Props are read-only at run time; `readonly` makes the compiler say so when code tries to assign one.

## `react/prefer-stateless-function` — A class with only render is a function

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX

### What it checks

A class component whose only member is `render`, and which reads no state, refs or `this` beyond `this.props` and `this.context`, is written as a function component.

```js
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Hello extends Component {
  render() {
    return <p>{this.props.name}</p>;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  render() {
    return <p>{this.props.name}</p>;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Hello(props) {
  return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}
```

## `react/prop-types` — Props are declared in propTypes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`

### What it checks

A component that reads a prop declares it: in `Component.propTypes`, or with a type on its props parameter (TypeScript). The rule reads destructured props of function components and `this.props.x` in class components, and checks a component only when its file assigns it no `propTypes` at all.

```js
function Hello({ name }) {
```

```js
Hello.propTypes = { name: PropTypes.string };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Hello({ name }) {
  return <p>{name}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Hello({ name }) {
  return <p>{name}</p>;
}
Hello.propTypes = { name: PropTypes.string };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Hello({ name }) {
  return <p>{name}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Hello({ name }) {
```

## `react/props-type-name` — A component's props type is named <Component>Props

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (renaming a type other files import would break them, so it is offered, not applied)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/props-type-name.md

### What it checks

The type of a component's props is named after the component: `CardProps` for `Card`.

**Why:** One naming pattern makes props types easy to find and import.

```tsx
type CardOptions = { title: string };

  return <h2>{props.title}</h2>;
```

```tsx
type CardProps = { title: string };
export function Card(props: CardProps) {
```

### Differences from the source

The type is renamed with its uses in the file; an exported type is reported without a fix.

## `react/purity` — Render doesn't call Math.random(), Date.now() or other impure functions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an impure value that a body-level `const` or the final `return` computes moves into a `useState` initializer, computed once; the value then stays the same across renders, which the reviewer confirms is meant. Any other impure call is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/purity.md

### What it checks

A component or hook doesn't call `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, `performance.now()`,
`crypto.randomUUID()` or `crypto.getRandomValues()`, or make `new Date()` with no argument, in its
own body. Calls in callbacks — effects, event handlers, a `useState` initializer — are fine, and so
is a local binding that shadows the global (`Math` as a parameter).

**Why:** React may render a component any number of times and expects the same output for the same props and state; a value that changes on every call makes the output change on every render and breaks hydration.

### How to fix

1. For a value made once, compute it in a `useState` initializer: `useState(() => Date.now())`.
2. For an id, use `useId()`.
3. For a value that should change, set it in an effect or an event handler.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useRandomKey() {
  return Math.random().toString(36);
}
```

##### Fixed

```js
function useRandomKey() {
  const [value] = useState(() => Math.random().toString(36));
  return value;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useRandomKey() {
  const [key] = useState(() => Math.random().toString(36));
  return key;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Clock() {
  const now = Date.now();
  return <p>{now}</p>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Clock() {
  const [now] = useState(() => Date.now());
  return <p>{now}</p>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useToday(): string {
  return new Date().toDateString();
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
function useToday(): string {
  const [value] = useState(() => new Date().toDateString());
  return value;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useToday(): string {
  const [today] = useState(() => new Date().toDateString());
  return today;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Field({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const id = crypto.randomUUID();
  return <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
function Field({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const [id] = useState(() => crypto.randomUUID());
  return <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Field({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const id = useId();
  return <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>;
}
```

### Differences from the source

- eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7 knows `Math.random`, `Date.now` and `performance.now`; codelaw adds `crypto.randomUUID`, `crypto.getRandomValues` and `new Date()` from @eslint-react's list, and leaves out the rest of that list (DOM, storage, network and timer calls), which reads as side effects more than impurity and is better reported by a rule of its own.
- Upstream follows a global through an alias (`const { random } = Math`); codelaw reports only the direct `Math.random()` form.
- A call in a function the component calls during render is not followed.

## `react/require-default-props` — Every optional prop has a default

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the default value is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/require-default-props.md

### What it checks

Each prop in a component's `propTypes` that is not `.isRequired` has an entry in its `defaultProps`.

**Why:** An optional prop with no default is `undefined` in the component, and every use of it has to guard for that.

### How to fix

1. Add a default for the prop to `defaultProps`, or mark it `.isRequired`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
```

##### Do

```js
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
Badge.defaultProps = { label: "" };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
```

##### Do

```jsx
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
Badge.defaultProps = { label: "" };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
```

##### Do

```tsx
Badge.propTypes = { label: PropTypes.string };
Badge.defaultProps = { label: "" };
```

## `react/require-optimization` — Class components say when to skip a render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: extending `PureComponent` or writing `shouldComponentUpdate` changes when the component renders, which the author has to confirm)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/require-optimization.md

### What it checks

A class extending `Component` defines `shouldComponentUpdate`, or extends `PureComponent` instead.

**Why:** Without either, the component re-renders whenever its parent does, changed props or not.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
class Row extends Component {

    return null;
  }

```

##### Do

```js
class Row extends PureComponent {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Row extends Component {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Row extends PureComponent {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Row extends Component {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Row extends PureComponent {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

## `react/require-render-return` — A class component's render() returns

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a `render()` whose last statement is a bare JSX expression gets `return` in front of it, so it draws what it builds; any other `render()` is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/require-render-return.md

### What it checks

The `render()` method of a class component returns a value on every path.

**Why:** A `render()` that falls off its end returns `undefined`, which is almost always a forgotten
`return`.

### How to fix

1. Return the element, or `null` to render nothing, on every path.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    return <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    return <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Title extends React.Component {
  render() {
    return <h1>{this.props.text}</h1>;
  }
}
```

## `react/rule-suppression` — The hooks rules are not switched off

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

No `eslint-disable` comment switches off a React hooks rule (`react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`, `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks`, …). The fix deletes the comment, which changes no code; the findings it hid come back.

##### Do

```js
function T({ id }) {
```

##### Do

```jsx
function T({ id }) {
```

##### Fixed

## `react/rules-of-hooks` — Hooks are called at the top level of components and hooks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a hook called after an early return moves above the statement holding it, when nothing it reads or declares sits in between; it then runs on renders that returned early, which is the fix but is a change. Every other misplaced hook is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/rules-of-hooks.md

### What it checks

Hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, any `use…`) are called only at the top level of a function component
or a custom hook: not in conditions, loops, nested functions, after an early return, in classes, or
in plain functions.

**Why:** React matches hook calls to state by their order, so a hook that runs on some renders and
not others mixes up every hook after it.

### How to fix

1. Move the hook call to the top level of the component or hook, before any early return.
2. Put the condition inside the hook (e.g. inside the effect) instead of around it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function Profile({ id }) {
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  const [user] = useState(null);
  return user;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function Profile({ id }) {
  const [user] = useState(null);
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  return user;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Profile({ id }) {
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  const [user] = useState(null);
  return user;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Profile({ id }) {
  const [user] = useState(null);
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  return user;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function Profile({ id }) {
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  const [user] = useState(null);
  return user;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function Profile({ id }) {
  const [user] = useState(null);
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  return user;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Profile({ id }) {
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  const [user] = useState(null);
  return user;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Profile({ id }) {
  const [user] = useState(null);
  if (!id) {
    return null;
  }
  return user;
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving methods carries their comments, and a class field's initialiser may read one declared before it, so the order is the author's to change)

##### Do

```js
  componentDidMount() {}
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

```tsx
    return null;
  }
  componentDidMount() {}
}
```

##### Do

```tsx

    return null;
  }
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the field moves into a constructor, which may not exist yet)

## `react/static-property-placement` — Static component properties are assigned after the class

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the property moves out of the class body to an assignment after it)

##### Don't

## `react/style-prop-object` — style is an object

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (each value stays a string, where React would also take a number for a length; a value with quotes or `!important`, or a `style` that is not a plain string, is rewritten by hand)

## `react/unsupported-syntax` — No eval or with in components and hooks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: what the evaluated code does is written as ordinary code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/unsupported-syntax.md

### What it checks

Components and hooks do not use `eval`, `new Function` or a `with` statement.

**Why:** Code built at run time can read and change any variable, so neither a reader nor the React Compiler can tell what a render depends on.

### How to fix

1. Replace the evaluated string or the `with` block with ordinary code.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{eval(expr)}</b>;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{evaluate(expr)}</b>;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{eval(expr)}</b>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{evaluate(expr)}</b>;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{eval(expr)}</b>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Calc({ expr }) {
  return <b>{evaluate(expr)}</b>;
}
```

## `react/use-memo` — useMemo's callback computes and returns a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an `async` callback with no `await` loses `async`, so the value is cached instead of a promise of it, and parameters nothing reads are dropped; every other misuse is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:react/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/use-memo.md

### What it checks

`useMemo(fn, deps)`'s callback is a plain synchronous function with no parameters that returns a
value, and the call's result is used. Reported: an `async` or generator callback, a callback that
takes parameters, a callback with a block body and no `return` of a value, and a `useMemo(…)` call
whose result is thrown away.

**Why:** `useMemo` caches the value its callback returns, calling it with no arguments: an `async` callback caches a promise, a parameter is always `undefined`, and a callback that returns nothing is a side effect in render, which belongs in `useEffect`.

### How to fix

1. For a side effect, use `useEffect` instead.
2. For an async value, load it in an effect (or a data library) and keep it in state.
3. Read the values the callback needs from the component's scope instead of parameters, and return the result.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(async () => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(() => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(async () => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(() => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(async () => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(() => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(async () => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function useTotal(items) {
  return useMemo(() => sum(items), [items]);
}
```

### Differences from the source

- Upstream also reports a `useMemo` callback that reassigns a variable from outside it, and a callback given by name (`useMemo(fn, deps)`) rather than written in place; codelaw does neither.
- An unused result is reported only when the call is a statement of its own; upstream follows the value through the function.

## `react/void-dom-elements-no-children` — Void elements have no children

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-react` · `codelaw-rules-react` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the children have to go somewhere else in the markup, which is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/react/void-dom-elements-no-children.md

### What it checks

A void DOM element (`<br>`, `<img>`, `<input>`, …) has no children, no `children` prop and no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

**Why:** React throws when a void element is given children.

### How to fix

1. Move the children next to the element, or wrap both in a container.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const l = <br>Line</br>;
```

##### Do

```js
const l = <>Line<br /></>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const l = <br>Line</br>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const l = <>Line<br /></>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const l = <br>Line</br>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const l = <>Line<br /></>;
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-blind-payload-return` — A reducer builds its state, not the action's payload

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`return action.payload` in a slice whose `initialState` is an object literal becomes one assignment per key of it; a payload with other keys then stops reaching the state, which the reviewer confirms. Any other return is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-blind-payload-return.md

### What it checks

A reducer doesn't return `action.payload` as the new state, return an object spreading
`...action.payload`, or `Object.assign` the payload onto an Immer draft.

**Why:** Whoever dispatches the action then decides the shape of the state, and a payload with a missing or
extra field changes it without the reducer knowing. *Style Guide, Priority B: Reducers Should Own the
State Shape.* The guide allows a spread for a form that edits every field; `redux-toolkit/recommended`
warns rather than errs.

### How to fix

1. Copy the fields the state owns from the payload by name: `state.name = action.payload.name`.
2. If replacing the whole state is the point (a cache reset), write that as its own case with a
   descriptive action name, and suppress the finding there.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      return action.payload;
    },
  },
});
```

##### Do

```js
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      state.name = action.payload.name;
      state.email = action.payload.email;
    },
  },
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      return action.payload;
    },
  },
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      state.name = action.payload.name;
      state.email = action.payload.email;
    },
  },
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      return action.payload;
    },
  },
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      state.name = action.payload.name;
      state.email = action.payload.email;
    },
  },
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      return action.payload;
    },
  },
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const userSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', email: '' },
  reducers: {
    userUpdated(state, action) {
      state.name = action.payload.name;
      state.email = action.payload.email;
    },
  },
});
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-immutable-js` — State is plain JavaScript, not Immutable.js

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (every read and update of the state is rewritten for plain objects)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-immutable-js.md

### What it checks

Nothing is imported from `immutable` (Immutable.js).

**Why:** Immutable.js values spread through the code that reads them, need conversion at every boundary and
don't serialize as plain data; Redux Toolkit's Immer gives immutable updates on plain objects. *Style
Guide, Priority B: Use Plain JavaScript Objects for State.*

### How to fix

1. Store the state as plain objects and arrays (`fromJS(x).toJS()` once, at the boundary).
2. Rewrite the reducers with `createSlice`, and the reads (`state.get('a')`) as property access.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { Map } from 'immutable';
```

##### Do

```js
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { Map } from 'immutable';
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { Map } from 'immutable';
```

##### Do

```ts
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { Map } from 'immutable';
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-legacy-create-store` — The store is made with configureStore

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (`configureStore` takes its options in another shape, and the middleware and enhancers move)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-legacy-create-store.md

### What it checks

`createStore` and `legacy_createStore` are not imported from `redux`; the store is made with Redux
Toolkit's `configureStore`.

**Why:** `configureStore` sets up the thunk middleware, the DevTools and the mutation and serializability
checks that catch the Priority A mistakes; `createStore` sets up none of them. *Style Guide, Priority
B: Use Redux Toolkit for Writing Redux Logic.*

### How to fix

1. Import `configureStore` from `@reduxjs/toolkit`.
2. Replace `createStore(rootReducer, preloadedState, enhancer)` with
   `configureStore({ reducer: rootReducer, preloadedState })`; pass extra middleware through
   `middleware: (getDefault) => getDefault().concat(…)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { createStore } from 'redux';
```

##### Do

```js
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { createStore } from 'redux';
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { createStore } from 'redux';
```

##### Do

```ts
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { createStore } from 'redux';
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-mutating-reducer` — A hand-written reducer doesn't change its state in place

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a `state.push(x)` or `state.key = v` followed at once by `return state` becomes `return [...state, x]` or `return { ...state, key: v }`; whoever held the old state no longer sees the change, which is the fix but is a change. Any other mutation is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-mutating-reducer.md

### What it checks

A hand-written reducer — a function `(state, action)` that tests `action.type`, outside
`createSlice`, `createReducer` and `produce` — does not assign to, delete from, or call a mutating
method (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, `Object.assign(state, …)`, …) on its `state`.

**Why:** Redux compares state by reference: a state changed in place is the same object, so the UI doesn't
update, and time-travel debugging shows the wrong history. *Style Guide, Priority A: Do Not Mutate
State.* Inside `createSlice` the state is an Immer draft, and changing it is how updates are written.

### How to fix

1. Return a new value: `[...state, item]`, `{ ...state, field: value }`, `state.filter(…)`.
2. Better, rewrite the reducer with `createSlice`, where the in-place update is correct.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      state.push(action.payload);
      return state;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      return [...state, action.payload];
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      state.push(action.payload);
      return state;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      return [...state, action.payload];
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      state.push(action.payload);
      return state;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      return [...state, action.payload];
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      state.push(action.payload);
      return state;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function todos(state = [], action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'todos/added':
      return [...state, action.payload];
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-non-serializable-state` — State holds only serializable values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the data has to be stored in another shape, and the code reading it changed)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-non-serializable-state.md

### What it checks

A slice's `initialState` (in `createSlice` or `createReducer`, followed through a `const`) and the
values a reducer assigns into its state are plain objects, arrays and primitives: no `Map`, `Set`,
`Date`, `Promise`, class instance, `Symbol`, function or regular expression.

**Why:** The DevTools, persistence and time-travel all serialize the state; a value that doesn't survive
`JSON.stringify` breaks them, and Redux Toolkit's serializability check warns at run time. *Style
Guide, Priority A: Do Not Put Non-Serializable Values in State or Actions.*

### How to fix

1. Store a `Map` or `Set` as an object keyed by ID, or as an array.
2. Store a `Date` as its ISO string or its timestamp, and make the `Date` where it is displayed.
3. Keep functions and class instances outside the store; store an ID that finds them.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: new Map() },
  reducers: {},
});
```

##### Do

```js
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: {} },
  reducers: {},
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: new Map() },
  reducers: {},
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: {} },
  reducers: {},
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: new Map() },
  reducers: {},
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: {} },
  reducers: {},
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: new Map() },
  reducers: {},
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const usersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'users',
  initialState: { byId: {} },
  reducers: {},
});
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-object-selector` — useSelector selects one value per call

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are one `useSelector` per value, when the result is destructured by exactly its keys (the default), or `shallowEqual` as the equality function when the file imports from `react-redux`; each changes when the component re-renders)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-object-selector.md

### What it checks

A selector passed alone to `useSelector` (or a typed `use…Selector` hook) doesn't return a new object
literal.

**Why:** `useSelector` re-renders when the selected value changes by reference, and a new object is a new
reference after every dispatched action, so the component re-renders on all of them. *Style Guide,
Priority B: Call useSelector Multiple Times in Function Components.* An equality function such as
`shallowEqual` as the second argument avoids it, and is left alone.

### How to fix

1. Call `useSelector` once per value: `const todos = useSelector((state) => state.todos)`.
2. Or pass `shallowEqual` as the second argument when one object is really wanted.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function TodoList() {
  const { todos, filter } = useSelector((state) => ({ todos: state.todos, filter: state.filter }));
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

##### Do

```js
function TodoList() {
  const todos = useSelector((state) => state.todos);
  const filter = useSelector((state) => state.filter);
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function TodoList() {
  const { todos, filter } = useSelector((state) => ({ todos: state.todos, filter: state.filter }));
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function TodoList() {
  const todos = useSelector((state) => state.todos);
  const filter = useSelector((state) => state.filter);
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function TodoList() {
  const { todos, filter } = useSelector((state) => ({ todos: state.todos, filter: state.filter }));
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function TodoList() {
  const todos = useSelector((state) => state.todos);
  const filter = useSelector((state) => state.filter);
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function TodoList() {
  const { todos, filter } = useSelector((state) => ({ todos: state.todos, filter: state.filter }));
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function TodoList() {
  const todos = useSelector((state) => state.todos);
  const filter = useSelector((state) => state.filter);
  return [todos, filter];
}
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-sequential-dispatch` — One event is one action, not a run of dispatches

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the actions have to be merged into one that the reducers all respond to)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-sequential-dispatch.md

### What it checks

A block doesn't dispatch more than `max` (2) actions in a row, statement after statement.

**Why:** Each dispatch re-renders the subscribers and leaves the state halfway between the first action and
the last, a state no reducer meant. *Style Guide, Priority B: Avoid Dispatching Many Actions
Sequentially; Model Actions as Events, Not Setters.*

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `2` | how many `dispatch` statements in a row are accepted |

### How to fix

1. Dispatch one action that describes what happened (`orderPlaced`), with what the reducers need in
   its payload.
2. Let each slice that cares respond to it in `extraReducers`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(setPizzas(1));
  dispatch(setCokes(1));
  dispatch(setTotal(12));
}
```

##### Do

```js
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(orderPlaced({ pizza: 1, coke: 1 }));
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(setPizzas(1));
  dispatch(setCokes(1));
  dispatch(setTotal(12));
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(orderPlaced({ pizza: 1, coke: 1 }));
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(setPizzas(1));
  dispatch(setCokes(1));
  dispatch(setTotal(12));
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(orderPlaced({ pizza: 1, coke: 1 }));
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(setPizzas(1));
  dispatch(setCokes(1));
  dispatch(setTotal(12));
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function placeOrder(dispatch) {
  dispatch(orderPlaced({ pizza: 1, coke: 1 }));
}
```

## `redux-toolkit/no-side-effects-in-reducer` — A reducer has no side effects

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a case reducer whose side effect sits in an object built from `action.payload` gets a `prepare` callback that builds the object, and reads it from the payload; the action creator's argument stays the same, the effect now runs when the action is made. Any other effect is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/no-side-effects-in-reducer.md

### What it checks

A reducer — a `createSlice` case reducer, a builder's `addCase`/`addMatcher`/`addDefaultCase`
callback, or a hand-written `(state, action)` reducer — doesn't fetch, wait, start timers, read the
clock or a random source, touch storage, or dispatch.

**Why:** A reducer must give the same next state for the same state and action, so that replaying actions
reproduces the state. *Style Guide, Priority A: Reducers Must Not Have Side Effects.*

### How to fix

1. Make random IDs and timestamps in the action's `prepare` callback, so they arrive in the payload.
2. Move fetching, timers and storage into a thunk (`createAsyncThunk`) or a listener.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const todosSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'todos',
  initialState: [],
  reducers: {
    todoAdded(state, action) {
      state.push({ id: nanoid(), text: action.payload });
    },
  },
});
```

##### Fixed

```js
const todosSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'todos',
  initialState: [],
  reducers: {
    todoAdded: {
      reducer(state, action) {
        state.push(action.payload);
      },
      prepare(payload) {
        return { payload: { id: nanoid(), text: payload } };
      },
    },
  },
});
```

##### Do

```js
const todosSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'todos',
  initialState: [],
  reducers: {
    todoAdded: {
      reducer(state, action) {
        state.push(action.payload);
      },
      prepare(text) {
        return { payload: { id: nanoid(), text } };
      },
    },
  },
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const todosSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'todos',
  initialState: [],
  reducers: {
    todoAdded(state, action) {
      state.push({ id: nanoid(), text: action.payload });
    },
  },
});
```

##### Fixed


## `redux-toolkit/object-shorthand-mapdispatch` — connect's mapDispatch is an object of action creators

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a `mapDispatch` whose every member is `(a) => dispatch(creator(a))` becomes the object `{ creator }`, and its `const` goes when nothing else reads it; `connect` then passes every argument to the creator, not only those named. Any other `mapDispatch` is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/object-shorthand-mapdispatch.md

### What it checks

The second argument of `connect` from `react-redux` is an object of action creators, not a function
of `dispatch`. A function that takes `ownProps` too is left alone.

**Why:** `connect` binds an object of action creators to `dispatch` itself; the function form only repeats
that by hand. *Style Guide, Priority B: Use the Object Shorthand Form of mapDispatch with connect.*

### How to fix

1. Replace the function with an object of the action creators it wraps: `{ todoAdded }`.
2. Remove the function.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

const mapDispatch = (dispatch) => ({
  todoAdded: (text) => dispatch(todoAdded(text)),
});

export default connect(mapState, mapDispatch)(TodoList);
```

##### Do

```js
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

export default connect(mapState, { todoAdded })(TodoList);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

const mapDispatch = (dispatch) => ({
  todoAdded: (text) => dispatch(todoAdded(text)),
});

export default connect(mapState, mapDispatch)(TodoList);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

export default connect(mapState, { todoAdded })(TodoList);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

const mapDispatch = (dispatch) => ({
  todoAdded: (text) => dispatch(todoAdded(text)),
});

export default connect(mapState, mapDispatch)(TodoList);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

export default connect(mapState, { todoAdded })(TodoList);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

const mapDispatch = (dispatch) => ({
  todoAdded: (text) => dispatch(todoAdded(text)),
});

export default connect(mapState, mapDispatch)(TodoList);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';

export default connect(mapState, { todoAdded })(TodoList);
```

## `redux-toolkit/prefer-create-slice` — Reducers are written with createSlice

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the reducer, its action types and its action creators are rewritten together)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/prefer-create-slice.md

### What it checks

A Redux reducer isn't written by hand as a `switch` on `action.type` (or a chain of comparisons with
it); it is written with `createSlice`. A reducer handed to React's `useReducer` is component state,
and is left alone.

**Why:** `createSlice` writes the action types and action creators, and its reducers update an Immer draft,
so the immutable-update mistakes can't happen. *Style Guide, Priority B: Use Redux Toolkit for
Writing Redux Logic; Use Immer for Writing Immutable Updates.*

### How to fix

1. Move the initial state and each `case` into `createSlice({ name, initialState, reducers })`, one
   case reducer per action.
2. Export the generated action creators (`slice.actions`) and the reducer (`slice.reducer`), and
   replace the hand-written action types and creators with them.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function counter(state = 0, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'counter/incremented':
      return state + 1;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: 0,
  reducers: {
    incremented: (state) => state + 1,
  },
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function counter(state = 0, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'counter/incremented':
      return state + 1;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: 0,
  reducers: {
    incremented: (state) => state + 1,
  },
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function counter(state = 0, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'counter/incremented':
      return state + 1;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: 0,
  reducers: {
    incremented: (state) => state + 1,
  },
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function counter(state = 0, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'counter/incremented':
      return state + 1;
    default:
      return state;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: 0,
  reducers: {
    incremented: (state) => state + 1,
  },
});
```

## `redux-toolkit/prefer-hooks-api` — Components read the store with hooks, not connect

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the component's props and its wrapper are rewritten as hook calls)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/prefer-hooks-api.md

### What it checks

`connect` is not imported from `react-redux`; function components use `useSelector` and
`useDispatch`.

**Why:** The hooks are simpler to read and type than `connect`'s wrapper and its `mapState` and `mapDispatch`
props. *Style Guide, Priority B: Use the React-Redux Hooks API.*

### How to fix

1. In the component, call `useSelector` for each value `mapState` gave it, and `useDispatch` for the
   actions `mapDispatch` gave it.
2. Remove the `connect(…)` wrapper and export the component itself.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { connect } from 'react-redux';
```

##### Do

```js
import { useDispatch, useSelector } from 'react-redux';
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useDispatch, useSelector } from 'react-redux';
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { connect } from 'react-redux';
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useDispatch, useSelector } from 'react-redux';
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { connect } from 'react-redux';
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useDispatch, useSelector } from 'react-redux';
```

## `redux-toolkit/slice-key-names` — State slices are named after their data

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-redux-toolkit` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the key is the state's shape, so every selector that reads it changes too)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:redux-toolkit/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/redux-toolkit/slice-key-names.md

### What it checks

The keys of `combineReducers`, `combineSlices` and `configureStore`'s `reducer` object name the data
each slice holds (`users`), not the reducer that manages it (`usersReducer`).

**Why:** The key is the field every selector reads: `state.usersReducer.list` reads as code, not data.
*Style Guide, Priority B: Name State Slices Based On the Stored Data.*

### How to fix

1. Rename the key after the data: `users: usersReducer`.
2. Update every selector and test that reads the old key.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ usersReducer, postsReducer });
```

##### Do

```js
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ users: usersReducer, posts: postsReducer });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ usersReducer, postsReducer });
```

##### Do

```jsx
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ users: usersReducer, posts: postsReducer });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ usersReducer, postsReducer });
```

##### Do

```ts
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ users: usersReducer, posts: postsReducer });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ usersReducer, postsReducer });
```

##### Do

```tsx
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ users: usersReducer, posts: postsReducer });
```

## `scss/at-extend-no-missing-placeholder` — `@extend` targets a placeholder

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-scss` · `codelaw-rules-scss` · **Languages:** SCSS
- **Fix:** `manual` (turning a class into a placeholder changes the stylesheet's output)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:scss/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:scss/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/scss/at-extend-no-missing-placeholder.md

### What it checks

`@extend` names a `%placeholder`, not a class or an element.

**Why:** Extending a class drags every selector that mentions the class into the output, including ones far from the code at hand.

### How to fix

1. Move the shared declarations into a `%placeholder`.
2. `@extend` the placeholder from each place that needs it.

### Examples

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
.a {
  @extend .b;
}
```

##### Do

```scss
%b {
  color: red;
}

.a {
  @extend %b;
}
```

### Differences from the source

A target with interpolation is not judged.

## `scss/at-function-named-arguments` — Function arguments are passed by name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-scss` · `codelaw-rules-scss` · **Languages:** SCSS
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the function is defined in the same file, whose parameter names the edit writes; otherwise reported without an edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/scss/at-function-named-arguments.md

### What it checks

A call to a `@function` passes its arguments by name: `size($base: 2)`.

**Why:** A named argument says what it is, and survives a reordered signature.

### Examples

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
@function size($base) {
  @return $base * 2;
}
a {
  width: size(2px);
}
```

##### Do

```scss
@function size($base) {
  @return $base * 2;
}
a {
  width: size($base: 2px);
}
```

## `scss/at-function-pattern` — Function names follow the project's pattern

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-scss` · `codelaw-rules-scss` · **Languages:** SCSS
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming the function must also rename its callers, possibly in other files)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/scss/at-function-pattern.md

### What it checks

A `@function`'s name matches `pattern`, kebab-case by default.

**Why:** Consistent names are predictable.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | `string` | `"^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*$"` | a regular expression names must match |

### How to fix

1. Rename the function and its calls.

### Examples

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
@function myFn($a) {
  @return $a;
}
```

##### Do

```scss
@function my-fn($a) {
  @return $a;
}
```

## `scss/at-if-no-null` — No comparing to `null` in `@if`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-scss` · `codelaw-rules-scss` · **Languages:** SCSS
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:scss/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:scss/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/scss/at-if-no-null.md

### What it checks

`@if` tests a value directly: `@if $x`, `@if not $x`, not `@if $x != null` or `@if $x == null`.

**Why:** Every value other than `null` and `false` is truthy in Sass, so testing the value says the same thing in fewer words.

### Examples

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
@if $x != null {
  a: b;
}
```

##### Do

```scss
@if $x {
  a: b;
}
```

### Differences from the source

`$x != null` is fixed to `$x` and `$x == null` to `not $x`. A comparison that is only part of a condition is reported without a fix.

## `scss/at-import-partial-extension-allowed-list` — `@import` extensions the project allows

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-scss` · `codelaw-rules-scss` · **Languages:** SCSS
- **Fix:** `manual` (which extension the project uses is its own convention)
