```jsx
xit("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
it.skip("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
xit("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
it.skip("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
xit("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
it.skip("rounds", () => {
  expect(round(1.5)).toBe(2);
});
```

## `testing/no-test-return-statement` — No `return` from a test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (`await` needs the callback to be `async`, and a returned value that is not a promise is a mistake to remove)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/no-test-return-statement.md

### What it checks

A test callback does not `return` a value; an async test is `async` and `await`s.

**Why:** A returned promise is easy to lose in a refactor, and then the test passes before the assertion runs; `await` reads plainly.

### How to fix

1. Make the callback `async`.
2. Replace `return <promise>` with `await <promise>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/no-unneeded-async-expect-function` — No async wrapper around an awaited promise in `expect`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/no-unneeded-async-expect-function.md

### What it checks

`expect(async () => await p)` and `expect(async () => { await p; })` pass the promise itself: `expect(p)`.

**Why:** The wrapper adds nothing: `resolves` and `rejects` already await the promise.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(async () => await save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(async () => await save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(async () => await save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(async () => await save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("fails", async () => {
  await expect(save()).rejects.toThrow();
});
```

## `testing/no-untyped-mock-factory` — Typed `jest.mock` factories

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/no-untyped-mock-factory.md

### What it checks

A `jest.mock(path, factory)` call names the module's type: `jest.mock<typeof import("./api")>("./api", () => …)`, so the factory is checked against the real module.

**Why:** Without the type argument the factory can return anything, and a mock that drifts from the module still compiles.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
jest.mock("./api", () => ({ get: jest.fn() }));
```

##### Do

```ts
jest.mock<typeof import("./api")>("./api", () => ({ get: jest.fn() }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
jest.mock("./api", () => ({ get: jest.fn() }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
jest.mock<typeof import("./api")>("./api", () => ({ get: jest.fn() }));
```

## `testing/playwright-expect-expect` — Every test asserts

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the assertion a test is missing is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-expect-expect.md

### What it checks

A test body calls `expect` (or `expect.soft`, `expect.poll`), Vitest's `expectTypeOf` or `assertType`, or an `assert` at least once. `test.todo` has no body and is left alone. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/expect-expect`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** A test with no assertion passes as long as nothing throws, so it reads as coverage and checks nothing.

### How to fix

1. Add an `expect` on the result the test is about.
2. If the test only checks that nothing throws, say so: `expect(() => run()).not.toThrow()`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
  expect(store.get(1)).toStrictEqual(user);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
  expect(store.get(1)).toStrictEqual(user);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
  expect(store.get(1)).toStrictEqual(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  save(user);
  expect(store.get(1)).toStrictEqual(user);
});
```

## `testing/playwright-max-expects` — At most five assertions in a test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting the test decides which assertions belong together)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-max-expects.md

### What it checks

A test body holds at most five `expect` statements; the sixth is reported. (The source's default; the limit is fixed here, and only statements directly in the test body are counted.) The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/max-expects`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** A test that asserts many things stops at the first failure and hides the rest; smaller tests each report their own.

### How to fix

1. Split the test into several, each asserting one behaviour.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("user", () => {
  expect(u.a).toBe(1);
  expect(u.b).toBe(2);
  expect(u.c).toBe(3);
  expect(u.d).toBe(4);
  expect(u.e).toBe(5);
  expect(u.f).toBe(6);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("user", () => {
  expect(u).toMatchObject({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6 });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(u.a).toBe(1);
  expect(u.b).toBe(2);
  expect(u.c).toBe(3);
  expect(u.d).toBe(4);
  expect(u.e).toBe(5);
  expect(u.f).toBe(6);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(u).toMatchObject({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6 });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(u.a).toBe(1);
  expect(u.b).toBe(2);
  expect(u.c).toBe(3);
  expect(u.d).toBe(4);
  expect(u.e).toBe(5);
  expect(u.f).toBe(6);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(u).toMatchObject({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6 });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(u.a).toBe(1);
  expect(u.b).toBe(2);
  expect(u.c).toBe(3);
  expect(u.d).toBe(4);
  expect(u.e).toBe(5);
  expect(u.f).toBe(6);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(u).toMatchObject({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6 });
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

### What it checks

```js
        describe("e", () => {});
```

## `testing/playwright-missing-playwright-await` — `await` Playwright's async assertions and steps

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-missing-playwright-await.md

### What it checks

A web-first assertion (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`, `toHaveURL`, …), a `.resolves`/`.rejects` assertion, `expect.poll(…)` and `test.step(…)` are awaited. The fix adds `await` inside an `async` function.

**Why:** Each returns a promise; without `await` the test ends before the retrying assertion has finished, and its failure is lost.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("shows", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (dropping the timeout makes the action use the configured one, which may be shorter)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

An action (`click`, `fill`, `press`, …) is not given its own `timeout`; the project's `actionTimeout` applies. The suggested edit removes the option.

**Why:** A per-call timeout hides a slow page behind one long wait and drifts from the configured limit.

#### TSX

## `testing/playwright-no-conditional-expect` — No `expect` inside a condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the test has to be split or its setup fixed so the assertion always runs; no edit can tell which)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-conditional-expect.md

### What it checks

A test does not call `expect` inside an `if`, a `switch`, a `catch`, a `? :` or a `&&`/`||`, where it may silently not run. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-conditional-expect`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** A conditional assertion passes when the condition is false, so the test can pass while checking nothing.

### How to fix

1. Split the test so each case sets up the state it asserts on, and assert unconditionally.
2. For an expected error, use `expect(() => …).toThrow()` or `await expect(p).rejects…` instead of `try`/`catch`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-conditional-in-test` — No conditional logic in a test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each branch becomes its own test, with its own setup; how to split is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-conditional-in-test.md

### What it checks

A test body has no `if`, `switch` or `? :`: each test runs one path. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-conditional-in-test`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** A test that branches checks different things on different runs; a failure is harder to trace and a path can go untested.

### How to fix

1. Write one test per branch, each with the setup that makes that branch happen.
2. Use `test.each` when the branches differ only in data.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("formats", () => {
  if (isWindows) {
    expect(fmt()).toBe("a\\b");
  }
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("formats", () => {
  expect(fmt()).toBe("a/b");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("formats", () => {
  if (isWindows) {
    expect(fmt()).toBe("a\\b");
  }
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("formats", () => {
  expect(fmt()).toBe("a/b");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("formats", () => {
  if (isWindows) {
    expect(fmt()).toBe("a\\b");
  }
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("formats", () => {
  expect(fmt()).toBe("a/b");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("formats", () => {
  if (isWindows) {
    expect(fmt()).toBe("a\\b");
  }
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("formats", () => {
  expect(fmt()).toBe("a/b");
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-duplicate-hooks` — One hook of each kind per block

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (merging two hooks means choosing the order of their statements)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-duplicate-hooks.md

### What it checks

A `describe` block (or the file) has at most one `beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` and `afterAll`. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-duplicate-hooks`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Two hooks of one kind run in declaration order, which is easy to miss; one hook keeps the setup in one place.

### How to fix

1. Move the second hook's statements into the first, in the order they should run.
2. Delete the second hook.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  seed();
});
```

##### Do

```js
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
  seed();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  seed();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  reset();
  seed();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  seed();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
  seed();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  seed();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  reset();
  seed();
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`

## `testing/playwright-no-element-handle` — Locators, not element handles

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a locator is lazy and strict where a handle was resolved once, so later lines may behave differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-element-handle.md

### What it checks

`page.$(selector)` and `page.$$(selector)` are written `page.locator(selector)`. The suggested edit makes the change.

**Why:** An element handle points at one DOM node, which goes stale when the page re-renders; a locator finds the element again each time and auto-waits.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.$("button");
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.locator("button");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.$("button");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.locator("button");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.$("button");
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.locator("button");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.$("button");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const b = await page.locator("button");
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-eval` — No `$eval` and `$$eval`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the evaluation becomes a locator assertion or `locator.evaluate`, which needs knowing what is checked)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-eval.md

### What it checks

A test does not call `page.$eval` or `page.$$eval`; it uses a locator (`locator.evaluate`, or a web-first assertion).

**Why:** `$eval` runs once against whatever matches at that instant, without waiting; a locator waits and retries.

### How to fix

1. Replace `page.$eval(sel, fn)` with `page.locator(sel).evaluate(fn)`, or with a web-first assertion on the locator.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.$eval("h1", (e) => e.textContent);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toHaveText("Hi");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.$eval("h1", (e) => e.textContent);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toHaveText("Hi");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.$eval("h1", (e) => e.textContent);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toHaveText("Hi");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.$eval("h1", (e) => e.textContent);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toHaveText("Hi");
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-export` — No exports from a test file

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the exported code moves to a module of its own, and its importers change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

```js
test("a", () => {});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-hooks` — No setup and teardown hooks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the hook's work moves into each test or a helper the tests call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-hooks.md

### What it checks

A test file has no `beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` or `afterAll`: each test sets up what it needs. Opt-in; a style some teams choose. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-hooks`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Setup in hooks is shared state that each test reads implicitly; a helper the test calls makes it explicit.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("a", () => {
  const db = freshDb();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
beforeEach(() => {
  db.reset();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("a", () => {
  const db = freshDb();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  db.reset();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("a", () => {
  const db = freshDb();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  db.reset();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("a", () => {
  const db = freshDb();
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-identical-title` — No two tests with one title

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

## `testing/playwright-no-magic-timeouts` — No literal timeout values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the named constant, and where it lives, are the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-magic-timeouts.md

### What it checks

A `timeout` option, `test.setTimeout(…)` or `page.waitForTimeout(…)` is given a named constant, not a number literal. Opt-in.

**Why:** A bare number says nothing about why that wait is right, and the same value repeated drifts.

```js
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
```

##### Do


##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do


##### Don't

## `testing/playwright-no-networkidle` — No `networkidle`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the wait becomes an assertion on what the page shows, which needs knowing what it waits for)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-networkidle.md

### What it checks

A test does not wait for the `"networkidle"` load state (in `waitForLoadState`, `goto`, `waitForURL` or `reload`).

**Why:** Network-idle is a guess: pages that poll never reach it and pages that load lazily reach it early. A web-first assertion waits for what the test needs.

### How to fix

1. Replace the wait with a web-first assertion on the element the test needs: `await expect(page.getByRole("table")).toBeVisible()`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole("table")).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");
});
```

##### Do


## `testing/playwright-no-nth-methods` — No `first()`, `last()` and `nth()`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a unique locator needs knowing what distinguishes the element)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-nth-methods.md

### What it checks

A locator is made unique by what it matches, not narrowed with `.first()`, `.last()` or `.nth(i)`. Opt-in.

**Why:** Position-based locators break when the order of the page changes, and pick the wrong element silently.

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByRole("button").first().click();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByRole("button").first().click();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  await page.getByRole("button").first().click();
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();

```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the assertion moves into a test, which needs a title)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-standalone-expect.md

### What it checks

`expect` is called inside a test or a hook, not at the top level or directly in a `describe` callback. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-standalone-expect`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** An `expect` outside a test runs while the file is collected: its failure is reported as a broken file, or not at all.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
describe("cart", () => {

});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("cart", () => {

  });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

    expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  test("starts empty", () => {
    expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  test("starts empty", () => {
    expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-test-return-statement` — No `return` from a test

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (`await` needs the callback to be `async`, and a returned value that is not a promise is a mistake to remove)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-test-return-statement.md

### What it checks

A test callback does not `return` a value; an async test is `async` and `await`s. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/no-test-return-statement`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** A returned promise is easy to lose in a refactor, and then the test passes before the assertion runs; `await` reads plainly.

### How to fix

1. Make the callback `async`.
2. Replace `return <promise>` with `await <promise>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", () => {
  return expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/playwright-no-unused-locators` — No locator created and left unused

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the locator was for — an action or an assertion — is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-unused-locators.md

### What it checks

A locator (`page.getByRole(…)`, `page.locator(…)`) is not created as a statement on its own: it does nothing until it is acted on or asserted.

**Why:** Locators are lazy, so a bare one neither waits nor checks; it reads as if it asserted that the element exists.

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })).toBeVisible();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })).toBeVisible();
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-useless-await.md

### What it checks

Creating a locator (`page.locator(…)`, `getByRole(…)`, `.first()`, `.filter(…)`, …) is synchronous and is not awaited; the fix drops the `await`.

**Why:** Awaiting a locator does not wait for the element; it only suggests that it does.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = await page.getByRole("button");
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = page.getByRole("button");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = await page.getByRole("button");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = page.getByRole("button");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = await page.getByRole("button");
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = page.getByRole("button");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = await page.getByRole("button");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  const save = page.getByRole("button");
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`

`not.toBeVisible()` is `toBeHidden()`, `not.toBeHidden()` is `toBeVisible()`, `not.toBeEnabled()` is `toBeDisabled()` and `not.toBeDisabled()` is `toBeEnabled()`; the fix uses the positive matcher.

## `testing/playwright-no-wait-for-navigation` — No `waitForNavigation`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the replacement assertion on the URL needs the URL the author expects; deleting the call is the suggested half)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-no-wait-for-navigation.md

### What it checks

A test does not call `page.waitForNavigation()`, which Playwright deprecates; it waits for the URL with `page.waitForURL(…)` or `expect(page).toHaveURL(…)`. The suggested edit deletes the call.

**Why:** `waitForNavigation` races the action that triggers it, so it can miss the navigation and hang.

### Examples

```js
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
```

##### Do

```js
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  await page.waitForNavigation();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.waitForNavigation();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  await page.waitForNavigation();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("/next");
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

## `testing/playwright-prefer-comparison-matcher` — Comparison matchers for comparisons

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-comparison-matcher.md

### What it checks

`expect(a > b).toBe(true)` is written `expect(a).toBeGreaterThan(b)`, and likewise for `>=`, `<` and `<=` and their `false` forms. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-comparison-matcher`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.


#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-ending-with-an-expect` — A test ends with an assertion

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what to assert after the last action is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-ending-with-an-expect.md

### What it checks

A test's last statement is an `expect`. Opt-in. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-ending-with-an-expect`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Work after the last assertion is unchecked: it either belongs before the assertion or needs one of its own.

### How to fix

1. Add an assertion on the effect of the last statement, or move that statement before the last assertion.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("saves", () => {
  expect(form.valid).toBe(true);
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("saves", () => {
  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(form.valid).toBe(true);
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  expect(form.valid).toBe(true);
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(form.valid).toBe(true);
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

```js
  expect(a.id === b.id).toBe(true);
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-hooks-in-order` — Hooks in the order they run

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (reordering hooks moves their statements; the author checks nothing depends on the old order)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-hooks-in-order.md

### What it checks

In a block, hooks are declared in the order Jest runs them: `beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`, `afterAll`. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-hooks-in-order`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Hooks run in that order whatever their position; declaring them out of order makes the file mislead its reader.

### How to fix

1. Move the hook above the hooks that run after it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```js
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-hooks-on-top` — Hooks before the tests

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a hook above tests changes nothing at run time but the author places it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-hooks-on-top.md

### What it checks

In a block, every hook comes before the first test. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-hooks-on-top`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

```js
  setup();
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-locator` — Locator methods over `page` actions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a locator is strict — it fails on more than one match where the page method took the first)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-locator.md

### What it checks

An action or query on a selector is made through a locator: `page.locator(sel).click()`, not `page.click(sel)` (and likewise `fill`, `check`, `hover`, `textContent`, `isVisible` and the rest). The suggested edit makes the change.

**Why:** The page-level selector methods are discouraged: a locator is strict, re-finds the element and composes with filters.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.click("#save");

});
```

##### Do

```js
  await page.locator("#save").click();
  await page.locator("#name").fill("Ann");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.click("#save");
  await page.fill("#name", "Ann");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  await page.locator("#save").click();
  await page.locator("#name").fill("Ann");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  await page.click("#save");
  await page.fill("#name", "Ann");
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  await page.locator("#save").click();
  await page.locator("#name").fill("Ann");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  await page.click("#save");
  await page.fill("#name", "Ann");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  await page.locator("#save").click();
  await page.locator("#name").fill("Ann");
```


## `testing/playwright-prefer-strict-equal` — `toStrictEqual` over `toEqual`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toStrictEqual` also checks `undefined` properties, sparse arrays and class types, so an assertion that passed may now fail)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-strict-equal.md

### What it checks

Deep equality is asserted with `toStrictEqual`, not `toEqual`. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-strict-equal`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** `toEqual` ignores `undefined` properties and object types, so `{ a: undefined }` equals `{}` and a class instance equals a plain object; that hides real differences.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-to-be` — `toBe` for primitives, `toBeNull`, `toBeUndefined`, `toBeNaN`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-to-be.md

### What it checks

A comparison with a number, string or boolean literal uses `toBe`, not `toEqual` or `toStrictEqual`; and `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` have their own matchers: `toBeNull()`, `toBeUndefined()`, `toBeNaN()`. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-to-be`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** For a primitive, `toBe` is the exact check and reads as one; the dedicated matchers say what is expected and print better failures.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

## `testing/playwright-prefer-to-contain` — `toContain` for an `includes` check

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-prefer-to-contain.md

### What it checks

`expect(list.includes(x)).toBe(true)` is written `expect(list).toContain(x)`, and the `false` form `expect(list).not.toContain(x)`. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/prefer-to-contain`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

```jsx

  expect(tags.includes("new")).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  expect(tags).toContain("new");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("tags", () => {
  expect(tags.includes("new")).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expect(tags).toContain("new");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  expect(tags.includes("new")).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  expect(tags).toContain("new");
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

## `testing/playwright-require-hook` — Setup code in a hook

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the code moves into a `beforeAll` or `beforeEach`, chosen by when it must run)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-require-hook.md

### What it checks

A call at the top level of a test file or directly in a `describe` callback — other than a test, a `describe`, a hook or a `jest.*`/`vi.*` call — is in a hook. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/require-hook`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Code outside a hook runs while tests are collected, before any of them, even when the test that needs it is filtered out.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the statement in `beforeAll` (once) or `beforeEach` (per test).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

## `testing/playwright-require-soft-assertions` — Soft assertions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a soft assertion lets the test go on after a failure, which changes what runs after it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-require-soft-assertions.md

### What it checks

Assertions use `expect.soft(…)`, so a test reports every failure, not only the first. The suggested edit changes `expect` to `expect.soft`. Opt-in.

**Why:** In a long end-to-end test, stopping at the first failed check hides the others.

### Examples

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect.soft(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect.soft(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect.soft(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async ({ page }) => {
  await expect.soft(page).toHaveTitle("Home");
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Do


## `testing/playwright-valid-describe-callback` — `describe` takes a plain synchronous callback

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (async work moves into a hook or test, and parameters out of the callback)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-valid-describe-callback.md

### What it checks

A `describe` has a title and a callback; the callback is not `async`, takes no parameters (except in `describe.each`) and returns nothing. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/valid-describe-callback`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** The runner calls the callback synchronously to collect tests: an async one registers its tests after collection is over, and they never run.

### How to fix

1. Move async setup into `beforeAll`.
2. Drop the callback's parameters and any `return`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

## `testing/playwright-valid-expect` — `expect` is called right and awaited when async

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-valid-expect.md

### What it checks

`expect` takes one argument (and, in Vitest and Playwright, an optional message string) and is followed by a matcher call; an assertion with `.resolves` or `.rejects` is awaited or returned. The fix adds `await` to an unawaited `.resolves`/`.rejects` assertion inside an `async` test; the other mistakes are reported for a hand edit. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/valid-expect`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** `expect(x)` with no matcher, `expect(x).toBe` without the call, or an unawaited `.resolves` all pass without checking anything.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/playwright-valid-expect-in-promise` — A promise with assertions is awaited

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the test becomes `async` and the chain is awaited or returned)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/playwright-valid-expect-in-promise.md

### What it checks

In a test, a `.then`, `.catch` or `.finally` callback that calls `expect` belongs to a promise that is awaited or returned. The Playwright Test counterpart of `testing/valid-expect-in-promise`, for `test`, `test.describe` and `test.beforeEach`.

**Why:** Otherwise the test finishes before the callback runs, and its assertion is never counted.

### How to fix

1. Make the test `async` and `await` the promise, or return it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", () => {
  load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", () => {
  load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", () => {
  load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", () => {
  load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/playwright` at `error`

```js
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(user);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith(user);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(user);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(user);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith(user);
```
```tsx
});
```

## `testing/prefer-called-with` — `toHaveBeenCalledWith` over `toHaveBeenCalled`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the expected arguments are the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-called-with.md

### What it checks

A call is asserted with its arguments, `toHaveBeenCalledWith(…)`, not only `toHaveBeenCalled()`. Negated forms are left alone.

**Why:** Checking the arguments catches a call made with the wrong values, which `toHaveBeenCalled` passes.

### How to fix

1. Replace `toHaveBeenCalled()` with `toHaveBeenCalledWith(<the expected arguments>)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 1 });
});
```

## `testing/prefer-comparison-matcher` — Comparison matchers for comparisons

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-comparison-matcher.md

### What it checks

`expect(a > b).toBe(true)` is written `expect(a).toBeGreaterThan(b)`, and likewise for `>=`, `<` and `<=` and their `false` forms.

**Why:** The comparison matchers print both values on failure; a boolean prints only `true` and `false`.

##### Do

```js
test("grows", () => {

});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size >= 2).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("grows", () => {
  expect(size).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

##### Do

## `testing/prefer-each` — `test.each` over a loop of tests

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the loop's data becomes a table and its body a parameterised test)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-each.md

### What it checks

Tests generated in a loop are written with `test.each` / `describe.each`.

**Why:** `each` names every case in the report and can run one case alone; a loop does neither.

### How to fix

1. Turn the loop's values into a table: `test.each([[1, 2], [3, 4]])`.
2. Move the loop body into the test callback, with the values as its parameters.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) {
  test(`doubles ${n}`, () => {
    expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
  });
}
```

##### Do

```js
test.each([1, 2, 3])("doubles %i", (n) => {
  expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) {
  test(`doubles ${n}`, () => {
    expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
  });
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
test.each([1, 2, 3])("doubles %i", (n) => {
  expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) {
  test(`doubles ${n}`, () => {
    expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
  });
}
```

##### Do

```ts
test.each([1, 2, 3])("doubles %i", (n) => {
  expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) {
  test(`doubles ${n}`, () => {
    expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
  });
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
test.each([1, 2, 3])("doubles %i", (n) => {
  expect(double(n)).toBe(n * 2);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-ending-with-an-expect` — A test ends with an assertion

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what to assert after the last action is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-ending-with-an-expect.md

### What it checks

A test's last statement is an `expect`. Opt-in.

**Why:** Work after the last assertion is unchecked: it either belongs before the assertion or needs one of its own.

### How to fix

### Examples

```js
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```js
  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

  expect(form.valid).toBe(true);
  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```ts

});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  form.submit();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("saves", () => {
  form.submit();
  expect(form.saved).toBe(true);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-equality-matcher` — An equality matcher for an equality

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toBe` compares with `Object.is`, not `===`: `NaN` and `-0` compare differently, so the author confirms the edit)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-equality-matcher.md

### What it checks

`expect(a === b).toBe(true)` is written `expect(a).toBe(b)` (and `!==` or `false` as `not.toBe`). The suggested edit uses `toBe`; `toEqual` or `toStrictEqual` fits when the values are objects.

**Why:** An equality matcher prints both values when it fails; a boolean prints only `true` and `false`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id === b.id).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id).toBe(b.id);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id === b.id).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id).toBe(b.id);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id === b.id).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id).toBe(b.id);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id === b.id).toBe(true);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("ids", () => {
  expect(a.id).toBe(b.id);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-expect-assertions` — Async tests count their assertions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`expect.hasAssertions()` fails a test that passed without asserting; the author may prefer `expect.assertions(n)`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-expect-assertions.md

### What it checks

An `async` test starts with `expect.hasAssertions()` or `expect.assertions(n)`. The suggested edit adds `expect.hasAssertions();`. Opt-in.

**Why:** An assertion in a callback or a `catch` may never run; counting assertions makes the test fail when it does not.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.hasAssertions(); await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.hasAssertions(); await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.hasAssertions(); await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.hasAssertions(); await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-expect-resolves` — `await expect(p).resolves` over `expect(await p)`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-expect-resolves.md

### What it checks

A promise's value is asserted with `await expect(promise).resolves.<matcher>(…)`, not `expect(await promise).<matcher>(…)`.

**Why:** `resolves` keeps the promise inside the assertion, so a rejection fails with the assertion's message, and the form matches `rejects`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(await load()).toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(await load()).toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(await load()).toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(await load()).toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-expect-type-of` — `expectTypeOf` for a type check

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`expectTypeOf` checks the static type at compile time; the runtime `typeof` check stops running, so the author confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-expect-type-of.md

### What it checks

`expect(typeof x).toBe("string")` is written `expectTypeOf(x).toBeString()` (and likewise for the other `typeof` names). The suggested edit makes the change.

**Why:** The `typeof` form asserts at run time what the type checker already knows; `expectTypeOf` states it as a type test.

```js
test("types", () => {
```

```jsx
test("types", () => {
  expect(typeof id).toBe("string");
```

##### Do

```jsx
  expectTypeOf(id).toBeString();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("types", () => {
  expect(typeof id).toBe("string");
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expectTypeOf(id).toBeString();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

});
```

## `testing/prefer-hooks-in-order` — Hooks in the order they run

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (reordering hooks moves their statements; the author checks nothing depends on the old order)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-hooks-in-order.md

### What it checks

In a block, hooks are declared in the order Jest runs them: `beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`, `afterAll`.

**Why:** Hooks run in that order whatever their position; declaring them out of order makes the file mislead its reader.

### How to fix

1. Move the hook above the hooks that run after it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```js
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

## `testing/prefer-hooks-on-top` — Hooks before the tests

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a hook above tests changes nothing at run time but the author places it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-hooks-on-top.md

### What it checks

In a block, every hook comes before the first test.

**Why:** A hook applies to every test in its block, the ones above it too; declaring it after a test hides that.

```js
test("a", () => {});

beforeEach(() => {
```

```js
test("a", () => {});
```

```jsx
  setup();
```


#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("a", () => {});

  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  setup();
});

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("a", () => {});
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  setup();
});
test("a", () => {});
```

## `testing/prefer-jest-mocked` — `jest.mocked()` over a type assertion

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-jest-mocked.md

### What it checks

A mocked value is typed with `jest.mocked(fn)`, not asserted with `fn as jest.Mock`, `jest.MockedFunction<…>`, `jest.MockedClass<…>`, `jest.MockedObject<…>` or `jest.Mocked<…>`.

**Why:** `jest.mocked` keeps the function's own parameter and return types; an `as` assertion throws them away.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("calls", () => {
  (fetchUser as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("calls", () => {
  (jest.mocked(fetchUser)).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("calls", () => {
  (fetchUser as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("calls", () => {
  (jest.mocked(fetchUser)).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-lowercase-title` — Test titles start in lower case

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-lowercase-title.md

### What it checks

A test or `describe` title starts with a lower-case letter: `test("adds")`, not `test("Adds")`. A title that starts with an acronym (`"API returns"`, two capitals) is left alone. The fix lowers the first letter.

**Why:** Titles read as a sentence after the block name in reports (`cart › adds an item`); one style keeps them readable.

#### TSX

## `testing/prefer-mock-promise-shorthand` — `mockResolvedValue` and `mockRejectedValue`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-mock-promise-shorthand.md

### What it checks

A mock that returns a settled promise uses the shorthand: `mockResolvedValue(x)` for `mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(x))` or `mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve(x))`, `mockRejectedValue(e)` for the rejecting form, and the `Once` variants.

**Why:** The shorthand says what the mock does in one word, and builds a fresh promise for each call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(user));
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(user));
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(user));
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(user));
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", () => {
  api.get.mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-mock-return-shorthand` — `mockReturnValue` for a constant

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-mock-return-shorthand.md

### What it checks

A mock implementation that only returns a primitive literal, `mockImplementation(() => 42)`, is written `mockReturnValue(42)` (and the `Once` form). An implementation that builds an object, reads a variable or calls something is left alone: it runs on every call, and the shorthand would evaluate it once.

**Why:** The shorthand states that the mock returns a constant.

##### Do

```js
test("counts", () => {

});
```

##### Don't

```jsx
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockImplementation(() => 3);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockReturnValue(3);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockImplementation(() => 3);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockReturnValue(3);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockImplementation(() => 3);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("counts", () => {
  count.mockReturnValue(3);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-snapshot-hint` — A hint on each of several snapshots

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

### What it checks

When a block has more than one `toMatchSnapshot()`, each is given a hint: `toMatchSnapshot("after save")`.

**Why:** Snapshots are keyed by test title and a counter; without hints, adding one in the middle renumbers the rest and the diff is unreadable.

```js
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot("filled");
```

```jsx
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  expect(a).toMatchSnapshot("empty");
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot("filled");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("form", () => {
  expect(a).toMatchSnapshot();
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("form", () => {
  expect(a).toMatchSnapshot("empty");
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot("filled");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("form", () => {
  expect(a).toMatchSnapshot();
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("form", () => {
  expect(a).toMatchSnapshot("empty");
  expect(b).toMatchSnapshot("filled");
});
```

## `testing/prefer-spy-on` — `spyOn` instead of overwriting a method

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-spy-on.md

### What it checks

A method is mocked with `jest.spyOn(obj, "m").mockImplementation(…)` (or `vi.spyOn`), not by assigning `obj.m = jest.fn(…)`.

```js
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("logs", () => {
  console.error = jest.fn();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("logs", () => {
  jest.spyOn(console, "error").mockImplementation();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("logs", () => {
  console.error = jest.fn();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("logs", () => {
  jest.spyOn(console, "error").mockImplementation();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("logs", () => {
  console.error = jest.fn();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("logs", () => {
  jest.spyOn(console, "error").mockImplementation();
});
```

## `testing/prefer-strict-boolean-matchers` — `toBe(true)` over `toBeTruthy()`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toBe(true)` fails for truthy values other than `true` (`1`, `"x"`), so an assertion that passed may now fail)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-strict-boolean-matchers.md

### What it checks

`toBeTruthy()` and `toBeFalsy()` are written `toBe(true)` and `toBe(false)`. Opt-in; the opposite of `prefer-to-be-truthy` and `prefer-to-be-falsy`.

**Why:** The loose matchers pass for `1`, `""` or `null`, which hides a value of the wrong type.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBeTruthy();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBe(true);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBeTruthy();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBe(true);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBeTruthy();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBe(true);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBeTruthy();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("valid", () => {
  expect(isValid(x)).toBe(true);
});
```

## `testing/prefer-strict-equal` — `toStrictEqual` over `toEqual`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toStrictEqual` also checks `undefined` properties, sparse arrays and class types, so an assertion that passed may now fail)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-strict-equal.md

### What it checks

Deep equality is asserted with `toStrictEqual`, not `toEqual`.

**Why:** `toEqual` ignores `undefined` properties and object types, so `{ a: undefined }` equals `{}` and a class instance equals a plain object; that hides real differences.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("user", () => {

});
```

##### Do

```js
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("user", () => {
  expect(user).toStrictEqual({ id: 1 });
});
```

## `testing/prefer-to-be` — `toBe` for primitives, `toBeNull`, `toBeUndefined`, `toBeNaN`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-to-be.md

### What it checks

A comparison with a number, string or boolean literal uses `toBe`, not `toEqual` or `toStrictEqual`; and `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` have their own matchers: `toBeNull()`, `toBeUndefined()`, `toBeNaN()`.

**Why:** For a primitive, `toBe` is the exact check and reads as one; the dedicated matchers say what is expected and print better failures.

### Examples

```js
test("parses", () => {

  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do
