```js
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toEqual(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBe(null);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
  expect(find("x")).toBeNull();
});
```

## `testing/prefer-to-be-falsy` — `toBeFalsy()` over `toBe(false)`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`toBeFalsy` also passes for `0`, `""`, `null` and `undefined`, so the assertion gets looser)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-to-be-falsy.md

### What it checks

`toBe(false)` is written `toBeFalsy()`. Opt-in; the opposite of `prefer-strict-boolean-matchers`.

**Why:** For a check that only cares whether a value is falsy, the named matcher says so.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("empty", () => {
  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBe(false);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("empty", () => {
  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBeFalsy();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("empty", () => {
  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBe(false);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx

  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBeFalsy();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBe(false);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBeFalsy();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBe(false);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  expect(isEmpty(list)).toBeFalsy();
```
```tsx
});
```

## `testing/prefer-vi-mocked` — `vi.mocked()` over a type assertion

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/prefer-vi-mocked.md

### What it checks

A mocked value is typed with `vi.mocked(fn)`, not asserted with `fn as Mock`, `MockedFunction<…>`, `MockedClass<…>`, `MockedObject<…>` or `Mocked<…>` (Vitest's types, with or without a `vi.` prefix).

**Why:** `vi.mocked` keeps the function's own parameter and return types; an `as` assertion throws them away.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("calls", () => {
  (fetchUser as Mock).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("calls", () => {
  (vi.mocked(fetchUser)).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("calls", () => {
  (fetchUser as Mock).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("calls", () => {
  (vi.mocked(fetchUser)).mockResolvedValue(user);
});
```

## `testing/require-awaited-expect-poll` — `expect.poll` is awaited

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/require-awaited-expect-poll.md

### What it checks

An `expect.poll(…)` assertion (and an `expect.element(…)` one) is awaited or returned. The fix adds `await` inside an `async` function; elsewhere it is reported for a hand edit.

**Why:** `expect.poll` returns a promise; without `await` the test ends before the polling does, and a failure is lost.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await expect.poll(() => count()).toBe(3);
});
```

## `testing/require-hook` — Setup code in a hook

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the code moves into a `beforeAll` or `beforeEach`, chosen by when it must run)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/require-hook.md

### What it checks

A call at the top level of a test file or directly in a `describe` callback — other than a test, a `describe`, a hook or a `jest.*`/`vi.*` call — is in a hook.

**Why:** Code outside a hook runs while tests are collected, before any of them, even when the test that needs it is filtered out.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the statement in `beforeAll` (once) or `beforeEach` (per test).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
describe("db", () => {
  seed();
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
describe("db", () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    seed();
  });
  test("reads", () => {});
});
```

## `testing/require-local-test-context-for-concurrent-snapshots` — Concurrent snapshot tests use their own `expect`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the test takes its context's `expect` as a parameter, which changes the callback's signature)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/require-local-test-context-for-concurrent-snapshots.md

### What it checks

A snapshot assertion in a `test.concurrent` (or `describe.concurrent`) test uses the `expect` from the test's context, `({ expect }) => …`, not the global one.

**Why:** Concurrent tests share the global `expect`, so snapshots can be written into the wrong test's file.

### How to fix

1. Take `expect` from the context: `test.concurrent("…", async ({ expect }) => { … })`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test.concurrent("renders", async () => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test.concurrent("renders", async ({ expect }) => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test.concurrent("renders", async () => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test.concurrent("renders", async ({ expect }) => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test.concurrent("renders", async () => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test.concurrent("renders", async ({ expect }) => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test.concurrent("renders", async () => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test.concurrent("renders", async ({ expect }) => {
  expect(html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

## `testing/require-mock-type-parameters` — `vi.fn` with a type parameter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the mocked function's type is the author's to write; a placeholder like `any` would hide the check)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/require-mock-type-parameters.md

### What it checks

`vi.fn()` is given the type of the function it stands for: `vi.fn<(id: string) => User>()`. Opt-in.

**Why:** Untyped, a mock accepts any call and returns `any`, so a test can drift from the code it mocks and still compile.

### How to fix

1. Add the function's type: `vi.fn<typeof realFn>()` or `vi.fn<(id: string) => User>()`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const get = vi.fn();
```

##### Do

```ts
const get = vi.fn<(id: string) => User>();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const get = vi.fn();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const get = vi.fn<(id: string) => User>();
```

## `testing/require-test-timeout` — Every test sets a timeout

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right timeout depends on what the test does)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset

### What it checks

Each test passes a timeout, as its third argument or `{ timeout }`. Opt-in, for suites where the global default is not wanted.

**Why:** A per-test timeout documents how long the test is expected to take and stops a hung one quickly.

```js
  await load();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
  await load();
```

##### Do

```ts
  await load();
}, 5000);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await load();
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("loads", async () => {
  await load();
}, 5000);
```

- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-await-async-events.md

### What it checks

A `userEvent.<action>(…)` call — asynchronous since user-event 14 — is awaited. The fix adds `await` inside an `async` function; elsewhere the finding is a hand edit (make the function `async`). `userEvent.setup()` is synchronous and left alone.

**Why:** Without `await` the assertion after the event runs before the event has been dispatched, so it checks the old state.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("submits", async () => {
  userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("submits", async () => {
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("submits", async () => {
  userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("submits", async () => {
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("submits", async () => {
  userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("submits", async () => {
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("submits", async () => {
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `error`

### What it checks

A `findBy…` or `findAllBy…` query, which returns a promise, is awaited. The fix adds `await` inside an `async` function.

```jsx
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  const title = screen.findByText("Hi");
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  const title = await screen.findByText("Hi");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
});
```

##### Do


## `testing/testing-library-consistent-data-testid` — `data-testid` values follow one pattern

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a new test id has to be chosen, and every query that names the old one changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-consistent-data-testid.md

### What it checks

A `data-testid` value is made of letters, digits, `-` and `_` only (a project pattern such as `<component>-<element>` is the source's option and is not configurable here). Runs on every file, since test ids are written in components.

**Why:** Test ids are an API between components and tests; one shape makes them predictable to query and to search for.

### How to fix

1. Rename the test id to the project's pattern, and update every query that names it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const b = <button data-testid="save button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```js
const b = <button data-testid="save-button">Save</button>;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const b = <button data-testid="save button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const b = <button data-testid="save-button">Save</button>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const b = <button data-testid="save button">Save</button>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const b = <button data-testid="save-button">Save</button>;
```

## `testing/testing-library-no-container` — No DOM queries through `container`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the query becomes a Testing Library query by role, label or text, which needs knowing what the user sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-no-container.md

### What it checks

A test does not query the DOM through the render result's `container` (`container.querySelector(…)`); it uses Testing Library's queries.

**Why:** `container` queries test markup structure, not what the user sees, so they break on harmless refactors and miss accessibility regressions.

### How to fix

1. Replace the selector with a query on what the user sees: `screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { container } = render(<App />);
  container.querySelector(".save");
});
```

##### Do

```js
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
  screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { container } = render(<App />);
  container.querySelector(".save");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
  screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { container } = render(<App />);
  container.querySelector(".save");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
  screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
});
```


#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx

```

```js
  screen.getByText(/save/i);
```

##### Don't

```ts

  screen.getByText(/save/gi);
});
```

##### Do


#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `testing/testing-library-no-node-access` — No DOM traversal in Testing Library tests

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the traversal becomes a query by role, label or text, which needs knowing what the user sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-no-node-access.md

### What it checks

In a file that imports Testing Library, a test does not walk the DOM — `.parentElement`, `.children`, `.firstChild`, `.closest(…)`, `.querySelector(…)` and their kin; it queries.

**Why:** Walking the DOM ties the test to markup structure; a harmless wrapper `div` breaks it, and it checks nothing a user perceives.

### How to fix

1. Replace the traversal with a query: `within(row).getByRole("cell", { name: "Total" })`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  screen.getByText("Total").parentElement;
});
```

##### Do

```js
import { screen, within } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  within(screen.getByRole("row")).getByText("Total");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  screen.getByText("Total").parentElement;
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { screen, within } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  within(screen.getByRole("row")).getByText("Total");
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  screen.getByText("Total").parentElement;
});
```

##### Do

```ts
import { screen, within } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  within(screen.getByRole("row")).getByText("Total");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  screen.getByText("Total").parentElement;
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { screen, within } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  within(screen.getByRole("row")).getByText("Total");
});
```

## `testing/testing-library-no-render-in-lifecycle` — No `render` in a setup hook

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the render moves into each test, or into a helper the tests call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-no-render-in-lifecycle.md

### What it checks

`render(…)` is called in the test, not in `beforeEach` or `beforeAll`.

**Why:** Rendering in a hook shares one rendered tree across tests and hides what each one renders; Testing Library cleans up after every test, so a `beforeAll` render is gone by the second.

### How to fix

1. Move the `render` call into each test, or into a `setup()` helper the tests call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
beforeEach(() => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
beforeEach(() => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
beforeEach(() => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", () => {
  render(<App />);
});
```

## `testing/testing-library-no-test-id-queries` — No queries by test id

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the query becomes one by role, label or text, which needs knowing what the user sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-no-test-id-queries.md

### What it checks

A test does not query by `data-testid` (`getByTestId` and its kin). Opt-in.

**Why:** Users cannot see test ids; a query by role, label or text tests what they can, and fails when that breaks.

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

## `testing/testing-library-no-wait-for-multiple-assertions` — One assertion per `waitFor`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the other assertions move after the `waitFor`, which the author orders)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-no-wait-for-multiple-assertions.md

### What it checks

A `waitFor` callback holds one `expect`; the others follow the `waitFor`.

**Why:** `waitFor` retries the whole callback until it passes, so one slow assertion delays the rest, and a failure reports only the last.

### How to fix

1. Keep the assertion that waits in the callback; move the others after the `await waitFor(…)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
    expect(b).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
  });
  expect(b).toBe(2);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
    expect(b).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
  });
  expect(b).toBe(2);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
    expect(b).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
  });
  expect(b).toBe(2);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", async () => {
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
    expect(b).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(a).toBe(1);
  });
  expect(b).toBe(2);
});
```

##### Do

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

## `testing/testing-library-prefer-presence-queries` — `getBy` for presence, `queryBy` for absence

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

```jsx

});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

});
```

##### Do

```ts

});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't


##### Do

```tsx

});
```

## `testing/testing-library-prefer-query-matchers` — The query each matcher is meant for

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which query pairs with which matcher is the project's configuration)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-prefer-query-matchers.md

### What it checks

A matcher the project lists in `get_matchers` is used with a `getBy…` query, and one it lists in `query_matchers` with a `queryBy…` query: `get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"]` reports `expect(screen.queryByText("x")).toBeVisible()`. Both lists are empty by default.

**Why:** `getBy` fails with the DOM printed when the element is missing; `queryBy` returns `null` for absence checks. Pairing each matcher with its query keeps failures readable.

|---|---|---|---|
| `get_matchers` | `string[]` | `[]` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `query_matchers` | `string[]` | `[]` | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Swap `queryBy…` for `getBy…` (or the reverse) as the project's pairing says.

### Examples

```js
test("t", () => {

});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx

```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"] }`

```jsx
test("t", () => {
  expect(screen.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();

```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"] }`

```ts

  expect(screen.queryByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();

```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"] }`

```ts

  expect(screen.getByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"] }`

```tsx

  expect(screen.queryByText("Hi")).toBeVisible();

```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ get_matchers = ["toBeVisible"] }`

## `testing/testing-library-prefer-screen-queries` — Queries through `screen`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the render result's queries are bound to its container, which `screen` is not when `render` was given another one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/testing-library` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-prefer-screen-queries.md

### What it checks

A test queries through `screen` (`screen.getByText(…)`), not through queries destructured from `render`. The suggested edit adds `screen.` when the file imports `screen`; otherwise it is a hand edit.

**Why:** `screen` is always the document; the destructured queries make each test carry the render result around and are easy to take from the wrong render.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  getByText("Hi");
});
```

##### Do

```js
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  screen.getByText("Hi");
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  getByText("Hi");
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  screen.getByText("Hi");
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  getByText("Hi");
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
test("t", () => {
  const { getByText } = render(<App />);
  screen.getByText("Hi");
});
```

## `testing/testing-library-prefer-user-event` — `userEvent` over `fireEvent`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (`userEvent` calls are async and need a `setup()` instance, so the test changes shape)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/testing-library-prefer-user-event.md

### What it checks

A test simulates input with `userEvent` (`await user.click(…)`), not `fireEvent`. Opt-in.

**Why:** `fireEvent` dispatches one DOM event; `userEvent` plays the whole interaction a user makes (focus, pointer, keyboard), so it catches what a single event misses.

### How to fix

1. Create `const user = userEvent.setup()` at the start of the test, make it `async`, and replace `fireEvent.click(x)` with `await user.click(x)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
test("t", () => {
  fireEvent.click(button);
});
```

##### Do

```js
test("t", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  await user.click(button);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
test("t", () => {
  fireEvent.click(button);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
test("t", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  await user.click(button);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
test("t", () => {
  fireEvent.click(button);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
test("t", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  await user.click(button);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
test("t", () => {
  fireEvent.click(button);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
test("t", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  await user.click(button);
});
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the calls move onto an instance created at the start of the test)

```js
  await user.click(button);
```

```jsx
  await userEvent.click(button);
```

##### Do

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TSX

### What it checks

```js
  view.unmount();
```

## `testing/valid-describe-callback` — `describe` takes a plain synchronous callback

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (async work moves into a hook or test, and parameters out of the callback)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/jest` at `error` · `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/valid-describe-callback.md

### What it checks

A `describe` has a title and a callback; the callback is not `async`, takes no parameters (except in `describe.each`) and returns nothing.

**Why:** The runner calls the callback synchronously to collect tests: an async one registers its tests after collection is over, and they never run.

### How to fix

1. Move async setup into `beforeAll`.
2. Drop the callback's parameters and any `return`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```js
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
describe("api", async () => {
  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```ts
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  await connect();
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
describe("api", () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await connect();
  });
  test("a", () => {});
});
```

## `testing/valid-expect` — `expect` is called right and awaited when async

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/jest` at `error` · `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/testing/valid-expect.md

### What it checks

`expect` takes one argument (and, in Vitest and Playwright, an optional message string) and is followed by a matcher call; an assertion with `.resolves` or `.rejects` is awaited or returned. The fix adds `await` to an unawaited `.resolves`/`.rejects` assertion inside an `async` test; the other mistakes are reported for a hand edit.

```js
test("loads", async () => {
```

##### Don't

```jsx
test("loads", async () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
```

##### Do

```jsx

  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

  expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

##### Do

```ts

  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

});
```

##### Do

```tsx

  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe(1);
```

## `testing/valid-expect-in-promise` — A promise with assertions is awaited

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-testing` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the test becomes `async` and the chain is awaited or returned)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:testing/jest` at `error` · `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error`

```jsx
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
  load().then((v) => {
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
```

##### Do

```ts
    expect(v).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
  });
```

##### Do

## `toml/deps-sorted` — pyproject.toml dependencies are sorted by name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/deps-sorted.md

### What it checks

The requirement lists in `[project].dependencies` and in each `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra are sorted by package name. Names compare the way pip compares them: case, `-`, `_` and `.` don't matter.

**Why:** A sorted list is quicker to scan, shows a duplicate at once and gives smaller diffs; installers don't depend on the order.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.31",
    "click>=8",
    "attrs",
]
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
dependencies = [
    "attrs",
    "click>=8",
    "requests>=2.31",
]
```

### Notes

A list with comments in it is reported without a fix, because the comments would stay on their lines while the requirements move.

## `toml/no-duplicate-keys` — No key or table defined twice in TOML

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the key is set twice to the same value, so the later one goes; otherwise the choices keep the first or the last, since TOML refuses both and only the author knows which was meant. A table defined twice is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/no-duplicate-keys.md

### What it checks

A key is defined once in its table, and a `[table]` header appears once. That covers dotted keys (`a.b = 1` and then `a = 2`), a table defined both by a header and by dotted keys, and keys inside inline tables.

**Why:** TOML forbids defining a key or table twice and conforming parsers refuse the file, so the mistake breaks every tool that reads it.

### How to fix

1. Decide which definition is right.
2. Delete the other one, or merge the two tables into one.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
[tool.pytest]
addopts = "-q"
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-q"
```

##### Fixed

```toml
[tool.pytest]
addopts = "-q"
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

##### Do

```toml
[tool.pytest]
addopts = "-ra"
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

## `toml/pyproject-requires-python` — pyproject.toml declares requires-python

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the supported Python range is a project decision; the fix inserts the `python` option, which may not be the right range)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/pyproject-requires-python.md

### What it checks

A `pyproject.toml` with a `[project]` table says which Python versions the package supports, in `requires-python`, unless it lists the field in `dynamic`.

**Why:** pip uses `requires-python` to pick a release that works on the running interpreter; without it, users on an old Python install a version that then fails at import.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python` | `string` | `">=3.11"` | the range the fix writes into `requires-python` |

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0.0"
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

## `toml/pyproject-schema` — pyproject.toml matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a value the schema rejects is wrong in a way only its author knows how to correct)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/pyproject-schema.md

### What it checks

A `pyproject.toml` matches SchemaStore's schema for it: `[build-system]` and `[project]` hold the keys PEP 517, PEP 518 and PEP 621 define, each in the form they define.

**Why:** Build backends reject or ignore a `[project]` key of the wrong shape — `authors` as a string, `dependencies` as a table — and the error appears only when someone builds the package.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and the form the schema expects.
2. Rewrite the value in that form, or move a tool's setting under `[tool.<name>]`.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0"
authors = "Ada Lovelace"
dependencies = { requests = ">=2" }
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0"
authors = [{ name = "Ada Lovelace" }]
dependencies = ["requests>=2"]
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `pyproject.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/pyproject.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. The `[tool.*]` tables whose schemas live in other SchemaStore files (ruff, black, mypy, poetry, setuptools, uv, …) accept any value. TOML dates and times are read as strings.

## `toml/todo-marker` — TOML TODO comments carry a ticket and, when asked, a date

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a ticket and a date are facts about the work that only the author knows; the engine can't invent them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/markers` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/todo-marker.md

### What it checks

A comment line that opens with a marker tag (`TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` by default) in a `#` comment carries a ticket, and a date when the project asks for one: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): text`. The ticket and the date go in the parentheses, in either order, either one optional unless required; any other item in them (an owner's name) is ignored. The tag must start the comment line, so a sentence that merely mentions a TODO is not a marker.

A date that is written is always enforced, whether or not `require_date` is set: it is **expired** from the as-of date on (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date, never the clock: [SR-BASELINE](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md) decision 9) and is a **warning** for the `warn_days` before it. A date that is not a calendar day is reported too. With no as-of date, only the missing and the malformed are reported.

**Why:** A TODO with no ticket has no owner and no place to be tracked, and one with no date never comes due; both outlive the people who wrote them. Naming a ticket ties the comment to the work, and a date makes the comment fail loudly the day it is overdue instead of rotting quietly.

**Configuration** is the `[todo]` table of `codelaw.toml` ([SR-CONFIG](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0110_config.md) decision 11a), one for every language:

```toml
[todo]
tags           = ["TODO", "FIXME", "HACK"]   # the words that open a marker
require_ticket = true                         # a ticket is required (default)
require_date   = false                        # a date is required (default: only a written date is enforced)
ticket_pattern = "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\\d+"        # a whole ticket must match this regular expression
warn_days      = 14                           # warn this many days before the date
```

**A repo full of bare TODOs** gets every one of them at once. Take them into the baseline (`codelaw baseline`) and pay them down, or set `require_ticket = false` and let the rule enforce only the dates that are written.

### How to fix

1. Open or find the ticket for the work and write it in the parentheses: `TODO(ABC-123): …`.
2. When the project asks for a date (`require_date`), or the work has a deadline, add it: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): …`.
3. For an expired marker: do the work and delete the comment; or, if the work really moves, change the date and say why in the text.
4. If the comment is not a to-do, rewrite it so it does not open with the tag.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
# HACK: pinned until the upstream fix
requests = "2.31.0"
```

##### Do

```toml
# HACK(DEP-3): pinned until the upstream fix
requests = "2.31.0"
```

## `ts/adjacent-overload-signatures` — Overloads of one name sit together

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (each overload moves up below the one before it, keeping their order; a comment above it stays where it was)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/adjacent-overload-signatures.md

### What it checks

The overload signatures of one function or method are written one after another, with no other member between them.

**Why:** Overloads read as one declaration; one split from the others is easy to miss when the function changes.

### How to fix

1. Move this signature up so that every overload of the name is together, before the implementation.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Store {
  get(id: string): Item;
  clear(): void;
  get(ids: string[]): Item[];
  get(x: string | string[]) { return lookup(x); }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Store {
  get(id: string): Item;
  get(ids: string[]): Item[];
  get(x: string | string[]) { return lookup(x); }
  clear(): void;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Store {
  get(id: string): Item;
  clear(): void;
  get(ids: string[]): Item[];
  get(x: string | string[]) { return lookup(x); }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Store {
  get(id: string): Item;
  get(ids: string[]): Item[];
  get(x: string | string[]) { return lookup(x); }
  clear(): void;
}
```

## `ts/array-type` — T[] rather than Array<T>

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/array-type.md

### What it checks

A simple array type is written `T[]`, not `Array<T>` (and `readonly T[]`, not `ReadonlyArray<T>`).

**Why:** One spelling for one type reads faster; `T[]` is the one TypeScript prints.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let names: Array<string>;
```

##### Do

```ts
let names: string[];
```

##### Fixed

```ts
let names: string[];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let names: Array<string>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let names: string[];
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
let names: string[];
```

### Differences from the source

Only `Array<T>` whose element type needs no parentheses (a name, a builtin type, another array or generic) is reported; `ReadonlyArray<T>` and union elements are left for now.

## `ts/await-thenable` — `await` only what can be awaited

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing `await` also removes the pause it makes, which code after it may rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/await-thenable.md

### What it checks

`await` is applied only to a Promise, another thenable, or a value typed `any` or `unknown`.

**Why:** Awaiting anything else does nothing but delay the code after it; it usually means a call
that was thought to be asynchronous is not, or a Promise was unwrapped twice.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
async function main() {
  const n = await 42;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
async function main() {
  const n = await Promise.resolve(42);
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
async function main() {
  const n = 42;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
async function main() {
  const n = await 42;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
async function main() {
  const n = await Promise.resolve(42);
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
async function main() {
  const n = 42;
}
```

### Differences from the source

None for the rule's checks: a value typed `any` or `unknown` may be a thenable, so awaiting it is
allowed, as typescript-eslint allows it.

## `ts/ban-ts-comment` — No @ts-ignore or @ts-nocheck; @ts-expect-error says why

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the reason the error is expected has to come from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/ban-ts-comment.md

### What it checks

Type-checking is never switched off with `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck`, and a `@ts-expect-error`
says why the error is expected.

**Why:** `@ts-ignore` hides an error for good, even after the code it excused changes; `@ts-expect-
error` fails as soon as the error is gone.

### How to fix

1. Fix the type error if you can.
2. Otherwise replace the comment with `// @ts-expect-error: <why>`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
// @ts-ignore
const n: number = "1";
```

##### Do

```ts
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the compiler's message
const n: number = "1";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
// @ts-ignore
const n: number = "1";
```

##### Do

```tsx
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the compiler's message
const n: number = "1";
```

## `ts/class-literal-property-style` — A literal getter is a readonly field

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a field is set on each instance and is visible to `Object.keys`, where the getter lived on the prototype)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/class-literal-property-style.md

### What it checks

A getter whose whole body returns a literal (`get kind() { return "user"; }`) is written as a `readonly` field instead. A getter with a setter of the same name is left alone.

**Why:** A getter that always returns the same literal is a constant; a `readonly` field says so in one line and keeps the literal type.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class User {
  get kind() { return "user"; }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class User {
  readonly kind = "user";
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class User {
  get kind() { return "user"; }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class User {
  readonly kind = "user";
}
```

## `ts/consistent-generic-constructors` — Type arguments on the constructor, not the annotation

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/consistent-generic-constructors.md

### What it checks

`const m = new Map<K, V>()` is written instead of `const m: Map<K, V> = new Map()`.

**Why:** Writing the type once, on the constructor, avoids repeating the name and lets the variable's type be inferred.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const seen: Set<string> = new Set();
```

##### Do

```ts
const seen = new Set<string>();
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const seen = new Set<string>();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const seen: Set<string> = new Set();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const seen = new Set<string>();
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const seen = new Set<string>();
```

## `ts/consistent-indexed-object-style` — Record rather than an index signature

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/consistent-indexed-object-style.md

### What it checks

A type made only of one index signature is written `Record<K, V>`.

**Why:** `Record<string, T>` says the same in a form readers recognise at once.

### Examples

```ts
type Counts = { [name: string]: number };
```

```ts
type Counts = Record<string, number>;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
type Counts = Record<string, number>;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
type Counts = { [name: string]: number };
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Counts = Record<string, number>;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
type Counts = Record<string, number>;
```

## `ts/consistent-type-assertions` — as, not angle-bracket assertions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/consistent-type-assertions.md

### What it checks

A type assertion is written `x as T`, not `<T>x`.

**Why:** The angle-bracket form cannot be used in TSX and reads like a generic.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const n = <number>value;
```

##### Do

```ts
const n = (value as number);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const n = (value as number);
```

## `ts/consistent-type-definitions` — interface for object types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/consistent-type-definitions.md

### What it checks

An object type is declared with `interface`, not `type X = { … }`.

**Why:** Interfaces give clearer errors, can be extended and merged, and are the form the TypeScript handbook recommends for object shapes.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
```

##### Do

```ts
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
```

##### Fixed

```ts
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
```

### Differences from the source

A type alias with type parameters is left alone.

## `ts/explicit-function-return-type` — Functions declare their return type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the return type is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/explicit-function-return-type.md

### What it checks

A function declaration or method declares its return type.

**Why:** An explicit return type documents the contract and catches a wrong return at the function, not at every caller.

### How to fix

1. Add `: ReturnType` after the parameter list.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function total(xs: number[]) {
  return xs.length;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function total(xs: number[]): number {
  return xs.length;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function total(xs: number[]) {
  return xs.length;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function total(xs: number[]): number {
  return xs.length;
}
```

### Differences from the source

Function and arrow expressions are not checked; the source checks them unless they are typed by their context, which needs type information.

## `ts/explicit-member-accessibility` — Class members say public, protected or private

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/explicit-member-accessibility.md

### What it checks

Every class method, field, accessor, constructor and constructor parameter property carries an accessibility modifier. The fix writes `public`, which is what an unmarked member already is. `#private` members, `declare` fields and fields with a decorator are not reported.

**Why:** An explicit modifier makes the class's surface readable at a glance and makes a member's widening a visible change in review.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Counter {
  count = 0;
  increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Counter {
  private count = 0;
  public increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
class Counter {
  public count = 0;
  public increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Counter {
  count = 0;
  increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Counter {
  private count = 0;
  public increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
class Counter {
  public count = 0;
  public increment() { this.count += 1; }
}
```

## `ts/explicit-module-boundary-types` — Exported functions declare their types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the types are the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/explicit-module-boundary-types.md

### What it checks

An exported function declares its return type.

**Why:** The exported signature is the module's contract; inferring it lets an internal change silently change the API.

### How to fix

1. Add `: ReturnType` after the parameter list.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export function load(id: string) {
  return fetch(id);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export function load(id: string): Promise<Response> {
  return fetch(id);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export function load(id: string) {
  return fetch(id);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export function load(id: string): Promise<Response> {
  return fetch(id);
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only exported function declarations' return types are checked; the source also checks arrow functions, parameters and class methods.

## `ts/member-ordering` — Class members are in a set order

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving members carries their comments, and a field's initialiser may read one declared before it, so the order is the author's to change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/member-ordering.md

### What it checks

Members come in this order: index signatures, static fields, instance fields, static blocks, the constructor, accessors, static methods, instance methods; within each, public, protected, private, then `#private`.

**Why:** A reader finds a member where they expect it.

### How to fix

1. Move the member up to its group.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class A {
  run(): void {}
  name = "a";
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class A {
  name = "a";
  run(): void {}
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class A {
  run(): void {}
  name = "a";
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class A {
  name = "a";
  run(): void {}
}
```

## `ts/method-signature-style` — Property signatures for methods

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/method-signature-style.md

### What it checks

A method in an interface or type literal is written as a property with a function type (`m: () => void`), not a method signature (`m(): void`).

**Why:** Property signatures are checked strictly (contravariantly) under `strictFunctionTypes`; method signatures are not.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Logger {
  log(msg: string): void;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
interface Logger {
  log: (msg: string) => void;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
interface Logger {
  log: (msg: string) => void;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Logger {
  log(msg: string): void;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface Logger {
  log: (msg: string) => void;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
interface Logger {
  log: (msg: string) => void;
}
```

### Differences from the source

Generic and optional methods are left for a manual rewrite.

## `ts/no-array-constructor` — No Array constructor with several arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-array-constructor.md

### What it checks

Arrays are built with literals; `new Array(n)` with one argument (a length) is allowed.

**Why:** `new Array(a, b)` and `new Array(n)` mean different things, and the literal says what it
means.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const xs = new Array(1, 2, 3);
```

##### Do

```ts
const xs = [1, 2, 3];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const xs = new Array(1, 2, 3);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const xs = [1, 2, 3];
```

## `ts/no-confusing-non-null-assertion` — No non-null assertion next to = or ==

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the `!` may have been meant as the start of `!=`/`!==` or as a stray assertion; the reviewer picks which)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-confusing-non-null-assertion.md

### What it checks

A non-null assertion is not written directly before `=`, `==` or `===`.

**Why:** `a! == b` reads like `a !== b`, which means the opposite.

### How to fix

1. Drop the `!`, or write `!==` if that was meant.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (user! === other) run();
```

##### Fixed (drop the !)

```ts
if (user === other) run();
```

##### Fixed (not equal)

```ts
if (user !== other) run();
```

##### Do

```ts
if (user === other) run();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (user! === other) run();
```

##### Fixed (drop the !)

```tsx
if (user === other) run();
```

##### Fixed (not equal)

```tsx
if (user !== other) run();
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (user === other) run();
```

## `ts/no-const-enum` — enum, not const enum

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX

```ts
enum Color { Red,
  Blue, }
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const enum Color {
  Red,
  Blue,
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red,
  Blue,
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
enum Color { Red,
  Blue, }
```

## `ts/no-duplicate-enum-values` — No two enum members share a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are an explicit alias of the first member with that value, keeping both equal, or the next unused number, making them differ; which one is meant is the reviewer's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-duplicate-enum-values.md

### What it checks

Each member of an enum given a literal value has a different value.

**Why:** Two members with one value are indistinguishable at run time, which is usually a copy-paste
slip.

### How to fix

1. Give each member its own value.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 1,
}
```

##### Fixed (alias)

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = Red,
}
```

##### Fixed (next value)

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

##### Do

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 1,
}
```

##### Fixed (alias)

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = Red,
}
```

##### Fixed (next value)

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

## `ts/no-dynamic-delete` — No delete with a computed key

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (a `Map` or a rest-destructure changes the data structure)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-dynamic-delete.md

### What it checks

`delete` is not used with a computed key (`delete obj[key]`).

**Why:** Objects used as dictionaries are better as `Map`; deleting dynamic keys is slow and defeats typing.

### How to fix

1. Use a `Map` and its `delete`, or build a new object without the key.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
delete cache[key];
```

##### Do

```ts
cache.delete(key);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
delete cache[key];
```

##### Do

```tsx
cache.delete(key);
```

## `ts/no-empty-object-type` — No empty interfaces or {} types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the right replacement — `object`, `unknown`, `Record<string, never>` or `NonNullable<unknown>` — depends on intent, so each is offered (an interface with a generic or `extends` clause carries no edit))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-empty-object-type.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't declare an empty interface or use the type `{}`.

**Why:** `{}` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, which is almost never what an
empty-looking type was meant to say.

### How to fix

1. For any object, use `object`.
2. For any value, use `unknown`.
3. For an object with no keys, use `Record<string, never>`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Options {}
type Empty = {};
```

##### Fixed (object)

```ts
type Options = object;
type Empty = object;
```

##### Fixed (unknown)

```ts
type Options = unknown;
type Empty = unknown;
```

##### Fixed (no keys)

```ts
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Empty = Record<string, never>;
```

##### Fixed (any non-null value)

```ts
type Options = NonNullable<unknown>;
type Empty = NonNullable<unknown>;
```

##### Do

```ts
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Anything = unknown;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Options {}
type Empty = {};
```

##### Fixed (object)

```tsx
type Options = object;
type Empty = object;
```

##### Fixed (unknown)

```tsx
type Options = unknown;
type Empty = unknown;
```

##### Fixed (no keys)

```tsx
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Empty = Record<string, never>;
```

##### Fixed (any non-null value)

```tsx
type Options = NonNullable<unknown>;
type Empty = NonNullable<unknown>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Anything = unknown;
```

## `ts/no-empty-type-parameters` — No empty type parameter list

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`

A type parameter list `<>` is not left empty.

#### TSX

##### Don't

##### Do

```tsx
  value: string;

```

## `ts/no-explicit-any` — No explicit any

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`unknown` may need narrowing code where the value is used)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-explicit-any.md

### What it checks

Types are not written as `any`.

**Why:** `any` silently disables checking for everything it touches; `unknown` keeps the checks and
forces a narrowing.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function parse(input: any) {
  return input;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function parse(input: unknown) {
  return input;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function parse(input: any) {
  return input;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function parse(input: unknown) {
  return input;
}
```

## `ts/no-extraneous-class` — No class used as a namespace

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the members become module-level functions, which changes every caller)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-extraneous-class.md

### What it checks

A class is not empty and does not hold only static members.

**Why:** A class that is never instantiated is a module in disguise; plain exports are simpler.

### How to fix

1. Export the static members as module-level functions and constants.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class MathUtil {
  static double(n: number) {
    return n * 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class MathUtil {
  static double(n: number) {
    return n * 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export function double(n: number) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

## `ts/no-floating-promises` — A Promise is awaited, returned or handled

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`void` marks the Promise as deliberately not awaited; awaiting it instead changes when the code after it runs, which only the author can decide)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-floating-promises.md

### What it checks

A statement that makes a Promise awaits it, returns it, handles its rejection (`.catch(…)`,
`.then(…, …)`) or marks it with `void`.

**Why:** A Promise nobody awaits can reject with nobody listening: the error is lost, or stops the
process as an unhandled rejection far from the line that caused it.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
save();
```

##### Do

```ts
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
async function main() {
  await save();
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
void save();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
save();
```

##### Do

```tsx
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
save().catch((e) => console.error(e));
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
async function save(): Promise<void> {}
void save();
```

### Differences from the source

Only a call or `new` alone in a statement is checked: typescript-eslint also checks a Promise left
in an array, a comma or a conditional expression.

## `ts/no-implicit-any-let` — A let without a value has a type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the variable's type is the author's to write)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-implicit-any-let.md

### What it checks

A `let` declared without a value carries a type annotation.

**Why:** Without one its type is `any` until TypeScript's control-flow analysis guesses, and type errors slip past.

### How to fix

1. Add the type (`let count: number;`) or initialise the variable.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let count;
count = 1;
```

##### Do

```ts
let count: number;
count = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

count = 1;
```

##### Do

```tsx

count = 1;
```

## `ts/no-import-type-side-effects` — An import of only types is import type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-import-type-side-effects.md

### What it checks

An import whose every named specifier is marked `type` (`import { type A } from "m"`) is written `import type { A } from "m"`. The first keeps a bare `import "m"` in the output under `verbatimModuleSyntax`; the second is removed whole. For now the rule reads an import of one specifier with no alias; a longer list waits for a native fix.

**Why:** An inline-`type`-only import still loads the module at run time, with whatever side effects it has.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { type User } from "./user";
```

##### Do

```ts
import type { User } from "./user";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { type User } from "./user";
```

##### Do

```tsx
import type { User } from "./user";
```

## `ts/no-invalid-void-type` — void only as a return type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`undefined` is what `void` means outside a return type; where the author meant a return type, the diff is wrong)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-invalid-void-type.md

### What it checks

`void` is used only as a return type or a generic argument, not as a variable, parameter or union member type.

**Why:** Elsewhere `void` is confusing: it means "ignored", not `undefined`.

```ts
let result: string | void;
```

##### Do

```ts

```

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Do

```tsx
let result: string | undefined;
```

## `ts/no-mergeable-namespace` — A namespace is declared once per file

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (restructure: the two bodies are merged into one, and their order and exports are the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-mergeable-namespace.md

### What it checks

Two `namespace` (or `module`) declarations of the same name in one file are written as one.

**Why:** TypeScript merges them silently; a reader who finds one rarely looks for the other.

### How to fix

1. Move this body into the first `namespace $N` and delete this one.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
namespace Shapes { export const square = 1; }
namespace Shapes { export const circle = 2; }
```

##### Do

```ts
namespace Shapes {
  export const square = 1;
  export const circle = 2;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
namespace Shapes { export const square = 1; }
namespace Shapes { export const circle = 2; }
```

##### Do

```tsx
namespace Shapes {
  export const square = 1;
  export const circle = 2;
}
```

## `ts/no-misused-new` — No constructors declared in interfaces, and no `new` methods in classes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended constructor signature needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-misused-new.md

### What it checks

An interface doesn't declare a method named `constructor`, and a class doesn't declare a method
named `new`.

**Why:** Both look like constructors but are ordinary methods; constructors in types are written
`new (): T`.

### How to fix

1. In an interface, describe a constructor with `new (…): T`.
2. In a class, use `constructor(…)`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Point {
  constructor(): void;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
interface PointConstructor {
  new (): object;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Point {
  constructor(): void;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface PointConstructor {
  new (): object;
}
```

## `ts/no-misused-promises` — No async function where a `void` callback is expected

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the caller should wait for the work, or the work should handle its own errors, is the author's decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-misused-promises.md

### What it checks

A function that returns a Promise is not passed or assigned where a function returning `void` is
expected.

**Why:** Whoever calls a `void` callback ignores what it returns: the Promise is never awaited, a
rejection inside it goes unnoticed, and the caller carries on before the work is done
(`forEach`, an event listener, a `setTimeout`).

### How to fix

1. Use a caller that waits: `for … of` with `await` instead of `forEach`, `await Promise.all(…map(…))`
   instead of a `forEach` of async work.
2. Or keep the callback synchronous and handle the Promise inside it:
   `() => { void work().catch(report); }`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
async function save(n: number): Promise<void> {}
[1, 2].forEach(async (n) => {
  await save(n);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
async function save(n: number): Promise<void> {}
export async function main(): Promise<void> {
  for (const n of [1, 2]) await save(n);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
async function save(n: number): Promise<void> {}
[1, 2].forEach(save);
```

##### Do

```tsx
async function save(n: number): Promise<void> {}
export async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await Promise.all([1, 2].map(save));
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only typescript-eslint's `checksVoidReturn` is checked, for a function written in place (passed,
assigned or returned) or a function passed by name. `checksConditionals` is TypeScript's own
TS2801, reported once by `ts/type-error` (SR-TYPES decision 10), and `checksSpreads` is not checked.
A callback whose expected type has several signatures is reported only when every one returns `void`.

## `ts/no-namespace` — No TypeScript namespaces

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a namespace's members into a module changes every import)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-namespace.md

### What it checks

Code is organised with ES modules, not `namespace` or `module` blocks; `declare module "x"` and
`declare global` are allowed.

**Why:** Namespaces predate ES modules and don't work with modern bundlers and tooling as well.

### How to fix

1. Move the namespace's members to a module of their own.
2. Export them, and import them where the namespace was used.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
namespace Geometry {
  export const pi = 3.14;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export const pi = 3.14;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

  export const pi = 3.14;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const pi = 3.14;
```

## `ts/no-non-null-asserted-nullish-coalescing` — No ! before ??

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing `!` is right if the left side may be null, which is the point of `??`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-non-null-asserted-nullish-coalescing.md

### What it checks

The left side of `??` is not non-null asserted.

**Why:** `a! ?? b` says `a` is never null, so `b` can never be used — one of the two is wrong.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const name = user.name! ?? 'anon';
```

##### Do

```ts
const name = user.name ?? 'anon';
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const name = user.name! ?? 'anon';
```

##### Do

```tsx
const name = user.name ?? 'anon';
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing `!` widens the type to include `undefined`, which later code may not handle)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-non-null-asserted-optional-chain.md

### What it checks

An optional chain (`a?.b`) is not followed by a non-null assertion (`!`).

**Why:** The two contradict each other: `?.` allows `undefined`, and `!` asserts it never happens.

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do

```ts

```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const name = user?.name!;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const name = user?.name;
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (optional chaining turns a null into `undefined` instead of failing; the reviewer confirms that is the handling wanted (offered where the `!` is followed by `.name`))

## `ts/no-require-imports` — No require() calls

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX

```tsx
import * as fs from "node:fs";
```

##### Fixed (import equals)

##### Do


## `ts/no-this-alias` — No aliasing this to a variable

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the callbacks that use the alias must become arrow functions by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-this-alias.md

### What it checks

`this` is not stored in a variable such as `self` or `that`; destructuring it is fine.

**Why:** Arrow functions keep the outer `this`, so an alias only adds a name to keep track of.

### How to fix

### Examples

```ts
  self.save();
};
```

##### Do

```ts
button.onclick = () => {
  this.save();
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const self = this;
button.onclick = function () {
  self.save();
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
button.onclick = () => {
  this.save();
};
```
