## `ts/no-unsafe-argument` — No argument typed `any` for a typed parameter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type the value should have comes from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-argument.md

### What it checks

A value typed `any` is not passed to a parameter declared with another type.

**Why:** The parameter's type is a promise the caller makes; an `any` argument breaks it unchecked,
and the function receives whatever the value turns out to be.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a type before passing it: annotate it, narrow it, or validate it.
2. If the parameter really accepts anything, declare it `unknown`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
declare const loose: any;
function double(n: number): number {
  return n * 2;
}
double(loose);
```

##### Do

```ts
declare const loose: unknown;
function double(n: number): number {
  return n * 2;
}
double(typeof loose === "number" ? loose : 0);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
declare const loose: any;
function double(n: number): number {
  return n * 2;
}
double(loose);
```

##### Do

```tsx
declare const loose: any;
function show(value: unknown): void {}
show(loose);
```

### Differences from the source

A spread argument (`f(...values)`) and an `any` nested in an argument's type (`any[]` passed for
`number[]`) are not checked.

## `ts/no-unsafe-assignment` — No value typed `any` assigned to a typed target

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type the value should have comes from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-assignment.md

### What it checks

A value typed `any` does not initialise or get assigned to a variable or property declared with
another type.

**Why:** The declared type is what every later reader trusts; an `any` assigned to it puts an
unchecked value behind a type that says it was checked.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a type before assigning it: annotate it, narrow it, or validate it.
2. If the target really holds anything, declare it `unknown`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const port: number = JSON.parse("8080");
```

##### Do

```ts
const raw: unknown = JSON.parse("8080");
export const port: number = typeof raw === "number" ? raw : 8080;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let port: number;
port = JSON.parse("8080");
```

##### Do

```tsx
let port: number;
port = Number("8080");
```

### Differences from the source

Only a target with a declared type is checked: typescript-eslint also reports `const x = value`
with `value` typed `any`, which makes `x` itself `any` (`ts/no-unsafe-member-access` and
`ts/no-unsafe-call` report what is done with it), and an `any` nested in the value's type (`any[]`
assigned to `number[]`) or in a destructuring.

## `ts/no-unsafe-call` — No call of a value typed `any`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type the value should have comes from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-call.md

### What it checks

A function is called only through a value TypeScript knows the type of.

**Why:** Calling a value typed `any` switches off every check on the call: the arguments, the
result and whether the value is a function at all.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a type: annotate it, or narrow it with a check before the call.
2. If it comes from an untyped library, add a declaration (`.d.ts`) for it.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
declare const handler: any;
handler(1);
```

##### Do

```ts
declare const handler: (n: number) => void;
handler(1);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
declare const handler: any;
handler(1);
```

##### Do

```tsx
declare const handler: (n: number) => void;
handler(1);
```

### Differences from the source

`new` on a value typed `any` and a tagged template on one are not checked yet.

## `ts/no-unsafe-declaration-merging` — No interface that merges with a class of the same name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the interface holds only property signatures, has no `extends` or type parameters, is not exported and names nothing the class declares: they become `declare` fields of the class, which emit nothing, so the type and the runtime are unchanged; any other interface is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-declaration-merging.md

### What it checks

An interface doesn't share its name with a class in the same scope.

**Why:** The merged interface adds members to the class's type that the class never initialises, and
the compiler can't tell.

### How to fix

1. Move the interface's members into the class, or rename the interface.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Point {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Fixed

```ts
class Point {
  declare z: number;
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
interface PointLike {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Point {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
class Point {
  declare z: number;
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface PointLike {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

## `ts/no-unsafe-function-type` — No Function type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right signature needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-function-type.md

### What it checks

The built-in `Function` type is not used as a type.

**Why:** `Function` accepts any function and its calls are unchecked, like `any` for functions.

### How to fix

1. Write the function's real signature, e.g. `(event: Event) => void`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let handler: Function;
```

##### Do

```ts
let handler: (event: Event) => void;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let handler: Function;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let handler: (event: Event) => void;
```

## `ts/no-unsafe-member-access` — No member access on a value typed `any`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type the value should have comes from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-member-access.md

### What it checks

A property is read or written only on a value TypeScript knows the type of.

**Why:** Every property of a value typed `any` is `any` too, so one untyped value spreads unchecked
code through everything that reads from it.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a type: annotate it, or narrow it with a check before reading from it.
2. If it comes from `JSON.parse` or another untyped source, validate it into a typed value first.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
declare const config: any;
const port = config.port;
```

##### Do

```ts
declare const config: { port: number };
const port = config.port;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
declare const config: any;
const port = config.port;
```

##### Do

```tsx
declare const config: { port: number };
const port = config.port;
```

### Differences from the source

In a chain on an `any` value (`a.b.c`), only the first access is reported, as typescript-eslint does.

## `ts/no-unsafe-return` — No `return` of a value typed `any`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the type the value should have comes from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-return.md

### What it checks

A function returns only values TypeScript knows the type of.

**Why:** A returned `any` takes the place of the function's declared result: every caller gets an
unchecked value, however carefully the function is typed.

### How to fix

1. Give the value a type before returning it: annotate it, narrow it, or validate it.
2. If the function really returns anything, declare its result `unknown` so callers must check it.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load(text: string): number {
  return JSON.parse(text);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load(text: string): number {
  const value: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
  return typeof value === "number" ? value : 0;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function load(text: string): number {
  return JSON.parse(text);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load(text: string): number {
  const value: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
  return typeof value === "number" ? value : 0;
}
```

### Differences from the source

An arrow function's expression body (`() => value`) is not checked yet, and a function whose result
is declared `any` or `unknown` is reported too; typescript-eslint allows it.

## `ts/no-unused-expressions` — No expression statements that do nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the statement does nothing, so the choices are what it was meant to do: delete it (the default), call it, or make a comparison an assignment; the reviewer picks, since only the author knows the intent)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unused-expressions.md

### What it checks

Every expression statement does something: a call, an assignment, an update, `await`, `yield`,
`delete` or `void`. Directives such as `"use strict"` are allowed.

**Why:** An expression whose value is thrown away is usually a forgotten call or assignment.

### How to fix

1. Add the call or assignment that was meant, or remove the statement.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close;
}
```

##### Fixed (delete)

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
}
```

##### Fixed (call)

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close;
}
```

##### Fixed (delete)

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
}
```

##### Fixed (call)

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

## `ts/no-unused-vars` — Every declared name is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto for a name nothing reads or writes: an import with another binding left, a variable (an initialiser that could do something kept as a statement), a function, an interface or type alias, a catch binding; removing an import's last binding drops the module's load and is suggest; a parameter, a destructured name or a class is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unused-vars.md

### What it checks

Every variable, function, class, type, interface, enum, import, parameter and caught error is used
somewhere. Parameters before the last used one are allowed (`args: after-used`).

**Why:** An unused declaration is dead code or a sign the code doesn't do what it was meant to.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vars` | `string` | `"all"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `args` | `string` | `"after-used"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrors` | `string` | `"all"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `ignoreRestSiblings` | `boolean` | `false` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `varsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `argsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrorsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `destructuredArrayIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Check the initialiser has no side effect that matters.
2. Remove the declaration, or use it where it was meant to be used.
3. For a parameter that must stay for its position, prefix it with `_` and set `argsIgnorePattern: "^_"`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`

**Why:** It only turns a script into a module, which the other import or export already does.


```ts
export const a = 1;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
export const a = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx

export {};
```

##### Do

```tsx

```

##### Fixed

```tsx

```

## `ts/no-wrapper-object-types` — Primitive types, not wrapper object types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-wrapper-object-types.md

### What it checks

Types use `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `bigint` and `object`, not the wrapper objects
`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Symbol`, `BigInt` and `Object`.

**Why:** The wrapper types describe boxed objects almost no code uses, and accept values the
primitive types reject.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let label: String = "a";
```

##### Do

```ts
let label: string = "a";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let label: String = "a";
```

```tsx
let label: string = "a";
```

## `ts/parameter-properties` — No parameter properties

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the property becomes a field in the class body and an assignment in the constructor, placed after any `super()` call; where the field goes among the others is the author's layout)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/parameter-properties.md

### What it checks

Class properties are declared in the class body, not as constructor parameter properties (`constructor(private x: T)`).

**Why:** A parameter property hides a field declaration in the constructor's signature, and is not plain JavaScript.

### How to fix

1. Declare the field in the class and assign it in the constructor.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Repo {
  constructor(private db: Db) {}
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Repo {
  private db: Db;
  constructor(db: Db) {
    this.db = db;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Repo {
  constructor(private db: Db) {}
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Repo {
  private db: Db;
  constructor(db: Db) {
    this.db = db;
  }
}
```

## `ts/prefer-as-const` — as const instead of repeating a literal as its type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/prefer-as-const.md

### What it checks

A literal cast to its own literal type (`"a" as "a"`) uses `as const` instead.

**Why:** `as const` says the same thing once, and stays right when the literal changes.


```ts
const mode = "dark" as const;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't


```tsx
const mode = "dark" as const;
```

## `ts/prefer-enum-initializers` — Enum members have initialisers

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the suggested value fixes today's order; review it before relying on it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/prefer-enum-initializers.md

### What it checks

Each enum member is given its value explicitly.

**Why:** Implicit values change when members are reordered or inserted, which silently changes stored data.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
enum Status {
  Open,
}
```

##### Do

```ts
enum Status {

}
```

##### Don't


## `ts/prefer-for-of` — A loop that only reads arr[i] is a for-of

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (value: the loop variable needs a name the code does not contain)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/prefer-for-of.md

### What it checks

A counting `for` loop over `arr.length` whose index is used only to read `arr[i]` is written `for (const item of arr)`.

**Why:** The index is noise when only the element is wanted; `for…of` cannot go out of bounds or skip an element.

### How to fix

1. Write `for (const item of $A)`, naming the element.
2. Replace each `$A[$I]` in the body with that name.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
  greet(names[i]);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (const name of names) {
  greet(name);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
  greet(names[i]);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (const name of names) {
  greet(name);
}
```

## `ts/prefer-namespace-keyword` — namespace, not module, for a TypeScript namespace

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`

```ts
module Shapes {
```

```ts
namespace Shapes {
```

## `ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check` — A `switch` on a union handles every member

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what each missing member should do is the author's decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check.md

### What it checks

A `switch` whose value is a union of literal types (string, number or boolean literals, enum
members, `null`, `undefined`) has a `case` for every member, or a `default`.

**Why:** When a member is added to the union, a `switch` that silently skips it lets the new value
fall through to whatever comes after; with every member handled, TypeScript points at each `switch`
that needs the new case.

### How to fix

1. Add a `case` for each member of the value's type the `switch` leaves out (hover the value, or
   read its type, to list them).
2. If the members left out really share one behaviour, add a `default` instead.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
  }
  return -1;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
    case "square":
      return 4;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
  }
  return -1;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
    default:
      return 4;
  }
}
```

### Differences from the source

A `switch` with a `default` is never reported (typescript-eslint's
`considerDefaultExhaustiveForUnions` set to `true`), and none of the rule's options are offered: a
value whose type is not made only of literal types (`string`, an object union) is not checked
(`requireDefaultForNonUnion`), and a `default` in an exhaustive `switch` is allowed
(`allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch`). typescript-eslint's suggestion that writes the missing cases
is not offered: SR-TYPES's questions answer whether members are missing, not which.

## `ts/triple-slash-reference` — No /// <reference path> directives

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the matching import needs the module path and what it provides)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/triple-slash-reference.md

### What it checks

Files are connected with `import`, not `/// <reference path="…" />`.

**Why:** Reference directives predate ES modules and hide dependencies from bundlers and other
tools.

### How to fix

1. Replace the directive with an `import` of the module it pointed to.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/// <reference path="./globals.d.ts" />
export const x = 1;
```

##### Do

```ts
import "./globals";
export const x = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/// <reference path="./globals.d.ts" />
export const x = 1;
```

##### Do

```tsx
import "./globals";
export const x = 1;
```

## `ts/type-error` — TypeScript's own errors

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (TypeScript 7.1's API offers no code fixes yet, so each error is fixed by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/type-error.md

### What it checks

A file has none of the errors the project's own TypeScript reports for it.

**Why:** These are the errors `tsc` would stop on; reporting them with the rest of the check means
one run, one report, and no second tool to wire up.

### How to fix

1. Read the TypeScript error code and message in the finding (`TS2322: …`).
2. Fix the code, or the type it is checked against, the way `tsc` would ask you to.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const port: number = "8080";
```

##### Do

```ts
export const port: number = 8080;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const port: number = "8080";
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const port: number = 8080;
```

## `ts/type-only-imports` — Names used only as types are imported with type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a type-only import is erased, so code that relied on the module's side effects changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/type-only-imports.md

### What it checks

An imported name that the file uses only in type positions is marked `type`.

**Why:** Type-only imports are erased at compile time, which keeps runtime imports honest and helps
bundlers drop unused modules.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

##### Do

```ts
import { type Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { type Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

### Differences from the source

Only within the file, without type information: a name used as a value anywhere is left alone.
Default and namespace imports are reported without a fix.

## `ts/unified-signatures` — Overloads that one signature can say are one signature

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (merging two overloads changes the declared API callers see; the union is offered for an agent or a person to accept)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/unified-signatures.md

### What it checks

Two adjacent overloads don't differ in only one parameter's type (write a union), or only by a trailing parameter (make it optional).

**Why:** Fewer overloads are easier to call and to read.

### How to fix

1. Write one signature with a union type or an optional parameter.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function f(x: string): void;
function f(x: number): void;
function f(x: unknown): void {}
```

##### Do

```ts
function f(x: string | number): void;
function f(x: unknown): void {}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function f(x: string): void;
function f(x: number): void;
function f(x: unknown): void {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function f(x: string | number): void;
function f(x: unknown): void {}
```

## `yaml/document-start` — A YAML document starts with ---

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/document-start.md

### What it checks

Every YAML document begins with an explicit `---` line. Comments and directives may come before it. Markdown front matter is not checked: its `---` belongs to the Markdown file.

**Why:** An explicit start marks where a document begins, so a file can grow to hold several documents, and tools that concatenate YAML files keep the boundaries.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
name: build
on: push
```

##### Do

```yaml
---
name: build
on: push
```

## `yaml/gha-action-schema` — GitHub Actions action metadata matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a misshapen input or run step has several possible meanings; the author picks the one they intended)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-action-schema.md

### What it checks

An `action.yml` matches SchemaStore's schema for action metadata: `name`, `description` and `runs` are present, and the inputs, outputs and steps have the keys and forms GitHub reads.

**Why:** GitHub reads an action's metadata only when a workflow uses it, so a misspelt `steps:` or `using:` breaks every workflow that calls the action, not the action's own repository.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and what the schema expects.
2. Add the missing key, or correct the key or the value.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=action.yml
name: Setup
description: Set the toolchain up
runs:
  using: composite
  step:
    - run: ./setup.sh
      shell: bash
```

##### Do

```yaml path=action.yml
name: Setup
description: Set the toolchain up
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - run: ./setup.sh
      shell: bash
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `github-action.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/github-action.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`.

## `yaml/gha-pin-sha` — GitHub Actions are pinned to a commit SHA

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (finding the commit a tag points to needs the network, and the engine never uses it (L5))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-pin-sha.md

### What it checks

A `uses:` in a GitHub Actions workflow or composite action names a full 40-character commit SHA, not a tag or branch. Local actions (`./…`) and `docker://` images are not checked.

**Why:** A tag or branch can be moved to different code at any time, so a compromised or careless upstream changes what your workflow runs; a commit SHA can't change.

### How to fix

1. Look up the commit the tag points to, for example with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> <tag>`.
2. Replace the tag with the 40-character SHA and keep the tag as a comment: `uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.2.2`.
3. Let Dependabot or Renovate update the pinned SHAs.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
```

##### Do

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
```

## `yaml/gha-workflow-schema` — GitHub Actions workflows match their schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a misshapen job or step has several possible meanings; the author picks the one they intended)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-workflow-schema.md

### What it checks

A GitHub Actions workflow matches SchemaStore's schema for workflows: every key of a trigger, a job and a step is one GitHub reads, with a value of the form it takes.

**Why:** GitHub rejects a malformed workflow only when it is pushed, and a misspelt key such as `runs_on` or `timeout-minute` fails the whole workflow file, so the mistake shows up as a red run instead of in review.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and what the schema expects, and suggests the key meant when the name is misspelt.
2. Correct the key or the value.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs_on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
```

##### Do

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `github-workflow.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/github-workflow.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. YAML is read as YAML 1.2, as GitHub reads it, so `on:` is a key. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`.

## `yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans` — No yes/no/on/off as unquoted values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (quoting keeps the YAML 1.2 meaning (a string); if a boolean was meant, write `true` or `false` instead)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans.md

### What it checks

A value is not a bare `yes`, `no`, `on` or `off` (in any of their capitalisations). Quote it if it is text, or write `true` or `false` if it is a boolean. Keys are not checked, so a GitHub Actions `on:` is fine.

**Why:** YAML 1.2 reads these words as strings, but YAML 1.1 loaders, still common (PyYAML, Ruby's Psych, many tools built on them), read them as booleans: `country: no` becomes `false`.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
country: no
```

##### Do

```yaml
country: "no"
```

##### Do

```yaml
enabled: true
```

### Differences from the source

The idea comes from the YAML 1.1 and 1.2 specifications. `y` and `n` are not reported: the YAML 1.1 type repository lists them, but the common 1.1 loaders don't treat them as booleans.

## `yaml/no-ambiguous-numbers` — No numbers that YAML 1.1 and 1.2 read differently

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the choices are quoting it (the default: the string YAML 1.2 reads, for a time), the number YAML 1.2 reads, or the number YAML 1.1 reads, each now read the same by both)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-ambiguous-numbers.md

### What it checks

A value is not an unquoted integer with a leading zero (`0755`) or an unquoted base-60 form (`22:22`, `1:30:00`).

**Why:** YAML 1.1 reads `0755` as octal (493) and `22:22` as the number 1342; YAML 1.2 reads them as 755 and the string "22:22". The same file means different things to different loaders — the classic case is port mappings in `docker-compose.yml`.

### How to fix

1. For an octal number, write it as `0o755`; for a decimal one, drop the leading zero.
2. For text such as a port mapping or a time, quote it: `"22:22"`.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
mode: 0755
ports:
  - 22:22
```

##### Fixed

```yaml
mode: "0755"
ports:
  - "22:22"
```

##### Do

```yaml
mode: 0o755
ports:
  - "22:22"
```

### Differences from the source

The idea comes from the YAML 1.1 and 1.2 specifications.

## `yaml/no-duplicate-keys` — No key twice in one YAML mapping

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `auto` (auto when the key is set twice to the same value, so the later one goes; otherwise the choices keep the last (the default: what most YAML readers keep) or the first)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-duplicate-keys.md

### What it checks

Each key appears once in a mapping, block or flow. Quoted and plain spellings of a key are the same key.

**Why:** YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, but many loaders accept duplicates and keep only the last value, so the first one is silently lost.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Delete the other entry, or give it a key of its own.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
service:
  image: nginx
  restart: always
  image: caddy
```

##### Fixed

```yaml
service:
  restart: always
  image: caddy
```

##### Do

```yaml
service:
  image: caddy
  restart: always
```

## `yaml/no-undeclared-alias` — Every alias refers to an anchor defined before it

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the anchors defined before the alias within two edits are choices, nearest first; an alias whose anchor comes later, or with none near, is manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-undeclared-alias.md

### What it checks

An alias `*name` refers to an anchor `&name` defined earlier in the same document.

**Why:** An alias with no anchor before it is an error: YAML loaders refuse the whole file, and anchors don't carry over from one document to the next.

### How to fix

1. Find the anchor the alias meant.
2. Move the anchored node above the alias, fix the spelling, or add the anchor.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  port: 443
production:
  <<: *default
  host: example.com
```

##### Fixed

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  port: 443
production:
  <<: *defaults
  host: example.com
```

##### Do

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  port: 443
production:
  <<: *defaults
  host: example.com
```

## `yaml/todo-marker` — YAML TODO comments carry a ticket and, when asked, a date

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a ticket and a date are facts about the work that only the author knows; the engine can't invent them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/markers` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/todo-marker.md

### What it checks

A comment line that opens with a marker tag (`TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` by default) in a `#` comment carries a ticket, and a date when the project asks for one: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): text`. The ticket and the date go in the parentheses, in either order, either one optional unless required; any other item in them (an owner's name) is ignored. The tag must start the comment line, so a sentence that merely mentions a TODO is not a marker.

A date that is written is always enforced, whether or not `require_date` is set: it is **expired** from the as-of date on (`--as-of`, `CODELAW_AS_OF`, else `HEAD`'s commit date, never the clock: [SR-BASELINE](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md) decision 9) and is a **warning** for the `warn_days` before it. A date that is not a calendar day is reported too. With no as-of date, only the missing and the malformed are reported.

**Why:** A TODO with no ticket has no owner and no place to be tracked, and one with no date never comes due; both outlive the people who wrote them. Naming a ticket ties the comment to the work, and a date makes the comment fail loudly the day it is overdue instead of rotting quietly.

**Configuration** is the `[todo]` table of `codelaw.toml` ([SR-CONFIG](https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/records/0110_config.md) decision 11a), one for every language:

```toml
[todo]
tags           = ["TODO", "FIXME", "HACK"]   # the words that open a marker
require_ticket = true                         # a ticket is required (default)
require_date   = false                        # a date is required (default: only a written date is enforced)
ticket_pattern = "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\\d+"        # a whole ticket must match this regular expression
warn_days      = 14                           # warn this many days before the date
```

**A repo full of bare TODOs** gets every one of them at once. Take them into the baseline (`codelaw baseline`) and pay them down, or set `require_ticket = false` and let the rule enforce only the dates that are written.

### How to fix

1. Open or find the ticket for the work and write it in the parentheses: `TODO(ABC-123): …`.
2. When the project asks for a date (`require_date`), or the work has a deadline, add it: `TODO(ABC-123, 2027-01-31): …`.
3. For an expired marker: do the work and delete the comment; or, if the work really moves, change the date and say why in the text.
4. If the comment is not a to-do, rewrite it so it does not open with the tag.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
# TODO: pin the image digest
image: app:latest
```

##### Do

```yaml
# TODO(OPS-18): pin the image digest
image: app:latest
```

## Engine rules

### `codelaw/no-rules` — No rule pack and no local rule is configured

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw init` to install the rule packs for the languages in this repo, or add a rule under `.codelaw/rules/`.

### `codelaw/not-utf8` — File is not valid UTF-8 and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Re-encode the file as UTF-8, or exclude it in `codelaw.toml`.

### `codelaw/file-too-large` — File is larger than `[files] max_file_size` and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Exclude the file, or raise `[files] max_file_size` in `codelaw.toml`.

### `codelaw/generated` — File is marked generated and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the generator instead, or set `[files] lint_generated = true`.

### `codelaw/internal-error` — A rule failed on this file

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Report the rule and file to the rule's maintainer; the rest of the run is unaffected.

### `format/unformatted` — File is not formatted

Severity `warn` · fix `auto`

1. Run `codelaw format` (or `codelaw fix`) on the file.

### `format/failed` — The formatter left the file as it was

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. If the file does not parse, correct the syntax error and run `codelaw format` again.
2. Otherwise the formatted text failed verification; add the file to `[format] exclude` and report it with the file attached.

### `codelaw/file-changed-during-run` — File changed on disk during the run, so the fix was not written

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw fix` again once the file is no longer being edited.

### `codelaw/write-failed` — The fixed file could not be written, so it is unchanged

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Make the file writable (its permissions, a read-only disk, a full disk), then run `codelaw fix` again.

### `codelaw/suppression-needs-reason` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment has no reason

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Write the reason after a colon: `codelaw-ignore <rule>: <reason>`.

### `codelaw/unused-suppression` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment suppresses nothing

Severity `info` · fix `auto`

### `graph/no-deprecated-usage` — A deprecated symbol is used

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Replace the use with the replacement `.codelaw/deprecations.toml` names (or the deprecation marker's message gives).
2. An existing use may stay until its deadline only through `.codelaw/baseline/graph--no-deprecated-usage.toml`, which a person adds with `codelaw baseline add`.

### `codelaw/stale-baseline` — A baseline entry allows more findings than its file has

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw baseline prune` (or `codelaw fix`, which prunes too) to lower the entry; lowering is always safe.

### `codelaw/expiring-exception` — An exception (a baseline entry, a deprecation, a `codelaw-ignore`) expires within its warning window

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the findings the exception covers before its `expires` date: on that day they are reported again and the exception is an error.
2. To keep it longer, a person moves `expires` later with `codelaw baseline add --expires …` (a baseline entry) or edits the comment; `codelaw baseline check` flags an extended deadline for review.

### `codelaw/expired-exception` — An exception reached its `expires` date and no longer covers anything

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the findings it covered; they are reported again at their rule's own severity.
2. Then remove the exception: `codelaw baseline prune` (or `codelaw fix`) lowers a baseline entry, and the `codelaw-ignore` comment is deleted by hand.

### `codelaw/exception-without-expiry` — An exception has no `expires` date while `[exceptions] require_expiry` is on

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Add `expires = "YYYY-MM-DD"` (the first day it no longer holds): `codelaw baseline add --expires …` rewrites a baseline entry; a `codelaw-ignore` takes `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` before its colon.

### `codelaw/exception-author` — An exception's `added_by` is not an email address, or not the git author of the change

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Set `added_by` (`by=` in a `codelaw-ignore`) to your own git email, `git config user.email`; `codelaw baseline add` writes it for you.

### `codelaw/unknown-suppression` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment names a rule that does not exist

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Correct the rule id, or remove the comment.

### `graph/untested-function` — A new or edited function is reached by no test file

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Write a unit test that imports the function (or its module, for a function the module does not export) and calls it: a test needs judgment, so codelaw does not write one.
2. If the function should never need its own test (a thin wrapper, generated code), exempt it in `.codelawignore` — `<path>#<name> graph/untested-function forever: <reason>`; to defer the test, give the line `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` and `on_touch=…` and a reason.

### `graph/function-coverage` — A new or edited function's line coverage is under `[coverage] min`

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Add test cases that run the lines the coverage report shows as missed, regenerate the lcov report in the same job, and run `codelaw check --coverage <report>` again: a test needs judgment, so codelaw does not write one.
2. If the function cannot reasonably be covered, exempt it in `.codelawignore` — `<path>#<name> graph/function-coverage` with `expires=` or `forever`, `on_touch=` and a reason.

### `codelaw/stale-coverage` — The coverage report does not match this file, so its coverage is not judged

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Regenerate the lcov report from the code being checked — in the same CI job, after the tests and before `codelaw check` — and pass it with `--coverage` or `[coverage] report`.

### `codelaw/stale-ignore` — A `.codelawignore` line matches no file or function

Severity `warn` · fix `auto`

### `codelaw/incomplete-ignore` — A `.codelawignore` line is missing a field or contradicts itself, so it exempts nothing

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Give the line what the message names: the rules it exempts after the target, each a rule this project has or a namespace (`js/*`); a reason after a colon (always, with `expires=` or `forever`); `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` or `forever` (`[codelawignore] require_expiry`); and `on_touch=error|warn|keep` unless it is `forever` (`[codelawignore] require_on_touch`).
2. `forever` takes no `expires=`, `warn_days=` or `on_touch=`; a glob takes no `on_touch_scope=function`; no line exempts a `codelaw/` rule.

### `codelaw/off-without-reason` — A rule is turned `"off"` in the config without a `reason` while `[rules] require_reason` is on

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Write the entry as a table with a reason: `"py/no-print" = { severity = "off", reason = "CLI tool: print is the output" }` (SR-CONFIG decision 11c).

### `git/commit-message` — A commit message does not follow `[commits]` (Conventional Commits by default)

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Reword the message to the form the finding shows: `git commit --amend` for the last commit, `git rebase -i <base>` and `reword` for an earlier one; a message is never rewritten for you.
2. If the convention is wrong for this repository, change `[commits]` in `codelaw.toml` (`preset`, `types`, `scopes`, `subject_max`, `subject_case`, `ticket`, `skip`).

### `git/branch-name` — The branch name does not follow `[branches]`

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Rename the branch (`git branch -m <new-name>`), push it under the new name and open the pull request from it; the finding shows a name that passes.
2. Or change `[branches] pattern` or `max_length`, or add the branch to `[branches] protected`.

### `git/pr-size` — The pull request changes more lines than `[pr] max_lines`

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Split the change into pull requests that each stand alone — the refactor first, then the feature that uses it.
2. Lockfiles and generated files are not counted: add other generated paths to `[pr] exclude`, or raise `[pr] max_lines`.

### `git/pr-description` — The pull request's title or description does not follow `[pr]`

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Edit the pull request as the finding says: a title that matches `[pr] title_pattern`, a ticket in the title or description, each section of `[pr] template_sections` filled in.
2. Then run the CI job again: the description is read from what the CI hands the job, never fetched.
